s13-bonus-factory-orchestration-coordinating-people-processes-and-machines-in-one-model-with-david-caputo-co-founder-of-harmoniio

Custom Hardware Paid Off: Harmoni built its own hardware instead of using off-the-shelf boards, adding a year or more to the MVP. It enabled differentiators like embedded far-field RFID and edge inference, and Caputo says it was worth it.

Two-Plug Installation: Most U.S. factories are small and many lack IT staff, so Harmoni designed its device to plug into power and the machine. Pre-built integrations avoid heavy professional services that would limit scale.

No Free Pilots: Caputo believes a product is worth what a customer will pay, even in a pilot. Refusing free pilots likely meant fewer devices in the field, but he calls it one of the company's best decisions.

Simpler Dashboards Won: An early customer asked for dashboards, and the team built highly configurable ones that drew crickets. The customer wanted pre-made charts showing what to care about, so Harmoni rebuilt them.

Fewer People, No Titles: Harmoni aims for fewer, smarter people, with no titles and a pod system for work across functions. Caputo says this lets people be valued for their contributions rather than their rank.

q: What is factory orchestration?
a: David Caputo describes factory orchestration as a new product category built on three pillars: automation, process control and observability. He says the goal is "to simply automate non-productive work so that you have more productive time from operators," [04:18] and to prevent mistakes that lead to scrap.

q: Why did Harmoni build custom hardware instead of using off-the-shelf devices?
a: Caputo says key differentiators, including embedded RFID, on-device TPUs and connections to many types of equipment, depend on custom hardware. It slowed the early build by a year or more, "but it was worth it" [10:26] a thousand times over, in his words.

q: How does Harmoni keep CNC program changes from being lost?
a: Caputo lost a year re-engineering a part after a retiring operator left with the only current copy of its program. Today, he says, "we have a feature called program change detection, where we can detect whether changes are made" [14:04] while programs run, and it sends a change request back to engineering.

q: Does Harmoni offer free pilots?
a: No, Caputo says the company decided early on that "we are not going to run free pilots of the system." [20:04] He believes free pilots drive the wrong behavior and that you can't expect commitment or engagement from a customer who doesn't see value.

q: What is HAL, the Harmoni AI Lieutenant?
a: HAL is Harmoni's AI agent, which operators can talk to through the device at their work center, while management can also use a cloud interface. Caputo calls it "context-aware AI delivered at the point of production" [26:40] that knows details such as the operator, job, machine and running program.

s13-bonus-the-generative-media-shift-scaling-real-time-ai-content-creation-with-sky-yang-founder-ceo-of-imagine-ai

Deposits Before Building: Sky Yang ran discovery calls, mapped ghostwriters' workflows and collected 10 deposits from ghostwriters and agencies before building an AI that drafts posts in a client's voice.

From Voice to Strategy: Matching a client's voice found product-market fit, but the market was small. Imagine AI moved into strategy and ROI by using its own AI to run an agency-like service for B2B companies.

Productizing Manual Know-How: After reaching $1M annual run rate during YC with three people, the team spent December rebuilding the product, baking its LinkedIn know-how into an agent instead of adding headcount for manual work.

Don't Stop Selling: When growth strained capacity again, the team paused go-to-market to focus on R&D and existing customers. Yang calls that a mistake: he should have hired so some people built while others kept momentum.

Data-Driven LinkedIn Content: Imagine AI tracks engagers and CRM stages to steer content toward revenue. Its newest agent has its own computer, makes graphics and creates posts, aimed at companies of about 20 to 200 people.

q: What does Imagine AI do?
a: Imagine AI is a research company focused on B2B growth, with agents that help marketing and growth teams work more efficiently on LinkedIn. As Sky Yang put it, "we have a content agent that focuses on data-driven content" [04:37].

q: How did Imagine AI validate its MVP?
a: Sky Yang did cold outreach to ghostwriters and agencies, held discovery calls to understand their workflows, and asked for deposits before building. "We got 10 deposits from 10 different ghostwriters" [10:00], he said, adding that agencies were among them.

q: How does Sky Yang define product-market fit?
a: Yang describes it as demand so strong that a company must hire or build a more scalable product to survive. In his words, "you have so much demand that your company will literally die" [12:04] if you don't respond.

q: What was Imagine AI's biggest mistake while scaling?
a: Yang says the team stopped go-to-market and selling to go back to R&D, which cost it some momentum. As Yang put it, "I think it was a mistake that we just stopped" [26:51], and he now believes they should have hired more people and kept selling while others did R&D.

q: What has Imagine AI learned about LinkedIn engagement?
a: Yang says the company found that engagement follows a log-normal distribution, with some posts doing very badly and others very well. Rather than expecting every post to be a hit, he said, "what you can do is that you can optimize your posts" [26:14].

s13-e13-frictionless-group-payments-the-collaborative-checkout-revolution-with-cam-richardson-founder-ceo-of-paysquad

Holds Instead of Credit: Paysquad's early design used authorized holds and an extended, crowdfunding-style checkout, avoiding credit licensing and underwriting. That pushed the team into retail first, though ticketing and travel were obvious fits.

Three Ways Groups Pay: Cam sees three main patterns: crowdfunding, where people chip in any amount (great for gifts); even splits (tickets and group travel); and claiming individual items (food orders).

Merchant Brand as Hero: A bold, gradient-heavy design aimed at Gen Z was toned down after merchants asked for a slicker, co-branded look. Putting the merchant's brand first also helped build shoppers' trust.

Platforms Before Custom Builds: Paysquad prioritized Shopify's invite-only global payment partner program and payment orchestrators, so one integration could switch it on across multiple merchants and speed up learning.

Alignment Over Interest: Chasing interested but poorly suited merchants, especially smaller ones needing lots of help, wasted time. Furniture also disappointed, proving to be a mostly taste-driven solo purchase.

q: What is Paysquad and how does pay together at checkout work?
a: Paysquad, founded by Cam Richardson, adds a pay together option at checkout for retail, ticketing and travel merchants. Shoppers can "invite friends family or colleagues from anywhere in the world to contribute" [03:11], and the order goes through automatically once it is 100% funded.

q: What inspired Cam Richardson to start Paysquad?
a: At Cam's 21st birthday, his friends, then struggling students, all chipped in for a gift he never expected. Cam said that for him "it was a complete paradigm shift where I realized how much more is possible when people do" [03:49] things together.

q: How does Paysquad handle group payments without offering credit?
a: Cam explained that, without huge funds to burn, the team chose "to architect the product in a way that uses authorized" [06:16] holds for each person's contribution. This meant they did not guarantee payment to merchants up front or need to get into credit licensing or underwriting.

q: How did Paysquad scale its merchant distribution?
a: Cam said the team aimed for platform distribution ahead of custom builds, and "seeing Shopify's continued ascendance meant that we really had to do everything in our power to get" [13:41] into its global payment partner program. Paysquad was the first pay together option in that invite-only program, and payment orchestrators offer a similar one-integration advantage.

q: What mistake did Paysquad make when choosing merchants?
a: Cam said one mistake "is just prioritizing interest over alignment" [16:29], taking on stores that lacked the volume or natural fit to drive transactions. The team also expected furniture to be a strong category, only to find it is usually a solo, taste-driven purchase.

s13-bonus-reinventing-banking-bitcoin-native-global-financial-services-with-shah-ramezani-founder-ceo-of-noahcom

Stablecoins Bridge Local Instant Payments: Noah's API connects local methods like ACH, SEPA, UPI and GCash with stablecoins, moving money without correspondent banking. Shah likens the shift to Skype cutting through chains of telecom carriers.

More Than a Blockchain Build: Shah put the first product at one and a half to three years of work across regulation and licensing, bridging old payment rails to stablecoins, and liquidity management. The first two took the most time.

Biggest Market, Simplest Product: Early on, Noah prioritized moving stablecoins into US dollar rails like ACH and Fedwire over smaller payment systems. It also shipped something simple to explore use cases before building further.

Hire Underdogs, Then Stretch Them: Shah bets on people with something to prove, gives them full responsibility and promotes them quickly. He says Noah accepted slower growth rather than make hires who would erode its culture.

Hire Before You Think Necessary: Coming out of a difficult period, Shah was slow to hire once product-market fit appeared, which cost time. Notice periods and onboarding mean new people take months to contribute.

q: What does Noah.com do?
a: Noah is a stablecoin company offering an API platform that connects local payment methods around the world with stablecoins. Founder and CEO Shah Ramezani said, "we are an API first company whereby we make sure that companies are able to reap the full benefits" [03:22].

q: How do stablecoin payments differ from correspondent banking?
a: Shah Ramezani explains that stablecoins run through one protocol, with instant local payment systems serving as the on and off ramps. In his words, "You don't need to touch so many different databases of banks to actually make a simple payment" [05:33].

q: How long did it take to build Noah's first product?
a: Shah put it at one and a half to three years, covering regulation and licensing, the technical bridge between old and new payment rails, and liquidity management. He noted that "there are many components to building that product besides just blockchain" [06:13].

q: What hiring mistake did Noah make while growing quickly?
a: Shah said he did not hire fast enough once the company had clear product-market fit and a strong revenue model, and time was lost as a result. His advice to leaders of high-performance teams is that "you should always hire earlier than what you think" [17:52].

q: What is next for Noah.com?
a: Shah pointed to agentic payments, expansion of the payment infrastructure network and global card issuing. On where he sees banking heading, Shah predicted that "a large number of people will start banking on a simple chat interface" [18:57].

s13-bonus-building-generative-ai-tools-multiplayer-engines-for-game-developers-with-anupam-singh-vp-of-eng-at-roblox

Planning for Massive Spikes: Creator events, often Saturday mornings, can draw millions of players, and one hit 45.7 million at once. GPUs can't be bought that morning, so capacity is worked out with partners and vendors.

From Recommendations to Four Models: The AI platform was first built to power homepage recommendations, then safety became a major workload. Today the focus is foundation models for coding, 3D, NPCs and video.

3D Must Be Functional: Anupam names understanding 3D as creators' biggest technical barrier. A car in a game needs a door that opens and a wheel that turns, an insight that led to the Cube foundation model.

Prompt to Playable Game: Roblox's Build product takes a text prompt, asks follow-up questions about things like controls and style, then builds a game. Further prompts add mechanics such as irregular gravity.
One Happy Customer First: Anupam urges founders to be less anxious about company size and fundraising. Take the next step, find one customer passionate about the idea and make them really successful.

q: What AI foundation models is Roblox building?
a: Anupam Singh says Roblox is building foundation models for coding, 3D, non-player characters (NPCs) and video, aimed at taking a creator from an idea to an evolving game. The platform started with recommendations, and then, as Anupam put it, "safety became the most important AI product for us." [07:39]

q: Why is generative AI for 3D game objects so hard?
a: Anupam explains that a 3D object has to work inside a game, such as a car whose door opens and whose steering wheel turns. He describes the goal as "an object that is functional, not just pretty to look at" [10:37], an insight that led to the Cube foundation model.

q: Can you create a Roblox game from a text prompt?
a: According to Anupam, "we have product called build where you can write a text prompt" [13:31] describing your game idea. It asks a series of questions, builds the game, and lets you keep prompting to add mechanics without writing the code yourself.

q: How does Roblox handle huge traffic spikes and thundering herds?
a: Anupam recalls a three-day outage shortly after he joined, and says that each time the team tried to restore the platform, "we would get a thundering herd of players trying to log into Roblox.com." [04:53] Solving for thundering herds was his first project, and he also describes planning capacity with partners and vendors for events that can far exceed forecasts.

q: What mistake does Anupam Singh say he made with AI coding models?
a: Anupam says he underestimated how quickly coding models would be adopted, partly because AI was so chat-based at the time and code has a particular structure. He admitted, "If I would go back two years, I would invest way more in coding models." [20:59]

s13-bonus-eliminating-friction-in-digital-market-discovery-deal-flow-with-demetrie-king-founder-ceo-of-marketmatch

Vending Machines Sparked The Idea: Demetrie had vending customers rate products, stocked the top request, iced honey buns, and sold out. Feedback asking for something easier than ratings led him to swiping, then a rebrand to MarketMatch for multiple industries.

Web App Over Downloads: Stickers and flyers rarely drove downloads, and users asked for a web-based option. With no technical background, Demetrie built that version himself in about six months using Claude and other AI tools.

Retail Was The Wrong Start: Early efforts in places like smoke shops got some traction but not the data needed. MarketMatch shifted to large audiences like universities, where even 10% of TCU's student body could yield substantial data.
Swipes That Change Campus Life: UTA students swiped through food trucks, and the top pick was brought to campus, booked three times, and then given a permanent Monday-through-Friday spot.

A Solopreneur With Student Help: Though bootstrapped and technically a solopreneur, Demetrie has 12 college students working with him through TCU and UTD, including a TCU team working on version three of the product.

q: What is MarketMatch and how does it work?
a: MarketMatch gathers community feedback through swipeable, gamified surveys to help brands and vendors before they launch or spend money in a market. Founder Demetrie King explained that it "is a marketing app that utilizes swipable surveys to conduct market research" [02:48]. On campus, every 50 swipes gives students a chance at prizes such as cash, school merchandise or a case of Celsius.

q: How did Demetrie King come up with the idea for MarketMatch?
a: Demetrie ran a vending machine business and asked customers to rate products so he could stock what was really in demand. When customers wanted an easier way to respond, he changed the format: "So I went to swiping, very similar to dating apps." [05:09]. He then realized the idea could reach well beyond vending and rebranded as MarketMatch.

q: Can a non-technical founder build an app with AI tools?
a: Demetrie King says he built MarketMatch himself in about six months, despite having no technical background, using Claude and other AI tools. As he put it, "with AI tools that are out right now, I was able to build the version of MarketMatch" [05:51]. A founder he met through his partnership with Tech Fort Worth introduced him to those tools.

q: What results has MarketMatch had on college campuses?
a: In one example Demetrie shared, UTA students swiped through food trucks and the number one choice was put on campus and booked three times. He said that "now it has a permanent spot on UTA campus Monday through Friday" [19:45].

q: What advice does Demetrie King have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Demetrie's mantra is to keep going through the many no's, including yeses that turn into no's, and to keep a positive circle around you. He also advises, "You have to make sure to find people that are going to say your name or pitch your business" [21:29] when you're not in the room.

s13-e11-optimizing-deep-sleep-cycles-through-intelligent-biometric-hardware-with-igor-me-founder-ceo-of-neera-sleep
Vibroacoustics in the Bed: Neera is a bed topper that adapts to your physiology in real time, using sound and vibration patterns to help you wind down, rejuvenate and move into certain sleep stages.

Two Months to Prototype: Igor's team reached a first prototype in about two months, thanks to suppliers, logistics, procurement and engineers already in place from years of building hardware together.
Comfort Was the Hard Part: A separate mat or chair was the initial idea, but Neera took on fitting its technology into a comfortable bed topper that adds no extra space or hassle to the bedroom.

Homework Before Manufacturing: One wrong component on a circuit board can cost a month. Igor advises rigorous testing protocols, fixing physical mistakes during EVT and DVT, and vetting manufacturing partners closely.
One Market at a Time: Chasing the US, Europe, South America and Asia at once in a business derailed the team. Now Igor launches in one market and vertical, and expands only once it converts.

q: What is Neera Sleep and how does it work?
a: Igor Me describes Neera as a neurological regulation platform built around a "VibroAcoustic Bed Topper that adapts to your physiology in real time" [05:45]. It creates vibroacoustic patterns meant to put you into certain sleep stages and help you wind down.

q: How long did it take to build the first Neera prototype?
a: Igor says that from the start, "it took us only probably two months" [07:20] to get to a first prototype. He credits a long-standing team and having suppliers, logistics, procurement and rapid prototyping already at hand.

q: What was the biggest challenge in designing a vibroacoustic bed topper?
a: Igor says it was hard to squeeze all the technology into a bed topper rather than a separate mat or chair. The team set out to "make it really comfortable, really nice from a sleep perspective" [08:34], and he says that challenge is still ongoing.

q: What advice does Igor Me have for scaling a hardware product?
a: Igor's first pillar is preparation: the key "is to do the homework before you manufacture." [14:44] He also advises tracking finances carefully and staying open to unexpected opportunities, such as a B2B client when you see yourself as a direct-to-consumer brand.

q: What is the zombie test for new product ideas?
a: Igor describes a zombie product as one that shouldn't exist, and his filter checks an idea for signs such as it already existing or having already bankrupted someone. He argues that in hardware recently, "90% of the products shouldn't exist." [27:59]

e13-bonus-storage-to-inference-powering-high-speed-ai-nvme-infrastructure-with-eran-kirzner-ceo-of-lightbits

Inventing a Protocol Isn't Enough: Lightbits created NVMe over TCP, pushed it into a standard, then built the ecosystem across Linux, VMware, OpenStack and Kubernetes. A production-grade MVP took about three years.

Breaking the GPU Memory Wall: Infera creates a virtual HBM from the system's memory and storage tiers and prefetches data just in time. Eran says GPU effective utilization, often stuck at 30%, can reach 80%.

Standards Versus Speed: Storage had to comply with existing environments, while Infera plugs into frameworks like vLLM, Dynamo and llm-d with no certification. Its first MVP took about six months, with 12 to 18 months for full GA.

Design for Failure at Scale: Lightbits assumes NICs, SSDs and whole servers will fail, so the product needs auto-healing. It also tells customers both the scale it was designed for and the scale it has actually been tested to.

Customers Over Marquee Validation: Eran says working with industry giants to prove the technology brought glory but no meaningful commercial upside. His lesson: stay close to customers and be very selective about partners.

q: Who invented NVMe over TCP?
a: Eran Kirzner says Lightbits invented the protocol, then pushed it through the community to make it a standard. In his words, "Lightbits is the one that invented the protocol and actually brought it first to the market" [15:45].

q: What is the GPU memory wall in AI inference?
a: Eran explains that each GPU has a limited amount of high-speed memory (HBM), which very large models can use up. As a result, he says, "it's basically the case that people are buying more GPU" [12:02] just to get access to more memory.

q: How does Lightbits Infera improve GPU utilization?
a: Eran says Infera extends GPU memory with a virtual HBM that uses the system's memory and storage tiers and shares them between GPUs. It also reduces stall cycles because, as he puts it, "it actually predicts the information the GPU needs to process and brings it just" [14:14] on time.

q: How long did it take Lightbits to build Infera?
a: Eran estimates it took "six months to get the first MVP and maybe 12 to 18 months to get the full GA product" [17:44]. By comparison, he says the first production-grade storage solution took probably three years because the standard and ecosystem had to be built.

q: What advice does Eran Kirzner have for startup founders?
a: Eran advises founders to "be close to your customers and stay close to them" [33:34] and to be very selective about partners, even large ones. He also recommends finding co-founders with complementary skills who can be trusted for the whole journey.

e13-bonus-the-edge-vision-shift-privacy-first-computer-ai-for-smart-security-eldercare-with-mike-link-vp-of-kami-vision

Field Data Beat Test Data: Kami trained fall detection on test and proprietary data, but real-world misses drove improvement. Early churn was high, and stabilizing the product took roughly eight months to a year.

From Detection to Prevention: Serious injuries typically come after repeated falls. Kami wants to combine fall detection with vitals, medications, comorbidities and behavior changes to flag decline and help people age in place.

Partners Over Direct Sales: A team of about 10 sellers produced pipeline that wasn't real. Link let the whole team go and shifted to partners who earn a fee for offering the product to existing customers.

Never Skip Hardware QA: A rush shipment arrived without proof of testing, and faulty cables made devices overheat a bit. Replacements stalled things for about a month, a problem manufacturer QA could have prevented.

Trust Depends on Support: With thousands of users, many falls are detected, and families may need alerts or clips quickly, including for medical reasons. Kami now relies on an outsourced team that responds 24/7.

q: What does Kami Vision do?
a: Mike Link describes a business that started in home security in 2014 and now also covers elder care fall detection and an enterprise security product. In his words, "Kami Vision is an AI vision company." [02:51] He expects it to add AI agents as well.

q: How did Kami Vision improve the accuracy of its AI fall detection?
a: Link says the model was first trained largely on test data, then retrained using misses and mistakes from customers using the product. As he put it, "there really is nothing quite like field data or data that's like in real environments." [08:15]

q: Why does early fall detection matter for seniors?
a: Mike Link explains that people typically aren't hurt in their first few falls, and that hospital visits often come around the sixth, seventh or eighth. He said, "if we can capture the early falls, we have a greater chance preventing the serious falls." [12:19]

q: How did Kami Vision scale without a large sales team?
a: Link let the sales team go and turned to partners who already had customer relationships, paying them a fee. He said "we moved away from selling directly and just started going to partners" [20:23], and the company also stays slim by using AI for design, email automation and back-end operations.

q: What is Mike Link's advice for early-stage founders?
a: Link urges founders to find real users quickly, even lining up people who agree to try the product before it is built. His advice is to "Get as many people to use it as fast as possible." [31:31] He also values users who feel comfortable giving blunt negative feedback.

s13-e10-decoupling-authorization-scalable-policy-as-code-for-enterprise-apps-with-alex-olivier-co-founder-cpto-of-cerbos

Borrow the Engine, Differentiate Policy: The first dozen or so Cerbos releases ran on Open Policy Agent underneath, translating simpler YAML and CEL policies into it. This let the team iterate quickly on what the policy format needed.

Users' Workarounds Became the Roadmap: After about two years of gathering feedback on the open source engine, Cerbos built Cerbos Hub, a paid control plane addressing extra work users faced, such as policy distribution, audit logs and testing changes.

Authorization Must Be Extremely Fast: Authorization runs on every request, often many times within one, so evaluation needs to be in milliseconds, ideally sub-millisecond. Cerbos also built in telemetry, tracing and metrics from day one.

Distributed by Design: The fully remote company hired mostly senior people and intentionally spread them out, including an early engineer in New Zealand. That forced documentation and async work, with very few meetings and no daily stand-up.

Agents Expose Coarse Permissions: An intern may skip systems unrelated to a task, but an agent will try any access it has to reach its goal. Alex argues authorization must happen at every step, including delegation chains between services.

q: What is Cerbos and how does it work?
a: Cerbos is an authorization system whose core, the policy decision point, is an Apache 2 licensed open source project that returns allow or deny decisions. Alex Olivier explained that it moves the logic about who "can do what under what context and when and why to an external service that's running alongside" [06:14] your system.

q: Why did Alex Olivier and his co-founders start Cerbos?
a: Alex had to solve application permissions for enterprise customers repeatedly across several companies, and found no off-the-shelf product designed for it. He and his co-founders also saw from peers that it was becoming "a blocker to enterprise adoption of any product you're building." [04:46]

q: How is Cerbos different from Open Policy Agent's Rego approach?
a: Alex said Open Policy Agent had the right model, but its Rego language was too complicated to put in the hands of product, security or business teams. Cerbos chose YAML policies with Common Expression Language conditions, which he described as "a much simpler manifest driven way of defining policy." [07:33]

q: Why do AI agents make fine-grained authorization more important?
a: Alex argues that agents will use every tool and access they have to achieve a goal, even in systems a human would know to leave alone. In his view, this exposes that the security models "that have been placed to date are not fine-grained enough." [22:41]

q: What mistake did the Cerbos team make with integrations and SDKs?
a: Alex said the team spent time on demos, extensions, plugins and SDKs that were never looked at again, when its data now shows only one or two major architectures and tech stacks. As he put it, "We probably went too broad too quickly with some of those integrations and SDKs and such," [19:10].

s13-bonus-the-99-reliability-shift-foundation-models-for-robotic-manipulation-with-yash-sinha-founder-of-intelligence-factory

Deployment Over Data Sales: Intelligence Factory could have made money selling robotics data, but chose to train its own models and deploy them. Sinha calls it riskier, but says selling data lacks defensibility and erodes the moat.

Pick and Place First: The first prototype targets picking and packing most objects. The team identifies what interested customers handle, collects data in its data factories, and trains the model, widening its action space with each deployment.

Buy Hardware, Build Intelligence: The company doesn't build robots, since hardware has become good and cheap. Sinha says its models are hardware agnostic and adapt to any robot with 20 to 25 minutes of extra training.

Hiring Beyond Credentials: Sinha screens for first principles and extrapolative thinking, integrity and resilience. He admits over-indexing on credentials led to offers that could have hurt the company had they worked out.

Problem Before Solution: At his previous startup, Sinha spent 18 months on AI and robotics for materials discovery. He says the team fit a solution to a problem, lacked founder-idea fit and took too long to see the market didn't exist.

q: What does Intelligence Factory build?
a: Yash Sinha says Intelligence Factory is building models, the "intelligence to deploy general purpose manipulation robots." [02:47] Its focus is manipulation, meaning anything you do with your hands, with deployments in warehouses, groceries, data centers and electronics.

q: Why doesn't Intelligence Factory just sell robotics training data?
a: Sinha says selling data looked like a good way to make a lot of money in the short term, but the team realized that "selling data doesn't have a defensibility attached to it." [07:22] They chose deployment instead, reasoning that customers find it very hard to switch between robotics providers.

q: Can Intelligence Factory's models run on different robot hardware?
a: Yes, Sinha describes the models as hardware agnostic, able to adapt to any robot hardware "in 20 to 25 minutes of extra training." [14:49] Because the hardware is bought rather than built, he says the company isn't constrained by hardware or shipping time.

q: What does Yash Sinha look for when hiring for a robotics startup?
a: Sinha looks for first principles thinking, integrity and resilience, a combination he calls extremely rare. On being willing to be wrong, he wants someone where "a person believes in their hypothesis but is ready to change" [12:45] when there is enough evidence.

q: What did Yash Sinha learn from his previous startup?
a: Sinha says product-market fit and founder-idea fit need to be assessed extremely early. Reflecting on his earlier work in AI and robotics for materials discovery, he said the mistake "was that we fit a solution to a problem." [17:52]

s13-bonus-accelerating-zero-knowledge-hardware-driven-zk-proof-generation-with-leo-fan-co-founder-ceo-of-cysic

Pausing the Custom Chip: After more than a year of effort, Cysic paused its ZK chip. Off-the-shelf GPUs and FPGAs met demand, ZK algorithms hadn't settled, and potential buyers wouldn't pay. The call meant letting some team members go.

Revenue Defines the MVP: To Leo, an MVP has to earn money from customers. Cysic spent over half a year on GPU proving, sharply cutting a CPU job of about two hours on a two-card 4090 machine, and customers were willing to pay.

An Expensive FPGA Lesson: Cysic put too many resources into its own FPGA server, which cost around $200,000 to $300,000. It couldn't handle many parallel computations, and fast-moving GPU acceleration outperformed it, so the team stopped building new ones.

Creating Demand for Proofs: As layer two demand for proving declined, Cysic expanded into AI computing and designed a dark pool. It hides transaction details on-chain while using Cysic's open-source ZKVM and creating demand for compute.

Technology Is Not Enough: Leo advises founders not to expect too much from a first product and to iterate heavily. Technology is only part of success; marketing, business development and getting customers to pay matter too.

q: What is Cysic and what does its name mean?
a: Cysic combines "Cy" from cipher, meaning cryptography, with "sic" from ASIC, a specialized chip. Co-founder and CEO Leo Fan explained, "So it means we are going to build some hardware for some crypto systems" [03:16]. The company also built the Cysic Network, a blockchain that incentivizes people to contribute idle computing power.

q: Why did Cysic pause development of its ZK proof chip?
a: Leo Fan said GPUs and FPGAs could meet current proving demand without spending several million on a chip tape-out. As he put it, "those hardware is like off the shelf hardware. They are good enough" [09:02]. The market was also unclear and ZK algorithms had not converged, so potential buyers were reluctant to pay.

q: What is Cysic's ZKVM and how does it help developers?
a: ZKVM stands for Zero Knowledge Virtual Machine, and Cysic open sourced its version so developers don't have to write ZK circuits by hand in a new language. Leo Fan explained, "You just write your normal Rust program and then it will be converted to the opcode" [16:30]. He said it remains one of the best performing ZKVMs in the space.

q: How can zero-knowledge proofs be used to verify AI inference?
a: Leo Fan said ZK proofs could show that a result came from the model a user is paying for, not a different one. In his example, "the ZK can be used to certify the result" [19:22]. He added that current GPU proving is too slow for this, so ASICs are really needed.

q: What advice does Leo Fan give young entrepreneurs about their first product?
a: Leo Fan advises founders to temper expectations and keep pace with the market, especially now that AI helps products iterate quickly. He said not to expect too much from "your first product. You need to iterate it a lot" [25:16]. He also stressed that marketing, business development and customer acquisition matter alongside technology.

s13-e9-forward-deployed-ai-moving-enterprise-pilots-into-real-production-with-pooja-brown-cto-at-tribe-ai

Production MVPs, Not Pilots: Tribe's MVP is a first real use case running for actual users inside the enterprise's security and governance, with a business owner and clear metric. Pooja calls POCs a pre-sales artifact.

The First Build Pays Forward: The first product in an enterprise is expensive because integrations, evals, security and the agent harness must be set up. Later use cases reuse that foundation and compound its value.

Autonomy Is Earned: Clients want fully autonomous agents immediately, but Pooja says that right is earned one run at a time. People check the work, and their corrections give the agent more room to act on its own.
Everyone Still Builds: Every Tribe hire, at every level, does the same take-home, including Pooja for the CTO job. It tests whether they work well with agents and have the judgment to steer them.

Bring People Along: At DocuSign, Pooja's far better replacement platform met what she calls "organ rejection" because she hadn't understood how people worked with the old system or brought them through the change.

q: What does Tribe AI do?
a: Tribe AI builds AI products for large enterprises that live inside the company's own systems and do real work. Pooja Brown, its CTO, says the company fills the gap between demos and running products: "We don't advise, we build through it." [04:31]

q: How do you move an enterprise AI pilot into real production?
a: Pooja Brown says it takes a business owner, a clear metric and a path from an engineer's laptop to production through evals, audit trails and security guardrails. Proofs of concept help align people, "but those are a pre-sales artifact." [07:34]

q: How much autonomy should AI agents have on day one?
a: Pooja Brown describes this as a constant trade-off, because everybody wants fully autonomous versions running immediately. Her view is that teams need to "earn the right to do that one run at a time" [09:16], with agents creating output, getting corrections from people and improving.

q: How does Tribe AI avoid starting from scratch on each engagement?
a: Pooja says Tribe captures what its engineers learn across enterprises, which she calls Tribe knowledge, so common platform and learning-loop problems aren't rebuilt each time. In her words, "Every engagement that we walk into, we're not starting from zero." [17:36]

q: What did Pooja Brown learn from replacing the platform at DocuSign?
a: She found that a much better system can still go unused if you don't understand the norms and processes built around the old one. Pooja said, "I hadn't made the effort of actually bringing them along." [21:00]

s13-bonus-eliminating-paperwork-manual-data-entry-in-manufacturing-with-brian-mckeown-ceo-of-harmony-ai

One Data Layer Underneath: Harmony digitizes floor paperwork and connects machine data, ERP, CMMS, MES and internal tools into an ontological data layer that powers AI scheduling, quality and inventory intelligence.

Pilots Tackle the Hardest Problem: Harmony spends four to six weeks in a plant solving its toughest problem. McKeown said every pilot so far had closed, but the work must be fast without leaving a shoddy foundation for the full rollout.

Factories Share Common Patterns: Sawmills and gun makers may seem unalike, but both run machines and turn material into products. Weekly roadmap meetings compare problems across plants to find what can be repeated.

Discipline About Ideal Customers: Harmony targets mid-market, high-volume, family-owned manufacturers. Taking poor-fit customers for short-term revenue can create siloed deployments and a mountain of maintenance.

Hiring Builders, Not Just Engineers: Candidates are asked, "How are you a dog?" McKeown looks for people who can code, understand AI, talk with operators and turn loosely defined problems into working solutions.

q: What is Harmony AI and what does it do for manufacturers?
a: Brian McKeown describes Harmony AI as an AI operating system for factories that digitizes paperwork and connects machine data and software tools into one data layer. The reason, as McKeown put it, is that "AI is only as good as the data it has access to" [03:40].

q: How does Harmony AI's factory pilot work?
a: Harmony goes into a plant for four to six weeks to solve its hardest problem and prove the value of its software. McKeown said that at the time of the interview, "every single pilot we've done as it stands has closed." [08:20]

q: Can one manufacturing software platform work across very different factories?
a: McKeown argues that it can, because plants as different as a sawmill and a gun maker both rely on machines and materials. In his words, "everyone does things slightly differently, they do it just similar enough for this kind of" [13:45] ontological data solution to work.

q: How is Harmony AI approaching scalability?
a: McKeown said the team limits its early focus so it can spot repeatable trends, port solutions between factories and speed up each deployment. He explained, "the way we've approached scalability is by targeting these mid-market, high volume," [18:18] family-owned manufacturers.

q: What mistake did Harmony AI make with speed versus quality?
a: At an earlier deployment, McKeown's team prioritized speed and later had to weigh patching solutions against rewriting them. He said that as you gather more context on what the customer wants, "you really realize this was not the way to do it." [21:35]

s13-bonus-spotting-property-red-flags-using-the-carfax-of-real-estate-with-jeff-emalaba-founder-ceo-of-investfusion

Born From a Bad Duplex: Jeff paid over $11,000 in fees and deposits on a North Carolina duplex before an inspector told him to run. A contractor put the cost of pursuing the deal at over $65,000, and the seller refused to refund his money.

Score Deals Before Committing: InvestFusion pulls over 400 data points and returns an evaluation in under 60 seconds. A deal score above 50 signals a likely good investment, while a score below 50 comes with the reasons why it isn't.

Paying More to Build: About 10 companies bid on the project, and Jeff chose one priced over $10,000 above the rest. The build took over two and a half years, with loan officers, agents, appraisers, inspectors and investors getting beta access.

A $5 Million Lesson: A Dallas commercial property with a single government tenant led to a loss of over $5 million when the tenant left. The platform now flags tenant concentration and reviews lease terms and tenant financials.

Feedback Drives the Roadmap: Jeff watches clients walk through the platform and passes requests to developers. One example: investors with 100+ properties want to scan them quickly and focus on the few with the strongest deal scores.

q: What is InvestFusion, the "Carfax for real estate"?
a: InvestFusion is an AI-powered platform that Jeff Emalaba founded to surface property risks, such as foundation, structural, mold and roofing issues, at the deal level. As Jeff put it, "The platform is able to go behind the scene and uncover hidden issues before you spend" [05:09].

q: How does InvestFusion analyze a property so quickly?
a: Jeff says the platform draws on industry APIs, government sites and professional reports, then interprets that data for the buyer. In his words, "The platform is able to pull up over 400 data points and evaluates everything you're seeing on those data points in under 60 seconds." [08:44].

q: What is the "no representation" loophole in real estate disclosures?
a: Jeff explains that on a disclosure document, a seller can answer yes, no or "no representation" about a property's issues or condition, and the last option can act as cover. As he described it, "So it's now left for the buyer to go and uncover those risks." [06:38].

q: Why did Jeff Emalaba start InvestFusion?
a: Jeff lost over $11,000 on a duplex where the inspection revealed foundation, structural, electrical and roofing problems that the seller had not disclosed. Reflecting on why he created the tool, Jeff said "I built from a place of pain." [29:17].

q: What red flags did Jeff learn from losing money on a commercial property?
a: Jeff points to two in his Dallas deal: the property had only one tenant, and that government tenant could leave if its contract changed. He noted that "in the lease they signed, the lease allowed them to leave if there's" [20:29] any change on their contract.

s13-e8-democratizing-real-estate-fractional-wealth-building-for-modern-investors-with-alex-blackwood-ceo-of-mogul

Born From a Painful Purchase: Buying his first rental, Alex saw 10 to 12 people scraping fees. He used a month of garden leave to write a fractional investing thesis, then pitched Joey, who had grown Goldman's single-family rental platform from zero to $1 billion.

Shrink the MVP: Mogul spent months toiling with an outsourced firm in India before deciding it didn't need the full platform, just an entry point to list properties and let people invest. Alex now wishes he had first tested demand with a simple Webflow signup.

Hire for the Seat: An early technical hire chosen for prestige hadn't touched code much lately. The CTO Alex later cold messaged on LinkedIn rebuilt in a month what had been a two-year struggle, and the team began shipping updates almost daily.

Own the Marketing Data: After a marketing hire didn't work out, Alex took a month to learn Snowflake and SQL and stand up data infrastructure. By the end of August, Mogul launched Google ads with its own tracking, and Alex says they're now very profitable.

Buying Mogul.com: The domain was priced at $4 million, and Mogul got it for about $1.3 million after modeling the return with and without it. Alex sees it as brand legitimacy for a goal bigger than fractional investing: owning the word for residential real estate.

q: What is Mogul and how does fractional real estate investing work on it?
a: Mogul, which Alex Blackwood likens to a Robinhood for real estate, lets people buy shares in single-family rentals and receive rental income, appreciation and tax benefits. Alex describes the idea as "you can buy shares in single family rentals that are vetted by institutional professionals" [03:02].

q: How was the first version of Mogul built?
a: Alex Blackwood and his co-founder outsourced development to a firm in India, funding it themselves with friends and family money while moonlighting alongside their day jobs. Off-the-shelf platforms didn't fit, and as Alex put it, "We realized that it had to be a custom built software." [09:43]

q: What did Mogul's CEO learn about early startup hiring?
a: Alex Blackwood learned that prestige can help sift candidates, but it shouldn't decide who gets hired. His lesson was "that we need to hire people for the seat rather than caring about any sort of prestige." [20:47]

q: How much did Mogul pay for the mogul.com domain?
a: Alex Blackwood said the asking price was $4 million, and the company modeled scenarios with and without the domain before buying. In his words, "ultimately we were able to get it for about 1.3, which was incredibly exciting." [38:12]

q: What advice does Alex Blackwood give young entrepreneurs?
a: Alex advises founders to stop comparing themselves with others, trust their gut and use data to change course when they're wrong. He also says to "Take lessons from everyone, but don't take it as Bible." [42:27]

s13-bonus-from-lab-to-market-scaling-high-growth-tech-startups-with-caitlinn-mcminn-programs-director-at-techfw

Equity-Free by Design: TechFW is a nonprofit that provides no funding and takes no equity, so pre-revenue founders keep their company intact. The hope is that members who make it big will reinvest in the next generation.

Keeping Promises Builds Ecosystems: McMinn calls broken promises the most fragile part of an ecosystem. She says TechFW strayed amid multiple leadership changes, then recovered by owning up to it and showing up again.

Beyond Medtech and Biotech: After focusing heavily on medtech and biotech for about two decades, TechFW now also sees drones, robotics, advanced manufacturing and AI, and highlights its 25-plus-year relationship with TMAC.
Validate the Real Market Gap: A common first-time founder mistake is confusing an assumed need with an actual one. ThinkLab focuses on finding a real gap and whether the founder is filling it.

Audit Before You Scale: In FastForward, coaches act as consultants, auditing existing processes to find inefficiencies and cut noise. Communication and a clear roadmap are central to building the team.

q: Why doesn't TechFW take equity from startups?
a: Caitlinn McMinn explains that TechFW is a nonprofit that doesn't provide funding, so it doesn't take equity either, which protects founders while they are still building. As McMinn put it, "It also just takes away the money exchange conversation with our members." [03:10]

q: What kinds of startups does TechFW support in Fort Worth?
a: McMinn says TechFW concentrated heavily on medtech and biotech for roughly its first two decades, while also helping some apps and SaaS platforms. More recently defense-related work and AI have grown, and she noted, "So we get a lot of drones, a lot of robotics, advanced manufacturing" [04:29].

q: What is the biggest misconception first-time founders have when validating a business idea?
a: According to McMinn, it is failing to see "the difference between an actual market need and something you think is a market need." [10:24] TechFW's ThinkLab program spends much of its time on identifying whether there is a real gap and whether the founder is filling it.

q: How does TechFW help founders avoid feeling isolated?
a: McMinn points to the incubator's building, which has about 20 tenants and hosts events and networking, along with its coaching team. She said there are "10 coaches on staff, all different subject matter experts, and they are highly encouraged to meet" [12:43] and collaborate with members.

q: How can a mid-sized city start a tech startup community from scratch?
a: McMinn advises first learning what it takes to start a business, then confirming that entrepreneurs in the region actually need an innovation hub, and then setting a mission to attract founders and partners. "My first advice would be to become an entrepreneur yourself." [21:55]

s13-bonus-automating-local-lead-growth-high-intent-prospecting-ai-verification-with-david-moore-founder-ceo-of-stalexai

Built for the Little Guy: Stalex is an exclusive B2B lead pipeline and custom CRM with scoring and prompting tailored to what, how and to whom you sell. It targets small sellers, not big companies already set on their CRM.

Checks Against False "Done": The AI repeatedly claimed the MVP was finished when it wasn't. Christian, David's brother, who built it by directing AI agents, added a system of checks and balances that David estimates now numbers about 20.

Simplicity Beat the Trading Terminal: David's first interface resembled his old trading platforms and overwhelmed his buddy. That feedback became a design cornerstone: make it usable by someone with no time to learn a new system or syntax.

Review Fixes Like New Code: A fix for one bug broke something worse, making the system show an operator the opposite of the truth in a test run. A rule to re-review every fix from scratch caught it, avoiding a possible full revert.

Headcount Is the Constraint: David says traffic was never the limit and most of it is already automated. The constraint is that the team is just him and Christian, so they want hungry, driven hires who can learn their roles using shared Obsidian knowledge.

q: What is Stalex.ai?
a: Stalex is a B2B lead pipeline paired with a custom CRM that supports lead scoring and individualized prompting. As David Moore put it, "Now we are an exclusive B2B lead pipeline" [03:20].

q: How was the Stalex MVP built?
a: David Moore started with a crude HTML tool for internal use, then handed the project to his brother Christian, who built the MVP by directing AI agents. Of his own early approach, David said, "I was only using Claude at the beginning with no infrastructure" [05:41].

q: How does Stalex verify work built with AI?
a: After the AI repeatedly reported work as finished when it wasn't, David Moore and his brother built a series of checks and balances into their process. David said that without them, "we wouldn't be able to push a product that we could verify" [09:00].

q: Who is Stalex designed for?
a: David Moore says it is built for small B2B sellers rather than large companies that are already committed to a CRM. Describing how easy they wanted it to be, he said, "We made it so your grandmama could sell on this thing" [11:16].

q: How can a bug fix in AI-built software make things worse, and how did Stalex catch it?
a: David Moore described a fix that broke something even worse, causing the system to print the opposite of the truth to an operator during a test run. He said it was caught only because of an earlier lesson, "that a fix gets reviewed" [18:07] again from scratch, as if it were brand new code.

s13-e7-the-ai-legal-shift-giving-sme-law-firms-biglaw-leverage-with-dave-berner-co-founder-ceo-of-parachute

Lean Team, Buy Over Build: After raising what Dave recalls as AUD 1.8 million, Parachute kept engineering to about two and a half people and bought tooling for authentication and real-time collaboration, accepting that each addition must be justified in compliance audits.

Lawyers Selling to Lawyers: Parachute decided it was easier to hire lawyers to do sales than to teach salespeople law. Its three lawyers, plus in-person events for 40 to 50 firms, help shape the roadmap.

Solo Users Strain the System: The heaviest load came from solo practitioners, not larger firms, including uploads of 10,000-page documents needing OCR. Keeping token usage and costs from blowing out is now the main scaling concern.

Roll Out Infrastructure Slowly: Moving AI inference to Australian-hosted models passed local and staging tests, then hit throughput limits in production and cost a major pilot. Dave says they should have tried it first with trusted, heavy-use firms.
Book the Gig First: As in his band days, Dave advises committing publicly to a launch date or event before the product feels ready, because the deadline forces you to be good enough by then.

q: What is Parachute and who is it for?
a: Parachute is an AI platform covering drafting, document review, advice, client meeting notes and email intake across a legal matter. Dave Berner explains that "Parachute is an AI platform for SME law firms and all their clients that they serve." [02:45]

q: How did Parachute build its MVP with such a small engineering team?
a: Dave Berner says the company has been AI native from day one, with about two and a half engineers and Codex used for adversarial code review. In his words, "we're leaning heavily on Claude Code at the moment, using a range of models" [04:34].

q: What scaling challenges does an AI legal platform like Parachute face?
a: Dave says the main concern is stopping token usage and costs from blowing out as users grow. The surprise was that big firms did not hit the platform hardest; instead, "It's the solo practitioner who comes in" [10:05] and tries to use it in place of hiring a whole legal team.

q: What went wrong when Parachute moved AI inference to Australia?
a: Responses from the Australian-hosted models differed, and production throughput was restricted despite provider assurances, which cost Parachute one of its biggest pilots. Reflecting on it, Dave said "we probably should have rolled it out slower," [13:24] starting with trusted firms rather than pilot customers.

q: How can law firms use Parachute with their clients?
a: Firms can extend a version of Parachute to clients, who draft there and share the work, prompts and documents with their lawyer in one click. Dave Berner's reasoning is that people will "use ai tooling one way or the other so there's no point in just asking them not to" [15:28].

s13-bonus-the-ai-marketing-cloud-harnessing-predictive-intent-to-scale-growth-with-christian-monberg-cto-of-zeta-global

Enterprise Grade Took a Year: After Zeta acquired his SMB-focused company in 2017, Monberg's team spent the first year hardening it to meet enterprise SLAs, including moving beyond a purely real-time, streaming approach to support batch too.

Customers Drive the Roadmap: Zeta's customer advisory board feeds a large share of the yearly roadmap and shapes upcoming beta programs. Industry research and internal vision are the other inputs, and some customers react to paper prototypes early.

Scale From Day One: Zeta builds for the biggest throughput customers. Zero-to-one products stay that way only long enough to confirm product-market fit, then get scaled up and tested using internal frameworks.

Fix the Leaky Bucket First: In his startup days, Monberg poured on marketing growth before fixing enough of the mess from moving fast. In hindsight, he would have waited another six months to scale go-to-market.

Side-by-Side Spreads New Capabilities: Monberg says the best predictor of how fast teams adopt a new capability is having culture carriers sit down beside them, even if that means flying someone from Prague to Bangalore.

q: What is Zeta Global and what makes it different from competitors?
a: Christian Monberg describes Zeta Global as a technology company building AI, historically for marketing use cases such as acquiring, retaining and growing customers. He points to its proprietary data approach to identity and to its solutions being "all predicated on one platform, which is really important in today's industry" [03:30].

q: How did Christian Monberg's startup become part of Zeta's platform?
a: Zeta acquired Monberg's AI marketing company in 2017, and its platform, built largely for small and medium-sized businesses, became the backbone of what Zeta was doing. That required hardening it for enterprise customers, and as Monberg put it, "we really spent the first year focused on that" [06:12].

q: How does Zeta Global decide what to build next?
a: Monberg says customers are the most important input, led by the customer advisory board held before the Zeta Live event, alongside industry research and internal vision. Beta programs follow, and he explains they "are predicated on having real customers inside the platform providing feedback" [10:37].

q: What is generative UI in enterprise software?
a: Monberg describes it as software on demand at enterprise scale, an answer to the frustration of rigid workflows that were never built for the individual user. In his words, "if you want software to do something, you just tell it what to do and it should reorganize itself" [26:48].

q: What advice does Christian Monberg give young entrepreneurs?
a: Monberg first asks whether they want feedback as a friend, feedback as an investor or just support. As a friend, he urges them to picture what failure looks like, because "Identifying failure early is the key to success." [31:55] As an investor, he asks why the opportunity is big enough.

s13-bonus-scaling-real-time-search-data-secure-apis-for-ai-infrastructure-with-alaa-abdulridha-engineering-director-at-serpapi

Born From a Blocker: SerpApi's founder hit CAPTCHAs while collecting Google images for a food-identification app, so he built an API that scraped them. The company now serves structured search data to developers and businesses.

Prove the Security Impact: Alaa found SSRF risks in this new kind of API, but engineers didn't see them as vulnerabilities until he showed a proof of concept with significant impact. Those security steps are now standard before any new API ships.

Public Roadmap Guides Builds: SerpApi posts new product ideas on a public GitHub roadmap and builds when clients show interest. Clients also request features and new APIs directly by email or website chat.

JSON Consistency Matters: Customers expect a stable JSON structure, but search engine changes can force updates. When the Naver API structure had to change, the team contacted each client using it before pushing to production.

Start Compliance Early: Clients began insisting on certified vendors, which SerpApi didn't see coming. Alaa had to go through all company documentation, rewrite policies and prepare for external audits in a short period.

q: What is SerpApi and what is it used for?
a: Alaa Abdulridha describes SerpApi as a SaaS API that delivers structured search data at scale for uses such as AI training, real-time chatbot search, news monitoring and SEO. As Alaa put it, "We basically provide data for companies, for developers." [03:32]

q: Why was SerpApi created?
a: According to Alaa, the founder was building an app that identified food from pictures and ran into CAPTCHAs when gathering information and images from Google. Alaa explained, "The blocker was how can he collect this information and images from Google without limitation." [04:01]

q: What security challenges come with building search data APIs?
a: Alaa says securing this type of API was a mystery early on, and the team found it could be exposed to server-side request forgery (SSRF). Convincing engineers took evidence, as they did not see the issues as vulnerabilities "unless I managed to introduce a proof of concept that has a significant security impact there." [09:28]

q: How does SerpApi decide which APIs and features to build?
a: Alaa says the team posts ideas for new products publicly and goes ahead when clients show interest, while some products are requested by clients directly. "We have a public roadmap on GitHub." [11:56]

q: When should a startup start working on security compliance?
a: Alaa advises business owners to keep compliance in mind early, because some clients will only contract with compliant companies. Having had to do the work on a short timeline, Alaa warned, "you do not want to deal with all that compliance at once and into a short amount of time." [19:34]

e13-bonus-the-ai-sast-shift-eliminating-vulnerability-backlogs-with-santiago-castineira-co-founder-cto-of-maze

Cloud Context First: To simplify early triage, Maze limited its data to cloud context, such as environment metadata and some runtime configuration in AWS. It initially left out customers' code repositories and other security tools' datasets.

Engine Before Product: From mid-2024, Maze spent until November building an MVP of its vulnerability-ranking engine, then validated it with security engineers and design partners. A version customers could fully use took another six to eight months.

Built for Enterprise Scale: Maze targeted environments with tens of millions of open vulnerabilities. It loads data upfront to avoid API throttling during agent runs, and designed for thousands of concurrent agents per customer.

Multi-Agent Costs Add Up: An early prototype had multiple agents debating each other, which reasoned deeply but was costly. The team moved to a single agent consulting experts as needed, while also migrating from AutoGen to LangGraph.

A Reusable Agent Platform: Santiago is proudest of generic foundations for data ingestion and for building, orchestrating and evaluating agents. That makes standing up an agent with a completely new function and new datasets fairly straightforward.

q: What does Maze do?
a: Maze, co-founded by CTO Santiago Castiñeira, helps companies of very different sizes deal with their security vulnerabilities, with products focused on cloud, SCA and SAST. In Santiago's words, "We at Maze basically triage and remediate cloud and code vulnerabilities for companies" [02:53].

q: How did Maze use LLMs to prioritize vulnerabilities in its MVP?
a: Santiago Castiñeira's team set out to connect much more contextual data to vulnerabilities to decide which should be handled first. Using early, buggy versions of LangGraph, he said, "what we managed to prove with LangGraph is that basically LLMs could understand configuration" [06:31] metadata and produce an assessment on aspects of a vulnerability.

q: How does Maze run AI agents at enterprise scale?
a: Santiago explained that collecting data while agents run would mean too many external API calls and quick throttling. Instead, "we need to load the data upfront so we can read it as many times" [13:22] as needed, supported by a horizontally scalable data pipeline.

q: Is a multi-agent system better than a single agent?
a: Santiago Castiñeira found that Maze's early multi-agent prototype showed impressive depth of reasoning but came with costs the team hadn't anticipated. He now believes that for a lot of applications "a single agent can achieve the same reasoning levels" [16:08].

q: What does Maze look for when hiring?
a: Santiago uses a phrase he read elsewhere and has practiced for years: "high energy, high intelligence and high integrity" [10:41]. He pairs those traits with a strong vision people buy into, and says the result is a team where engineers often find their own problems to solve.

e13-e6-the-spatial-web-shift-building-decentralized-ai-knowledge-graphs-with-yaniv-tal-co-founder-ceo-of-geo
Protocol Meets Consumer App: Geo's core challenge is being both a web protocol, which should be perfect and never change, and a consumer app that must iterate almost daily on user feedback.
An Integrated, Apple-Like Stack: Geo builds the pieces together: a knowledge graph standard, on-chain governance, indexing, an SDK, and the Geo Browser, which shows who published what and when.
Iterate Before Locking In: Geo had real users within six months and worked in roughly six-month learning cycles, but took time on foundations before scaling, when structural changes get hard.
Restarting on the Web: After six months on a React Native app, the team saw that full native would perform better but ship too slowly. They started over on the web to iterate faster.
Mission Alignment Comes First: Yaniv hires people who have run into Geo's core problem themselves and have kept pushing their limits. He finds skill fairly easy to evaluate and often learnable.

q: What is Geo and what problem does it solve?
a: Geo, co-founded and led by Yaniv Tal, tackles the difficulty of knowing what is true amid a constant flood of information. As Yaniv put it, "Geo is a network for organizing knowledge" [02:54] that we can trust, using a knowledge graph that communities organize and govern together.

q: How does Geo relate to the semantic web?
a: Yaniv Tal describes Geo as the realization of what the web's original architects wanted: an open, interconnected web of data. In that vision, he explained, knowledge and information should "live outside the context of any one application." [05:07]

q: How does the Geo Browser verify where information comes from?
a: Yaniv says everything in the Geo Browser is attributable, cryptographically signed and carries its history, which he likens to Git for data. In his words, "You can see exactly who published what, when, right?" [10:25]

q: Why did Geo move from React Native to the web?
a: Yaniv Tal said the team realized full native would have performed better than React Native, but any native approach would slow down shipping updates. As he explained, development "velocity was too slow for any type of native compared to web." [20:34] They started over after six months on the initial version.

q: How do decentralized knowledge graphs fit with AI?
a: Yaniv Tal sees a global, verifiable knowledge graph as a kind of collective memory system that can matter for what AI models learn from and answer against. "I think intelligence is no longer the bottleneck." [24:36] His concern is whether the information fed to models is accurate, up to date and complete.

s13-bonus-the-enterprise-ai-chip-war-rethinking-llm-silicon-inference-with-vasanth-mohan-director-of-product-at-sambanova

Mix Models Across Agents: Mohan suggests a frontier model for planning, the most complicated step, and open models like GLM, Kimi or MiniMax for code execution. SambaNova's own teams do this to cut run time and cost.

Split Prefill From Decode: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound. In disaggregated inference, GPUs can handle prefill while RDUs or custom ASICs handle decode, with fast networking tying them together.

Keep Chip Ratios Fungible: Mohan puts the ideal prefill-to-decode chip ratio between 1:2 and 2:1, so hardware stays utilized as workloads shift. SRAM-only decode can balloon node counts because of limited memory.

Air Cooling Opens Capacity: Mohan estimates about 80% of data centers are air-cooled. He says SambaNova's data flow design cuts energy spent on memory movement, so its racks can run in them without liquid cooling.

Peel Back Closed APIs Gradually: Rather than rushing on-prem, build agents on closed APIs, then test individual sub-agents on open models with careful evaluations. Neoclouds and inference providers can handle the hardware complexity.

q: What is SambaNova's Reconfigurable Data Flow Unit (RDU)?
a: The RDU is SambaNova's AI chip, which Vasanth Mohan says works fundamentally differently from GPUs and is tuned to the data flow graphs of AI models. He explains that it "maps the hardware in a way that is much more spatially oriented to how AI operations work" [02:31].

q: Why can SambaNova racks run in air-cooled data centers?
a: Mohan says SambaNova's data flow architecture significantly reduces the energy needed for inference, which lets its racks fit into air-cooled facilities. As he put it, "the reason at the simplest level is because memory movement is the most" [16:17] energy-expensive thing a chip can do.

q: What is disaggregated inference?
a: It runs the prefill and decode stages of inference on different hardware to improve utilization and deliver faster tokens. Mohan describes "using GPUs on the prefill side, using custom ASICs or RDUs in our case, in the decode" [13:27] side.

q: What is the right ratio of prefill to decode chips?
a: Vasanth Mohan says operators should avoid over-engineering for one workload and keep the hardware fungible as demand changes. He recommends "balancing pre-fill and decode, ideally in the range of 1 to 1 or 1 to 2 or 2 to 1." [23:16]

q: How should companies move from closed AI APIs to open models?
a: Mohan expects most to start with closed providers like OpenAI or Anthropic, build their agent infrastructure, and then move pieces over gradually, with evaluations playing an important role. He describes the step as "okay, let me test this sub-agent on an open model," [27:45] and then seeing how it performs.

s13-bonus-dynamic-observability-eliminating-telemetry-waste-at-scale-with-peter-morelli-co-founder-ceo-of-bitdrift

Built for Mobile's Bad Networks: Data center-style tools lost telemetry when phone connections dropped. Bitdrift's first version stored data on the device and uploaded it once the network was good, without blowing out storage or hurting the user experience.

Rust Core, Native Wrappers: The team wrote the core in Rust for speed, performance and memory safety, wrapped it in Swift and Kotlin layers, and kept work asynchronous to avoid lag a user would notice.

Runtime Control Beats Release Trains: Mobile release cycles averaged 10 to 15 days. Making observability configurable at runtime lets teams gather more detail on a problem, then turn it off, in minutes instead of weeks or months.

Stop Shipping Unused Data: Morelli says 90% of observability data is never looked at. Bitdrift keeps data on devices and can summarize logs into small counters. Some customers spent 70% of data bandwidth on telemetry, which Bitdrift can cut to 2%.

Early Deals Can Backfire: Some early contracts were break-even or money-losing, with unexpected cost overruns. The team fixed them through engineering and by working with customers, who are still with Bitdrift and growing.

q: Why do traditional observability tools struggle on mobile apps?
a: Peter Morelli explains that most tools assume the reliable bandwidth, CPU and storage of a data center, which phones don't have. When connections dropped at Lyft, he said, "We were seeing that the data was being dropped on the ground." [05:01]

q: How does Bitdrift reduce wasted mobile telemetry?
a: Bitdrift stores data locally and uses a server-side control plane to ask for only the observability needed at that moment. As Morelli put it, "It keeps data at the edge on the devices until something on the control plane" [14:18] requests it.

q: What technology is Bitdrift built with?
a: Morelli says the core library is wrapped in native Swift and Kotlin layers, with early work focused on performance, memory safety and network reliability. Of the core, he said, "We wrote it in Rust and it still is to this day." [06:14]

q: How can mobile teams add logging without waiting for an app release?
a: Bitdrift makes observability configurable at runtime, so teams can collect more information on a problem and switch it off afterward. Morelli said "that's something that used to take you weeks or months" [10:20], and now it can be done in a few minutes.

q: What advice does Peter Morelli have for technical founders?
a: Morelli urges founders to understand customers deeply and not to underestimate how hard it is to get a product in front of people. He advises them "not to underestimate the story that you tell around these things." [23:26]

s13-e5-the-dynamic-compute-revolution-eliminating-cache-invalidation-with-julien-verlaguet-founder-ceo-of-skiplabs

Reactive Means Spreadsheets, Not Streams: Julien's Skip language generalizes how Excel and ReactJS work. Developers define dependencies, and the system handles updates when something changes, instead of maintaining caches and invalidating them by hand.

Coding Agents Are Reactive Systems: Agents make changes, then must update what they know is left to do. SkipLabs paired a Skip-suited harness with fast tooling, including a sound, incremental TypeScript rebuilt from scratch, to create Skipper.

Tooling Is the Next Bottleneck: Julien expects that as models get much faster, infrastructure won't keep up with AI-written code. He contrasts an hour to test and deploy a change with under a second each in an incremental, reactive setup.

Hear Problems, Question Solutions: From years of language design, Julien finds users usually know the source of their pain but propose easy fixes for their own use that may not fit the product. Zero-to-one work needs vision; feedback drives more later.

A Quicksort Copy-Paste Backfired: Changing the pivot in code copied from the internet subtly broke sorting in Skip's C runtime. It passed tests and usually worked, but led to data corruption and his hardest deterministic bug.

q: What is Skipper from SkipLabs?
a: Skipper is SkipLabs' coding agent, which Julien Verlaguet says you can use a little like a compiler: you give it a spec and let it iterate until it produces something that works. In his words, "Skipper is a coding agent that works in a closed loop" [03:54].

q: What does reactive programming mean in the Skip language?
a: Julien Verlaguet distinguishes it from streaming: when you change something, everything that depends on it updates. As he put it, "I mean something that works like a spreadsheet." [05:53]

q: Why is manual cache invalidation a problem for coding agents?
a: Julien explains that a coding agent has to keep updating its state after every change, and building that without a reactive language means maintaining many caches yourself. He warns that "trying to do your cache invalidation by hand" [07:45] is going to lead to bugs, and Skip is his way of getting it right.

q: How will AI-generated code affect developer tooling?
a: Julien believes faster models will produce more code than current infrastructure can take in, which is where he sees incremental, reactive tools mattering. "I think given that AI is now in the mix, the bottleneck is going to switch to tooling very soon." [23:38]

q: What was Julien Verlaguet's hardest deterministic bug?
a: While writing Skip's runtime in C, Julien changed the pivot in a Quicksort implementation found online, not realizing it only worked with the original pivot. The badly sorted memory pages led to corrupted data, and he vowed, "I will never copy paste code from the internet ever, ever, ever again." [21:56]

q: How did GitLaw get started?

q: How has AI changed the way GitLaw builds its product?

Automation Without Coding: Kilter AI offers insights on which vulnerabilities matter and turns them into automations engineers can test and run without writing code. It targets network experts who don't necessarily choose to be Python coders.

AI as Accountable Advisor: Backbox keeps engineers in control and shows how AI reaches conclusions. Customers worry that autonomous AI could take down infrastructure, and AI doesn't hold itself accountable when it makes a mistake.

q: What does Backbox do?

q: Why doesn't Backbox let AI run networks autonomously?

q: How does responsible AI shape what Backbox builds?

Federated From Day One: Rather than start with one Kubernetes cluster and fix scaling later, Aranya built a management cluster with many subclusters. Growth means adding clusters to a federation, which is nearly as straightforward as adding a node.

Text Before Web UI: The team had planned to launch a web UI early, then put its AI in Slack, email and other text channels first. Compute is already operated there, so customers don't have to change their behavior.

q: Why can you manage GPU clusters from Slack and other text channels with Aranya?
a: Christian explained that compute was already being operated over email, Slack, phone and messaging apps before the LLM era, so Aranya put its AI there first instead of rushing out a web UI. In his words, "It allows us to meet people where they're at" [10:37].

a: Christian says it is very difficult to quickly build a data center over about 20 megawatts, at least in the U.S. and some other jurisdictions.
