Fraud Detection Started It: At Airbnb, the trust team wanted real-time signals to fight payment fraud, but data pipelines for training and serving caused most of the friction. The tooling eventually cut iteration from months to days.

Own the Compute Problem: Rather than offer a key-value store and leave feature computation to users, the team took on computation end to end. It was a much harder scope, but it addressed the core user challenge.

Incubation Allowed Costly Rework: Building inside Airbnb let the team redo batch architecture and run big data migrations with real use cases at scale. Varant says such changes would be close to impossible now, with multiple customers.

Design for Skew, Then Optimize: Hot keys, such as a fraudulent IP address flooding a site, can bottleneck distributed jobs. The engine handled skew early, and later added an unskewed mode that gets much better performance on evenly spread data.

Don't Let Early Prospects Steer: Zipline spent four or five months going deep on one part of the stack that early prospects wanted. It adds value today, but other work would have unblocked far more growth, teaching the team to say no.

q: What is Zipline AI?
a: Varant Zanoyan, Co-Founder and CEO, describes it this way: "Zipline AI is a feature and embedding platform for machine learning." [02:45] Data scientists and engineers use it to automate complex infrastructure, use more data, improve model performance and iterate faster.

q: How is Zipline AI related to Airbnb's Chronon engine?
a: Chronon grew out of infrastructure Varant's team built at Airbnb, first for fraud detection and then for search and personalization. Varant said that as Stripe faced similar challenges, "we collaborated with Stripe across company bounds" [05:32], and Chronon later went fully open source, with Zipline building an enterprise platform around it.

q: Why does Zipline AI handle feature computation instead of letting users bring their own compute?
a: Varant explained that a key-value store with some metadata, leaving users to compute their own features, did not fit the use cases the team was supporting. Of that approach, he said, "It's tempting because it's far simpler, but it really doesn't solve the core of the user" [08:30] challenge.

q: How does the Chronon engine deal with data skew at scale?
a: Skew happens when some keys have far more data than others, creating bottlenecks on a few machines, so Varant's team architected for it early while supporting fraud detection. More recently they added a separate path for evenly distributed data, and as Varant put it, "for unskewed cases, we can actually get much better performance" [14:19].

q: What early mistake did Zipline AI make with customer requests?
a: Varant said the team over-indexed on early prospective customers and invested months in an area that probably wasn't the right priority. They shifted to work that would generalize to more users, and he reflected, "It's tough to say no, but you learn to say no a little bit" [17:20].

Consulting Fires Became a Product: Tools built to rescue customers' failing databases grew into a platform. It hit $1 million ARR within 18 months of launch, fully bootstrapped.
Correlating Metrics With Queries: Early scripts went beyond CPU and memory to examine query patterns, so an unexpected 10 PM query surge could explain resource pressure and a struggling application.

Speed Over Code Quality: With customers on fire, the team traded code quality and scale for speed. Some early MVP pieces remain, sometimes causing problems or costing money, while the team builds ahead.

a: The MVP was a scrappy collection of scripts that gathered metrics existing tools did not traditionally surface and graphed them. q: How does NeverBlink find the root cause of database performance problems?

q: Why do AI agents create new challenges for databases?
a: Itamar says agentic workflows are non-deterministic, so the load they create often cannot be planned for. He warns that "agents are making life harder over there because they sometimes really hammer the databases" [20:02].

q: How was NeverBlink's expertise built into the platform?
a: Lessons from consulting work fed back into the product as decision trees and detectors. Itamar explains that the people who built the platform and its root cause analysis "are the same people who consult companies and help them improve their database" [12:55].

Pivot to Survive: In December 2024, Liminal saw its application security route would fail. It combined that security tooling with a multi-model chat interface, giving regulated companies observability and control over how data is handled.

Interest Is Not Demand: Liminal hired salespeople too early after mistaking plentiful inbound calls for demand. It couldn't close the deals and had to let those salespeople go.

Agents That Assemble Themselves: Liminal's vision is to spot repeated, high-value workflows in its observability logs, then offer to run them automatically, so non-power users never have to build an agent.

q: Why did Liminal pivot from its application security platform?

s13-bonus-the-intention-layer-why-coding-agents-need-product-judgment-with-drew-dillon-founder-ceo-of-brief

The Why Is Repeatable: Drew found build processes vary, but the why runs the same: company direction, roadmap, features, then build. Operationalizing it in his consultancy more than doubled clients' engineering velocity.

A Deliberately Tiny MVP: Brief's first version, built in about three days, was a log of product decisions. Much of the work was getting older models to understand what a decision meant and how an agent should use the log.
Scale Limits Become Decisions: Choices on databases, rate limits and security are logged in Brief with the scale at which they should change, so agents can flag when it's time to invest.

Judging Advice by Voice: With no numerical correctness to test against, Drew's bar for Brief's advice is whether it sounds like a decision he would have made. He calls the weekly learnings-and-focus email the product's crown jewel.

Ask for Money Early: Brief followed a pivot from an idea where the best response to asking for money was to come back next quarter. Drew's lesson: charge upfront, don't work free forever and don't hear feedback with happy ears.

q: What is Brief and what does it do?
a: Brief is Drew Dillon's product that extends a product team's knowledge and capability, helping companies operate the why of building software alongside the how. In Drew's words, "Brief is basically your AI product brain." [02:53]

q: Why do AI coding agents need product context?
a: Drew found that when using Cursor, he got results by explaining the user, what the user wants and why a feature matters, rather than just giving UI instructions. He drew on his product management background: "I've been explaining to engineers why we need to build stuff for 20 years." [05:14]

q: What did the first version of Brief look like?
a: Drew describes the MVP as very dumb and built in about three days, growing out of his habit of copying and pasting prompts, then using Markdown documents and MCPs. As he put it, "it was a log of all the decisions" [05:59] the team had made about the product, its users and what they were doing.

q: How does Brief help plan for scaling challenges?
a: Drew records technology choices, API rate limits, security and similar concerns early, along with the point at which each approach should be revisited. q: How do you evaluate an AI agent that gives advice?
a: Drew says it is hard to build evals for advice because there is no numerical correctness to work toward. His test is personal: "my bar for me is like, does it sound like me?" [12:21]

s13-bonus-why-local-on-device-ai-compute-is-the-future-of-privacy-with-behnam-bastani-co-founder-ceo-of-openinfer

Built for Agentic Inference: In 2024, while others focused on model training and chatbots, OpenInfer bet that inference would dominate compute, with long-lasting, interdependent AI workloads that existing infrastructure couldn't scale.

Virtualizing Inference for Neoclouds: OpenInfer's software stack abstracts mixed GPUs and CPUs so neoclouds can sell tokens instead of only renting GPUs. Behnam says their profit margin typically rises by as much as 50.

Follow the Market Pull: OpenInfer began with portable ecosystem devices, where inference was underserved, then adjusted as neocloud demand pulled it toward the cloud. Its early bet on collaborative robotics proved ahead of revenue.

Design Partners Shape the Roadmap: The team studied the problem before building and worked with large design partners, including Fortune 500s. Their feedback informs priorities, though OpenInfer doesn't take every direction.

Small, Local, Handpicked Team: OpenInfer has under 20 people, mostly meeting in person in the Bay Area, with some exceptions. Candidates do trial work so both sides can judge fit, and many teammates have built together before at Meta.

q: What does OpenInfer do for neocloud providers?
a: OpenInfer gives neoclouds an inference software stack, so they can sell tokens rather than only rent out GPUs. Behnam Bastani likens the approach to VMware, saying "we are now virtualizing inference" [10:04].

q: Why should AI inference run where the data lives?
a: Behnam Bastani says banks, robotics and drones generate huge amounts of data, and sending it to the cloud can be costly or mean losing sovereignty. Prove What AI Did: Higdon says the CISO question has shifted from whether you use AI to what it did last week and whether you can prove it. Management, boards and customers are now asking at once.

Enforcement Closes the Loop: Discovery maps what AI exists and runtime monitoring shows what it actually does. Enforcement stops a rogue agent or non-human identity in real time, keeping the blast radius small.

Governance Enables Speed: Citing a CrossFit line, "slow is smooth is fast," Higdon argues that upfront work on compliance, auditing and access keeps AI projects from stalling at a late security review.

Quarterly Reviews Fall Short: Static inventories, quarterly access reviews and after-the-fact log reading assume systems barely change between checks. AI can call a different API tomorrow than it did yesterday.

Evidence as a By-Product: A mature program generates proof of owners, policies, violations and responses as systems run. Higdon expects a widening gap with companies still assembling it by hand before reviews.

q: Why is now the accountability moment for enterprise AI?
a: Shayne Higdon says AI has stopped being a side project and now touches production data, calls APIs and can affect customers before a human looks. As he puts it, "It used to be, are you using AI? Now it's, what did your AI do last week?" [03:13].

q: How can CIOs balance AI speed with governance?
a: Higdon doesn't see speed and governance as opposed, and says teams that skip early security and compliance questions can stall months later. In his view, "good governance is what lets AI scale really past the pilot stage" [10:54].

q: Why do traditional governance and security models struggle with AI?
a: According to Higdon, they rely on static inventories, quarterly access reviews and logs read after the fact, which is too slow for systems that keep changing. He says they "were just simply built for a slower, more predictable world" [13:03].

q: What does a mature AI governance model need to prove?
a: Higdon says it must show that AI assets are continuously discovered and owned, and record what they did, which policies applied, what was violated and how the company responded. He says "the real dividing line is whether that evidence gets generated as a by-product" [18:20] of the running system or built by hand before an audit.

q: How do discovery, runtime monitoring and enforcement create a closed loop for AI accountability?
a: Higdon describes discovery as the map of what AI exists and what it connects to, while runtime monitoring shows what it is actually doing. He adds that "Enforcement, though, is what really closes the loop." [20:43], because it can stop risky behavior before the consequences compound.

the-ai-control-loop-whats-missing-in-ai-security-today-with-craig-thomas-of-wallarm

Security Must Move Past the Gate: Firewalls, IAM and segmentation control who gets in. With AI agents, the question becomes what they do next with legitimate access: whether they stay in scope and match business intent.

Late Remediation Can't Undo Harm: Restarting pods or rotating credentials can't unsend an email or reverse an agent's actions. Craig Thomas calls these stateless remediations applied to stateful harm.

Contain the Session, Not Everything: Revoke the token or freeze pending tool calls for one misbehaving agent, preserve its artifacts for forensics and leave other sessions running. Most teams don't have this capability yet.

Containment Can Widen Agent Permissions: Fast containment bounds the blast radius by detection latency, so CISOs can grant agents broader access instead of restricting them until they're barely useful.

Observe First, Then Enforce: Keep policy as code in version control, start in audit mode to learn baseline behavior, then move to blocking. Show developers what production would block, and why, before they deploy.

q: Why is detect-and-respond security not enough for AI agents?
a: Craig Thomas of Wallarm explains that traditional incident response assumes a human attacker moving at human speed, leaving time to detect, triage and contain. AI can act in seconds or less, and as he describes that older approach, "That mental model all assumes time. AI just doesn't" [02:40].

q: What can kernel-level runtime visibility see that network and application layers miss?
a: Craig says network and identity layers see who and where, while the application layer sees inputs and outputs but not intermediate behavior. Kernel-level visibility captures system "calls, the file IO, the process behavior, what the model is actually doing" [07:02].

q: How can you contain a compromised AI agent session without taking down the whole deployment?
a: Craig recommends revoking the session token or freezing pending tool calls, preserving artifacts for forensics and letting other sessions continue. In his words, "look at it like killing a single process without rebooting the whole server" [08:31].

q: What AI behaviors should runtime enforcement be able to stop?
a: Craig lists data movement to unapproved endpoints, executing prompt injections, tools exceeding their scope, query rate spikes and lateral movement between agents. On scope, he gave the example of an agent that is "supposed to have read access only, but now it's making write and delete calls" [12:52].

q: How do runtime controls change AI governance and accountability?
a: Craig says accountability gets tied to specific AI sessions and tool calls, with continuous logs that show whether policy was actually enforced. As he put it, "Governance becomes evidence-based rather than attestation-based." [16:39]

Detection Trails AI Speed: The detect-then-respond model was designed for human-speed incidents. Tim says data exfiltration that took hours now takes seconds, so by the time an alert is investigated, the data is already gone.

Static Policies Fall Short: AI agents pick tools, pass data and call services at runtime based on model outputs. That behavior can't be fully listed in a policy written before deployment, so controls must watch agents as they run.

Kernel-Level Enforcement: Working at the kernel needs no application patches, ties actions to specific sessions, users and traces, and can block a transaction while the pod keeps running and other sessions stay unaffected.

Separate Enforcement From Deployment: If policy changes require a release, teams avoid touching them. Push rules at runtime without restarts, and let teams see what would be blocked, and the blast radius, before turning enforcement on.

Accountability Means Proof: Auditors and regulators will ask whether a policy worked and how you can prove it. Evidence should trace sessions, users and tool calls with timestamps and outcomes, showing what was observed and what was stopped.

q: Why is detection alone not enough for AI security?
a: Tim Ebbers argues that the detect-then-respond model was built for human-speed incidents, while AI-driven attacks move far faster. As he put it, "detection tells you what happened, but it doesn't really change what happened." [02:09]

q: How is kernel-level enforcement different from network or application-layer controls?
a: According to Tim, enforcing at the kernel works without the application being patched or updated, and it can block a transaction while the pod keeps running. He also said "you can act on the identity that's visible at the workload" [05:38], including the specific session, user and trace.

q: What AI agent behaviors should organizations be able to stop immediately?
a: Tim points to unauthorized data access through tools, calls to external services outside the approved scope, and compliance boundary violations, along with prompt injection patterns and unusual tool sequences. He said "it's not 300 things that you have to think about. It's really a few categories" [08:04].

q: How can teams enforce AI security without slowing down development?
a: Tim recommends separating enforcement from deployment so teams can iterate on policies independently of application changes. In his words, "enforcement rules have to be pushed at runtime," [09:45] and he adds that teams adopt enforcement faster when they can first see what would have been blocked.

q: What will auditors and regulators ask about AI agent accountability?
a: Tim believes simply showing a log will no longer be enough, because it doesn't help you understand what the agent did. He said the question "isn't, did you have a policy? It's, did the policy work? And how can you prove it?" [10:44]

Rogue Isn't Always Malicious: Craig Thomas says the most common rogue AI cases are legitimate systems acting outside intended boundaries. He groups the risk into unsanctioned, unmonitored and unpredictable AI.
Drift Without a Deploy: Prompt injection through support tickets, scraped pages or user messages can redirect an agent. A hosted LLM update can also shift its behavior with no code change or review.

Judge the Whole Sequence: Reading a customer record, summarizing it and sending it to a third-party API may each pass checks, yet fail an audit together. Session tracing links every step into one record.

Know, See, Stop, Prove: Thomas says policy alone isn't oversight. Teams need runtime enforcement that can inspect, block or rate limit AI-generated API traffic, with humans placed at high-risk decision gates.
Make the Safe Path Fast: Offer a usable sandbox with no production data and logging enabled, plus an AI intake process that takes days. Slow official routes push people toward shadow AI.

q: What is rogue AI, and does it have to be malicious?
a: Craig Thomas of Wallarm says rogue AI often involves legitimate systems behaving outside their intended boundaries rather than attacks. As he put it, "rogue doesn't necessarily mean malicious" [02:54].

q: What are shadow LLMs and why are they risky?
a: Thomas describes shadow LLMs as endpoints or AI tools running without approval, often because the internal approval process takes too long, leaving no security review, data handling policy or logging. In his words, "I'd define shadow LLMs that they are the new shadow IT" [06:09].

q: How can authorized AI agent actions still create compliance risk?
a: Thomas explains that each action can be allowed on its own while the automated chain, run at scale without human review, creates a problem such as a GDPR concern. He warned that individual steps may pass, "but the sequence could fail the audit" [08:37].

q: Is an AI governance policy enough to control AI agents?
a: No. Thomas argues that real oversight requires runtime enforcement that can inspect, block or rate limit AI-generated API traffic in real time. As he said, "Policy document does not stop an agent mid-call" [15:08].

q: What is the difference between detecting AI risk and controlling it?
a: Thomas says detection tells you what happened, while control stops the action before the damage compounds, which matters when an agent can make thousands of API calls before anyone is alerted. In his words, "detection without prevention is just documentation of damage" [19:36].

See Data Flows, Not Just Logs: With non-deterministic AI, Tim Ebbers says security must see the models, endpoints, what models call, the data moving between them, and the downstream effects of each person's actions.

Identity Gets Murky Across Agents: Identity may change as a request passes through an AI gateway to an MCP server. Teams must ask whether the original requester should really get the data returned when another identity asks on their behalf.

Watch Shadow AI, Don't Block: Shadow AI usually starts with developers and business users chasing speed. Ebbers advises discovering it, setting policies and flagging deviations, since early blocking makes enemies of people trying to move faster.

Risk Lives on the Edges: The same agent carries very different risk with a read-only search API than with payment or email-send tools. Policies should define which tools an agent can use and send alerts when it tries others.

Move From Inventory to Enforcement: Many programs can list their AI, but few can act on it. Ebbers points to blocking unsanctioned models, cutting off misbehaving sessions, stopping PII leaving, proving it to auditors, and knowing who owns what.

q: How is AI discovery different from traditional API or cloud asset discovery?
a: Tim Ebbers says the fundamentals of inventory, ownership and continuous coverage still apply, but AI is behavioral, has fuzzy boundaries, treats data as part of the asset and changes in minutes. In his view, "The teams that do well will treat AI discovery as an extension" [10:43] of API and cloud discovery rather than a replacement.

q: Should companies try to prevent shadow AI?
a: Ebbers argues against leading with prevention, because it recreates the old shadow IT problem of blocking people who are trying to get work done. He said "it shouldn't be prevented because then you're going back to the" [06:37] shadow IT ways, and recommends discovering usage, adding policies and getting notified when agents stray from them.

q: Why do an AI agent's tools and connections change its risk level?
a: Ebbers explains that a read-only search API and a payments or email-send API create very different risks, even for the same agent. As he put it, "the same model becomes high risk as soon as you connect a tool to it" [08:13] that can act on a data source.

q: What does continuous AI discovery mean?
a: For Ebbers, it means always watching traffic for changes in applications and agents, including releases and new libraries that may have CVEs, instead of relying on quarterly scans or spreadsheets. He warns that if your discovery cadence "is slower than your deployment cadence, you're permanently behind." [13:04]

the-ai-control-loop-ai-security-is-api-security-with-tim-erlin-of-wallarm
APIs Underpin Every AI Interaction: Chat interfaces, AI embedded in apps, and agents calling tools or MCP servers all run on APIs. That is why Tim Erlin argues AI security starts with API security.

Internal APIs Are Exposed Too: Teams may rate internal APIs as lower risk than external ones, but when AI tools use them, there can be a route in from outside. Mapping those connections is where organizations fall short.

The Data Shows Overlap: Wallarm's ThreatStats counted 439 published AI vulnerabilities in 2024 and 2,185 in 2025. AI-API overlap fell from nearly 100% to 36%, yet overlapping flaws still grew from about 438 to 786.

Old Controls Still Apply: Agents need strong authentication, least privilege and zero trust as a principle. Erlin warns that rushing to adopt AI leads teams to make exceptions, and he expects breaches to follow.

Start With Inventory: Catalog AI tools and workloads, plus the MCP servers, APIs and data they use. Then understand their behavior and connections, move to blocking bad actions, and ultimately to governance and compliance.

q: Why is AI security considered API security?
a: Tim Erlin of Wallarm explains that users, applications and agents all reach models, tools and data through APIs, including MCP servers. In his words, "all of the AI interactions are underpinned by API interactions" [03:09].

q: Where do organizations underestimate API risk when adopting AI?
a: Erlin points to the internal tools and APIs that AI applications and agents connect to, which may be treated as lower risk than public ones. If AI tools use them, he said, "there is actually a route to them from an external standpoint" [04:14].

q: What does Wallarm's ThreatStats research say about AI and API vulnerabilities?
a: Erlin said published AI vulnerabilities rose from 439 in 2024 to 2,185 in 2025, while the share overlapping with APIs fell from nearly all to about 36%. The overlap still grew in raw numbers: "you've still got massive growth of 80% from 439 to 786" [08:29].

q: What API security assumptions break down with autonomous AI agents?
a: Erlin says many of the faulty assumptions involve authentication and authorization, and that teams are making exceptions to principles like least privilege. As he put it, "the assumption is often that if an agent can do something, it's allowed to do that" [06:04].

q: What is the first step to strengthen API security before expanding AI adoption?
a: Erlin advises inventorying AI tools and workloads, then extending that to the MCP servers, APIs and data sources they access. He said "the first practical step is inventory. It's discovery." [13:24].

s12-e21-why-your-health-app-is-drowning-in-wearable-noise-and-missing-real-insights-with-marco-benitez-co-founder-ceo-of-rook

Clients Shape the Roadmap: Marco pairs a data science vision with heavy client interviews on delivery, time zones and useful data. An early beta API had so many issues that complaints arrived by email at 3 a.m.

q: Why did ROOK pivot from building a wearable device to an API?

Ship in Small Pieces: Over three-plus years at Meta, mostly in ads logging and reliability, Daulet handled at least millions of logs daily. He learned to break problems into the smallest shippable pieces and test hypotheses fast.

Shared Memory Across Frameworks: At Cognee, Daulet decoupled the MCP layer so agents built on different frameworks, such as Google's Agent Development Kit and LangGraph, could work concurrently on one knowledge graph.

Distributed Systems Lens on Agents: Once memory moved beyond one local machine to shared, distributed compute, idempotency, retries, competing requests and shared state across processes became increasingly important.

Sandboxing as the Boundary: Daulet argues that, at least for now, sandboxing is the only safety boundary you can rely on for autonomous agents, despite prompts and other layers. That view guides his safety decisions at Bead AI.

Evals and the Production Gap: Daulet owns evals at Bead AI to measure performance and guard against regressions. The challenge is that each client's data has quirks, leaving a small gap between local evals and production.

q: Why is Bead AI applying autonomous agents to compliance audits?
a: Daulet Amirkhanov believes agentic systems are improving quickly and can match or beat humans in many more areas when used well. He argues that for audits, the wave of model progress has "already surpassed the capabilities necessary to solve this very efficiently" [14:11].

q: How can AI agents built on different frameworks share the same memory?
a: At Cognee, Daulet worked on decoupling the MCP architecture so separate agentic systems were no longer isolated from each other and could build on one knowledge graph. After that change, as Daulet put it, "you could mix and match all of them" [10:31].

q: Is sandboxing necessary for autonomous AI agents?
a: Daulet Amirkhanov says yes, pointing to supply chain attacks and the need to protect client data when things don't go as planned. In his words, "I firmly believe that at least right now, sandboxing is the only" [16:02] boundary for autonomous agents, though he allows this might change.

q: Why are evals important for agentic systems?
a: Daulet explains that evals measure a system's performance, safeguard it against regressions and act as a sanity check. He said "evals are the backbone of how you evaluate your system's performance" [17:59], while noting that replicating unique client data locally remains difficult.

q: What agent infrastructure might be needed in the next few years?
a: Daulet predicts a need to identify individual agents so that responsibility for their actions can be traced, with the European Union possibly leading the way. He envisions an "identity and capability registry for individual agents" [20:19].

Attack AI's Own Bottlenecks: Hexo's roadmap prioritizes problems that limit AI itself, especially energy and compute. Lab partners get help with frontier problems, and the work could unlock new, potentially monetizable IP.

Hiring Through Trial Projects: Beyond technical skill, Hexo looks for people who think big, take bets and have grit. Two or three-week projects help both sides judge mutual fit, which a couple of interviews often can't.

a: Kunal says the challenge is mainly on the backend, where even small experiments can use thousands of dollars of GPU expense, so Hexo is working with partners at hyperscalers to gather more capacity. In his words, "any kind of self-improving AI system needs a lot of compute" [10:02].

q: How does Hexo Labs hire AI researchers?

q: Can startups compete with big AI labs on superintelligence?
a: Kunal expects a few big labs to hold superintelligence and warns that agents could wipe out entire industries. He still sees room for a counter-narrative, which Hexo is pursuing: "But there is space for sovereign superintelligence" [16:46], provided you can afford that sovereignty.

s12-bonus-the-bearer-token-trap-why-api-secrets-are-leaking-and-the-rise-of-dynamic-zero-trust-machine-identity-providers-with-anusha-iyer-founder-ceo-of-corsha

q: What does Corsha do?
a: Corsha builds an industrial identity security platform that helps customers securely connect legacy systems and machines to modern AI and data tools. Anusha Iyer describes it as a platform that "is almost like focused on managing and securing connections for machines first over humans" [03:19].

q: How was Corsha's MVP built?
a: Anusha Iyer says it probably took about six months with four core engineers and herself, using containerization and Kubernetes. The team made a conscious choice "to be Kubernetes native, but cloud agnostic" [05:27] so the MVP could run on really any cloud.

q: Why did Corsha pivot to industrial cybersecurity?
a: An Air Force customer pushed the team to think beyond Kubernetes pods to physical equipment such as room-size robotic arms on manufacturing lines. Iyer recalls, "we realized that this was a pretty unserved space from a cybersecurity perspective" [09:26], and Corsha chose to go after it.

q: What makes securing industrial and manufacturing systems different?
a: According to Anusha Iyer, security cannot be considered on its own because these operational systems run real-time processes and production lines where downtime is expensive. She says it is "super important to prioritize availability and safety as much as it is to think about security" [12:05].

Draw Requests Are Pull Requests: Construction loans are largely reimbursed as work gets done. Built manages the compliance, proof and money flow as requests move from subcontractors to general contractors, developers and lenders.

Cracking Home Builder Finance: Thomas's first Built project handled huge revolving credit lines where updates to homes cascade into borrowing math. Design partners helped, and he recalls a 14-month scope shipping in about six months.

q: What is home builder finance and why is it so complex?

a: Thomas's innovation group explores ideas ahead of the rest of the organization, tries to get them to production within 30 days and shelves most of them. He describes the role this way: "my job is to run out in front, fall in the holes, step on the landmines" [13:40].

q: Why did Weekend Will start with only a Texas will?

Three Flavors of Agents: Offload agents take on repetitive busywork, elevate agents help people do what they already do better, and extend agents give them new capabilities. Brown says the real impact comes from the last two.

Enablement Is Only the Start: Brown puts AI tools like copilots at roughly 3-5% of the impact. Re-engineering workflows across humans, agents and robots brings about 30-40%, and becoming truly AI-first about 60%.

Reinvention Beats Reduction: If two rivals only automate to cut costs, they erase their differentiation and everybody loses. Brown urges leaders to use AI to amplify their people, grow impact and create new products and services.

Fix Data and Involve Employees: AI fails without clean, organized company data. It also fails when IT builds agents without frontline input; at one client, employees refused to use them and some quit.

Leaders Must Drop the Sage Role: AI is uncharted territory, so leaders need to admit they don't have all the answers, explore alongside their teams, and still set a bold vision with the courage to pursue it.

q: What are the three types of AI agents Steve Brown describes?
a: Steve Brown identifies offload agents that handle tasks you don't want to do, elevate agents that improve your performance, and extend agents that let you do things you couldn't before. q: What are the biggest AI rollout mistakes companies make?

q: Should companies use AI mainly to cut costs and headcount?

Clean First, Then Predict: Glasswall's CDR breaks a file down, removes malware and rebuilds it to specification. Foresight adds what cleansing alone doesn't: the likelihood that the original file was malicious.

Structure as the Signal: The research phase tested whether CDR's deep structural telemetry could separate malware from goodware. It found a statistical difference, though some features first chosen fell short of commercially viable results.

One File Type at a Time: Rather than detect malware in every format at once, the roadmap starts with a model for one type, such as PDF, then repeats the method, backed by testing on unseen threats and continuous drift monitoring.

q: What is Content Disarmament and Reconstruction (CDR)?
a: Dr. Aqib Rashid explains that CDR breaks a file into its components, removes any malware, validates it and rebuilds it to the manufacturer's specification. The result, he says, is "a deterministic guarantee that the file is safe to use regardless of where it came from" [04:57].

q: How does Glasswall use AI to predict whether a file is malicious?
a: Glasswall trains machine learning models on the structural telemetry CDR produces while analyzing and cleaning files, and the model returns the likelihood that a file contains malware. Rashid said the research showed that "There is a statistical difference between the CDR data that represents malware versus the CDR data" [09:03] that represents goodware.

q: Can AI malware detection keep working as threats evolve and models drift?
a: Rashid says Glasswall Foresight can predict zero-day threats and still perform months later as the threat landscape changes, while the team also monitors for drift. He credits the training data, saying that "because we have trained models on deep CDR structural telemetry," [20:52] the models are somewhat inoculated against that change.

q: How fast is Glasswall Foresight, and can it run offline?
a: Rashid says the product was designed for file verdicts in milliseconds and can be deployed in air-gapped environments or SaaS solutions. As he put it, "When you're doing this at scale, you need to have the efficiency of millisecond scale inference." [10:43]

q: What advice does Dr. Aqib Rashid give founders building AI products?
a: Rashid advises building something that deserves trust, getting early validation from prospects and customers, and avoiding problems an AI agent could soon solve. He warns that in cybersecurity "it's very easy to build an AI model that looks good on a benchmark." [27:32] Performing well in the real world under adversarial conditions is a very different problem.

Untangling the Monorepo: Community pull requests helped turn the codebase into a tech-debt-heavy "spaghetti monster." The team paused to factor the agent code into the Software Agent SDK, which the front end, CLI and integrations now consume.

Betting on Early Adopters: OpenHands does less to meet developers inside today's IDEs and CLIs and more to help early adopters chart cloud-based, multi-agent development. Brennan wants it to become the open source standard for running agents at scale.

q: What is OpenHands and why was it started?
a: OpenHands, originally called OpenDevin, is an open source platform for AI-driven development, started after Cognition's Devin demo in March 2024. Robert Brennan said the goal was "making sure that the community is able to guide this change" [03:54] to how software gets written.

q: How was the first version of OpenHands built?
a: Co-founder Graham Neubig first created a functionless front end with a chat window, terminal and file editor, which got the community contributing. Brennan then added an agent, recalling that he "wrote the first like agent, which was basically like a long prompt" [04:38] with a for loop around an LLM.

q: Why run AI coding agents in sandboxes instead of directly on a laptop?
a: Robert Brennan explains that sandboxed agents each have their own code, file system and terminal, so you can run many without them stepping on each other. They also protect your environment: "Because they have a sandbox, they're not going to delete all the files in your hard drive" [11:41].

q: What is the OpenHands Software Agent SDK?
a: It holds the agent code, including prompts, file system and terminal interaction, sandboxing, context window management and security analyzers, and developers and companies build their own experiences on it. Brennan said that "the SDK now contains basically everything you" [14:54] would need to build an agentic developer experience.

q: How does OpenHands interview engineers in the AI era?
a: Candidates build an application from scratch using whatever tools they want, leaning into front end, back end or DevOps strengths. Brennan said "we have folks record their screen for two to three hours and build an application" [09:36], which shows how they think, solve problems and use AI.

s12-bonus-the-predictive-model-trap-moving-beyond-static-ltv-forecasting-to-unleash-causal-ai-and-dynamic-multi-armed-bandits-with-tobias-tobi-konitzer-phd-vp-of-ai-at-growthloop

Upgrade What Customers Already Use: Rather than building an autonomous agent in a vacuum, GrowthLoop adds pieces of the vision to heavily used products like audiences and journeys, validating each with customer feedback.

Experimentation Comes First: An autonomous decisioning system needs a history of causal results to learn from. GrowthLoop forecasts efficient test splits, perhaps 10-90 instead of 50-50, and keeps measuring returns after winners are scaled.

Predictions Alone Don't Drive Growth: Tobi lost a company learning that accurate LTV predictions don't change outcomes by themselves. Judge AI by business impact, and how easily and early you can prove it.

q: What is GrowthLoop and what does its composable customer data platform do?
a: GrowthLoop unifies data on the customer's own data warehouse so marketers can build audiences and journeys without waiting on data engineers. As Tobi Konitzer explained, it "is what is called a composable customer data platform" [02:54].

q: Why isn't predicting customer lifetime value enough to grow revenue?
a: Tobi Konitzer found that a prediction describes the future under the status quo, while marketing is about changing what happens to customers. His lesson: "don't put too much stock into accuracy of machine learning" [27:02].

q: What is always-on measurement in marketing experimentation?
a: It is GrowthLoop's concept for continuing to measure ROI after a winning treatment has been rolled out to all traffic. Tobi Konitzer describes being able to measure "the returns of any experimental design that you ever did in the company" [13:10].

q: How should a company add AI to its product without building something nobody wants?
a: Tobi Konitzer recommends studying which parts of the product are actually used, then upgrading them one by one toward the larger vision. After a past venture built in a vacuum, he said, "I've really reworked the way that I'm thinking about tackling these big problems" [07:41].

q: Can LLMs and agentic AI take over marketing decisions without a human in the loop?
a: Tobi Konitzer is skeptical because LLMs can't give a truly quantitative explanation of a decision and may decide differently minutes later. Of that lack of replicability, he said, "I don't think that's what marketing wants" [31:43].

s12-e11-the-security-operations-center-hellscape-moving-beyond-broken-threat-feeds-to-empower-overworked-cyber-analysts-with-human-ai-collaboration-with-brian-carbaugh-co-founder-ceo-of-andesite

Compliance as Market Unlock: Targeting large, highly regulated enterprises, Andesite invested early in FedRAMP High, SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO. It cost money, time and engineering cycles, but has greatly helped the company scale.

Quiet for Too Long: Wary of overpromising in a noisy AI SOC market, Andesite invested heavily in product and engineering but under-invested in marketing. Brian owns that mistake and says the balance is now better.

q: What does Andesite do?
a: Brian Carbaugh describes Andesite as a data analytics company whose first product is an AI-driven cybersecurity product for Security Operations Centers. It keeps the analyst at the center, and as Brian put it, "we want to use technology, certainly not to replace the human, but to make the humans" [04:36].

q: What problem led Brian Carbaugh to start Andesite?
a: After retiring from CIA, Brian was asked by intelligence community colleagues to help with hard cyber problems, including how to 10x the impact of their workforce. q: How did Andesite approach building its MVP?
a: Brian said the team combined experienced cybersecurity practitioners with technologists and checked its own ideas against design partners, CISOs and cyber operators. His guidance was to "ask the question and have the humility to listen to the answer" [10:47].

q: Why did Andesite invest in FedRAMP High and SOC 2 compliance so early?
a: Andesite expected to serve large, well-resourced enterprise security teams, so it pursued what Brian calls "compliance high" from the beginning with support from its seed investors and board. Although it could slow the team down, Brian said, "we've looked at the compliance thing and said, this is a key market unlock for us" [19:53].

q: What mistake did Andesite make in the crowded AI SOC market?

Track the Deal Like Pizza: Reannah Wyatt saw that people could track pizzas and packages, but not what is typically their biggest purchase. Clients kept calling her about closing dates, next steps and documents.

q: What problem in real estate transactions does The Real Time solve?

q: What was Reannah Wyatt's $45,000 mistake?

s12-e10-the-childhood-smartphone-epidemic-re-engineering-android-os-to-stop-social-media-addiction-and-teach-kids-digital-wellness-with-dane-witbeck-founder-ceo-of-pinwheel

MDM Over an Android Fork: Dane spent four to six months forking open source Android, but lost compatibility with 25 to 30% of apps. Pinwheel switched to mobile device management layered on top of Android.

Solving the Problem Over Software-Only: Because MDM must be installed from the welcome screen, Pinwheel gave up a software-only model. It buys phones wholesale, configures them for kids, and sells each with a software subscription.

A Chaotic First Christmas: Pinwheel expected to sell 200 or 300 phones in 2020 and sold 1200, and things broke. Its AWS bill topped $10,000 until a new VP of engineering cleaned up, bringing it to about $800 by April.

From Allowlist to Blocklist: The curated app library grew from about 80 apps to roughly 1500. As kids aged up, Pinwheel let parents go to the Play Store for apps, blocking those it knows are inappropriate.
Dropping the Homegrown LLM: Pinwheel tried building its own LLM on teen text data to cut AI costs, but frontier models overtook it within 6 to 12 months. Dane's lesson: don't fall for sunk costs.

q: What is Pinwheel and how does its kids' phone work?
a: Pinwheel, founded by Dane Witbeck, buys Android phones wholesale, installs mobile device management software and kid-specific apps, and gives parents their own control app. Describing the model, Dane said they "see what's going on with the phone. And then sell that phone plus the software" [07:27].

q: Why didn't Pinwheel build its own version of Android?
a: Dane Witbeck first tried forking the open source Android project without Google's layers, but many apps depend on Google's proprietary software and would not work. In his words, "the real problem that we ran into was app compatibility" [05:43].

q: How does Pinwheel decide which apps are appropriate for kids?
a: Pinwheel built a team and process to vet apps for parents, looking at things like messaging with strangers and available parental controls. Dane explained, "we have a grading system for apps. And so it's this one's green, this one's" [16:20] yellow with some warnings, or red with real concerns.

q: How did Pinwheel's first product launch go?
a: The first product shipped for Christmas 2020 and far outsold expectations, which exposed scalability problems on Christmas morning. Dane recalled that "we ended up selling 1200 phones that first Christmas and everything" [09:01] broke, and dedicated customer service agents helped get customers working.

q: What is Pinwheel Home, the landline phone for kids?
a: Dane Witbeck described Pinwheel Home as a screen-free landline for kids that works over home internet, which the company was close to launching at the time of the interview. Calls among Pinwheel Home friends are free, other calling and 911 carry a $10 monthly subscription, and Dane said it sets a "hard boundary, which we're all about boundaries at Pinwheel, around a kid's tech use" [25:38].

s12-bonus-the-social-curation-revolution-moving-beyond-messy-bookmarks-to-build-an-intuitive-shareable-stacking-ecosystem-with-martina-zrnec-co-founder-cto-of-stacklist

From Bookmarks to Business Hub: Stacklist began as a way to save anything from anywhere and has become a branded content hub for businesses. A real estate agent can send a client one stack with homes, neighborhoods, restaurants, playgrounds and school district details.

B2B Now Drives the Roadmap: Early features like social profiles and a card redesign came from what the founders wanted to build. After moving to B2B, requirements from paying customers and agencies feed into the roadmap.

Mobile Couldn't Keep Pace: Web and backend features shipped faster than the mobile developer could follow, leaving the app always behind. Though people loved it, Martina would now hold off until the product was more stable and changing more slowly.

Try People Project by Project: Stacklist gave people project-based chances before any long-term commitment. After investment fell short of expectations, the team shrank to three, and it's hiring again after landing a 500K investment.

q: What is Stacklist?

q: Where did the idea for Stacklist come from?

Memory-First Inference Bet: Positron's founders saw in 2023 that memory use in inference would outstrip compute. The company targets memory-bound work such as video generation, code generation and reasoning models.
DRAM Instead of HBM: Mitesh says Positron will have about 2.3 TB of memory per chip versus 384 GB on NVIDIA's Rubin, at roughly one-fourth the cost, while giving up some memory bandwidth.

Fast Silicon Cadence: Positron shipped its first product within 20 months of founding and planned the next 18 to 20 months later, using customer feedback from deployments to shape the second generation.

Capital and People Efficiency: Fewer than 20 people built the first product. Mitesh says Positron has raised over $310 million, spent only $40 million and driven tens of millions in profitable revenue.

Aim Bigger on Deals: Mitesh says early caution on deal size and structure was a mistake. Even with $12 million raised and 10 people, he now believes they should have pursued huge orders and solved scale afterward.

q: What does Positron AI do?
a: Positron is a fabless semiconductor company that designs chips for AI inference, especially memory-bound workloads like video generation, code generation and reasoning models. Mitesh Agrawal explains that "what we are really focused on is performance per dollar and performance per watt." [05:47]

q: How is Positron's chip architecture different from NVIDIA's?
a: Positron has innovated on both on-chip memory and attached memory, favoring far more capacity over peak bandwidth. Mitesh says of the memory they "connect to our silicon, we're not using HBM, we're using DRAM, which has its both challenges," [07:51] and that architectural innovations address challenges such as its lack of speed.

q: How can a chip startup compete with NVIDIA?
a: Mitesh points to focus, finding a niche and growing revenue step by step rather than trying to become NVIDIA overnight. He argues that AI demand outstrips the supply of compute, chips and energy, so with a good "product, you will find demand curve for it because there's just so much requirement." [18:20]

q: Why does Positron prioritize launching silicon products quickly?
a: Frequent launches let the team learn from customer deployments and feed those lessons into the next generation. [14:39] He also acknowledges that this is not the only approach that can work.

q: What mistake did Mitesh Agrawal make in Positron's early days?

s12-bonus-why-spray-and-pray-job-applications-are-quietly-destroying-your-tech-career-momentum-with-ashwin-agrawal-founder-ceo-of-mobiusengine

Founded Hours After a Layoff: Laid off from Google by a 2am email in 2023, Ashwin Agrawal founded his company at 4:30am. He had decided after an earlier layoff that next time he would build a solution instead of just finding another job.

Humans First, a Little AI: Expecting the tech stack to shift with a disruptive new technology, Ashwin built the MVP mainly on human agentic workflows plus a bit of AI, starting with tasks like job applications and resumes.

Two Rules Instead of a Roadmap: Bootstrapping, Ashwin skipped a formal roadmap. He built only what customers wanted and would pay for, and aimed to be cash positive and profitable from the very first client.

Let Growth Expose the Cracks: Mobius pushed acquisition, then fixed what broke: building more tech to rely less on people, adding countries after a Philippines typhoon, and replacing third-party SaaS with homegrown systems.

Beware Long Vendor Contracts: A platform with good ROI led to a two-year contract. Two months later, policy changes sent returns plummeting. Ashwin now says paying a small premium beats a costly long-term tie-up.

q: What is MobiusEngine and who is it for?
a: MobiusEngine, founded by Ashwin Agrawal, aims to help people move from one job to another, whether they are unemployed or frustrated and stuck in a current role. As Ashwin put it, "Mobius is really a solution to making the transition" [02:57].

q: How was the first MobiusEngine MVP built?
a: Ashwin combined people and AI to handle basic job transition tasks, such as job applications and resumes, better than individuals could on their own. He chose to lean on human "agentic workflows and combine that with a little bit of AI to form an MVP" [06:09].

q: How can a bootstrapped startup decide what to build next?
a: Ashwin says he didn't really build a roadmap, and instead set two constraints: follow customer demand and stay cash positive from the first client. In his words, "I'm going to build what clients and customers are willing to pay for and they want" [07:27].

q: How did MobiusEngine handle scaling problems?
a: Ashwin let growth reveal weak points in operations and delivery, then stepped back to find longer-term fixes, including diversifying to more countries and building internal tools. He explained that "instead of relying on third party SaaS systems, both for cost reasons, but also for scalability, I've built my own homegrown systems" [12:12].

q: What is Ashwin Agrawal's advice for early-stage founders?
a: Ashwin advises founders to obsess over the customer's problem and to test early whether someone will actually pay. Of a first payment, he said that "even if it's a dollar, it's a huge milestone" [23:33].

Growth Exposed the Platform Gap: A team grew from about 10-15 to 80-90 people in half a year. Without cross-team standards, local development and service integration broke down, and internal testing showed the product couldn't handle the load.

Public APIs Are Contracts: Moving from B2C to B2B, the hardest part wasn't scaling infrastructure. It was backward compatibility, versioning, rate limits and careful naming of endpoints, parameters and errors.
Be Your Own API Client: Building an internal invoicing tool on the new public API surfaced design issues during prototyping, before real clients arrived, while also streamlining an internal workflow.

Open Source Raises the Bar: Piekhota says developers on his team put more care into a component once they know it will be open sourced, because the work becomes public and may become part of their resume.

Maturity Means Wise Trade-Offs: A mature system first makes money and covers customer use cases. Beyond that, it needs a responsible team and an architecture simple and flexible enough to follow business changes.

q: When does an engineering organization need a platform approach?
a: Oleksandr Piekhota saw the need after rapid hiring and a lack of cross-team standards made releases and integration very difficult at a previous company. As he described it, "local development is terrible. It's nearly impossible to run like the whole environment." [05:19]

q: What is the hardest part of moving from a B2C product to a B2B public API?
a: For Piekhota, the challenge in PDFfiller's shift was not mainly infrastructure scale. He said "it was more about contracts and formalizing interface, which you develop." [07:25] Backward compatibility, versioning strategy, rate limiting and endpoint design became much more important.

q: Why is it hard to decide when to stop an R&D experiment?
a: Piekhota warns that after weeks of research, proofs of concept and presentations, engineers are inclined to sell the tool they invested in. In his experience, "when you're trying to do some R&D work, it becomes very emotional." [12:28] Feedback from teammates and a skilled manager can redirect the work or slow it down.

q: How do you recognize a mature engineering system?
a: Piekhota starts with business value rather than code quality or tooling, saying "a mature system is like the system that makes basically money and where customers have their" [20:31] use cases covered. He also stresses balance, with a team that makes wise trade-offs and keeps the architecture simple but flexible.

q: How could AI change software architecture and engineering practices?
a: Piekhota expects that if codebases become largely AI generated, code elegance will matter less and the "shift is going to be is to focus more on tests and contracts." [24:24] He points to stronger CI/CD checks, canary deployments and rollback strategies, and suggests monoliths may regain popularity because agents work better with a single codebase.

s12-e8-h1b-paperwork-nightmare-why-hr-teams-stumble-on-visas-and-how-digital-first-frameworks-shift-ownership-back-with-satya-mishra-co-founder-cto-of-waylit

Scaling Complexity, Not Traffic: Satya says new immigration workflows for any country can be up in two days, and that WayLit does an H-1B in about two weeks versus the two months friends report.

LLMs With Human Review: WayLit plans to use LLMs for quick assessments that surface issues for its team, not to answer customers directly, because it doesn't yet trust them to be right.

q: How was the first version of WayLit built?
a: Satya Mishra and his co-founder Raj started by running the process manually with local St. Louis companies and a partner attorney who worked on paper. Once they understood how everything worked, Satya said they took that process "and built it into a workflow in Django." [06:17]

q: How does WayLit handle new types of immigration cases?
a: WayLit started with just one or two kinds of cases in the U.S. and designed its platform to take on more complexity with a very small team. Satya said "we built a platform flexible enough that we could, in two days, we could put up a new workflow" [11:10] for a new immigration process.

q: How is WayLit using AI and LLMs in immigration services?
a: Satya Mishra sees new opportunities for LLMs to make quick assessments that help the WayLit team review an employee's situation faster and more accurately. The output is not necessarily meant for customers, "because we still don't trust them to give the right answer." [14:47]

q: What advice does Satya Mishra give new entrepreneurs?

a: Max Denevich says the company cut what wasn't working, protected what was, and moved from direct sales to a partner-led model. The team stopped asking how to raise more money "and started asking how do we build something that doesn't need it" [17:42].

q: How do you sell B2B software to enterprise restaurant chains?
a: Max Denevich explains that many stakeholders have a say and buyers are approached by many vendors, so LoyaltyPlant relies on trusted technology partners and consultative selling. As he puts it, "You win by being already trusted" [24:20].

Trust Over Speed and Revenue: Dosy held back on rapid expansion, some automation and early monetization. That slowed short-term cash flow but built a committed community of users and instructors, which made scaling easier.

Users Wrote the Roadmap: Women who trusted Dosy for training asked for maintenance, self-defense, scooter access and jobs. Those requests shaped the next phase, backed by EV, maintenance and logistics partners.

Education Alone Wasn't Enough: Dosy underestimated fear, social pressure and safety concerns as barriers to adoption. The team responded by adding layers of reassurance, community support and trust building.

q: What is Dosy and what services does it offer?
a: Dosy is a women-only scooter ride-hailing platform in Egypt that also offers riding training, job opportunities, maintenance, self-defense and e-commerce services. Founder Nouran Farouk describes it as "the first women-only scooter ride-hailing platform in Egypt" [02:48].

q: What problem led Nouran Farouk to start Dosy?

the-gene-simmons-of-data-protection-ai-inference-time-guardrails

Assume the Agent Gets Jailbroken: Ave applies zero trust to agents: at scale, a bad actor will show up. Design around the worst a hijacked agent could do, such as reading sensitive data and sending it to a hacker.

Internal Agents Carry Higher Risk: Internal-facing agents usually get higher permissions and more sensitive data, and many large companies now expect bad actors among employees. Ave says their security matters more than for customer-facing agents.

Control What Agents Pass On: Role-based access still helps, but agents talking to agents can move data, like company payroll, to someone who shouldn't see it. Guardrails must restrict what an agent tells users and other agents.

Guardrails Are Breakable and Probabilistic: A smaller guard model can miss ciphers produced by a larger one, such as messages hidden in a poem. It might also catch 100 PHI strings and miss the 101st, a problem for compliance.

Prototype First, Then Secure Early: Build a non-production POC for maximum utility, then move it into a secure design with trusted and untrusted models plus guardrails. Ave says users usually value good results over speed.

q: What are inference-time threats in AI security?
a: Ave Gatton describes them as attacks on a model or agent while it is working, where someone gets it to take malicious actions or leak sensitive data. If an attacker jailbreaks an agent, Ave warns, "they can direct that agent to exfiltrate that data" [03:24].

q: Why is traditional security not enough for AI agents?
a: Ave says tools like role-based access control still apply, but they don't cover information passing between agents with different permissions. The challenge is not so much limiting initial access, "but it's restricting what that agent can then tell the users" [13:40] and other agents.

q: Why can AI guardrails be bypassed?
a: Guardrails typically use a smaller model to police a larger one, and Ave explains that "the smaller model by its very nature has less cognitive capabilities" [17:35]. An attacker can have the larger model hide data in ciphers or poems that the guard fails to recognize, and guardrails are also probabilistic.

q: What are secure-by-design architectures for AI agents?
a: Ave says "those boil down to having a trusted model and an untrusted model" [20:11], where the untrusted model handles sensitive data and its answers are constrained so a jailbreak can't filter back to the trusted one. Ave points to Google's CaMeL paper and notes it remains to be discovered whether these designs keep the full utility of agents.

q: Does adding security to AI agents hurt performance?
a: Ave believes the added security layers often don't affect performance much, and that latency is rarely the main complaint. In Ave's experience, people building with agents would say "they want a slow good result versus a fast bad result" [24:28].

From Drones to Cameras: Marc began by building warehouse drones for inventory checks. A drone-run injury and the realization that this was only a small part of the problem led OneTrack to a broader computer vision system capturing floor activity.

q: What does OneTrack do?
a: OneTrack uses cameras and sensors to capture what actually happens in warehouses and factories, then layers an agentic AI platform on top to automate work. Marc Gyöngyösi says that over the last 12 months it has been exciting that they "actually have the data you need to automate the physical world with agents." [06:14]

q: Why did OneTrack move away from warehouse drones?

q: How does OneTrack approach building MVPs?
a: Marc Gyöngyösi says there was no single MVP, pointing to an early drone demo in an unheated Evanston warehouse, a multi-sensor forklift system and a first chat box for agents. He explained, "I think we really take the mindset of stack a lot of small wins and move really fast." [07:29]

impact-how-to-inspire-align-and-amplify-innovative-teams-with-keith-lucas

Culture Is What You Do: A leader who holds long meetings, bottlenecks decisions and stalls on hiring or firing undercuts any "move fast" value. Stating the value anyway breeds inauthenticity, politics and low transparency.

Structure Serves the Mission: Keith sets where the team needs to be, backs out what it takes to get there, then organizes people around that. Quarters, funding rounds, pivots and scaling are natural moments to reorganize.

The Cost of Okay Contributors: People who meet every standard but excel at nothing and don't improve can be coached without short-term pain. Retaining many of them lowers belief that the team can succeed.

Hire With a Vision Document: Keith defines a role's long-term vision, near-term mission, values, scope, milestones, constraints and needed expertise. It guides the job description and interviews and helps new hires take ownership.

Don't Let Salary Bands Rule: A "can't lose" employee had gone over two years without a raise after maxing out her band. The company ultimately made an exception, which Keith says compensation plans must allow to serve the team and mission.

q: How can a startup leader create urgency without burning out the team?
a: Keith Lucas ties urgency to a purpose people believe in and an audience they can identify with, rather than a bare mandate to work hard. In his words, "The right kind of purpose drives urgency when it moves everyone from thinking about something that can be done to something that should be done." [04:26]

q: What is the cascade framework in Keith Lucas's book Impact?
a: The cascade is Keith's framework for what an entrepreneurial team should align to: "It is vision, mission, values, strategy, goals, and metrics." [11:05] He treats vision, mission and values as core alignment, and strategy, goals and metrics as hypothesis-based execution alignment that gets disrupted more often.

q: What is a mission athlete?
a: Keith describes it this way: "a mission athlete is my model for the type of person entrepreneurial teams need most." [20:23] These people are fueled by mission, operate by shared values, seek continuous growth and inspire and elevate their peers.

q: What is coaching out and how does the green, yellow, orange, red continuum work?
a: Keith says coaching out is not a euphemism for firing, because "it's really about coaching an individual" [26:44] toward higher performance, a turnaround or an exit. Green is the default of performing and being coached higher, yellow means disrupting the team, orange means a turnaround is possible but unlikely and the person's job is on the line, and red is exit.

q: Why does Keith Lucas oppose performance improvement plans (PIPs)?
a: Keith argues that PIPs tend to shift ownership to the manager and paint people into corners on the outcome. "I believe strongly that the person with the performance issue must drive their own turnaround." [32:13] Instead, he recommends a clear, concrete picture of the gap, its link to the mission, and offering help while the person owns the fix.

A Demo Became the Business: Krisp planned to license its noise cancellation to big companies and built a desktop app to demo it. Arto estimates the app now brings in about 80% of revenue, with licensing at 20%.

One Button, No Noise: For three years, Krisp built its go-to-market around noise cancellation alone, working to keep it stable across about 500 conferencing and calling apps and thousands of microphones and headphones.

q: How does Krisp remove background noise across different calling apps?
a: Arto explained that the desktop app, first built for Mac, was designed as a virtual microphone that audio passes through. There, Krisp can "basically modify the audio stream" [06:36] and get rid of the noise.

q: Why did Krisp run its voice AI on-device?

a: Dmytro's team goes beyond technical expertise and looks for evidence that someone has repeatedly been in the top 20%. The aim is to learn whether high "performance is something like a repeatable pattern, not just one-off results." [09:50]

q: Should startups outsource engineering or build their own team?
a: Dmytro recommends against outsourcing providers because he sees it as leasing a resource. He argues that "the earlier they look into long-term hiring and building their own engineering teams" [15:51], the better their chances of success.

s12-bonus-dismantling-legacy-hr-silos-to-automate-onboarding-scheduling-and-compliance-for-the-deskless-economy-with-arjun-vora-tito-goldstein-co-founders-of-teambridge

Borrowing Uber's Driver Experience: Drivers told the founders they chose Uber despite lower pay, largely for its self-service mobile app and flexibility. Teambridge set out to bring that to other hourly employers.

Value Beyond the Schedule: Teambridge began with a scheduler, then found the bigger pain in exceptions like late workers and missed clock-ins. Tito said handling them could consume 40 hours of a manager's week.

Lego Blocks Over Bespoke Features: Early customers ranged from a baseball maker to a Burger King franchise and nurse staffing. Unable to build custom features for each, the founders built composable blocks, turning the product into a platform.

Platform Jargon Missed the Mark: Pitching composability, automation and AI risked scaring off blue-collar buyers. The founders learned to go deep in an industry, speak its language and sell value against real problems.

Reliability Is Mission Critical: Customers run their operations on Teambridge, such as stadium staff getting tasks on game day. Downtime can stop the business, so the team invests heavily in keeping its automation engine and core platform up.

q: What inspired the creation of Teambridge?
a: Arjun Vora and Tito Goldstein saw at Uber how much drivers valued flexibility, control and a self-service app. Arjun said the technology was what they "wanted to build for any other business that has an hourly workforce" [04:58].

q: What was the first version of Teambridge?
a: The MVP was a scheduling product, shaped by visits to cafes, restaurants and movie theaters around Emeryville and San Francisco. Customer conversations changed its direction, and as Tito put it, "we started realizing that scheduling was a solved problem" [06:08].

q: How did Teambridge become a platform instead of just a scheduling tool?
a: Its first customers came from very different businesses, each with its own way of managing workers, so the founders built reusable building blocks. Arjun said casting a wide net early on "actually helped evolve the product to become more of a platform" [10:57].

q: Why do reliability and scalability matter so much for Teambridge?
a: Customers depend on the software to run their businesses, and workers rely on it for their livelihoods and pay. Tito explained, "We are the operating system by which most of our companies and our customers manage their entire business" [16:54].

q: What go-to-market mistake did the Teambridge founders make?
a: Arjun said they leaned on a tech-heavy story about their platform and features instead of focusing on customers' problems. In his words, "we completely missed the mark because if you are not talking about their problems" [26:11] and not speaking their language, you will scare them off.

c4f9bb8f-8a81-4995-abdd-2ca5a510ac43
s12-e3-overhauling-enterprise-deal-making-via-real-time-dynamic-deal-rooms-and-autonomous-investor-analytics-with-arsham-ghahramani-founder-ceo-of-ribbon

Interviews As the Signal: With AI-generated resumes flooding applications, recruiters told Arsham and co-founder Dave they were relying on interviews to filter people. That led them from a more efficient scheduling idea to building an AI interviewer.
Off-the-Shelf Voice Fell Short: The ElevenLabs-based MVP was demoable, but latency made conversations feel like turn-taking, and in about one in 20 interviews the AI would scream.

Choosing What to Build: Around eight AI models run in real time during an interview. Ribbon weighed build versus buy for each, chose three pieces it had to build in-house, and spent roughly nine months on those models.

Lean, Hands-On Senior Team: Ribbon has 10 people and does around a million interviews a year. It hires fairly senior, agentic people who still ship, have seen scale, and have the product sense to make many small decisions on their own.

Ship Sooner for Data: The team spent too long perfecting a feature that suggests next-round interview questions. Arsham's lesson is to release the simplest version, even a faked one, to learn how people react.

q: What is Ribbon's AI interviewer?
a: Ribbon is a voice AI that asks candidates complex questions, then helps recruitment teams score and analyze the interview. Arsham Ghahramani, its founder and CEO, says "it can interview people essentially in place of an initial screening interview" [02:43].

q: Why did Ribbon build its own voice AI technology instead of relying on off-the-shelf models?
a: Ribbon's early MVP used ElevenLabs, but latency was too high and the AI occasionally screamed during interviews. Arsham worried about deploying that to large customers, noting that "there's like screaming that will get in the news that's going to get us in trouble" [09:26].

q: How does an AI interview with Ribbon work behind the scenes?
a: Arsham explains that "there's around eight, eight different AI models that are all running in real time" [12:02]. These include speech-to-text, text-to-speech, a compliance engine that guards against off-limits statements, and a model that predicts when a speaker has finished a sentence.

q: How can an AI interviewer help job candidates who get ghosted?
a: Arsham says Ribbon gives candidates automatic feedback after every interview, without waiting for the recruiter. In his words, "We will give automatic feedback on this is how much of a match we think you are." [18:48]

q: What product lesson did Arsham Ghahramani learn while building Ribbon?
a: Arsham says the common theme in Ribbon's product mistakes has been taking too long to ship and get initial data. When it's unclear whether a feature will work, he advises that "the best thing honestly is just to get it out there" [20:46].

s12-bonus-overcoming-broken-right-sizing-models-to-automate-real-time-non-disruptive-cloud-cost-optimization-with-sharad-kumar-harshit-omar-co-founders-of-fluidcloud
Four Months Lost to AI: FluidCloud first tried using AI and its own models to generate Terraform for one-click migration. It never reached 100% accuracy without human intervention.

The In-House Mapping Breakthrough: The team built the cross-cloud mapping it had been avoiding. Harshit roughly put AWS configurations at 3 to 4 billion combinations, with similar amounts for Azure and GCP.
An MVP Without Shortcuts: The MVP shipped with dev, stage and prod environments, automated deployments, a custom QA framework and unit tests, and was performance benchmarked with 35 million records.

VMware Pricing as Tailwind: Sharad sees VMware customers facing steep price increases as a key opening, with FluidCloud offering a much cheaper route than a consulting project he pegged at $5 million.

Plan Distribution While Building: Sharad expected 200 leads on day one and learned selling is painful. His advice is to set a clear distribution strategy in parallel with the product, possibly splitting the two between co-founders.

q: What problem does FluidCloud solve?
a: FluidCloud targets cloud lock-in, aiming to let companies move infrastructure between cloud providers at the click of a button. Sharad Kumar explained that "People are still locked up into their cloud providers," [03:04] even as innovation around them accelerates.

q: Can AI generate accurate Terraform for cloud migration?
a: Not well enough for FluidCloud's goal of migration with no human intervention, based on the team's early experience. Harshit Omar said they spent four months on it, but "AI was never able to come up with a 100% accurate Terraform" [07:25].

q: How did FluidCloud build one-click cloud migration?
a: After the AI approach fell short, the team took on the huge upfront effort of mapping configurations across clouds. Harshit Omar said they built "on that mapping ourselves in-house." [08:34], and he later noted the company has a couple of patents on this core mapping engine.

q: How does the Broadcom acquisition of VMware affect FluidCloud?
a: Sharad Kumar described the resulting price rise as a tailwind, since affected customers are on a timeline to move to alternatives or go cloud native. By his approximate figure, "VMware has given almost 1000%" [19:42] in price increases.

q: What advice do FluidCloud's founders have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Sharad Kumar advises preparing for a painful marathon, picking a significant problem and not chasing hype waves such as rebranding around AI. He also urged that a solution be original and that "it should work, build for scale, don't build to flip" [34:22].

s12-bonus-decoupling-compute-and-storage-to-solve-the-petabyte-scale-log-cost-crisis-and-power-real-time-ai-sre-engines-with-david-sztykman-chief-architect-vp-of-product-at-hydrolix

Keep All the Data: Hydrolix rejects the idea that 90% of data is garbage. It indexes and compresses data, stores it in object storage with compute decoupled, and focuses on real-time streaming ingest with fast retrieval.

Leaving AWS-Only Services Behind: The first version relied on AWS services like EC2 and Kinesis. When Paramount wanted GCP for the Super Bowl, the team moved to its own Kubernetes operator, which David estimates was about a year of work.

Pre-Aggregate Data at Ingest: Query performance degraded at millions of logs per second, so Hydrolix built summary tables for Paramount. They aggregate data as it flows in, so dashboards query far fewer data points.

Stateful Buffering Broke at Scale: During the first Super Bowl, adding capacity to a stateful ingest component forced rebalancing and lost data. The team replaced it with stateless buffering and retries, using S3 as a queuing mechanism.

Autoscaling Beyond CPU and Memory: Standard Kubernetes autoscaling on CPU and memory wasn't enough for Hydrolix. The team built a custom autoscaler that can scale components on other metrics, such as incoming messages.

q: How does Hydrolix reduce the cost of keeping large volumes of log data?
a: David Sztykman explains that Hydrolix indexes and compresses data heavily, then keeps it in object storage while still retrieving it quickly. In his words, "we decouple completely storage from compute" [03:57].

q: Why was scaling Elasticsearch a problem for real-time log analytics?
a: While building a real-time video streaming data pipeline at Akamai, David found that more data meant adding nodes and rebalancing shards, which slowed things down when the data was needed most. He said "scaling elasticsearch was really hard" [05:46].

q: What went wrong for Hydrolix during its first Super Bowl?
a: A stateful component used to buffer incoming messages needed more capacity, and rebalancing it caused lost time and dropped data. As David put it, "for the Super Bowl, this component completely killed us" [17:38].

q: What are Hydrolix summary tables and why were they built?
a: David says they were a key feature for Paramount, whose dashboards needed aggregated views and saw query performance degrade at millions of logs per second. He described "the summary table, which allows us to pre-aggregate data as the data is flowing into the platform" [12:46].

q: How much log data has Hydrolix handled during a live event?
a: David says Hydrolix handled a terabyte a minute for Fox during the Super Bowl, with real-time queries and visibility into the edge. "We literally took a terabyte a minute of log" [20:12], he said, calling it probably the company's proudest day.

s12-e2-why-pure-ai-automation-fails-enterprise-procurement-and-how-customer-assurance-unlocks-hidden-deal-velocity-with-pukar-hamal-founder-ceo-of-securitypal-ai

Concierge MVP Before Software: The first version was Pukar behind an email address, using Airtable, Google Apps Script and Sheets. Customers sent questionnaires of 300 questions and got them back the next day.

Customers Wanted the Work Done: Pukar found customers didn't really want a tool that made forms easier to fill out; they wanted completed documents. They also asked for Uber-like status tracking, clear quality checks and predictability.
