From Services to AI Company: Bootstrapped on his savings, Pukar put revenue first and hired people to run the internal tools. The business started out more as a services operation and evolved into an AI technology company with a full engineering team.

Scaling Without Ballooning Costs: Venture-backed but not raising more, SecurityPal must run on its cash flows. The team is breaking work into steps, using AI and reorganizing to serve 3x to 10x more customers over 12 to 18 months.

Beyond Security Questionnaires: Pukar sees a "global assurance super cycle" driven by data laws. The roadmap aims at an assurance management platform spanning vendor assessments, trust center management, audits and new regulations.

q: What problem led Pukar Hamal to start SecurityPal AI?
a: At his previous company, a 200-page security due diligence questionnaire stalled a large enterprise deal just before signature. He later tested the idea by offering to answer questionnaires for a friend's company, saying "I basically told them, hey, listen, just hire me as a contractor." [04:33]

q: How was the first version of SecurityPal built?
a: Pukar handled requests himself behind an email address, using Airtable, Google Apps Script and Google Sheets to manage and route the work. To customers it felt like automation, and as Pukar described the experience, "I wake up the next day and it comes back" [08:26].

q: What did SecurityPal learn customers actually wanted from security questionnaire help?
a: Pukar found that many customers might have asked for a tool, when their real goal was to have the work finished. As he put it, "But really what customers wanted was they just wanted the documents" [10:33] done, and they also wanted visibility into progress and quality.

q: Why did SecurityPal build a team in Kathmandu, Nepal?
a: Pukar, who is originally from Kathmandu, saw top cybersecurity and consulting talent there that wasn't well known, noting "there's just a tremendous amount of hidden talent nestled amongst the Himalayas there." [05:36] The company has almost 200 people there, and Pukar champions the region as "Silicon Peaks."

q: Why does Pukar Hamal think demand for security assurance is growing?
a: Pukar argues that countries are creating data protection and privacy laws to reassert control over companies, which adds compliance and vendor assessment requirements to deals. In his words, "There are more speed bumps and points of friction during the commercial transaction today than ever before." [20:50]

s12-bonus-why-your-favorite-luxury-hotel-is-quietly-replacing-front-desk-forms-with-ai-agents-with-harman-singh-narula-co-founder-ceo-of-canary-technologies
Earn the Right First: Canary didn't ask hotels to swap out core platforms. It began with one specific workflow to prove it could solve hoteliers' problems before expanding.

Paper Form as MVP: The first product digitized the credit card authorization form, a PDF or paper that hotels likely send for non-standard bookings such as events. Narula says Canary is still one of the largest, or the largest, in that space.

Customers Lead the Roadmap: Hoteliers' needs are the biggest driver of what Canary builds, overlaid with its view of where the market is heading. Narula describes the growth pattern as "solution, scale, expand."
Hiring for Curiosity: Narula says Canary can teach hospitality and domain skills but can't teach someone to care. It looks for curiosity, a pursuit of excellence and high-agency entrepreneurial DNA.

Build Company Infrastructure Earlier: Narula says Canary was probably late building out finance and was late on recruiting, leaving it reliant on third parties. It is still catching up on some of that investment.

q: What does Canary Technologies do?
a: Canary provides hotel technology covering digital guest touchpoints, including messaging, purchases, digital tipping, AI voice and AI messaging. Harman Singh Narula says that "we basically are helping hoteliers provide better guest experience while generating more revenue" [03:34], and that the company works with more than 20,000 hotels in more than 100 countries.

q: What was Canary Technologies' first product?
a: The MVP was digital authorizations, which replaced the credit card authorization form that guests filled out and sent back to the hotel. Narula explained that "it literally digitized a piece of paper that's called a credit card authorization" [06:50].

q: How does Canary decide what to build next?
a: Canary spends a lot of time asking hoteliers about their needs and problems, then overlays its own vision of where the market is moving. Narula said of that customer input, "that tends to be the biggest driver of our roadmap" [08:58].

q: How is Canary approaching AI for hotels?
a: Canary is investing heavily in AI built specifically for hospitality, including an AI voice platform, an omni-channel communication platform and other native AI solutions. Narula said the company believes "that vertical players will be the drivers of vertical specific AI platforms" [16:38].

q: What mistake did Canary's founders make while scaling?
a: Narula said they were probably late to build out the finance function and were late on recruiting, so they had to rely on third parties. The thing he would change is that they didn't "invest in some of the like company infrastructure as early as we should have" [14:49].

s12-bonus-the-death-of-the-black-box-pos-solving-the-menu-api-nightmare-and-scaling-unified-commerce-across-2000-locations-with-niko-papademetriou-co-founder-evp-of-qu

Beyond the Countertop Box: Qu is a unified commerce platform for enterprise fast casual and quick service chains, built to handle orders from phone, web, mobile apps, kiosks, DoorDash and whatever channel comes next.

The MVP Isn't the Hardest Part: An early version took weeks to ring up items and tax. The later restack took 18 months, including rollout to early restaurants, and migrating existing customers took a couple of years.

Don't Become a Dev Shop: Even with a narrow focus, Qu faces a backlog of a thousand requests. The team filters them against broader market needs instead of letting the next exciting customer dictate the roadmap.

Edge-First for Uptime: Qu brings key AWS cloud services into the restaurant on edge nodes. Niko says customers could still open, take and close transactions inside their restaurants during recent major cloud outages.

Own the Contract Mistake: Niko left key protective language out of a huge contract and raised it late in negotiations. It added weeks, but both sides aligned, signed and still have a great relationship.

q: What is Qu and who is it built for?
a: Qu is a unified commerce platform for enterprise restaurant chains, primarily in the U.S., with a focus on fast casual and quick service brands such as Jack in the Box and Dave's Hot Chicken. Co-founder Niko Papademetriou says "the modern POS needs to go far beyond simply the black plastic box on the countertop." [03:04]

q: How can a restaurant POS keep working during a cloud or internet outage?
a: Qu uses edge nodes that bring the most valuable slice of its AWS cloud services inside the restaurant, adding resiliency, stability and speed. Niko Papademetriou says of operators, "They cannot have something like cloud outage or internet outage affect their ability to transact in a restaurant" [16:43].

q: How did Qu build its current platform?
a: Niko Papademetriou says Qu restacked its entire platform about six and a half years before this interview, reaching its first beta restaurants in about 12 months and expanding over another six or so. He said that MVP "was a behemoth when now you have to build an MVP that satisfies dozens of chains and thousands of restaurants." [06:57]

q: How does Qu decide what goes on its product roadmap?
a: Qu gathers challenges from its customers, weighs them against broader market opportunities and filters them through its product organization. Niko Papademetriou warns that "as soon as you become a custom dev shop for every single one of your customers, you immediately put a timestamp on your product." [09:36]

q: What is next for Qu?
a: Niko Papademetriou says Qu will stay focused on fast casual and quick service operators while investing in data access, insights and actionable intelligence. That includes helping multi-brand companies "to see that snapshot of the customer across your brands, across your portfolio" [25:50].

s12-e1-the-blast-radius-nightmare-shifting-from-blind-static-terraform-plans-to-real-time-predictive-change-intelligence-with-dylan-ratcliffe-founder-ceo-of-overmind

A Printer That Wasn't: A Friday 3 p.m. change to Linux server logins broke PDF saving through an undocumented server posing as a printer. It led Ratcliffe to quit and build automatic dependency discovery.

Discovery Alone Backfired: The first product mapped every cloud dependency, but users saw 500 things to review. The engine now sits mostly in the backend, feeding an LLM that assesses deployment risk.
Hiring for Ease and Ownership: Ratcliffe learned Go because he expected to hire infrastructure people who knew it. He looks for hires who say "I intend to fix this" rather than "we should fix this."

Roadmap Keyframed by Offsites: With AI moving too fast for a two-year plan, the team built proofs of concept at in-person events, then spent three months turning the chosen one into a shipped product.

Going Broad for Enterprises: Overmind started with AWS and Terraform, has launched GCP and is working on Azure, Pulumi and Argo CD. Larger companies use many tools, and users shouldn't have to change workflows.

q: What does Overmind do?
a: Overmind, founded by Dylan Ratcliffe, aims to remove the dread of deploying to production and to prevent outages before they happen. Ratcliffe explained, "We do that by simulating your infrastructure changes against your real-time actual production" [02:57] infrastructure before you make those changes.

q: What inspired Dylan Ratcliffe to start Overmind?
a: A change to Linux server authentication unexpectedly stopped a department from saving PDFs, because of a forgotten server that nothing documented. Ratcliffe quit his job because the incident convinced him that "it is totally reasonable to be afraid of pressing" [07:46] the deploy button.

q: Why wasn't real-time dependency discovery enough to prevent outages?
a: Ratcliffe found that showing users every dependency gave them a large new review job instead of an answer. He said the discovery engine "was not helpful. In fact, actively unhelpful to show to a human." [14:21]

q: How does Overmind use LLMs to assess infrastructure change risk?
a: The dependency data forms a directed graph that backs the LLM, which reasons about impact and risk. Ratcliffe described a "graph that it can traverse in real time of all of the dependencies and having certainty of it" [14:57], which he argues stops the model from hallucinating dependencies.

q: Which clouds and infrastructure tools does Overmind support?
a: Ratcliffe said Overmind started with AWS, recently launched GCP and is working on Azure. On tooling, he said, "We currently support Terraform, but we also are building Pulumi and Argo CD and even supporting manual changes." [26:18]

s11-e30-the-20-trillion-paper-trail-why-contracts-are-financial-assets-not-just-legal-documents-and-how-multi-agent-ai-slashes-enterprise-procurement-waste-with-brandon-card-co-founder-ceo-of-terzo

Contracts as Financial Assets: Brandon Card saw that contract software was built for legal teams, though he says 90% or more of contracts are negotiated by business people. Terzo uses AI to read contracts, invoices and purchase orders for finance and procurement.

Enterprise From Day One: Advisors and investors urged Terzo to start with SMB and mid-market. Card instead targeted the Fortune 500, relying on years at Oracle, IBM and Microsoft and his knowledge of large companies' problems.

The 70/30 Roadmap Rule: About 70% of the roadmap came from Terzo's own strategic initiatives and 30% from customer feedback. The team built nothing custom, favoring repeatable features that could sell across verticals.

Sales Hiring Came Too Early: Card brought in salespeople roughly six months before product-market fit, costing the company time and money. His lesson: don't build a revenue engine until fit is proven, especially in a new AI market.

A Bet on Contracts On-Chain: Card believes smart contracts will automate slow, manual contracting and payment processes. He says Terzo will be the first AI provider to put B2B contracts on chain, despite expecting many VCs to disagree.

q: What does Terzo AI do?
a: Terzo is a contract and financial intelligence platform that helps finance, procurement and supply chain teams understand supplier spend and reduce waste, and it is now working on customer contracts and revenue too. Brandon Card said the founding goal was to show the world "that contracts are financial assets" [04:35].

q: Why did Terzo sell to the Fortune 500 from the start instead of SMBs?
a: Brandon Card chose the enterprise despite many people telling him it was impossible, because he understood how large companies operate. As he put it, "I cope with those decisions because I spent my whole life working with the Fortune 500." [07:42]

q: How does Terzo decide what to build on its product roadmap?
a: Terzo balances its leadership team's strategic direction with feedback from large customers, and only builds repeatable features rather than custom work. Card explained that "about 70% of our roadmap was strategic initiatives that we designed." [09:35] The other 30% came from customer feedback.

q: What mistake did Brandon Card make when scaling sales at Terzo?
a: Card hired people to sell the product about six months before Terzo had product-market fit, which cost time and money and could have derailed the company. His warning is that "You cannot build out a sales team or a sales process" [15:12] without proper product-market fit.

q: What does Brandon Card see as the future of B2B contracts?
a: Card believes the future of finance is on the blockchain, with smart contracts replacing much of the manual work around PDFs, redlines, purchase orders and slow payments. "We believe the future is contracts on chain." [17:00]

s11-bonus-the-myth-of-sales-as-an-art-transitioning-from-gut-based-forecasts-to-algorithmic-crm-forensics-and-pipeline-cadence-with-juan-deangulo-co-founder-of-inselligence

Forecasting Rooted in Process: Inselligence plugs a deterministic AI engine into CRMs to expose process bottlenecks and bad data, improve reporting and forecast revenue. Juan says bad forecasts, reports and data are symptoms of a sales process problem.

Math Before Interface: The MVP took a little over a year and focused only on analysis. The team reproduced hundreds of interconnected formulas from Excel and Visual Basic, then showed business contacts results from their own CRM data without a finished UI.

Go to Market Sooner: Juan wishes the team had cut its year-plus beta short, because someone who isn't paying isn't a true test. They also built 10 CRM integrations when one or two would have revealed which best matched their ideal customer.

Direct Sales Before Partnerships: With a new concept, Inselligence committed to direct selling and tested agencies, SDR models and lead databases. It pursued strategic partnerships only after learning where it fit in the market.

Resisting Feature Chasing: Juan is proudest of staying committed to the core algorithm and process-driven intelligence, even though quick features could win deals. He accepts that companies that don't appreciate process won't be early adopters.

q: What is Inselligence and what does it do?
a: Inselligence is what co-founder Juan DeAngulo calls a RevOps navigation platform, designed to surface process bottlenecks, CRM data problems and better revenue forecasts. In his words, "We have a deterministic AI engine that plugs with multiple different CRMs." [02:53]

q: How does Inselligence forecast sales revenue?
a: Juan DeAngulo explains that the engine pulls CRM data through APIs and analyzes deal flow using KPIs that people usually view in isolation. As he describes it, "It's like hundreds of formulas working together real time to look at six or seven different" [07:46] KPIs.

q: When should a SaaS startup go to market?
a: Juan DeAngulo advises going as fast as you can, even if it feels early, because paying customers show what the product really needs. Reflecting on Inselligence's year-plus beta, he said "we should have just gone to market" [11:17].

q: Can AI replace salespeople?
a: Juan DeAngulo doesn't think so, arguing that selling is personalized and creative and still needs people in the loop, though teams might need fewer people to do more. Of AI, he said, "It's about augmenting human productivity. It's not about replacing it." [21:18]

q: What advice does Juan DeAngulo give young founders?
a: Juan stresses "understanding that your identity is not tied to what you're creating" [26:05]. He warns that tying the two together can inflate your ego or hurt your self-worth, and can cloud decisions such as when to step back as CEO or sell.

developer-chats-petr-petrenko

Rewrite Only as Last Resort: Petr sees a rewrite making sense when the tech stack must change to move forward or the system has drifted too far from its original requirements. Otherwise, refactoring and cleanup are almost always better.

Fix the Real Bottleneck: On a 10-plus-year-old reporting system, heavy queries on an outdated database were the problem. Two weeks of fixes cut reports from 30 minutes to 10 seconds, at under 10% of the planned rewrite budget.

Treat Every Cent Seriously: Different exchange rates across transaction, processing and conversion can obscure revenue, anomalies and fraud. Petr's advice is to track down even a one-cent difference and fix it.

Algorithms Beat Language Speed: Petr's image matcher hit a limit set by algorithmic complexity, not PHP. A better data structure, then a multithreaded C core, met the goal of about two searches per second across 100 million photos.

Don't Overbuild for the Future: Petr has seen ambitious small teams overcomplicate products by predicting 10 years ahead, then run out of budget. Build what users need now, without letting the code become a pile of hacks.

q: When should you rewrite a legacy system instead of refactoring it?
a: Petr Petrenko says it makes sense when you can't move forward without changing the tech stack, or when the system has drifted too far from its original requirements. As Petr put it, "For me, rewriting should always be the last resort." [02:29]

q: How can you speed up a slow legacy system without a full rewrite?
a: Petrenko analyzed a reporting project where each report took 10 to 30 minutes and found that heavy queries on an outdated database were the issue. The database couldn't simply be upgraded, so the queries were fixed, and in two weeks "reports went from 30 minutes to 10 seconds." [03:47]

q: How was the high-performance image matching system for real estate ads built?
a: Petrenko tested approaches on a database of 1 million photos, researched algorithms and academic papers, and prototyped a promising data structure in PHP. To make it faster, Petr said, "I wrote core on the C and added multithreading support that gave me the required performance." [12:13]

q: What do engineers underestimate about cross-border payment systems?
a: Petrenko says multiple exchange rates make it hard to know how much money was actually made, and systems built for one market often break when expanded. Petr's guidance is direct: "My main advice is always be careful with numbers." [07:48]

q: How do you write code that will still make sense years from now?
a: Petrenko argues that aiming for durability itself is a mistake, though a codebase full of hacks and quick fixes is the opposite extreme to avoid. In Petr's words, "Our real goal is to create a product that users need right now." [09:24]

s11-e29-the-60-second-behavioral-blueprint-why-great-on-paper-candidates-fail-and-how-voice-ai-biomarkers-predict-real-world-team-chemistry-with-sarah-lucena-founder-ceo-of-mappa

Voice as Behavioral Data: Mappa analyzes semantic and prosodic biomarkers, such as self versus other references, verb use, pitch, volume and jitter, to understand how people act, relate to others and react to situations.

A Spreadsheet Was the MVP: The first version ran an artisanal behavioral model in a spreadsheet, matching candidates to company culture. Some early clients who received talent that way have now worked with Mappa for over two years.
Profitable Before Scaling: Mappa focused on getting clients to pay, reached profitability within six months, and Sarah Lucena says it bootstrapped to over $4 million in annualized revenue.

Candidates Revealed the Voice Opportunity: Candidates short on time asked to send audio messages about their experience. Seeing how naturally they spoke led the team to academic research and made voice a key data point.

From Hiring to Infrastructure: Hiring gave Mappa the feedback loop to retrain its models. It has since launched a private API beta serving financial, education and dating companies, with a public launch planned for Q1 2026.

q: What does Mappa do?
a: Mappa, founded by Sarah Lucena, analyzes speech to understand the person behind the words and create connections that work in real life. As Lucena put it, "Mappa does behavior mapping at scale to help companies never make a bad hire" [02:44].

q: How does Mappa use voice biomarkers to predict behavior?
a: Sarah Lucena explained, "We extract biomarkers from voice, both semantic and prosodic biomarkers." [02:59] These include word choices, such as how often you refer to yourself versus others and how you use verbs, along with volume, pitch, jitter and the frequency of speech.

q: Why do great-on-paper candidates sometimes fail?
a: Sarah Lucena built her team of over 30 people multiple times, optimizing for the best schools and backgrounds, yet the chemistry and delivery fell short. She came to see that "compatibility with who we are and what we are looking for are deeper than just what the title" [05:05] on a CV suggests.

q: What was Mappa's first MVP?
a: Lucena said, "I'd say that our first MVP was actually a spreadsheet." [10:48] It held a rudimentary data model built from social and other online data about candidates and companies, which the team used to create compatibility matches.

q: What advice does Sarah Lucena give founders about going to market?
a: Lucena counts taking too long to get to market as an early mistake, because the market turned out to be completely different once the team got there after a lot of ideation. Her advice to founders chasing a perfect product is to "just get to the market and figure as you go." [21:38]

s11-bonus-headless-observability-why-dashboards-are-disappearing-and-how-context-engineering-achieves-a-90-drop-in-ai-sre-costs-with-tucker-callaway-ceo-of-mezmo

Storage Physics Forced a Rethink: Callaway concluded log management was largely reselling storage, so Mezmo shifted more compute and control into real-time data pipelines instead of storing all data on disk.

Context Over Model Training: Mezmo treats models as hot-swappable engines and uses machine learning to refine data into more specific context. Callaway says this reaches agentic outcomes at 10% of typical AI cost with much higher accuracy.

Scale Lessons From IBM Cloud: As a roughly 35-person startup, the company was suddenly deployed in 12 global data centers as IBM Cloud's log management provider. That experience now underpins its AI approach.

Build Access, Not Algorithms: With strong models readily available, Mezmo's roadmap centers on practical, efficient, scalable and accurate access to AI's value rather than proprietary algorithms as its defining IP.

Hire for the Company Stage: Callaway admits hiring people unsuited to the company's stage and not clearly explaining what that stage required. He stresses handling poor fits with empathy and candid two-way conversations.

q: What is Mezmo's approach to AI-driven observability?
a: Mezmo uses context engineering, refining telemetry data so an AI agent gets better inputs, rather than relying on prompt engineering or model training. Tucker Callaway says it delivers agentic outcomes "with 10% of the cost of what you might find in your typical AI approach with much higher accuracy." [03:15]

q: Why did Mezmo move beyond traditional log management?
a: Callaway saw customers face massive cost overruns and dealt with the same storage costs on his own side. In his words, "I realized that basically what I was doing was with reselling storage." [04:52] The company set out to move more processing and control into real-time data pipelines.

q: Why aren't bigger context windows enough for AI in observability?
a: Callaway argues that large context windows are not helping in high-scale, high-volume operational use cases, saying "they're actually bigger than it is useful." [12:46] Mezmo instead processes the data to make model inputs more dynamic and specific, aiming for cheaper and more accurate outcomes.

q: How did Mezmo learn to handle telemetry data at scale?
a: During the LogDNA era, the company was the log management provider for IBM Cloud and had to scale quickly while still a small startup. Callaway recalled, "we were operating at massive enterprise scale across 12 data centers worldwide" [06:22], which built deep knowledge of managing telemetry and log data.

q: What advice does Tucker Callaway give people hesitant to become entrepreneurs?
a: Callaway, who took his first CEO job at 45, wishes he had had the confidence to try earlier and encourages people to treat each move as a step they can learn from, even if they turn out to be wrong. As he put it, "You got to commit to the journey, not the outcome." [22:33]

s11-e28-the-temporal-correctness-crisis-why-static-rag-context-leads-to-broken-ai-agent-actions-and-how-to-engine-unify-real-time-streaming-data-with-hojjat-jafarpour-founder-ceo-of-deltastream

Cloud-Only by Design: DeltaStream skipped on-prem to avoid being stuck with the least common denominator of capabilities, taking cues from Snowflake and S3 to hide provisioning, cluster sizing and scaling from users.

Solutions Over Technologies: Users were pairing stream pipelines with databases like ClickHouse or Postgres to serve results. DeltaStream brought ClickHouse into the platform so a few SQL statements can build real-time materialized views.

Isolation for Every Streaming Job: Rather than sharing clusters, each streaming job runs in isolation and scales independently. This supports elasticity and fault tolerance, and keeps one bad job from affecting others.
Ship Sooner for Feedback: Jafarpour's admitted mistake was perfectionism that delayed going to market. Given another try, he would launch earlier and learn more from real-world scenarios.

Fresh Context for AI Agents: Jafarpour sees data, and how fresh it is, as a key differentiator for AI applications. DeltaStream's real-time context engine lets agents point to context that is continuously updated.

q: What is DeltaStream and why was it started?
a: DeltaStream is a cloud-only, serverless stream processing platform founded by Hojjat Jafarpour after his work on KSQL at Confluent, where he saw people struggle to run stream processing infrastructure. After raising a seed round, he started the company "to build a serverless stream processing platform" [04:36].

q: How was DeltaStream built, and does it use Apache Flink?
a: Jafarpour's team chose Apache Flink as the compute engine instead of building one from scratch, since it was already proven at large scale. The problem they set out to solve was running it, as Jafarpour described the thinking: "let's take away the complexity of operation" [06:30].

q: How does DeltaStream handle scalability for streaming jobs?
a: Jafarpour explained that the architecture separates compute and storage so each can scale independently, and avoids shared clusters across streaming jobs. In his words, "One decision that we made was to have each of the streaming jobs in isolation" [14:21].

q: How can real-time data help AI agents make better decisions?
a: Jafarpour argues that agents should act on what is happening right now, and positions DeltaStream as a real-time context engine for them. He said agents "would just point to the context and that context is continuously being updated and fresh" [18:37].

q: What mistake did DeltaStream's founder make early on?
a: Hojjat Jafarpour said the team was too perfectionist and did not go to market soon enough. Looking back, he noted that "we could go earlier and get much more feedback" [16:32].

developer-chats-svyatoslav-babinets-of-meta

Performance Is a Product Requirement: At 60 frames per second, everything must fit in about 16.7 milliseconds. Babinets makes budgets visible and enforced, using level of detail, budgeters and safe defaults so creators don't accidentally blow up CPU, GPU or memory use.

Integration Is Its Own Product: A cool prototype is far from a production feature. UI hooks, telemetry, configuration and rollout should be written down, estimated and scheduled, or you will likely pay later in delays or rework.

Squads Beyond the Org Chart: Virtual Mission Squads pull people from different teams and tech stacks into ad hoc groups with an end-to-end goal to ship. The bar isn't "I shipped my part" but a component that is live and trusted by its users.

Flip Conway's Law: Systems mirror how organizations communicate, so define the development pipeline you want and design for it. Clear contracts, versioned breaking changes, thin SDKs and templates make the standard path the fastest one.

Ownership Can Decide Designs: When multiple designs are valuable, Babinets weighs technical merit and who will maintain each with care and stay calm when edge cases hit. The strongest accountable owner is often the practical choice.

q: How do you manage performance in large-scale multiplayer and 3D applications?
a: Svyatoslav Babinets sets explicit frame-time and resource budgets, enforced with tools like level of detail and budgeters. He says he treats "performance and latency as product requirements, not nice-to-haves." [02:34]

q: How can large engineering teams move fast without sacrificing quality?
a: Babinets points to modular components, reliable end-to-end tests on real builds, clear documentation and easy local builds. In his words, "architecture succeeds when the easiest path is the right one" [09:47].

q: What are Virtual Mission Squads?
a: As Babinets describes them, they are ad hoc groups drawn from different teams and stacks, given an end-to-end objective to ship something, which recreates startup-like momentum inside a large company. His guiding principle is "don't let organizational charts limit impact." [11:35]

q: Which engineering decisions are really about trust rather than technology?
a: Babinets cites code reviews, design reviews, decision logs and choosing between similarly strong designs, where he considers who will maintain the system and respond well when something goes wrong. He says that "picking the option with the strongest accountable owner is often the practical choice." [19:02]

q: What should the next generation of engineers focus on: performance, presence or empathy?
a: Babinets says to combine them: performance makes an experience possible, comfortable and smooth, while presence makes it worth your time. His advice was "don't pick between performance, presence, and empathy." [29:58]

s11-bonus-the-new-ai-engineering-reality-decoupling-testing-and-orchestrating-the-next-gen-software-factory-with-spriha-baruah-tucker-field-cto-executive-leader-at-buildkite

A Customer Jingle Opened Doors: While running Aviator, Spriha found a customer had made an infomercial jingle to promote Buildkite internally. She told Buildkite's founder, who realized she knew more about his customers' technical context than he did.

Customers Sit on a Continuum: Some want raw "Lego blocks" while others want a curated set for CI or CD. Seeing these as stages of one journey let Buildkite share lessons from cutting-edge users with those earlier on.
AI Agents Shift Scaling Limits: Spriha says AI coding tools have driven a spike in pull requests, so 30-person engineering teams now bring feature requests once seen from 30,000-person teams.

CI as a Risk Knob: Instead of a pass/fail Boolean, Spriha sees CI tuning tests, time and compute to the risk at hand. Quick experiments run likely failures first, while high-stakes deploys run every test.

Pitching Without Listening Cost a Deal: Days into the job, Spriha pitched power and configurability to a prospect that wanted hand-holding and ease of use. She says she tanked a very large deal and avoided prospect calls for a month.

q: What is Buildkite and what does it do?
a: Buildkite is a CI/CD platform that Spriha Baruah Tucker says powers the building, testing and deploying of code at many popular apps and websites. She describes it this way: "Buildkite feels like Silicon Valley's best-kept secret" [02:45].

q: How are AI coding agents affecting CI/CD pipelines?
a: Spriha says AI coding tools have caused a big spike in pull requests, with downstream effects on the rest of the developer loop. Smaller companies are now hitting large-company scaling problems: "So 30-person engineering teams are now coming to us with feature requests that previously" [23:25] came from 30,000-person teams.

q: What is risk-based CI, and why does Spriha Baruah Tucker see it as the future?
a: Spriha argues that CI should move beyond a simple pass or fail, with the depth of testing matched to how much confidence a given action requires. In her words, "It's a risk knob that you sort of dial up or down depending on what you're trying to do." [24:58]

q: What mistake did Spriha Baruah Tucker make early on at Buildkite?
a: She pitched a prospect on Buildkite's power, scalability and configurability when they actually wanted ease of use and hand-holding. Spriha admits, "I didn't come in with my empathy ears on." [19:47]

q: What advice does Spriha Baruah Tucker give startup founders?
a: Spriha advises founders to watch their own energy, learn what inspires them, and focus on the one or two biggest things to de-risk, such as product market fit. She says, "the big advice I'd say is enthusiasm and energy is they're actually perishable." [34:27]

s11-bonus-dismantling-the-upwork-middleman-tax-and-scaling-a-global-freelance-network-without-percentage-slices-with-gajus-kuizinas-co-founder-cto-of-contra

Commission-Free Changes the Model: Contra dropped the marketplace commission fee, which forced it to innovate on how it makes money. The product evolved into a hybrid of a professional network and a marketplace.

Scrapping the Seed Prototype: Contra raised its seed round on an agency-built PHP and Vue prototype, then scrapped it and the team to rebuild from the ground up. Reaching feature parity with existing talent marketplaces took four years.

Single Player Mode First: Before the marketplace and network were ready, Contra put significant resources into customizable portfolio websites. These let people start building their identity on the platform right away.

Recruiting Through Stack Overflow: Gajus posted niche questions about Relay, Flow and GraphQL, then watched how people answered and debated. Those who were generous collaborators got his phone number, and this produced the first couple of hires.

Generalists Before Specialists: Hiring experts such as DBAs and QA specialists too early was Contra's biggest mistake. Early problems come and go, and most people who left were early hires too specialized to adopt the company's broader technology choices.

q: What is Contra and how is it different from other freelance marketplaces?
a: Contra is a talent marketplace for creatives that charges no commission fee and combines elements of a professional network. Describing the goal, Gajus Kuizinas said "you keep full of your entire earnings, and you're building something that has a long lasting value" [05:28].

q: Why did Gajus Kuizinas co-found Contra?
a: Gajus started freelancing on oDesk and eventually questioned why he was on a platform that controlled his client relationships. He recalled asking why he stayed on a service "that's taking a large chunk of my pay of the commission fee" [04:15].

q: How did Contra attract users before its marketplace was fully built?
a: Contra built what it called single player mode, giving people a way to establish their identity before work and networking features arrived. Gajus explained, "we allocated a pretty significant portion of our resources to building what we call custom portfolios" [08:04].

q: How did Contra hire its first engineers?
a: Gajus looked for people excited about emerging technologies like GraphQL and Relay who were also kind, generous collaborators. As he described it, "I started posting questions to Stack Overflow that I knew that" [11:35] only those people would be able to answer.

q: How does Contra use AI to help freelancers find work?
a: Gajus described Indie AI, a browser extension that collects social posts from users' friends on platforms such as Twitter and LinkedIn. He said it handles tens of millions of posts daily, "where we then analyze those posts using AI to identify work opportunities for them" [17:42].

the-railsware-way-mistakes-lessons-in-product-evolution-with-oleksii-ianchuk

A Mistake Became a Product: Mailtrap began after Railsware, then a consultancy, sent test emails to real recipients on a client project. The team built a fake SMTP tool for itself, found others had the same problem, and later turned it into a paid SaaS product.

Splitting the Product Backfired: Separating testing and sending into two repositories meant constant synchronization over gRPC, slower delivery and harder regional hosting. The team assigned engineers to merge them, and the work is almost finished.

Bring in Experts Early: After struggling with Redshift for logs and stats, Railsware hired experts who confirmed it was wrong for this use. For the move to OpenSearch, experienced help changed the speed of delivery and estimation.

Existing Users Don't Automatically Switch: Mailtrap expected sandbox users to adopt its email API and SMTP sending, but switching costs are high for critical flows like signups. Customers tend to move when their current provider fails them, and some did switch to Mailtrap.

Deliverability Needs Dedicated People: Spammers on shared IPs can damage other customers' reputation, and some mailbox providers are hard to reach. Mailtrap built a compliance system, a squad covering that area and a small deliverability team that also coaches customers.

q: How did Mailtrap get started?
a: Oleksii Ianchuk explained that Mailtrap grew out of a mistake at Railsware, where test emails reached real recipients during a client project. The team built a fake SMTP utility to prevent a repeat, and as Oleksii put it, "it's a problem that not only Railsware at the time had" [04:16].

q: Why did Mailtrap merge its email testing and email sending projects back together?
a: Oleksii said isolating the two sounded great, but they shared many parts, including the user database, which created synchronization work and extra costs. He noted that "if you add some feature, it became like not one task to add in one place" [07:12].

q: Why did Mailtrap move away from Redshift?
a: The team had chosen Redshift for logs and stats without prior experience with it, then hit limitations and heavy maintenance. Oleksii said the experts they later hired "confirmed that it's a great database, but not for the case that we used it" [11:23], and the team moved to OpenSearch.

q: Why didn't Mailtrap's sandbox users immediately adopt its email sending service?
a: Oleksii said email is a critical part of many products, so teams that are happy with their provider rarely move without a reason such as an unresolved block or poor support. In his words, "cost of switch is really high" [14:36] for some customers.

q: How does Mailtrap handle spammers and compliance?
a: Oleksii said Mailtrap forbids cold outreach and built a compliance system, including AI content checking, that tries to keep onboarding friction low while keeping bad actors out. He acknowledged that "it's impossible to create 100% ideal compliance system" [18:24], so false positives and some spammers still slip through.

s11-e27-why-conventional-saas-billing-fails-the-agentic-era-and-how-to-protect-margins-on-non-deterministic-actions-with-raj-dosanjh-co-founder-engineering-lead-at-paid

Token Costs Change the Math: Unlike many SaaS costs, token usage is billed as it happens, so some customers are more profitable than others. A voice agent customer who talks a lot costs more and may need to be billed accordingly.

Telemetry Over Manual Metering: Paid's SDK event submission stalled integrations, so the team leaned on OpenTelemetry. AI helps turn raw trace data into billable business metrics that map to what end customers pay for.

Paid Design Partners: Unpaid design partners agreed to help but put off integrating. Having partners pay put skin in the game, created a forcing function and drove the engagement Paid needed to iterate quickly.

Engineers Own the Customer: Paid has no real roadmap in the traditional sense. Engineers stay close to customers from implementation through expansion and retention, and can ship fixes within hours of hearing an objection.

Scale With Observability: Raj advises watching metrics like P95s and CPU usage and fixing bottlenecks as they appear. A cache or database proxy may help far more than a big bet like migrating to Kubernetes.

q: Why doesn't conventional SaaS billing work well for AI agents?
a: Raj Dosanjh explains that generative AI costs hit immediately and vary by customer, whereas SaaS costs did not always rise straight away. As he put it, "use a token at the moment you are getting billed for that so some customers are going to be more" [06:37] profitable than others.

q: How does Paid use OpenTelemetry to bill for AI agent activity?
a: Paid reads telemetry data to understand what an agent is doing, and initially proved the approach with cost tracking, identifying calls to OpenAI in Node.js apps. Raj said they "use natural language to create transformational queries that can then turn this sort of raw data" [23:20] into billable business metrics.

q: How did Paid find its early design partners and adopters?
a: Raj says early agent startups agreed to be design partners but kept delaying integration, which suggested the ideal customer profile or the approach was wrong. Repeatedly addressing objections helped, and so did charging partners, because "that now puts some skin in the game their side" [10:17].

q: How does Paid decide what to build without a traditional roadmap?
a: Drawing on his time at Palantir and its forward deployed engineer model, Raj keeps engineers embedded closely with customers so less information is lost in handoffs. He said, "if the engineer has seen it themselves, they have an opinion." [12:37]

q: What is Raj Dosanjh's advice on scaling a startup's application?
a: Raj advises against large architecture changes aimed at perceived problems, and favors forming a hypothesis, backing it with data and making targeted fixes. In his view, "it all comes down to good observability." [18:51]

unbreakable-how-to-thrive-under-fear-based-leaders-with-kate-lowry

Why It's Surging Now: Kate calls this the largest leadership-style shift of her career. Five years ago CEOs felt they had to at least pretend to care; now many tech leaders say get in line or get out.

Fear Chokes Innovation: Employees won't share big or unusual ideas under a my-way-or-the-highway CEO. Fear of reporting problems also leads to more mistakes, severe technical debt and hidden Achilles heels.

Predictable Means Influenceable: Fear-based leaders can seem chaotic, but they follow clear, simplistic logic. Once you can predict their decisions, you can reliably use tactics to protect what you care about.

Three Protective Tactics: Be intentional about what personal information you share, don't react (be boring, like a rock), and use your availability as leverage, such as taking a few extra hours to reply to an email.

Keep It From Taking Root: Run employee pulse surveys at least quarterly, celebrate failures as well as wins, and create forums for big ideas, including what customer success hears. And don't push your company into 996.

q: What makes someone a fear-based leader?
a: Kate Lowry explains that these leaders are driven by their own insecurity and use fear to motivate others because it is what motivates them. In her words, "leaders are called fear-based because they themselves are really insecure" [06:09].

q: Why is fear-based leadership bad for startup innovation?
a: Kate says people need to feel safe before they will share bold ideas or admit that something is going wrong. She finds that "companies that use fear-based leadership end up with very high levels of mistakes, really severe technical debt" [05:33].

q: How do you deal with a fear-based boss?
a: Kate advises being careful about what you reveal, withholding the negative reactions these leaders feed on, and not always being instantly available. On reactions, she suggests "trying to be boring like a rock in a landscape" [08:44] so the leader moves on.

q: How can CEOs prevent fear-based leadership in their company?
a: Kate recommends regular employee feedback, forums that celebrate mistakes and learning, and ways for teams such as customer success to share what they hear. "I'm a big fan of doing pulse surveys of your employees" [12:03], she says, with live feedback at least once a quarter.

q: How is the AI boom affecting the way leaders treat employees?
a: Kate says many leaders resent that employees have needs and lives outside of work, and she is seeing more extractive, transactional behavior. As she describes it, "now people are starting to compare that to agents, which have 100% uptime" [14:03].

the-railsware-way-how-an-mba-helps-or-doesnt-product-mgmt-with-julia-starun

MBA Theory Lags Startup Reality: Julia found the core program built around hierarchies and slow change. Time management still covered full inboxes and delegating to a secretary, and AI practices were missing from the main curriculum.

Monetization Beyond Subscriptions: Working through 35 monetization strategies pushed Julia past flat fees, subscriptions and pay-as-you-go, and widened how she thinks about go-to-market and brand positioning.
Frameworks Are Not Cages: Frameworks help when you're unsure where to start, but they can lead to over-structuring. Sometimes you should just do the job now and build the structure later.
Practice Strategy on Real Businesses: Julia applied her MBA work to Railsware Product Studio, Coupler.io and Tradezilla, setting multi-year goals and weighing revenue against market share.

A Neurodiversity Leadership Gap: The MBA only validated Julia's people leadership approach and offered nothing on managing neurodiverse teams, such as adapting goal setting and regular management for people with autism or ADHD.

q: Where does MBA theory fall short for product management in startups?
a: Julia Starun of Railsware found the main program geared toward big corporations, structured hierarchies and slow change, with no AI practices in the core curriculum. Recalling the time management material, she said, "I was taught that I need to have a secretary who would do it instead of me" [04:26].

q: How can an MBA change the way you make product decisions?
a: Julia says this was the best part of her MBA, especially working through 35 monetization strategies instead of defaulting to subscriptions. As she put it, "this exercise taught me that quantity actually can become a quality" [11:14].

q: How should product managers use business frameworks without overcomplicating things?
a: Julia says frameworks simplify uncertainty and support more conscious decisions, but not every situation needs a process. Her advice is to treat them "not as cages, but rather as a foundation to start something" [09:46].

q: Does an MBA teach you how to manage neurodiverse engineering teams?
a: Not in Julia Starun's experience, even though she notes that some great engineers are not neurotypical. She said "there is no fundamentals on how to manage, how to change the approaches" [07:41], and it is a topic she would like to research and teach.

q: When is an MBA worth it for someone already managing product teams?
a: Julia points to two cases: when you need to build and practice a helicopter view and vision, and when you want to broaden your network. On networking, she said, "It's about have connections with people who can actually help you to get investment or review your pitch deck." [16:04]

s11-e26-fusing-statistical-modeling-with-agentic-ai-to-silence-false-positives-and-dominate-saas-attack-surfaces-with-marco-rodrigues-co-founder-head-of-customer-engineering-at-exaforce

Data Before Agents: Exaforce spent its first six to nine months on data architecture, bringing in logs, events, configurations, code bases and threat intel so LLMs and agents had the context a human analyst would need.

Three Methods, One Platform: Exaforce fuses semantic understanding of security data with statistical reasoning and LLM-driven decision logic to create Exabots, AI agents that triage, investigate and respond at machine speed.

Baselines Change Alert Priority: Behavioral models learn what each identity and account normally does. Correlated signals can mark an alert as a likely false positive, or raise a low-severity Amazon GuardDuty alert to high.

Avoid Bespoke Detours: A technology decision shaped partly by one design partner's requests proved too bespoke for a broad customer base. The team peeled it back, and the partner was open to a more feasible approach.
Augment, Don't Replace Analysts: Marco hopes that by 2026 or 2027 every enterprise SOC pairs each human analyst with an AI one, moving teams toward "Q0": no backlog, no burnout and zero blind spots.

q: What is Exaforce and what problem does it solve?
a: Exaforce is an agentic SOC platform born from Marco Rodrigues watching security operations teams drown in data and tooling without better outcomes. He said the founding question was "what if AI itself could reason about security like an actual person, like an analyst?" [03:15].

q: How does Exaforce identify false positives and prioritize security alerts?
a: Marco Rodrigues explained that Exaforce packages the data needed for a specific situation and processes it through its knowledge model, which can judge an alert a likely false positive. It can also escalate a low-severity alert, as in his example where "we were able to correlate many other signals fairly quickly" [08:38].

q: How was the Exaforce MVP built?
a: Marco Rodrigues said the team started with data acquisition, pipelines and enrichment, which became its semantic data model, followed by behavioral and knowledge models. The company "for the first six to nine months was hyper-focused on getting that data architecture and thought" [07:07] process nailed down.

q: Will AI replace SOC analysts?
a: Marco Rodrigues does not frame Exaforce as a replacement for people, since the teams he talks to are drowning in alerts and short on staff. In his words, "I see it, we're just augmenting all the existing folks." [20:04]

q: What mistake did the Exaforce team make while building the product?
a: Marco Rodrigues described starting to deliver a technology decision based partly on feedback from a design partner, then pulling it back. The team realized "this was going to be more of a bespoke solution, not necessarily something that made sense" [18:21] for a large customer base.

fraud-awareness-week-how-seon-is-your-fraud-aml-command-center-with-husnain-bajwa

Fraud Costs Multiply: Bajwa says every dollar of fraud costs $3 to $4 to address and mitigate. Even healthy-margin businesses can run into real trouble if they put growth first and don't take the threat seriously.

Fraud and AML Converging: AML checks once relied on periodic reviews, spreadsheets and manual analysts. A single data and decisioning layer can expose fraud rings, layering schemes and mule networks with very low latency.

AI Supports Human Intuition: SEON enriches transactions with as many as 900 fields, then uses natural-language summaries to explain what matters. Bajwa says this can save 80-90% of the time a proficient user would spend making sense of it.

Under-Screening Draws Scrutiny: Independent auditors are testing screening systems with 30,000 or 50,000 names, and some legacy AML tools have been under-screening considerably. Regulators also want explainable AI with clear approval provenance.

Secure Onboarding First: Startups should block bots and multi-accounting, then check email and phone signals and digital footprint. Carry those controls into logins, profile changes and payments, watching for patterns like a test charge before a large one.

q: What is SEON's fraud and AML command center?
a: Husnain Bajwa describes SEON as a set of strong, composable capabilities that drive a single data layer and a single decisioning layer, rather than a conventional platform. As Bajwa put it, we "think of our system as a command center and not a conventional platform" [15:56].

q: Why are fraud prevention and AML compliance converging?
a: Bajwa explains that AML was traditionally handled through batch operations and manual review, while payments and account creation needed fast, real-time visibility. In a digital-first world, he says "it's important that we break down the silos and bring the data to a single place" [06:25].

q: How is AI being used in fraud detection and AML?
a: Bajwa says generative AI helps summarize large sets of mixed data points in plain language and helps users build decisioning rules that draw on more signals. He describes today's systems as keeping people in charge, saying "the systems are at an assisted cruise control kind of level" [17:30].

q: How can organizations prepare for AML regulatory pressure in 2026?
a: Bajwa points to demand for explainable AI, auditability, monitoring at smaller thresholds and platforms that can be reconfigured quickly as rules change. He notes that "the FIUs have a lot of focus on determining whether people are over-screening and especially under-screening" [14:14], referring to financial intelligence units.

q: Are early-stage startups too small to be targeted by fraudsters?
a: No. Bajwa says SEON was created after its co-founders' crypto exchange faced prohibitive fraud and they couldn't find a prevention platform that sold to small startups. His advice is that "it's important for organizations to protect themselves early on" [20:17] with appropriately sized, transparent solutions.

s11-bonus-why-babysitting-your-dev-team-is-killing-momentum-with-praveen-ghanta-founder-ceo-of-fraction-devhawk

Fractional Hiring Proved Itself First: At Hidden Levers, Praveen's bootstrapped fintech SaaS, 40% of the engineering team grew to be fractional. The first such engineer stayed nine years, and some fractional team members stayed through the 2021 exit.

No-Code Marketplace in Days: Fraction built its first talent marketplace on Softr's marketplace template, likely in under a week. The trade-off was less flexibility and the question of when to bite the bullet and rewrite it.

Ten Clients as the Test: The founders gave themselves six to eight months to reach 10 clients as proof the business was worth more investment. After hitting it, they built the team, hiring fractionally themselves.

Client Demand Rewrote the Plan: Fraction expected integration and DevOps roles to be big sellers, but startups most often needed full-stack help. Praveen now sees Python in about 50% of backend work and React in over 90% of front-end work.

Scaling People Led to DevHawk: To avoid layers of client managers, Fraction built DevHawk to monitor project boards, source control and chat, ping developers and flag problems early. It began as an internal tool and could become its own SaaS product.

q: What is Fraction and how does fractional engineering work?
a: Fraction, which Praveen Ghanta started in 2022, matches companies with senior engineers who work quarter time or half time, about 10 to 20 hours a week. Ghanta described helping startups and "growing companies engage with senior US based engineers on a fractional basis" [05:03].

q: How did Fraction build the MVP of its talent marketplace?
a: The team used Softr, a no-code platform with a marketplace template, to showcase its talent so potential buyers could shop for it. Ghanta said they were able "to spin up using that marketplace template, basically, in a couple of days, maybe a week" [07:43].

q: How did Praveen Ghanta validate the idea for Fraction?
a: Ghanta and his co-founders set an early target of 10 clients and gave themselves six to eight months to reach it, which they did. As he put it, "we need to see 10 expressions of interest in this business to prove that it's real enough" [16:25].

q: What is DevHawk and what problem does it solve?
a: DevHawk monitors signals from project management systems, source control, Slack and Teams, and handles low-level follow-ups so managers don't spend their days chasing developers. Ghanta said it brings attention to "problem areas before they really fester and a client becomes upset about it" [22:09].

q: What advice does Praveen Ghanta give early-stage founders?
a: Ghanta advises founders to share their ideas rather than stay secretive, and to charge even a very small price early. "I would say get someone to pay for it." [35:42], he said, because feedback from paying customers is worth far more than advice from people with no skin in the game.

the-railsware-way-conversational-analytics-data-focused-products-with-nika-tamayo-flores

Dashboards Monologue, Chat Dialogue: Dashboards assume you know where to look and what to ask. Conversational analytics lets users ask in plain language why a metric changed, with no SQL or pivot tables.

Schema Beats Context Limits: Coupler gives the model the data schema, source metadata and 5 to 20 sample rows. The LLM writes SQL, which Coupler then runs against the real data, even when it spans millions of rows.
Insights Shrink Decision Time: Coupler's AI Insights button turns aggregated dashboard data into key findings, trends and top recommendations. Nika reports an 89% satisfaction rate since launch.
Tailored Prompts Curb Hallucinations: Each template with insights has its own prompt, with rules such as not making up numbers. Schema knowledge, user feedback and human oversight add further checks.

Another Layer, Not Replacement: Nika expects dashboards to remain for KPI monitoring and alerts, while conversational analytics handles exploration and unexplained changes. Their dominance, though, is ending.

q: What is conversational analytics, and how is it different from traditional dashboards?
a: Nika Tamayo Flores describes traditional dashboards as a monologue, while conversational analytics lets you chat with your data and ask why something happened. As Nika put it, "And with conversational analytics, it's like a dialogue." [02:05]

q: How does Coupler handle large datasets that don't fit in an AI model's context window?
a: Coupler feeds the model a schema describing each column and its data type, source metadata, and 5 to 20 sample rows. Nika says that from this, "it can write SQL queries and it's very good at it" [07:11], and Coupler then runs those queries on the real data.

q: What does Coupler's AI Insights feature do?
a: On Coupler's native dashboards, it sends aggregated data to AI with custom prompts and returns key findings, trends and actionable recommendations. Nika says the most important result "is that users don't need so much time to understand what they need to check or do next." [10:16]

q: How can AI-generated data insights be kept accurate and reliable?
a: Nika points to prompt engineering with specific constraints, a tailored prompt for each template, schema knowledge and user feedback, while stressing that human oversight is still needed. One of the rules Nika describes is "Do not make up numbers. Or if you are referring to a number," [12:33] make sure it comes from the data.

q: Will conversational analytics replace traditional BI tools and dashboards?
a: Nika expects the two to complement each other, at least in the coming years, with dashboards monitoring KPIs and conversational analytics supporting exploration. In Nika's words, "dashboards are not going anywhere, but the dominance is ending." [20:36]

s11-e25-the-13m-bootstrapped-shield-moving-past-broken-point-scanners-to-unified-continuous-exposure-management-with-chris-wallis-founder-ceo-of-intruder

Start with a PDF: Intruder's first version was a monthly PDF telling customers whether they were secure and listing any issues. Three or four signed up before the team even thought about building a login UI.

Manual Work Behind the Button: Even with a front end, clicking scan sent the team a Slack notification and they did the work by hand. They had about 15 or 16 customers by the time a CTO was hired, who went on to fully automate the product.

Balance Feedback With Direction: Wallis warns that building only from customer feedback can leave you with something that already exists. Intruder weighs customer pain points against its own product direction to carve out its space.

Scale One Step Ahead: Intruder avoids over-engineering for scale. The app isn't built for millions of users because it doesn't have them, and the team stays one step ahead of current needs rather than five or six.

From Product to Awareness: Bootstrapped with no VC funding and around 56 people, Intruder now sees its main problem as not enough people having heard of it. Wallis points to go-to-market and a bigger marketing team as the next focus.

q: What is Intruder and what does it do?
a: Intruder is an exposure management platform covering applications, employee laptops and cloud systems. Founder and CEO Chris Wallis says of those weaknesses, "We find them before the hackers exploit them and we tell you about them so you can fix them" [02:52].

q: Why did Chris Wallis start Intruder?
a: Wallis had worked as a penetration tester and later used defensive tools inside one of the companies, where he found them confusing, time consuming and not very helpful. In his words, "what I really saw was those tools were really difficult to use" [03:56], and he thought he could build something better.

q: How did Intruder build its first MVP?
a: Chris Wallis, influenced by The Lean Startup, began with a service that used open source tooling behind the scenes and had nothing to log into. He recalls, "we just found our first customer and said, what we're going to do is send you a PDF once a month" [06:21].

q: How does Intruder balance customer feedback with its product roadmap?
a: Wallis weighs the pain points customers describe against the direction he wants to take the product. He cautions that relying only on feedback means "you might easily end up building something that looks like something that's out there already" [09:22].

q: What did Chris Wallis learn about building a startup team?
a: Wallis initially thought his job was building a product, but came to see it as building the team that builds it. As he puts it, "I'm not building a product, I'm building a team, and the team builds the product" [13:16].

s11-bonus-how-he-bypassed-enterprise-hospital-bureaucracy-to-build-an-ambient-ai-scribe-for-26000-independent-clinicians-with-erez-druk-co-founder-ceo-of-freed

Dinner Demo as Validation: Erez showed a doctor friend a recording, transcribed and run through the first ChatGPT with prepared prompts. Her reaction, and a next-day text asking when it would be ready, convinced him Freed would work.

HIPAA as the Hard Line: The MVP was a start-and-stop button that produced a simple clinical summary using off-the-shelf transcription and LLMs. The one non-negotiable was guaranteeing clinicians that recording patients was HIPAA compliant.

Quality, Then Workflow: Feedback showed that intelligence and accuracy mattered most, and that the clinical note was a gateway to other work. Freed expanded into visit prep and post-visit tasks such as referrals and billing.

Product-Led, AI-Only Growth: Freed was fully AI from the start, with no human scribes behind it. Clinicians can sign up, learn the product and invite their team without human help; Erez cites over 25,000 paying clinicians and 3 million visits a month.

Going In-Person Sooner: Remote work stopped working well as Freed grew. Erez moved to in-person in San Francisco despite no support from his leadership team, saw execution change, and wishes he had acted much earlier.

q: What is Freed and what does it do for clinicians?
a: Erez Druk, Freed's co-founder and CEO, says "Freed is an AI clinician assistant" [02:46]. It helps clinicians prepare for visits, get intelligence from patient visits and document them, with the aim of saving time and reducing burnout from administrative work.

q: How was the first version of Freed's AI medical scribe built?
a: Erez Druk and his friend Andre stitched it together in a few weeks using off-the-shelf tools: press start, talk to the patient, press stop and get a simple clinical summary. In Druk's words, "It was essentially a hyper-compliant conversation summarizer" [04:57].

q: How does Freed use product-led growth with clinicians?
a: Erez Druk says the goal is a product that requires no human intervention for users to succeed or pay. Clinicians sign up and learn the "product on their own, they can invite their team" [12:32] without help.

q: How is Freed expanding beyond clinical notes?
a: Erez Druk explains that the team learned "the clinical note is a gateway to many other workflows" [08:44], such as referrals, billing and preparing for the next visit. He says Freed is shifting from a scribe to a full assistant and is looking to become the AI platform for the clinic.

q: What was the biggest mistake Erez Druk made while building Freed?
a: Druk says it was probably staying remote too long, which cost time as the company grew and led to a lot of remote hiring. Of the move to in-person, he admits, "I felt it in my gut, but it took me a while to just act on it" [16:49].

the-railsware-way-delivering-value-through-bridges-with-sergiy-korolov

Separate Problems From Solutions: BRIDGeS maps benefits, risks, issues, goals and domain knowledge apart from solutions. Teams prioritize the problem side first, and those priorities then guide what to build.

Ship the Core Value First: Sign-up, password reset and pricing pages don't deliver your specific value. For a scheduling product, Sergiy says to get the first shareable booking link sent as fast as possible, even in a very simple wrapper.

Research Feeds the Problem Space: Before setting an AI direction in Coupler, the team used analytics, customer surveys and MeasureCamp conferences. They learned that data analysts worried about how AI would use their data and whether its results were reliable.

Test Assumptions Against the Funnel: A modern redesign may change nothing if the real drop-off happens later. Railsware used BRIDGeS in 2024 to assess marketing strategy for Coupler and Mailtrap against their issues, goals and resources.

Validate Demand Before Building: Mailtrap added an "email marketing soon" menu item linked to a Typeform. It drew more than 300 responses in the first few weeks, including which features users wanted prioritized.

q: What is the BRIDGeS framework from Railsware?
a: BRIDGeS stands for benefits, risks, issues, goals, domain knowledge and solutions, and Sergiy says it was inspired by the Pivotal Labs inception process. As Sergiy explains, "the goal of this framework is to separate the motivation, the problematic part, the problem part, and the solution part" [03:19].

q: What is the difference between delivering value and shipping features?
a: For Sergiy, value means leaving users better off by solving a problem, covering a risk or giving them a benefit. In his words, the "value is that you give something to the user" [05:05] that brings them to a better state.

q: How should a team approach the first version of a SaaS product?
a: Sergiy advises focusing on the core value before wrapper features such as pricing and settings. Using a scheduling product as the example, he said "the first link can be sent, should be sent as fast as possible" [10:11].

q: How does user research fit into the BRIDGeS process?
a: Research gathered beforehand becomes input to the problem space and helps the team prioritize its cards. For Coupler's AI direction, Sergiy said they found that for data analysts "it is an issue or a potential risk that they don't know what AI is going to do with their data" [16:08].

q: How did Mailtrap validate demand for email marketing?
a: Instead of building the feature right away, the team added a menu item marked as coming soon, with a Typeform asking about interest and feature priorities. Sergiy was surprised that within the first few weeks "there were more than 300 answers for that questionnaire" [22:44].

s11-e24-the-agent-swarm-architecture-moving-beyond-single-prompt-bots-to-orchestrate-5000-parallel-ai-agents-safely-in-production-with-mrinal-wadhwa-founder-cto-of-autonomy

Every Agent Is an Actor: Autonomy runs each agent as a stateful actor on a Rust runtime wrapped in Python. Agents can create thousands of sub-agents to finish jobs faster while keeping each agent's context small.

Scale Beyond Containers per Agent: Tests fit tens of thousands of agents in one 250 MB container. Connecting containers securely with Ockam pushed that to hundreds of thousands, even millions, working in parallel.

Demo First, Then Co-Build: After about two months of building in isolation, the team showed a demo to spark ideas. A bank asked for parallel loan document analysis, and building it exposed API and library interface gaps.

Documentation for Coding Agents: When a bank engineering director adapted their example in Cursor, the team made docs coding-agent friendly and began handing customers example prompts that build and deploy apps.

Prune Context to Stop Rot: Feeding full history back to the LLM worked for 5 or 10 steps but derailed longer runs. Carefully trimming each loop's input let agents stay coherent, including in hour-long voice interviews.

q: What is Autonomy and who is it for?
a: Mrinal Wadhwa, Founder and CTO, describes it this way: "Autonomy is a platform for developers to build and ship autonomous AI products." [02:46] It is meant for products delivered to internal or external customers, not personal scripts.

q: Why does Autonomy use the actor model for AI agents?
a: Mrinal explains that the properties of highly scalable actor systems suit agents because "agents are these long-lived concurrent state machines" [08:50]. Making each agent an actor lets developers create thousands of parallel agents easily and cheaply.

q: How many AI agents can run in parallel on Autonomy?
a: Mrinal says that after making the core design decisions, "we tested how many agents can we spin up in a single 250 megabyte container," [18:59] and the answer was tens of thousands. Across a distributed fleet of containers connected with Ockam, he puts it at hundreds of thousands, even millions.

q: How do you stop context rot in long-running AI agents?
a: Mrinal's team found that replaying the full history made the LLM noisy and confused over many iterations. As he put it, "the learning from that was actually what we need to do is prune and trim very carefully" [23:49] what goes to the model in each loop.

q: How did Autonomy build its MVP and find early customers?
a: The team spent two to two and a half months building before reaching out to people in their network. Mrinal says "It was minimum demo-able thing that we could go show to someone so it would evoke their ideas." [11:44] By the public announcement, five customers were live in production.

s11-bonus-the-canva-for-ai-agents-demolishing-the-code-barrier-to-build-connect-and-deploy-autonomous-multi-model-workflows-with-shamba-chowdhury-co-founder-cto-of-deforge

One Node Instead of Ten: Deforge is a visual no-code agent builder where a knowledge base, or RAG setup, is a single node. Shamba says n8n or Langflow would need 10 different nodes and many connections.
A Decoupled Node Library: The node library lives in its own repository, separate from the backend. New nodes can be added without backend changes, backed by a custom agent execution engine.
No Arrows for Execution Order: Users don't have to specify which node runs after which. The execution engine Shamba built from scratch works out the order, and it is the technical work he's proud of.
Copy-Paste Debugging Lesson: Shamba copied a node and forgot to edit its log messages, so errors pointed to a different node. The team lost hours before catching it in testing, before production.
Marketing Before Launch: The team did cold outreach and social media promotion before its August 23rd open beta, and was the number one product of the day on Product Hunt.

q: What is Deforge and who is it for?
a: Deforge is a visual no-code platform for building and deploying AI agents and workflows on a node-based canvas, aimed at everyone and not just coders. Agents can also be wrapped into a simple form, and as Shamba Chowdhury put it, "others give you the car parts, we hand you the keys." [04:00]

q: How is Deforge different from n8n or Langflow?
a: Shamba Chowdhury describes Deforge as similar to n8n and Langflow but much simpler and more user-friendly. For example, he says building a knowledge base elsewhere takes many nodes and connections, but "In Deforge, it's a single node." [03:21]

q: How does the Deforge agent execution engine work?
a: Shamba says the engine determines the order in which nodes should run without the user specifying it. Of users, he explained, "They don't have to drag arrows." [12:58] He did not go into the implementation, calling it part of the company's secret sauce that is not open source.

q: How did Deforge design its architecture to scale?
a: Shamba says the team made modularity a core philosophy so components could be built independently and still work together. The node library is kept apart from the backend and frontend, and he noted that "we can casually change our node library whenever we want" [07:04].

q: What advice does Shamba Chowdhury have for technical founders?
a: Shamba advises founders to have deep passion for the problem, since there will be setbacks, and to find a way to have fun. He also urges tech founders to market their work and to "remember that just building a great product isn't enough." [20:17]
