the-railsware-way-vibe-coding-vs-traditional-sdlc-with-sergiy-korolov

Separate Vibe Coding From Copilots: Railsware engineers use tools like Cursor and Copilot, which Sergiy finds especially strong for research, architecture options and learning unfamiliar projects, though not a 100%-plus boost for every engineer.

Iteration Is The Breaking Point: Prompting can produce a first version, but later changes may rewrite parts you never meant to touch. Sergiy doesn't see this as sustainable for software needing versioning, migrations and new features.

A Designer's Wheel Experiment: Designer Vlad spent days vibe coding a device simulator, then switched to Cursor and got an iPhone app with a spinning wheel. Asking for one turn gave him 10, but the progress still inspired him.

Best Fit Is Proof Of Concept: Product managers can prompt a standalone screen instead of building it in Figma, especially with detailed feature documentation. Fitting a feature into an existing interface's UX is much harder.

The Future Is Abstraction Layers: Sergiy expects vibe coding to assemble existing building blocks, as with n8n automations and potentially WordPress or Shopify. Coupler.io applies a similar idea, "vibe querying" data in natural language.

q: What is the difference between vibe coding and using AI coding tools like Cursor or Copilot?
a: Sergiy separates engineers using AI assistants in their development work from people without software experience generating apps from plain text. In his words, "it makes sense to separate vibe coding from the using AI tools for software development" [05:18].

q: Do AI coding tools really double developer productivity?
a: Sergiy says tools like Cursor and Copilot are handy and make reasonable contributions, particularly in research and architecture. However, he cautions that "it's not like 100 plus percent boost for every engineer as it is promised" [05:40].

q: What is vibe coding best used for?
a: Sergiy sees it as a good way for product managers to try out ideas, particularly separate features or pages designed from scratch. "I believe that proof of concept is the best applicable thing for product managers" [16:43], he said.

q: Can you build a scalable product with vibe coding?
a: Sergiy thinks a very simple, straightforward app, such as one for ordering a few flower packages, may be possible. For software that needs versioning and constant "iterations, improvements, development, then vibe coding is not a proper tool for this purpose" [19:48].

q: Where is vibe coding headed in the future?
a: Sergiy believes it will progress, partly because so much money has already been invested in it. He thinks "these vibe coding tools can move towards an abstract layer for more advanced systems" [21:31], pointing to n8n connecting automation blocks from a description.

s11-e23-why-generative-hype-fails-business-roi-and-how-predictive-ai-agents-solve-the-trillion-dollar-forecasting-gap-with-dr-zohar-bronfman-co-founder-ceo-of-pecan-ai

Talent Is the Bottleneck: Bronfman found that companies weren't doing predictive modeling mainly for lack of talent and expertise. Pecan's automated platform aims to let them build models with the people they already have.

A Prototype in Months: The first version took about two to three months. It accepted data as it natively existed in the business, produced predictive outputs, and started with revenue and demand forecasting.

Mid-Market Over Enterprise: Pecan chose a generic SaaS product over customized, big-ticket enterprise deals. It accepted higher risk, lower prices and slower short-term returns for a more sustainable, widely useful product.
Roadmap From Customer Pain: Pecan pairs usage data with interviews of customers, prospects, churned accounts and non-converters to learn what's missing, how alternatives compare and what people like.
Don't Overpromise Certainty: Bronfman told an all-hands no layoffs were planned, then cut staff weeks later after churn and canceled deals. He now says openly that startup conditions can change.

q: Why don't more companies use predictive modeling?
a: Dr. Zohar Bronfman's research pointed first to a shortage of people who can build the models. As he put it, "it's first and foremost a question of insufficient talent" [04:25], and Pecan AI was built to help organizations without large data science teams.

q: How was the first version of Pecan AI built?
a: Bronfman and his co-founder spent about two to three months building a prototype focused first on forecasting, such as revenue and demand. He described it as "a very simple system that takes data inputs in the way they exist natively in the business" [06:15].

q: Why did Pecan AI target the mid-market instead of enterprise customers?
a: Bronfman said the team chose a generic SaaS platform without custom work, despite the higher risk and potentially lower prices. He explained that this route sacrifices short-term returns, "but it forces you, on the other hand, also to develop a long-term sustainable product" [10:25].

q: What mistake did Zohar Bronfman make around layoffs at Pecan AI?
a: Bronfman told his team no reduction in force was planned, but bad news soon followed, including a major customer giving notice and big deals being canceled, and he ultimately decided to cut staff. Reflecting on it, he said, "that overconfidence is the mistake I'm regretting" [19:16].

q: What is next for Pecan AI's predictive platform?
a: Bronfman wants predictive modeling to be accessible to anyone, including executives without data aptitude, and to pair predictions with recommended actions. In his words, "you're also going to get a recommendation as to how you should be acting in accordance" [22:39].

s11-bonus-moving-past-semantic-layers-to-eliminate-hallucinations-and-build-dependable-enterprise-data-agents-with-tanmai-gopal-co-founder-ceo-of-promptql

Accuracy and Trust Come First: Tanmai's team concluded that the hardest problem for AI accessing business data isn't connectivity or API format. It's accuracy and trust, which they expect to matter even more as everything else improves.

Hasura as the Foundation: PromptQL kept Hasura's data connectors, security and policy engine, but swapped the GraphQL API for a virtual SQL API. Databases, APIs and vector stores can all be queried the same way.
Accuracy That Scales: A narrow pilot can look accurate with 10 users. PromptQL's North Star is staying accurate for thousands of users across hundreds of thousands of tables, metrics and APIs.

The One True Deck: To bridge product and go-to-market, Tanmai maintained a single messaging deck with two or three others. No copies or variations were allowed, and everyone had to learn the updates themselves.
From Agents to AI Co-Workers: Tanmai sees AI co-workers as the next step, defined by two traits: they're multiplayer, working with multiple stakeholders, and they learn continuously on the job.

q: What is PromptQL and how does it work?
a: PromptQL is a virtual AI analyst that business stakeholders or customers can ask for data insights or use to set up workflows on their data. Tanmai Gopal explains that the existing data team takes on a new role: "the analysts, they turn into teachers of the AI analyst." [03:15]

q: How does PromptQL connect AI to different data sources?
a: Tanmai says the team reused Hasura's data connectors, authorization policies and policy engine, replacing the GraphQL layer with SQL. Whether the source is a database, an API or a vector database, "it all feels like a SQL API, a virtual SQL API." [07:40]

q: Why do enterprise AI projects get stuck in the pilot stage?
a: Tanmai argues that narrow pilots don't do enough to change how users work, and their accuracy doesn't hold up when thousands of people start using them. In his view, accuracy has to "scale to a breadth of use cases, to a breadth of users, to the breadth and chaos of data" [13:15] inside an organization.

q: What is the One True Deck that Tanmai Gopal used at PromptQL?
a: It was a dense set of slides that served as the only definition of the product for both product and go-to-market teams, evolving for seven months as they learned from customers, product and sales. As Tanmai put it, "There was no other source of knowledge." [20:04]

q: What advice does Tanmai Gopal give to young entrepreneurs?
a: Tanmai advises founders to match their ambition to disrupt with a market deep enough to absorb it. He says that "the amount of disruption that you want to make has to be proportional to the depth that the market" [25:52] has.

s11-e22-the-support-capacity-paradox-managing-the-tri-border-workforce-of-humans-bpos-and-ai-agents-without-metric-depravation-with-ryan-wang-co-founder-ceo-of-assembled

Workforce Management Was the Problem: Ryan Wang and his co-founder first tried automating Stripe support tickets with machine learning. Stripe's head of support redirected them to the harder problem: forecasting volume and deciding who should work on what.

Productizing the Support Spreadsheet: Early customers' spreadsheets looked alike: one tab forecasting ticket volume, another working as a team calendar. Assembled turned that into software, though it took two years to launch.

Engineers Face the Customer: Assembled admits it was bad at roadmapping early on. What worked was sending engineers to customers, even shadowing support agents, and its engineering organization is still simply called "product."

Go as a Compounding Bet: After weighing Ruby, Python, Java and Haskell, the team chose Go for its simplicity, standard library and built-in tooling. Wang says it has saved time and is easy for AI coding tools to work with.

Second Product, Cultural Strain: Building AI agents with a separate team shipped a product quickly but almost broke the company. Customer feedback, shown to staff rather than sold to them, helped connect the new product to workforce management.

q: What does Assembled do?
a: Assembled, co-founded by CEO Ryan Wang, builds an AI platform for customer support, including AI agents for chat and phone, a copilot for human agents, and workforce management. Wang describes forecasting as central to the workforce side: "It's time series forecasting. All the things I described to you" [05:30].

q: Why did Assembled choose Go as its programming language?
a: The team considered Ruby, Python, Java and Haskell before choosing Go for its simplicity, standard library and built-in tooling. Ryan Wang explained, "we landed on Go because it was a very professional language" [17:53], and called it a compoundingly useful bet.

q: How did Assembled build its product roadmap in the early days?
a: Ryan Wang says the team was surprisingly bad at roadmapping for a long time and relied on close customer contact instead of product managers. As he put it, "the thing that did work for us was forcing engineers to be really customer-facing" [10:31].

q: How did a workforce management company move into AI agents?
a: Assembled added AI agent products after ChatGPT launched, starting the effort with a team in a separate room. Ryan Wang recalls a customer explaining why the move made sense: "okay, but I get it because you have all the data" [24:15].

q: How will human and AI agents work together in customer support?
a: Ryan Wang expects a lot of repeatable work to be automated, while human agents take on higher-leverage tasks such as training AI agents and creating policies. He sees Assembled providing "this orchestration layer of how much volume should go" [27:38] to AI agents versus human agents.

s11-bonus-the-agent-authentication-crisis-moving-past-prompt-engineering-to-build-zero-trust-tool-execution-and-secure-zktlsmcp-actions-planes-with-sam-partee-co-founder-cto-of-arcadedev

An SRE Agent Exposed the Gap: Arcade's first idea was an agent that autonomously solved bugs. Users kept asking how it reached Datadog and Grafana and whether it logged in as them, revealing agent authorization as an unsolved problem.

Sell Before You Build: Co-founder Alex Salazar pushed Sam to ask customers if they'd pay $100,000 before building. Sam built 10 V1 variants, and all shared a tool execution and authorization platform.

Auth Came First on the Roadmap: Tools were also locked inside client applications and couldn't scale separately. Arcade prioritized authorization because more people were blocked by it than by running computationally expensive tools.

Hire for What You Don't Know: Knowing he didn't know auth well enough, Sam first recruited auth expert Nate Barbatini, then Sterling Dreyer and Eric Gisson, infrastructure and open source engineers he had worked with before.

Instrument Agent Usage Early: Sam wishes Arcade had gotten analytics right sooner, since usage showed up in places the team didn't know about. Sporadic tool calls and runtime auth change how product feedback is collected; they now use PostHog and custom usage services.

q: What is Arcade.dev?
a: Sam Partee describes Arcade as an MCP platform where agents can access and manage tools from many servers and act on your behalf safely. He said Arcade "will provide you both an execution environment and an authorization environment" [03:21].

q: How did the idea for Arcade come about?
a: Sam's team was building an SRE agent to solve bugs, and feedback kept focusing on how it connected to services on users' behalf. Sam said it became clear that "there was a dire need for an authorization for the activities that agents wanted to be able to do" [05:01].

q: Why is authorization for AI agents different from traditional authorization?
a: Sam explained that an agent's runtime authorization can't be separated from the action it wants to take on your behalf. Agents also call tools sporadically, so "the auth is completely and utterly different" [16:13] and has to happen at runtime rather than being pre-authorized across thousands of services.

q: How did Arcade validate its first product before building it out?
a: Following Alex Salazar's playbook, Sam talked to many customers and showed them demos built on a set of tool calls the team knew would work. The question to prospects was "would you pay me $100,000 for this" [06:52], asked before going too far down any one path.

q: What advice does Sam Partee give to young entrepreneurs?
a: Sam advises getting comfortable being uncomfortable, taking risks and getting things done even when they aren't perfect, and starting as early as you can. In his words, "you just get used to being uncomfortable, and it's hard to do." [21:23]

s11-e21-synopsys-the-future-of-ai-how-we-are-building-it-with-raja-tabet-svp-at-synopsys

Three Phases of AI: Synopsys moved from AI as an optimization engine (2018 to 2021-22), to AI as an assistant (2022-23), to agentic AI as an engineer's colleague (since 2024). Each phase built on the one before.

DSO.AI Came First: The first AI MVP, DSO.AI for design space optimization, took about two to two and a half years from conception to early deployment. The approach then spread to other areas, including verification and test.

Roadmap From Engineers' Days: Synopsys studies a day in the life of digital, verification and implementation engineers to find high-toil work to automate. It pairs that with challenges customers face moving to new technology nodes.

Blending Domain and AI Skills: Core technologists who know chip design and algorithms built up AI knowledge, and were supplemented with data scientists and new AI talent to build models and semantic engines.

Agent Engineers Are Next: Tabet expects virtually every organization to stand up an agentic workforce, starting in the next 12 to 24 months. Synopsys is building agent engineers that customers could lease or buy to ease engineering bottlenecks.

q: What was Synopsys's first AI product for chip design?
a: Raja Tabet points to DSO.AI, a design space optimization product, as the first incarnation of the company's AI MVP, aimed at better results and faster time to market. He said "this product took about a couple of years, two, two and a half years from conception to early deployment" [07:57].

q: How is Synopsys using agentic AI in electronic design automation?
a: Tabet describes agentic AI as the third phase, after AI as an optimization engine and then as an assistant for knowledge, workflow and design generation. In his words, "we think about this new era as AI being a colleague or a companion to our engineering community" [10:19].

q: How does Synopsys decide what to build on its AI roadmap?
a: Tabet says the team looks at where different kinds of engineers spend their day and combines that with the challenges of moving to new technology nodes. As he put it, "the objective that we are driving for is to allow the engineer to continue really to solve engineering problems" [13:34], specifically high-value ones.

q: How did Synopsys build its AI engineering team?
a: According to Tabet, the company started with core technologists who understood design automation and chip design and were getting up to speed on AI, then added data scientists and other AI skills. He described the mix as "training technologists today in AI and bringing new AI talent into the fold" [16:47].

q: What are AI agent engineers, and what is Synopsys planning?
a: Tabet says Synopsys is working on agent engineers for personas such as digital, verification, implementation and analog engineering, to address capacity limits, time to market and design complexity. "We envision the future where our customers will be leasing from us or buying from us agent engineers" [21:17], he said.

a-startup-field-guide-in-the-age-of-robots-ai-with-oliver-mitchell

Five Rules for Automation Startups: Mitchell's tests are high utilization, reliability, reasonable payback, truly differentiated IP and target customers likely to adopt. A robot that lifts two tons once a week sits idle the rest of the time.

Kiva Started With the Problem: After seeing Webvan's costly fulfillment firsthand, Mick Mountz built robots that bring shelves to a stationary picker. Amazon later bought Kiva Systems for $775 million.

Interest Is Not a Purchase: Civ Robotics began with an autonomous staking drone that people loved but wouldn't buy. Pivoting to a ground robot helped it hit its stride, so ask early what customers will actually pay.

Match the Investor to the Business: VCs, corporate venture arms and government funders want different things. A corporate investor like GM Ventures looks for strategic integration into the core business, not just financial returns.
Escape Pilot Purgatory: Grants and pilots can stall if they're disconnected from the units that actually buy. Tie the work to end users' KPIs so a pilot can become a revenue-generating contract.

q: What are the essential rules for launching a successful robotics or automation company?
a: Oliver Mitchell points to high utilization, high reliability, reasonable payback, differentiated IP and customers with a high likelihood of adoption. On the first rule, he said, "So a robot, first off, needs high utilization." [05:49]

q: What can hardware founders learn from Webvan and Kiva Systems?
a: Mitchell says Webvan did too little customer discovery and built fulfillment centers without figuring out what it needed. Mick Mountz, who worked there, went on to start from the problem when creating Kiva, and as Mitchell put it, "He didn't say, I want to build a robot company." [10:55]

q: How do you validate product-market fit for a hardware startup?
a: Mitchell advises finding the decision maker and the ultimate customer, asking what they would pay and iterating on their feedback. He stresses "getting out of the lab and really getting out in front of customers early on" [19:14].

q: How can robotics and hardware startups attract investors?
a: Mitchell says the pool of hardware investors is small, so founders should research each fund's thesis, whether it is venture capital, corporate venture or government. He stresses that "it's not a homogeneous money pit" [15:02], and that early-stage decisions are driven first by the people, along with the product.

q: What is pilot purgatory when selling to government or large corporations?
a: Mitchell describes startups running grants and pilots that are divorced from the business units or military units that make purchasing decisions. He calls it "pilot purgatory, if you would, because they never make that crossover to actually getting a purchase" [22:31].
