s11-e20-the-death-of-the-black-box-algorithm-transitioning-from-rigid-rules-to-fully-autonomous-glass-box-contextual-ai-pricing-with-alex-halkin-founder-ceo-of-competera-ai

Spreadsheet Before Software: Competera's original version sent pricing advice in a Google spreadsheet. Alex Halkin landed first customers that way, with design layered on top and the customer's requirements, such as sharing and security, met.

A 300-Product Deadline Demo: Halkin promised 30,000 products live in 90 days, but only 300 were running at the deadline. He planned to show the larger number in the UI, and when one attendee noticed, tied delivering the rest to payment of the balance.

A Three-Part Healthy Backlog: Halkin balances releases that delight existing paying users, the most repeated requests from prospects, and paying down technical debt. Paying customers' feedback comes first.

Technical Debt Came Due: While bootstrapping, Competera put off technical debt. As the audience grew, it hit a Postgres table column limit during a Christmas season and went out of service, hurting customers who relied on its price recommendations.

Scaling Ahead of Adoption: After raising funding, Competera opened offices in places including Singapore, London and America in 2019, before the market was ready. Halkin calls it probably his biggest mistake and advises staying small as long as you can.

q: What does Competera AI do?
a: Competera, founded by Alex Halkin, uses AI to recommend optimal prices based on location, considering factors such as where a store is. Halkin describes it as "The kind of AI would guiding the retailers and brands" [03:07] to optimize prices, and cites cruise lines as customers.

q: How is contextual AI pricing different from rule-based pricing?
a: According to Alex Halkin, Competera's deep machine learning learns context, including business goals and how people interact with products in the store. It then advises prices "without the need of writing those rules" [05:04] or relying on consultants.

q: What did the first version of Competera look like?
a: It started far simpler than a full software product. Halkin recalled that "the original version of Competera was a spreadsheet where we're sending the advice" [12:11], and the team landed its first customers on Google Sheets.

q: How does Competera decide what to build next?
a: Alex Halkin uses what he calls a healthy backlog, saying "it's a healthy backlog has three things" [10:24]. Those are improvements for existing customers, the most frequently requested features from prospects, and technical debt.

q: What was Alex Halkin's biggest mistake while scaling Competera?
a: Halkin points to premature growth, including opening offices in several countries and hiring there after raising money, while AI pricing was still far from broad adoption. His lesson to founders is clear: "my advice is be small as long as you can" [18:29].

s11-bonusthe-spreadsheet-trap-why-custom-e-commerce-workflows-crash-in-the-back-office-and-the-rise-of-lightweight-fashion-erp-architecture-with-harish-chandramowli-co-founder-cto-of-flaire

Email CRM Came First: Flaire's MVP was a CRM for organizing email with manufacturers and buyers, because the first customer asked for it. Harish built it in Python from the ground up after studying the email protocols.

Backend-for-Frontend Paid Off: Splitting backend services from the front end let UI work be contracted out cheaply. Later, it let Harish and a founding engineer in India work independently with only an hour or two of overlap.

Piggyback on Shopify: Instead of building inventory logic first, Flaire sent received stock straight to Shopify's APIs and synced the data back. Shopify handled the math and concurrency, so features reached customers sooner.

Tie Roadmap to Revenue: Harish spent seven months letting customers without an e-commerce platform run their back office on Flaire, for $3,000 to $4,000 a year. He now links engineering spend and priorities to sales revenue.

Vibe Code Only Low-Stakes Pieces: For an AI-native rebuild, Harish wants money-related functions like invoicing kept standard and exposed through APIs with MCP tooling. Approval flows, UIs and reporting views can be vibe coded.

q: What does Flaire do for fashion businesses?
a: Flaire focuses on back-office operations in fashion, which co-founder and CTO Harish Chandramowli came to see as a workflow and data problem after observing a shop in Soho. As Harish put it, "We make the life for these business back office operations as easy as possible." [03:33]

q: What was the first version of Flaire?
a: It was a tool for organizing email, which the first customer said was hard when communicating with manufacturers and buyers. Harish recalled, "the very first version I built was literally a CRM, which is not like the back office operation management" [04:05].

q: How did Flaire build inventory management on top of Shopify?
a: Rather than updating its own database first, Flaire told Shopify through its APIs when items arrived from a manufacturer, then synced the data back. Harish explained that "Shopify takes care of all the complexities around like addition, subtraction," [09:19] along with concurrency when orders come in at the same time.

q: What mistake did Harish Chandramowli make when prioritizing Flaire's roadmap?
a: Harish spent seven months on a large build for customers without an e-commerce platform that did not bring in enough revenue. He described the error as "never tying down the business aspect of it to your prioritization, to your tech choices." [14:50]

q: How is Flaire thinking about AI and vibe coding?
a: Harish imagines rebuilding the product as AI native, where customers describe a workflow in natural language and the backend creates it. He draws a line at critical functions such as invoicing, saying that where money is involved, "you don't want to vibe code your entire stack." [16:53]

s11-e19-the-genai-fraud-wave-why-doc-uploads-and-pdfs-are-dead-and-how-zktls-generates-cryptographic-proof-with-madhavan-maddy-malolan-co-founder-ceo-of-reclaim-protocol

Proof Over Visual Cues: Maddy says checks that judge whether documents look authentic are being bombarded with AI-generated fakes. Reclaim instead proves what a user sees after logging into a source, such as a university portal.

From 15 Minutes to Seconds: The first version took six months and needed 15 minutes per proof, even on a top phone. Another year of research and engineering cut that to under one or two seconds, about 18 months from idea to real customer use.

Privacy Drove the Architecture: Reclaim chose to compute proofs client-side so it would not access users' sensitive data. The trade-off was heavy processing on phones. Pushing work to the client also eases some server scaling.

The B2C App Detour: Reclaim launched its own app, partly for low-level speed optimizations, but businesses didn't want users downloading another one. Maddy estimates delaying the shift to a B2B SDK wasted at least six months.

Verification for AI Agents: Maddy expects agents negotiating deals and discounts with other agents will need verifiable information, or they could be prompt-engineered. Reclaim wants to be ready to supply that infrastructure.

q: What is Reclaim Protocol and how does it verify users?
a: Reclaim Protocol, co-founded by CEO Madhavan "Maddy" Malolan, verifies information such as student status, employment and spending. A user logs into the relevant website, and as Maddy put it, "we generate a cryptographic proof that all of this happened" [05:06].

q: Why is document-based verification vulnerable to generative AI fraud?
a: Maddy explains that many verification companies look for visual cues that an ID is genuine or has been altered, and they are now being hit with AI-generated documents. His alternative to visual authenticity is that truth "should be grounded in cryptographic and mathematical proofs" [04:41].

q: How does Reclaim Protocol protect user privacy?
a: Maddy says the team decided early on to avoid having access to users' personally identifiable or sensitive information. He described the principle this way: "So all of the computation needs to happen client-side." [08:24]

q: How long does it take Reclaim Protocol to generate a zero-knowledge proof?
a: According to Maddy, the first version took 15 minutes to prove someone was a student, which was unacceptable. It took another year of engineering and research "to get to a point at which all of that could happen in under one or two seconds" [07:14].

q: What was Reclaim Protocol's biggest early mistake?
a: Maddy says the team stuck with its own consumer app for too long, despite customer feedback pointing toward an SDK for businesses. In his words, "we failed to realize that Verifications inherently is probably a B2B business." [16:11]

s11-bonus-the-100m-retirement-mistake-why-crypto-staking-regulatory-shifts-and-old-401k-rollovers-are-rescuing-the-next-generation-of-wealth-with-chris-kline-co-founder-coo-of-bitcoinira

Manual Trades to Real Technology: BitcoinIRA launched in June 2016 with small batches of accounts and phone trades. After the 2017 crypto run, the company hired a CTO, chief compliance officer and chief marketing officer to build it out.

Security Over Speed: Kline prioritized compliance and safety over launching features fast, despite client blowback and slower early growth. He credits that choice with building the credibility behind $14 billion in assets under custody.

Early Adopters Shaped the Roadmap: The first clients, including former NASA scientists, astronauts and athletes, told Kline what they needed. Their requests built the first roadmap, which later became a balance of efficiency and innovation.

A Fixed Security Budget: BitcoinIRA dedicates 30% of its roadmap points to security. Kline sees the user as the greatest weakness, exposed to SIM swaps and email hacks, and notes the company is now SOC 2 Type II rated.

Tokenization and Yield Ahead: Kline says four or five tokens already earn yield, paid in the asset held. Longer term, he sees tokenizing real estate, private equity and other assets, allowing fractional ownership.

q: Why was BitcoinIRA created?
a: Chris Kline was already working with self-directed IRAs when his partner asked him about Bitcoin, and it fit their mission amid what he calls a retirement crisis. In Kline's words, the vision "since we started was to help more Americans retire." [03:10]

q: What did the BitcoinIRA MVP look like?
a: Kline describes the original product, launched in June 2016, as down and dirty, with a lot of manual work and paper. "I remember being in the room helping people do phone trades back in 2016" [04:59], Kline recalled.

q: How does BitcoinIRA prioritize security on its product roadmap?
a: Kline says security has a permanent share of the roadmap, balanced against client requests and new features. As he explained, "we dedicate 30 percent of our points." [08:42]

q: Can you earn yield on crypto held with BitcoinIRA?
a: Kline says the company has created yield on certain tokens, with long-term holders paid back in the asset they hold, and he mentions Ethereum, Solana and Polkadot. "So we have four or five tokens that are making yield." [18:05]

q: What advice does Chris Kline give to startup founders?
a: Kline advises founders to focus on the problem rather than the technology, iterate quickly, take calculated risks and build a team that fills their weaknesses. He also stressed, "You have to be obsessed with the customer. I will repeat that three times." [20:44]

s11-e18-the-evolution-of-enterprise-automations-moving-beyond-fragile-rpa-to-natural-language-self-healing-workflows-with-theodore-bergqvist-co-founder-ceo-of-turbotic

Two Pivots to Vibe Automation: Turbotic began as an orchestration platform for enterprises with large automation installments, then pivoted to generative AI for mid-size companies. Its newest product lets non-engineers build their own automations.

Narrow Scope Beats Broad: Instead of covering everything, the team picked two or three core features and focused on usability, starting with simple automations for lightweight users who don't know coding or APIs.

Product-Market Fit Before Scale: Early talk centered on scaling, security and compliance. Theo now advises shoestringing technology and finding fit first, even if that means rebuilding an application that can't scale.

Don't Sell Before You're Ready: Turbotic spent heavily on sales reps, marketing and events before it had anything good to sell. Two attempts to set up a U.S. operation from Sweden also failed, burning funds and time.
Pivot the Team Too: Theo estimates 80 to 85% of the full team has turned over three times in about four and a half years. He sees a skilled, passionate and loyal core team as essential.

q: What is Turbotic's vibe automation product?
a: It is Turbotic's newest tool, built so people can create automations without being engineers or knowing a lot of coding. Co-founder and CEO Theodore Bergqvist described it this way: "Think of it more like Bolt or Lovable or anything else, but for automation." [04:27]

q: What problem led Theodore Bergqvist to start Turbotic?
a: While helping Ericsson with its transformation, Theodore saw that many companies investing in automation and AI faced a major challenge. In his words, "that was to scale the IT operational part." [03:10] He raised capital and began building Turbotic as an orchestration platform for enterprises.

q: What tools did Turbotic use to build its MVP?
a: Theodore said the team used Lovable to start prototyping the GUI and front end, alongside skilled developers who can spin up MVPs and demos. On the coding side, he said, "We've been using Cursor a lot for kind of building the code" [05:58].

q: What was Turbotic's biggest mistake?
a: Theodore pointed to heavy early spending on sales reps, marketing, events and sponsorships, which burned funds and time. As he put it, "we invested quite heavily in go-to-market sales and marketing machine before we even had a product." [13:55]

q: What advice does Theodore Bergqvist give young entrepreneurs?
a: Theodore advises being willing to pivot, whether that means the marketing idea, the team or the product, and building a highly skilled core team. He also recommends surrounding yourself with loyal people and rewarding them, and said of pivoting, "don't be afraid of pivoting because that is really, for me, it's been key." [17:47]

s11-e17-the-api-sprawl-cure-moving-beyond-graphql-federation-to-composable-type-safe-api-gateways-for-the-agentic-era-with-jens-neuse-founder-of-wundergraph

Pivot From a Dead End: After about a year and a half and nearly going broke, the team saw Apollo move from open to closed source, killed its first product, and built Cosmo because people had asked for open-source Apollo Federation.

Boring Stack, Fast Start: The bare-bones MVP paired a Go router with a TypeScript CLI and backend, a Next.js studio and Keycloak auth. Postgres and GCP Autopilot reflect Jens's rule to build on proven, boring tech.

Plan Queries Before Traffic: Cosmo caches query plans and uses analytics to warm up routers before they get a new config. A deduplication algorithm using fragments also cut oversized subgraph queries by 99%.
Commitment Before Code: The first product drew 2K stars but little success. Jens now asks prospects to commit early, such as by arranging an NDA, and moves on if they won't make the effort.

Senior Talent, Ambitious Juniors: Two junior hires from India helped CTO Dustin ship and, about three years later, know the domain deeply. When hiring, Jens weighs attitude and care heavily, since skill gaps can close quickly.

q: What is WunderGraph Cosmo and how does GraphQL federation work?
a: Cosmo is WunderGraph's fully open-source platform for GraphQL federation, also offered as a managed version. It splits one large API into services owned by different teams, and Jens Neuse said of API consumers, "They all think they talk to a monolith" [03:52].

q: Why did WunderGraph pivot to building Cosmo?
a: Jens Neuse said the company's first product wasn't working, and at a retreat in the Netherlands the numbers showed it was finished. Co-founder Stefan had notes from meetings, and Jens recalled, "a couple of people said, could you do Apollo Federation, but open source?" [07:32].

q: What tech stack did WunderGraph use to build the Cosmo MVP?
a: The first version had a router in Go, a CLI and backend in TypeScript, and a Next.js frontend, with Keycloak for auth, plus Postgres and GCP. Jens Neuse explained, "We try to use the most boring stack we can actually use." [10:19].

q: How does WunderGraph handle slow GraphQL query planning at scale?
a: Jens Neuse described a query planning cache plus a heuristics-based system that uses analytics to pick queries for warming up a router before it receives a new config. As he put it, "you never really plan a query, because we have planned it ahead of time." [20:40].

q: What is Jens Neuse's advice for technical founders?
a: Jens warns against hiding in code and adding features in the hope that success will eventually follow. He says that as a founder "your number one job is to talk to people, talk to customers" [26:23] and get them to commit to something.

s11-bonus-the-cloud-tax-the-10000-jvm-milestone-why-performance-optimization-is-the-only-way-to-scale-enterprise-ai-without-blowing-your-budget-with-simon-ritter-deputy-cto-of-azul

Pauseless Memory Management: Azul's early focus was letting Java applications keep updating objects while garbage collection moved them, safely. This cut latency pauses, which initially appealed to financial services such as stock and FX trading.

Performance as Cloud Savings: After tackling pauses, Azul changed the JIT compiler to win back lost throughput. Faster code lets customers carry the same transactions per second on smaller or fewer cloud instances.

Snapshots Beat Warm-Up Time: Java on CRaC checkpoints a running application, closing connections and files, then reopens them on restore. In an Azul benchmark, a Spring Boot app's four-second start to first transaction fell to 40 milliseconds.

Hiring for JVM Depth: The JVM is written in C++, so Azul seeks engineers who know its internal data structures and algorithms, not just Java programmers. That talent is scarce, so it looks to ex-Sun and Oracle people and academic researchers.

Knowing When to Quit: Azul tried bringing C-style struct memory layout to Java for better cache locality. It abandoned the project because the customer benefit was too small and getting it into standard Java would take too much effort.

q: What does Azul do?
a: Simon Ritter describes Azul's products as Platform Core, a supported build of OpenJDK; Platform Prime, a high-performance Java platform; and Intelligence Cloud. Of the supported distribution compared with Oracle's, Ritter said customers are "just paying a whole lot less" [05:16].

q: How can a faster JVM reduce cloud costs?
a: Ritter says many companies move workloads to the cloud and end up spending more than they did in their own data centers. With a better-performing JVM, he explained, "because it performs better, you can use smaller instances or less instances" [13:42] while handling the same number of transactions per second.

q: What is Java on CRaC (Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint)?
a: Ritter likens it to closing a laptop and reopening it later: a snapshot of a running Java application is restored from the same point, with the application closing and reopening resources such as database connections. Describing a Spring Boot benchmark, he said that restarting from a snapshot, "we reduced that four seconds to 40 milliseconds" [24:32].

q: How can you find which JVMs are actually using a vulnerable library like Log4j?
a: Ritter explains that Azul Vulnerability Detection monitors the class loader to see which classes are really being used, unlike a static software bill of materials that shows what could be used. In a Log4j-style incident, you could ask it to "show me all the JVMs that currently have Log4J loaded and are using it" [26:05].

q: What advice does Simon Ritter give to builders and entrepreneurs?
a: Ritter encourages builders to fail fast and iterate, but warns against a shotgun approach of trying everything. He advises not being afraid "to fail, but give it some thought before you go down different directions" [29:44].

s11-e16-the-vanity-metric-deception-why-counting-lines-of-code-fails-the-cursor-era-and-how-to-calculate-true-weave-hours-with-adam-cohen-co-founder-ceo-of-weave
Pivot From Summaries to Data: Weave began by using AI to summarize Slack, with plans to add Git and Jira. Users found the first release, built in about a week, noisy and not solving a real pain.

A Custom Model Measures Work: When users asked for proof, Weave trained its own machine learning model on thousands of hand-labeled PRs to gauge work done and how long PRs should take. The base version took two to three weeks.
Speed Can Outrun Performance: Pages began taking 30 seconds to a minute to load, and a couple of prospects said no because of it. The team blitzed the problem, largely by optimizing queries.

Customers Come Before Fundraising: Weave closed its seed round quickly but lost its biggest enterprise deal while Adam was busy with investors, the deck and negotiation. His lesson: prioritize customers and revenue.

Hire for Passion: Weave looks for people who have been fanatical about something, whether Ironman triathlons or watching a movie nearly every day, who are open-minded and passionate about bettering themselves.

q: What does Weave do for engineering teams?
a: Weave combines machine learning and LLMs to give engineering teams data on their work, including AI's role in it. Co-founder and CEO Adam Cohen said it works "with LLMs to show engineering teams how much work is getting done, how good it is" [02:46].

q: How does Weave measure engineering work?
a: Adam Cohen explained that Weave trained a custom machine learning model on thousands of hand-labeled pull requests, and has continued to fine-tune it. The goal is "to measure how much work is actually getting done and how long these PRs should take" [05:31].

q: Why didn't Weave's original Slack summarization tool work?
a: Adam Cohen said the first version drew very constructive feedback after its release. In his words, "people felt like it was noisy and it wasn't actually solving any pain" [03:51], so the team moved on to a separate platform focused on insights.

q: What scaling problems has Weave faced?
a: Adam Cohen said page loads slowed to 30 seconds or a minute, prompting customer complaints and costing some prospects before the team fixed it. He traced it to the fact that "we were shipping as fast as we possibly could without performance in mind" [10:29].

q: What mistake did Adam Cohen make while raising Weave's seed round?
a: Weave lost its biggest potential enterprise contract, a deal Adam Cohen believes was winnable, while the seed raise was underway. He said "we lost it because I was spending way too much time" [12:26] on investors and the work around fundraising.

s11-bonus-the-autonomous-railroad-revolution-replacing-time-consuming-visual-audits-with-computer-vision-wayside-tracks-at-120-kmh-via-kinetix-with-alan-fisher-group-vp-at-wabtec-corporation

Three Pieces of KinetiX: Wabtec assembled it through acquisitions: TrackIQ's acoustic and wheel condition detectors, Nordco's ultrasonic track inspection, and vision systems using lasers and high-resolution cameras.

Buying for Time to Market: Wabtec had prior vision products with strong qualities, but the math on re-engineering them for 20-plus years of harsh conditions favored acquiring. Fisher said that on some forums it was a bit of an emotional decision.

Roadmaps Built With Customers: With only six customers in North America, Fisher says a rail product team cannot work in a vacuum. Customers need to be involved in roadmapping, even at the early stages.

Gate Prototypes Before Production: A GoPro taped to a rail car can quickly become a fielded solution. Prototypes need a gate requiring design for manufacturing and long-term reliability before promotion to production.

Report Problems Solved, Not Algorithms: At a prior railroad job, Fisher's updates focused on algorithms instead of how many defect cases were solved. He thinks it cost momentum and sponsorship as the work felt like a science project.

q: What is Wabtec's KinetiX?
a: KinetiX is Wabtec's portfolio of rail inspection technologies, covering acoustic and wheel condition detectors, ultrasonic track inspection and computer vision. Alan Fisher describes it as "a set of inspection technologies that inspect" [03:19] trains as they travel along the track, looking for defects, some of which could be catastrophic.

q: How does computer vision inspect moving trains?
a: Fisher explains that the vision systems are "using lasers and high-resolution cameras to capture a train as it goes by a portal" [09:19]. The images are then inspected for defects, and the hard part is triggering lasers, lights and cameras at the right moment to capture a very small part on a train going 60 miles an hour.

q: Why did Wabtec acquire vision inspection technology instead of re-engineering its own?
a: Fisher says rail products are expected to last 20 or more years in harsh conditions, and Wabtec weighed that against its earlier vision solutions. In his words, "the time to re-engineer that, hey, time to market is really important and we've got to go acquire." [11:17]

q: How do you move a rail technology prototype into production safely?
a: Alan Fisher recommends balancing speed with "having a gating system around that prototype so that prototypes do not get" [18:07] promoted into production without a full phase of designing for manufacturing and long-term reliability. He considers finding that sweet spot the hardest part of scaling within rail.

q: What is the future of railroad inspection technology?
a: Fisher sees data science combining inputs such as vision images, microphone array readings and track temperature to improve preventive maintenance and prevent derailments. He is also interested in robots working in dangerous places, saying that "deploying robotics to perform some of those repairs is really interesting." [25:39]

building-identity-orchestration-for-ai-agents-with-granville-schmidt-of-strata

Translate Instead of Rewrite: One enterprise with hundreds of apps was quoted millions of dollars and years of rewrites to move identity to the cloud. Strata instead translates between old apps and the identity provider in real time.

Three Horsemen of Identity Debt: Granville names vendor lock-in, the rewrite trap and identity spaghetti. Orchestration makes apps vendor agnostic and adds SSO and stronger login flows without changing app code.

Identity That Survives Outages: Strata's platform can handle authentication and authorization fully disconnected, so a retail chain's cashiers can still log in and process transactions when a Category 5 hurricane takes down connectivity.

Agents Break Static Roles: Traditional identity assumes stable, long-lived human accounts. AI agents can be ephemeral, change roles at a moment's notice and spin up more agents, so the core challenge is governance rather than load.

Delegation Chains and Human Approval: Agent actions must trace back to a human decision across every system. Out-of-band, policy-based checks can require a person's approval for sensitive actions without approving every step.

q: What is identity orchestration?
a: Granville Schmidt of Strata compares it to a universal translator that sits between applications and the identity provider, whether an app uses SAML, OIDC or legacy headers. Apps keep their code, and as he put it, they "speak their old language, but we translate everything in real time." [03:26]

q: What identity tech debt problems does identity orchestration solve?
a: Granville describes three horsemen of identity tech debt: "You have vendor lock-in, you have what we call the rewrite trap, and identity spaghetti." [05:14] Orchestration lets companies move apps to a different identity provider, avoid risky authentication rewrites and standardize inconsistent login flows.

q: How can authentication keep working in DDIL (disconnected) environments?
a: DDIL stands for disconnected, disrupted, intermittent and limited bandwidth, such as a store trying to stay open during a hurricane. Granville said Strata built a platform that allows these "systems to operate in fully disconnected mode from the authentication and authorization perspective." [09:14]

q: Why do AI agents need a different approach to identity management?
a: Agents can change roles quickly, spin up other short-lived agents and act far faster than people can monitor. Granville explained that "the typical identity systems are meant for these static roles for humans, right?" [14:40]

q: How does Strata keep humans in the loop for AI agent actions?
a: Granville said Strata treats agents like air traffic control, giving each one permissions and constraints and tracking its life cycle. For sensitive operations, "an agent can prepare everything but needs human approval to execute." [17:14]

s11-e15-passing-telco-infrastructure-costs-to-advertisers-and-scaling-an-all-ip-wireless-carrier-to-300m-downloads-with-derek-ting-co-founder-ceo-of-textnow

Frugality Sparked the Product: Derek Ting built TextNow in college to avoid AT&T's $20 monthly texting fee on top of calling and data. Unlike other apps at the time, friends didn't need it installed to get his texts.
iPod Touches Revealed the Market: Many early users were on iPod Touches because they couldn't afford a phone plan. That insight widened the goal from free texting to free phone service.

Email Gateways Powered V1: The first version sent texts for free through carriers' email-to-text addresses. It could only send, and building the much harder receiving feature led Ting to recruit a classmate who became co-founder.

Roadmap From Repeated Signals: Early priorities came from patterns in user feedback, not a multi-year plan. Sometimes the response wasn't building anything, but testing price after users said a one-time $5 was too expensive.

Always Have Backups: Working solo and tired, Ting wiped the production database with a typo during a live edit. He rebuilt it with a script that replayed actions from log files, in what he recalls was an all-nighter.

q: How did TextNow get started?
a: Derek Ting was a college student with the first iPhone who didn't want to pay extra for texting. He explained, "TextNow first started as an app that I built to not have to pay for texting" [04:20].

q: How did the first version of TextNow send text messages for free?
a: Ting used carrier email addresses tied to phone numbers, so an email arrived on the recipient's phone as a text, and the app hid that process behind a normal messaging interface. As Ting put it, "lot of these carriers have what they call email gateways" [07:00].

q: What scaling problems did TextNow face early on?
a: Ting said the backend stopped working as usage grew and couldn't handle the load. In the first year, a Christmas morning spike from people opening new iPod Touches took the service down, and Ting recalled, "And it totally crashed our servers" [11:56], leading to all-nighters with his co-founder over the holidays.

q: What does TextNow offer for free?
a: In the interview, Ting described free talk and text through the app, plus a SIM card for cellular coverage where users pay about $5 for shipping. He also said, "we do have a basic free data plan where you can use our app" [18:06] and a few other apps such as email, maps and ride share, while broader data is a paid add-on.

q: What advice does Derek Ting give to startup founders?
a: Ting advises founders to trust their own instinct over the noise from venture capitalists and advisors, since each journey is different. He also said that "grit and persistent is the common thing that will prevail" [21:54].

s11-bonus-the-77-token-tax-why-fixed-token-chunking-is-poisoning-your-enterprise-rag-pipelines-and-how-to-fix-the-ingestion-layer-with-dr-alex-kihm-founder-ceo-of-poma-ai

Cost Exposed the Chunking Problem: In a private demo of a legal RAG chatbot, one question cost $1 because so much context was needed, and the full context became convoluted. That led Alex's team to focus on chunking.

Indent Text Like Code: POMA has an LLM repeat text verbatim with indentation that reveals its structure. Asking for summaries or other metadata was avoided because it can introduce bias and hallucinations.

Chunk Sets Over Chunks: Customers embed root-to-leaf paths through the document tree, from title through headings to sentence. Retrieved paths are then fused into a "cheat sheet" of only the relevant lines.

Narrow the Product Further: POMA, still pre-revenue with design partners, had planned to take PDFs and return chunks. When partners said they already had text, the team cut that scope to focus on chunking.

Sample Before Full Runs: A typo-level bug ran through a pipeline on all 200,000 parsed legal texts, costing a lot of money. Alex didn't blame anyone; the team reran on a 1% sample before going to 100%.

q: What problem led to the creation of POMA AI?
a: Dr. Alex Kihm's team was building a domain-specific chatbot for lawyers using retrieval augmented generation. At a private demo, they found that "in the end, one question would cost $1" [04:43], and the large context also became garbled, which pointed them to chunking.

q: What are POMA AI's chunk sets?
a: Kihm explained that "what our customers embed are not chunks anymore, but are what we call chunk sets" [07:31]. Each one follows a root-to-leaf path through the document's tree, running from the title through the headings down to a sentence.

q: Why doesn't POMA AI use LLM summaries when chunking documents?
a: Kihm said that asking an LLM for meta information, such as a chapter summary, is a risk in a system meant to avoid hallucinations: "This always creates a potential bias." [06:32] POMA instead keeps the text verbatim and has the LLM indent it to expose its structure.

q: How much energy can POMA AI's chunking approach save?
a: According to Kihm, "it saves between 50 and 80 percent of energy" [17:15] for the same question. He said it also delivers more accuracy.

q: How did POMA AI decide what product to sell?
a: Kihm drew on his earlier companies and kept reducing the offering, dropping PDF handling after design partners said they already had text. As he put it, "If we are the chunking guys, let's really focus on chunking." [14:17]

what-founders-need-to-know-with-dan-eyman-of-meld-valuation

A Cap Is Not a Valuation: A SAFE's valuation cap is a contractual term that protects investors. It ignores fundamentals like product traction and market dynamics, even as rolling SAFEs push caps from $5 million to $25 million.
SAFEs Differ From Debt: Convertible debt accrues interest, has a maturity date and gives investors recourse. SAFEs don't. With post-money SAFEs, which Dan recommends, dilution is fixed at signing.
Early Overvaluation Backfires: An inflated early round pressures later raises and risks a down round, which can create internal friction when newer employees get cheaper options than earlier hires.

Know Your Dilution Path: Dan typically sees founders hold 50-60% after seed, 30-40% after Series A and 10-20% after Series C or D. Model SAFEs, option pool expansion and exit waterfalls to avoid surprises.
Don't Dismiss the 409A: Auditors review past 409As at later rounds or an exit. If they reject them, you may have to redo them and reprice options, and rush jobs before a sale get expensive.

q: Is a SAFE valuation cap the same as my company's valuation?
a: No. Dan Eyman explains that nobody setting a cap is performing an independent analysis of the company's fundamentals: "It's a contractual term. It's not a valuation." [09:11]

q: What is the difference between a SAFE and convertible debt?
a: Dan Eyman stresses that a SAFE is a simple agreement for future equity, not a note, while convertible debt is true debt that accrues interest. Of convertible debt, he says, "It has a maturity date and has recourse for the debt investor." [06:17]

q: Why does a 409A valuation matter for startups?
a: A 409A sets the fair market value of common stock so that stock options can be issued under IRS rules. Dan Eyman warns that auditors will review past 409As later, and "if they won't accept them, you're going to have to redo them" [14:50].

q: How is a 409A valuation different from ASC 820?
a: According to Dan Eyman, a 409A is done at the company level and aims for a low but defensible value for common stock, while ASC 820 in venture applies to the fair value of a fund's holdings. He places it between the option value and the fundraising value: "ASC 820 aims to be in the middle for the investor." [16:27]

q: How should founders think about dilution when raising money?
a: Dan Eyman says dilution is a normal part of fundraising, but founders should model it so they aren't surprised and should weigh the value of their stake, not just the percentage. As he puts it, "I'd rather own 10% of a $500 million company than 100% of a $5 million one" [18:12].

s11-e14-dismantling-the-data-team-bottleneck-with-watsonx-powered-generative-business-intelligence-genbi-with-avi-perez-co-founder-cto-of-pyramid-analytics

A Full Rebuild After Silverlight: Pyramid's first generation used .NET and Silverlight, until Apple's iPhone and iOS undercut browser plugins. The second moved to a React and TypeScript front end with a Java back end built as "mini services."

Owning the Plumbing to Scale: After months lost to unexplained slowdowns, the team built its own networking protocols, compression and browser visualization mechanics. Avi says one customer runs about 100,000 users on roughly 150 nodes in a single instance.
Hire Thinkers Over Coders: Avi tests candidates on logical problem solving more than coding, looking especially for spatial thinkers. His view is that programming can be taught, but thinking can't.

Make Changes Additive, Not Destructive: Even legitimate bug fixes can break behavior customers rely on. Pyramid adds UI or back-end switches to preserve the old way, and Avi warns that big UI changes can cause churn.

Small Team, Giant Competitors: With a team Avi puts at probably a tenth the size of its nearest competitor, Pyramid wins what he estimates is eight in ten technical bake-offs. The harder fight is matching rivals' marketing and sales budgets.

q: What does Pyramid Analytics do?
a: Avi Perez describes Pyramid as a platform that takes raw business data through preparation, modeling and analysis so it can drive business decisions, including through natural language and AI. As Avi put it, the design concept "is to make the sophisticated simple" [03:46] for non-technical users.

q: Why did Pyramid Analytics rebuild its product from .NET and Silverlight?
a: Avi says Silverlight was a great programming experience, but Apple's iPhone and iOS effectively killed browser plugins. The team moved to JavaScript with React and switched the back end to Java, partly to connect more easily to many data technologies, and Avi said "the second generation of the product is like a complete redo" [07:32].

q: How does Pyramid Analytics scale to large enterprise deployments?
a: The team wrote much of its own plumbing, designed the platform to run across multiple machines or in containers with Kubernetes, and made the web client sessionless so it doesn't need sticky sessions. Avi said of building it themselves, "because we owned it, we knew where all the bodies were buried" [15:27].

q: What does Avi Perez look for when hiring developers?
a: Avi is most interested in strong thinkers, particularly spatial thinkers who can solve complex problems in their heads, and tests candidates on logic problems. As he put it, "Programming I can teach you, but thinking I can't." [13:31]

q: How can software teams avoid breaking existing customer workflows during upgrades?
a: Avi advises adding a user-facing or back-end switch that lets customers keep the old behavior, even when the change is a legitimate fix. He said of Pyramid's approach, "We always find a way to make the change additive rather than destructive." [22:28]

s11-bonus-the-on-call-burnout-cure-moving-past-noise-heavy-dashboards-to-autonomous-agentic-sre-triage-with-goutham-gou-rao-co-founder-ceo-of-neubird

Practitioners Building for Themselves: NeuBird's founding team had all held IT ops roles, which Goutham Rao says made the MVP fairly easy: use LLMs to dig through telemetry and cut incident response time for on-call teams.

Adapt to Existing Workflows: Users struggled to work out how to interface with an agent, so NeuBird moved Hawkeye behind the scenes as an agentic backplane inside existing IT service management tools.

Context Beats Data Volume: Too much telemetry creates noise, and LLMs will answer regardless. NeuBird's secret sauce is surgically extracting only what is relevant to the incident, while leaving storage to existing observability platforms.

Triage Before Inference: With GPUs limited and some companies facing thousands of alerts an hour, NeuBird uses AI for grouping, deduplication, correlation and causality analysis to distill the flood into a few core issues.

Beta With Co-Development Partners: Rao called on past customers to test a slow, half-baked Hawkeye that sometimes needed nudging. The beta took three to five months and showed what ops teams wanted first, leading to GA around December.

q: What is NeuBird and why was it created?
a: NeuBird builds Hawkeye, an agentic AI Site Reliability Engineer that helps manage the health of IT operations by triaging and remediating issues. Goutham Rao and co-founder Vinod wanted to clone their own troubleshooting skills because, as Rao said, "we've spent way too much time debugging issues at two in the morning" [04:41].

q: How does NeuBird's Hawkeye handle a PagerDuty alert?
a: Rao explains that Hawkeye picks up the alert within minutes and, a couple of minutes later, produces a report that engineers can review instead of doing the digging themselves. In his words, "it creates what's called this root cause analysis report, which contains detailed information about the incident, the evidence" [12:34].

q: How do you stop noisy IT telemetry from misleading an AI SRE agent?
a: Goutham Rao says the key is context: extracting exactly what could be relevant to the incident so the LLM can reason well, which he frames as an algorithmic and data structure problem. The challenge, as he put it, "is you are sitting on a sea of data and all of that is largely useless for the issue at hand," [18:40].

q: How does NeuBird deal with thousands of alerts at once?
a: Rao notes that GPUs are limited, so handling many incidents simultaneously adds time. Before running inference, NeuBird had to "deploy AI to do things like incident grouping, deduplication, correlation, causality analysis" [21:04], narrowing a barrage of alerts to a few core issues.

q: How did NeuBird get its first users and shape the product?
a: Rao called on customers who were fans of his and Vinod's prior products, including those from Portworx, and gave them beta versions of Hawkeye to get feedback. "I'm a firm believer in building alongside what we call co-development partners." [09:36], Rao said.

s11-e13-from-frictionless-saas-auth-to-eliminating-the-11-drone-pilot-bottleneck-at-the-tactical-edge-with-matt-hamann-co-founder-cto-of-rownd

Pivot to Passwordless: Rownd entered Y Combinator pitching a data privacy product, saw there probably wasn't a market for it, and pivoted to passwordless-first authentication that didn't support passwords at all.

A Deliberately Narrow MVP: The team aimed to build in two or three weeks on existing TypeScript, React and Node.js code. It only did email magic links, and they onboarded customers by hand, doing much of the integration work.

Weekly Iterations Over Long Roadmaps: Rownd skipped three- and six-month roadmaps for one-week cycles driven by customer needs, later moving to two weeks. Focused "jams" got features like passkeys ready ahead of demand.

Shaky Foundations Get Exposed: Serverless compute was hard to observe, and an outage or heavy degradation lasted most of a day. The team moved to more stable compute, improved visibility and apologized to customers, and Hamann doesn't think they lost any.

Migrating While Still Scaling: Rownd's database provider, already showing scaling issues, essentially went out of business and gave them two months to move all data. The team migrated while continuing to meet growing customer demand.

q: What is Rownd and why did it go passwordless?
a: Rownd is what Matt Hamann calls a next-gen, frictionless authentication platform, born from a pivot away from a data privacy idea and the founders' shared dislike of passwords. On the security logic, Hamann said, "If you don't support passwords, your password can't get hacked." [04:25]

q: What was in the first version of Rownd's passwordless MVP?
a: Users entered an email address, received a link and clicked it to authenticate their browser tab. Hamann said, "And all that it could do was email magic link authentication." [06:25] The team manually onboarded early customers and used what it learned to improve onboarding and the SDKs.

q: How does Rownd decide what to build next?
a: Hamann puts listening to customers first, with early design partners helping shape the product. He explained, "So we avoided creating a three-month roadmap or a six-month roadmap and early on actually focused" [08:01] on one-week iterations, which more recently became two-week cycles as features grew more complex.

q: What did Rownd learn from its major service outage?
a: Hamann said the team was running key business logic and APIs on serverless technology and lacked the data to make good scaling decisions. While triaging, "we realized that our foundation was shaky" [16:50], which led to a plan for more stable compute, better visibility and an apology to customers.

q: What scaling challenges has Rownd faced with its authentication platform?
a: Hamann pointed to raw compute and database capacity, which the team balanced by weighing added compute and its cost against more efficient queries. Rownd also had to migrate databases on short notice because, as Hamann put it, "the database provider essentially went out of business and gave us two months to" [13:48] move the data off.

s11-bonus-why-your-corporate-ai-pilots-are-yielding-zero-roi-with-greg-shove-ceo-of-section

Pivoting After the Pandemic Boom: Section's management training went from zero to $10 million in revenue, then sales crashed. Greg Shove cut the team and, from February 2023, repointed the business at training people for the age of AI.

Disrupting Your Own Courses: Shove asked how an AI-native rival would beat Section's $50-a-month learning product. His answer was to build ProfAI, a personalized AI coach, price it aggressively or give it away, and ship the MVP early.
Pricing Around Inference Cost: Certifying someone in AI takes about an hour of conversations and under 50 cents of inference. With that cost falling, Section made ProfAI free for consumers.

Innovate on the Business Model: Incumbents can usually catch a product innovation. Shove argues startups should pair a better product with a new way to charge, such as fixed prices for finished legal work instead of billable hours.

Don't Invent Scale Problems: Shove thinks founders and investors worry about scale too early. His advice is to drive adoption, usage and customer volume, then solve scaling pinch points when growth actually creates them.

q: What is Section AI and what does ProfAI do?
a: Section, led by CEO Greg Shove, helps companies transform their workforces for AI by combining services such as change management and workflow redesign with a SaaS product. That product, ProfAI, is a personalized AI coach, and as Shove put it, "we're using AI to coach you on how to use AI" [05:31].

q: Why did Section pivot to AI training?
a: Sales of Section's management courses crashed after the pandemic, and in February 2023 Greg Shove spent a few hours with GPT and decided to pivot. He saw that "the workforce would split and there'd be a bunch of people in the AI class" [04:30], while others would find the tools scary and hard to use.

q: How did Section build its AI product roadmap?
a: Greg Shove started with a course on setting an organization's AI strategy, then built a ProfAI MVP focused on teaching people to prompt in a way personalized to their job and company. He pushed it out early and let users guide what came next, saying "your roadmap starts to basically reveal itself" [09:17].

q: How much does it cost to train someone in AI with ProfAI?
a: Greg Shove said the figure he tracks is Section's inference cost, which covers about an hour of conversations in which a user learns to prompt and finds use cases. In his words, "It's under 50 cents to certify someone as being trained in AI" [09:50], and Section offers it free to consumers.

q: What is Greg Shove's advice for young entrepreneurs?
a: Shove says founders should care about the problem and the customer more than the solution they have built, because building a company takes years of struggle. His top advice is that "you better care a lot about the problem that you're solving" [17:46], and he warns against buying into AI hype about tiny teams reaching huge revenue.

s11-e12-the-agentic-auth-crisis-why-ai-agents-are-forcing-saas-to-shift-from-user-directories-to-short-lived-scoped-token-planes-with-ravi-madabhushi-co-founder-cto-of-scalekit

Customers Pulled the Agent Pivot: ScaleKit began with human-focused identity and auth. Repeated customer questions about MCP servers and API authentication revealed a pattern that moved the team into agent authentication.

A Deliberately Narrow MVP: After about four months of customer conversations, the team spent three to four months building only SSO and SCIM as a service, so companies with existing auth could become enterprise ready in days.

Reliability Built In Early: Because customers trust ScaleKit with product security, security, reliability, availability and performance came first. The stack is a Golang monolith on GCP with Cockroach as the persistent store.

Solve the 90% First: Knowing every auth edge case led the team to build for scenarios no customer had hit. They now focus on common problems and handle extreme corner cases only when there is a clear, present need.

Agents May Outpace Human Access: Ravi's hypothesis is that agentic access to apps and APIs will soon surpass human and machine-to-machine access, requiring auth that is secure and auditable, whether agents act alone or for users.

q: What is ScaleKit?
a: Ravi Madabhushi, Co-Founder and CTO, describes it this way: "ScaleKit is an authentication platform for AI applications and agentic workflows" [02:46]. It is modular, so customers can adopt the full package or only pieces such as MCP server auth, API auth, SSO or SCIM.

q: Why did ScaleKit move into AI agent authentication?
a: Ravi says customers pulled the company there by asking about MCP servers and API authentication, which the team first handled in an advisory role. As he put it, "when we keep hearing the same problems again and again, we realize that there is a pattern" [10:12].

q: How can developers add OAuth to an MCP server with ScaleKit?
a: ScaleKit offers an OAuth layer that developers can add without building the entire OAuth infrastructure themselves. Ravi explained, "we have a drop-in authorization platform for MCP servers where anyone can use a platform" [10:36].

q: What tech stack is ScaleKit built on?
a: Ravi says the team uses GCP as its cloud platform and Cockroach as its persistent store to get high availability from day zero. He added that "our entire platform is built as a monolithic platform on Golang" [07:58], which he said is not very memory intensive and is easy to scale.

q: What mistake did the ScaleKit team make with premature optimization?
a: Ravi says the team spent significant engineering effort covering edge cases and hypothetical scenarios that no customer had encountered. He admitted that "we were actually slowing ourselves down" [17:40], so they refocused on the problems customers face day to day.

s11-bonus-the-modern-playbook-for-pioneering-feature-flags-as-a-measurement-layer-with-trevor-stuart-co-founder-of-split-gmsvp-of-feature-management-at-harness

Born From an Internal Tool: Split grew out of a system built at RelateIQ to gate code in production. It proved itself one Friday when switching off a flag brought the website back, sparing the team a night of rollbacks.

Follow the Integration Signal: Every customer was using Split's impressions webhook to send flag evaluation data downstream and measure impact. That signal pushed the company into experimentation and release monitoring.

Always Build for 10X: Flag changes had to propagate worldwide in milliseconds, but data was the bigger scaling challenge. Split joins trillions of impressions with monitoring and analytics data, rebuilding repeatedly for 10X.

Naming Can Cost Discoverability: Split avoided calling its object a feature flag because it saw flags as an entry point to a bigger product. As developers searched for feature flags, that choice hurt discoverability and forced customer education.

Merging for One Plus Three: Harness is combining its flagging product's pipelines, policy enforcement and permissions with Split's data, monitoring and experimentation. Rollout to customers began within 12 months of the acquisition.

q: How did Split get started?
a: Trevor Stuart and his co-founders first saw the idea work at RelateIQ, where an internal tool helped the team release faster while limiting quality issues. Trevor said one future co-founder "spent his nights and weekends building this early primitive" [04:22], and after Salesforce acquired RelateIQ, the three started Split around it.

q: What was the hardest part of building Split's feature flag product?
a: Trevor Stuart said the first prototype, with a Java SDK, a UI, percentage rollouts and light logging, came together quickly. In his words, "the hardest part was not getting to that kind of early MVP, but it was about scaling it" [06:48] to serve flags around the world and across many kinds of devices.

q: Why did Split expand from feature flags into experimentation?
a: Trevor Stuart said the team already wanted to go that direction, and customer behavior validated it. Every customer was using one "integration within our product. It was our impressions webhook." [07:52] They were sending data on who saw which feature to other tools to understand the impact on their users.

q: What was one of the biggest mistakes Split made?
a: Trevor Stuart pointed to never calling the product's core object a feature flag, using terms like tests, experiments and splits instead. He said "that was probably one of the bigger mistakes, which just introduced friction" [15:34], since it hurt discoverability and meant customers had to be taught the language.

q: What happened to Split after Harness acquired it?
a: Trevor Stuart explained that Split is being merged with the feature flagging product Harness already had, pairing release automation and enterprise controls with Split's experimentation and monitoring. He said the effort is about "bringing those two products together into a one plus one equals three scenario" [19:20].

s11-e11-the-auth-to-growth-pipeline-eliminating-legacy-ciam-friction-and-building-customer-facing-infrastructure-for-the-product-led-growth-era-with-dave-berner-vp-of-product-at-kinde

Build for Most People: After early customers pulled the roadmap toward obscure auth features, Kinde adopted a rule: if 80% of users won't care about a feature, don't build it. The mantra became "build what most people need most of the time."

The Two-Year Thin Slice: The MVP was meant to be a thin slice of auth, billing and other app infrastructure. Widely varied mass-market auth needs, plus the need to earn trust in security, stretched it to about two years.

Dogfooding Shapes the Roadmap: Kinde runs on its own login, billing and feature flags, so features are battle-tested before customers get them. The team didn't charge for about a year, Dave thinks, while building billing the way they wanted it.

A Rule of Minimum Two: Because adding a second of something is harder than adding a third, Kinde started with two regions instead of only Australia. That set patterns for later expansion, such as into Europe.

Hiring Ahead of Reality: After raising on an idea, a prototype and a strong founding team, Kinde hired aggressively, including four marketers. About six months after seeing the mistake, it had cut the team roughly in half. Dave says he would now start much leaner.

q: What is Kinde and what does it do for SaaS businesses?
a: Kinde handles pieces such as authentication and billing so founders can focus on the product they are actually trying to sell. Dave Berner summed it up by saying "we're essentially Shopify for SaaS" [02:47].

q: How long did it take to build the Kinde MVP?
a: It took about two years before Kinde had something it could take to market, largely because auth needs vary so widely. Dave explained, "what I thought was going to be a thin slice ended up pretty much taking two years" [04:59].

q: How does Kinde decide what to build next?
a: Kinde focuses on indie hackers and others racing to market, and rules out features most users won't care about. It also builds what it needs itself, and Dave said one thing that has shaped the plan is that "we need to build what we need to use" [07:29].

q: How did Kinde approach scalability in the early days?
a: Dave said the team built for scale from the start and chose two regions even though its initial customers were in Australia. He recalled the decision as "we're going to do two regions, because that way when we need to add Europe" [11:29]. Those early infrastructure choices helped when one customer grew to what he recalled as about a million users in a matter of weeks.

q: What mistake did Kinde make after raising venture capital?
a: Kinde hired a large team quickly at a time when the market was pushing hyper growth, then had to scale back. Dave said, "we unfortunately ended up having to cut the team" [14:43], and noted that the company owned the mistake in public.

s11-bonus-redefining-the-merchant-lifecycle-reducing-integration-friction-and-capitalizing-on-the-gen-z-tap-to-mobile-shift-with-tiffany-johnson-chief-product-officer-at-nmi

Buying the Missing Piece: To offer all-in-one embedded payments, NMI needed underwriting, risk and merchant account issuing. It acquired part of Sphere's commercial business to gain both the technology and an experienced team.

Built for SaaS Novices: NMI Payments targets SaaS platforms, many of them new to payments and unable to stitch point solutions together. It combines payment acceptance, merchant underwriting, residual management and white labeling.

Outcomes Drive the Roadmap: The team picks outcomes to swarm on, such as payment volume or easier partner onboarding, then sorts ideas into now, next and later, guided by data and the voice of the customer.

Scale Without Chasing Perfection: Even after NMI's 10 billionth transaction, Johnson advises setting a North Star for scale, then iterating. Building for perfection on day one risks missing the customer experience and product-market fit.

Adding Product-Led Growth: Historically sales-led, NMI has launched a sandbox as phase one of a PLG motion, because new software buyers want to explore the API and learn by doing, including with AI and agents.

q: What is NMI and what does it do?
a: NMI provides white-labeled embedded payments infrastructure that its roughly 4,000 partners use to support about a million small businesses. Tiffany Johnson, its Chief Product Officer, said "we like to say we're the biggest payments company that no one's ever heard of" [02:57].

q: Why did NMI acquire part of Sphere's commercial business instead of building the capability?
a: NMI was missing the ability to take on risk, underwrite accounts and issue merchant accounts, which required operational support and expertise beyond its gateway business. Johnson explained that NMI "went the acquisition route to make sure we didn't just buy the tech, but also a great team of talent" [07:50].

q: How does NMI build the roadmap for its embedded payments platform?
a: According to Johnson, the team identifies the outcomes and biggest customer problems to focus on, then folds ideas into a now, next, later roadmap. To decide where each one falls, she said "we let data and voice a customer be our guide" [09:57].

q: Why is NMI adding a product-led growth motion?
a: Johnson said NMI has historically been sales-led, but new SaaS and software buyers don't necessarily want a lot of sales conversations. In her words, "They want a sandbox, they want to get in" [17:13], so NMI has gone live with a sandbox as phase one.

q: What does Tiffany Johnson look for when hiring product managers?
a: Johnson looks for people who are smart, adaptable and able to get things done, as well as customer-obsessed, business-minded and outcome-driven. On background, she said "my unicorns have both that payments experience as well as the craft of product management" [11:32].

the-gene-simmons-of-data-protection-navigating-the-future-of-data-management

Type Systems Fall Short: Michael Howard calls database type systems "lame" because they label values as characters, integers or decimals but don't check whether data is valid or complete, or add context.

A Deleted Quarter of Revenue: At a sales analytics company Howard led, a customer's own DBA deleted a quarter's revenue in Salesforce. He warns that an LLM relying on data with that kind of gap would fall apart.

Quantum Cuts Both Ways: Howard sees promise in drug discovery, materials science and financial modeling, but warns of threats to RSA encryption, with bad actors sharing the same cloud as their targets through hyperscaler quantum services.

Policies Attached to Data: Howard describes Protegrity as data-centric security, turning the idea of a type into dynamic policies tied to data elements, covering compliance rules like HIPAA and PCI and limits on what can be shown in each country.

Business Need Over Legislation: Howard doesn't expect lawmakers to catch up. He predicts adoption will come when major companies can't close their books because LLMs are inaccurate, making data integrity a matter of survival.

q: Why are traditional database type systems a problem for AI and LLMs?
a: Michael Howard argues that types such as character, integer or decimal don't tell you whether the underlying data is right, which matters when LLMs are used for analytics. As he put it, "they do nothing to determine the validity of the data" [04:40].

q: How can bad or missing data affect business analytics?
a: Howard recalled a major customer reporting wrong pipeline numbers from his sales analytics system. The cause was on the customer's side: "one of their own DBAs literally deleted all revenue in Salesforce" [05:27] for a quarter, and nothing in the underlying systems stopped it.

q: How could quantum computing affect data security and encryption?
a: Howard expects major benefits for certain use cases but also serious risk to RSA encryption and digital wallets. Michael also warned that "the bad guys and good guys are going to be on the same system in the cloud" [11:26] because hyperscalers are offering quantum services.

q: What does Protegrity do differently from other security vendors?
a: Howard contrasts Protegrity with vendors focused mostly on perimeter, network or DDoS security, saying "we're specialists in data-centric security" [14:23]. He explained that its mechanism lets organizations ascribe compliance and sovereignty policies to specific data elements.

q: What is Protegrity planning with Apache Iceberg and new data types?
a: Howard said Protegrity is researching a new type that can carry policies, and is aiming to be a first mover with the Iceberg format. In his words, "we're going to put this type of new type system into iceberg directly" [16:53], so platforms above it, such as Databricks and Snowflake, can use the policy mechanism.

s11-e10-the-berkshire-hathaway-of-ai-services-re-architecting-a-17m-holdco-to-disrupt-the-6-trillion-professional-services-market-with-brennan-pothetes-co-founder-ceo-of-infinity-constellation

Selling the Cake, Not Mixers: Infinity Constellation delivers full-stack AI services instead of selling software tools. Brennan says it created eight companies in a year and went from zero to over $7 million in revenue in 12 months.

Services MVPs Need a Wedge: Unlike a tightly focused SaaS MVP, a services MVP stays broad and end-to-end but needs an entry point. His example: an AI recruiting company placing hires in about 22 days versus an industry norm of about 75.

Dogfooding New Company Ideas: When the portfolio needs a service and lacks a good provider, Infinity considers recruiting a repeat founder to build it. It looks for a qualified operator, market demand, and its own share of that demand.
Headcount Kills as Culture: The average portfolio company has about six people. Brennan says avoiding hires only works if revenue still grows, which takes applied AI and a very strong tech team.

Centralize Finance, Not Sales: Central finance gives the holdco asymmetric data for monthly capital deployments. Centralizing sales failed because each business had a different funnel, so go-to-market now sits with each company.

q: What is Infinity Constellation?
a: Brennan Pothetes describes Infinity Constellation as an AI services holding company that builds, backs and grows businesses in full-stack service spaces. In his words, it is the "first AI services holding company, where we pair repeat founders with applied AI people" [05:50].

q: How is an MVP for an AI services company different from a SaaS MVP?
a: Brennan says a SaaS MVP stays as small and focused as possible, while a services MVP stays broad and end-to-end with a painful or poorly served entry point. As he put it, "you want to be like end-to-end, like we make cakes. But that services MVP has to have a wedge." [07:09].

q: How does Infinity Constellation scale without adding lots of headcount?
a: Brennan made avoiding headcount-driven growth a cultural pillar, pairing it with applied AI and strong developers so revenue can still grow. He said, "The biggest thing I'm fighting now is I made one of our cultural pillars headcount kills." [10:59].

q: Should a holding company centralize sales across its portfolio companies?
a: Brennan tried it, and even though founders said they wanted it, the businesses turned out to have different funnels. He concluded, "I really found it's best to like resource sales and go to market at the company level." [14:44], citing better results, accountability and growth.

q: What advice does Brennan Pothetes have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Brennan advises founders to do what they love and to search hard for whether they care about the business beyond its profit potential. He argues that people "forget how much leverage, like loving what you do and founder fit" [18:50] provide.

s11-bonus-the-data-warehouse-tax-using-neural-compute-optimizers-to-slash-snowflake-and-databricks-bills-by-70-on-autopilot-with-ben-lerner-co-founder-ceo-of-espresso-ai

Savings on Autopilot: Espresso AI uses machine learning models to learn Snowflake workloads and run them more efficiently. Lerner puts savings between 20-30% on the low end and 70-80% on the high end.

Ship Before You Research: The team confirmed demand with design partners, analyzed their data, then shipped a simple heuristics-driven system. Getting something live took about six months from the company's start.

Demand Real Commitment: Before major initiatives, the team approaches three to five customers or prospects and seeks a real commitment, such as a weekly meeting, because polite praise doesn't prove interest.

Scale When It Matters: Lerner says early startups should avoid overengineering, but know where their system's limits are so they hit them before a big customer arrives, not two weeks after onboarding.

Don't Neglect Customer Success: Because the product runs in the background, check-ins slipped. One customer shut it off after an invoice reached a manager who didn't know about it, forcing a scramble.

q: How much can Espresso AI save on a Snowflake bill?
a: Ben Lerner says results vary by customer, and for many users they amount to six or seven figures. In his words, "We save customers anywhere from 20, 30% on the low end to 70, 80% on the high end" [03:09].

q: How does Espresso AI reduce Snowflake costs?
a: Ben Lerner explains that, behind the scenes, "we train up a bunch of machine learning models that understand what workloads you're running and when" [03:22]. Espresso AI then works to run those workloads as efficiently as possible while keeping Snowflake's performance benefits.

q: How long did it take to build the Espresso AI MVP?
a: Ben Lerner says the team first worked with early design partners, then built a straightforward heuristics-driven system, shipping it within a couple of months once they knew what to build. He recalls, "From the start of the company, it took us maybe six or so months to get something live." [06:14]

q: How can founders tell whether customers really want a new feature?
a: Ben Lerner advises getting prospects to commit in some way, because early on people tend to say an idea is great. He says a recurring check-in is a good test, "Like setting up a weekly meeting is a really good example because they're not going to take" [10:34] that time unless they are genuinely interested.

q: Does Espresso AI plan to support Databricks, BigQuery and Redshift?
a: Ben Lerner describes the product today as helping Snowflake users, and names other platforms as part of the company's vision for the next few years. He expects Espresso AI to "turn into the default solution for most people running a data warehouse on Snowflake, on Databricks," [22:58] as well as BigQuery and Redshift.
