the-next-iteration-of-gremlin-with-kolton-andrus-ceo

Netflix Gains From Fault Injection: Kolton helped build Netflix's next-generation fault injection platform and test its services. He says outage time went from about eight hours a year to under 45 minutes.

Tools Alone Weren't Enough: Customers adopted chaos engineering unevenly, and many teams didn't know what to test. Gremlin added services, reliability scores, a default test suite and reporting so leaders could measure progress.

Homegrown Dependency Discovery: Gremlin expected to rely on customers' tracing tools, but most lacked a ubiquitous one. It built its own discovery from network traffic and ports, exposing services whose failures could bring a team's software down.

From Finding to Fixing: Gremlin 1.0 injected failure and 2.0 judged the system's response. The third arc aims to explain why a test failed and recommend fixes, such as a circuit breaker or a better timeout.

Guidance Before AI Autonomy: Kolton sees LLMs as useful for natural language interaction, but their probabilistic output makes him wary of letting AI act in production. For now, Gremlin will guide customers rather than fix failures for them.

q: What is chaos engineering and what does Gremlin do?
a: Kolton Andrus describes chaos engineering this way: "we want to go out and purposely inject failure in order to understand how the system responds" [06:15]. Gremlin provides fault injection across CPU, memory, disk, IO and network, designed to be safe, secure and simple to use.

q: How did Kolton Andrus get started in chaos engineering?
a: Kolton was on Amazon's retail website availability team, where the work was largely reactive and the team wanted to test proactively. Of the fault injection platform that followed, he said, "it was my job as an engineer to go build that platform" [03:12]. He later joined Netflix to work on fault injection there.

q: Why did Gremlin add Reliability Management on top of chaos engineering?
a: Kolton found that customers struggled to get consistent value from the tool alone, saying of chaos engineering, "It's a valuable tool, but you need some process and structure around it" [10:04]. Reliability Management added reliability scores, a default test suite, monitoring integrations and reporting.

q: What is the next phase of Gremlin's product?
a: Kolton wants Gremlin to go beyond showing whether a system responded correctly and help engineers fix what failed. In his words, "We want to give people actionable, credible advice on how to go fix their system," [16:21]. Letting Gremlin apply fixes itself is a possibility for someday, once he trusts it enough.

q: Can AI replace site reliability engineers?
a: Kolton Andrus is cautiously optimistic to skeptical, and doesn't think people are ready to let AI take actions in production that could bring down their systems. With large distributed systems, he said, "you really want deterministic results. You really want to trust your result." [17:21] He does see valid uses for AI, particularly natural language interaction.

s11-e9-the-appsec-illusion-demolishing-blind-spots-and-transitioning-from-legacy-api-monitors-to-unified-runtime-ai-security-planes-with-buchi-reddy-founder-ceo-of-levoai

Testing Before Production: Customer interviews showed Buchi Reddy and Harish Natraj that APIs weren't security tested before release, and authorization was broadly tested by hand. That gap led Levo to automated, proactive API security testing.

Minimal Sellable Over Minimal Viable: Levo scoped its first release as a minimal sellable product: automated testing for the top three common API vulnerabilities plus eBPF-based API discovery, with many extras pushed down the road.

Lost POVs Shape the Roadmap: Levo watched what customers used and why proofs of value stalled or failed. Missing integrations went on the roadmap and were stack ranked, and the biggest one built opened up the most POVs.

Scale From Day One: Selling to very large enterprises meant one eBPF sensor had to capture traffic on a machine using minimal resources. One customer ran 200-plus applications or application pods next to a single sensor.

GTM Came Late: Reddy says Levo tilted toward product over go-to-market early on. Technical differentiation still won notable logos and credibility, and the company has since made major progress in sales and marketing.

q: What is Levo.ai and what does it do?
a: Levo.ai, founded by Buchi Reddy, automatically discovers an enterprise's APIs and automates continuous security testing before production. Reddy describes it this way: "Levo is an API security platform, proactive API security platform to be precise." [02:52]

q: What gap in API security led Buchi Reddy to start Levo?
a: Reddy saw that other tools were mainly focused on production, while proactive testing got little attention. He and Harish Natraj ran more interviews, and he says "we spotted this wide gap where APIs were not security tested" [05:12] before going into production.

q: How did Levo decide what to build in its first version?
a: Buchi Reddy says scoping an enterprise product with a very small team was hard, and customer interviews helped. He explains, "we tried to follow the MSP rather than MVP" [07:51], meaning a minimal sellable product that combined automated security testing with eBPF-based API discovery.

q: How does Levo's eBPF sensor handle scale in large enterprises?
a: Reddy says some enterprise customers process millions, if not billions, of API calls every day, so scale was designed in from the start. The goal was to install one "sensor on a single machine that works with the most minimal resources but captures traffic from" [12:07] even dozens of applications.

q: What mistake did Levo make with go-to-market?
a: Buchi Reddy says the company leaned more toward product than go-to-market in its early days. He admits, "we haven't put enough weight on the GTM engine from early enough" [14:48], though technical differentiation still helped Levo close great logos.

s11-bonus-twitters-1st-employee-talks-about-agentic-programming-and-its-impact-on-team-building-with-rabble-of-rabble-labs
Agentic Coding Beat the Team: Running parallel Claude Code and Cursor sessions in the evenings, Rabble became more productive building prototypes alone than his entire team was on the main app.

Chorus as Proof of Concept: Five or six people in Switzerland took Chorus, a group app with a Cashu Bitcoin wallet for crowdfunding, from idea to launch largely through conversations with AI about the code.

Rebuild Instead of Patching: With language models writing tests and specs, Rabble says a failing part can be removed and rebuilt from scratch. MVPs can be running code built to learn, then cheaply thrown away.
Designers Can Now Ship: After a day learning the tools, designer Sebastian, who had never been a developer, went within a month to leading development on a new product the group plans to launch.

A Network, Not a Company: Rabble now favors a pop-star model: a small core plus a wider cloud of specialist collaborators, with enough money for people to live on and less pressure to be either in or out.

q: Why did Rabble start building open social media protocols?
a: Rabble was upset when Twitter shut down its open app ecosystem in 2012, which left him feeling he needed permission to innovate. He explained, "I want a way in which I can do something Twitter-like," [03:10] without Twitter being able to deauthorize his app.

q: How did agentic programming change the way Rabble builds software?
a: Rabble spent his days on management work and his evenings building prototypes with large language models, running Claude Code and Cursor sessions in parallel. He said it got to "the point where I was more productive in my evening time building my own apps than the entire" [07:51] team was on the main development.

q: What is the Chorus app and how was it built?
a: Chorus was a proof-of-concept social group app with mobile and desktop versions, where each group could crowdfund itself through a built-in Cashu Bitcoin wallet. Rabble's small group built it in Switzerland by talking with AI about the code, and he noted, "we did it without even very much looking at the code." [10:32]

q: How does Rabble handle technical debt with agentic programming?
a: Rabble has language models write the unit tests and specs that describe how the application works, then replaces whatever fails. As he put it, "If part of it isn't working, you take the entire part out" [14:04] and rebuild it from scratch based on what it was supposed to do.

q: How does Rabble think agentic programming will change startup teams?
a: Rabble believes the tight, live-or-die team can give way to a network of collaborators, similar to how a pop star brings in specialists for each project. He suggests we "think of what we're doing, not as a single organization, but a cloud of people who are" [20:08] collaborating.

s11-e8-the-10b-l2-juggernaut-re-architecting-coinbase-wallet-embracing-token-decentralization-and-scaling-ethereum-for-one-billion-users-with-jesse-pollak-creator-of-base-head-of-protocols-at-coinbase

Platform Before Products: After about a year of trying to bring Coinbase's products on-chain, Jesse's team concluded it first needed a scalable, secure, usable platform, much as AWS and Heroku served Web 2.0. That insight in December 2021 led to Base.

Open Source Sped the Build: Base started on Optimism's MIT-licensed OP Stack, collaborated with Paradigm on Reth for performance, and leaned on front-end tools like Viem and Wagmi to help developers go from zero to one.

Gas Per Second as Scoreboard: Base measures throughput in gas per second and has grown from about 2.5 million to about 35 million. Jesse's goal is to 10x again, and keep doing it, drawing on hard lessons from Coinbase's outage years.

Hiring Founders and Trusted Colleagues: Base's early team came from people Jesse had long worked with at Coinbase. It also asks candidates what they have invented and has made roughly six acquisitions in nine months, mostly for talent.

Local Leaders for Global Reach: Trying to serve builders abroad from California led to missteps. Base shifted by hiring about 15 leaders in countries around the world and empowering them to decide how to make its tools relevant locally.

q: What is Base and how does it work?
a: Jesse Pollak describes Base as a global economy made up of an underlying chain, tools for builders and easy access to apps for everyday people. Of the chain itself, he said, "It's called an Ethereum Layer 2, where people can go and deploy apps" [03:06]. Layer 2s batch many transactions together and submit them to Ethereum, which makes them much cheaper for users.

q: Why did Coinbase create Base?
a: Jesse set out to explore what Coinbase would look like if it were built with smart contracts and Layer 2 blockchains available. After about a year of ideas that didn't work, his team found a missing foundation, and as he put it, "The first thing we needed to do was actually have a platform where we could build those products" [07:21].

q: What technology was used to build the first version of Base?
a: Jesse said the team built on Ethereum, the EVM and open source tooling, including Reth, Viem and Wagmi. A key piece was Optimism's OP Stack, which he said "let us kind of start building our chain really, really quickly" [09:59]. A testnet launched in February, followed by the real-money version in August.

q: How does Base approach scalability?
a: Base sets long-term, specific throughput goals measured in gas per second and works to optimize its whole software stack to hit them. Jesse contrasted this with Coinbase's interlinked microservices, saying of Base that "you can kind of think about it like scaling a single computer" [23:15]. Improvements to that virtual machine benefit everything built on it.

q: What mistake did the Base team make with its global expansion?
a: Jesse said the team had good intentions but got ahead of itself in assuming it knew how to serve builders in other countries. To fix this, he said that in the last six months "we've actually hired kind of like 15 different leaders" [28:41] around the world and empowered them as decision makers. He said this is already leading to better results, though it is still early.

s11-bonus-slashing-patient-recruitment-cycles-from-years-to-weeks-with-federated-data-architectures-and-generative-ai-trials-with-gaurav-bhattacharya-founder-ceo-of-jeeva-ai

Pivot Born From Internal Tool: After five years without product-market fit at Involve AI, the team turned its internal sales tool into Jeeva. About nine months in, Gaurav reported almost $5M ARR, over 10,000 users and almost 300 enterprises.

Chrome Extension Cost Months: Pulling Salesforce and deal context made Jeeva's Chrome extension extremely slow, and users uninstalled or rejected it. The team moved to a SaaS app with native Gmail integration, losing about three months of head start.
Hypotheses Over Roadmaps: Jeeva works from about five unique insights, with an engineer prototyping each. The team then picks one to focus on, aiming to ship one big feature or release a month.

Small Team, Heavy AI: About six engineers generate 99% of their code with AI, though Gaurav says AI is horrible at systems design thinking. He hires for trust, speed and high agency, leaning heavily on his network.

Delay Scaling Until It Hurts: Gaurav's last company spent heavily designing for millions of concurrent users but never passed a thousand. Now he waits for real complaints before adding scalable systems, and uses Streak as a simple, cheap CRM.

q: What is Jeeva AI and what does it do?
a: Jeeva AI builds agentic tools that help salespeople find leads, research people and companies, and write hyper-personalized outreach across channels such as email and LinkedIn. Gaurav Bhattacharya, its co-founder and CEO, said "we're building these tools almost like a cursor or a windsurf for sellers" [04:40].

q: Why did Involve AI pivot to Jeeva AI?
a: Involve AI analyzed customer data for churn and revenue signals, but each customer's data was so unique that the team was building custom machine learning models. Gaurav said that "it just became like a consulting company" [03:28], so the company pivoted to the sales tool it had built for internal use.

q: Why did Jeeva AI drop its Chrome extension?
a: The extension needed deal context, including data from Salesforce, which made it heavy and slow to load. Gaurav said users would "install it, they would uninstall it or reject it within like a day of use" [09:31], and the team eventually moved to a SaaS application with a native Gmail integration.

q: What tech stack is Jeeva AI built on?
a: Gaurav described a Python FastAPI back end, a React front end, MongoDB, Pinecone and Azure hosting, with OpenAI, Llama and other models, including in-house classifiers. The team codes in Cursor, and Gaurav said "99% of our code is AI generated" [05:47].

q: When should a startup worry about scalability?
a: Gaurav Bhattacharya's view is that it depends on the situation, but founders often over-invest in scale before users need it. He said scalability is something "that can always be pushed out a little bit extra" [16:14], until people start complaining about glitches, and he would rather focus first on delivering value.

s11-e7-the-90-minute-daily-engagement-phenomenon-redefining-multimodal-conversational-ai-to-cure-the-loneliness-epidemic-with-artem-rodichev-founder-ceo-of-ex-human

Competing With All Entertainment: Artem says users average more than 90 minutes a day chatting with AI companions, and paying users more than two and a half hours. He sees the whole entertainment industry as the competition, not just other companion apps.

Feedback Loop From the MVP: Botify AI began with three people, text chat and a dozen preset characters. User upvotes and downvotes were fed back into training, starting with the open-source GPT-J model, so characters improved with each iteration.

Adults Only by Design: Seeing that users shared very private things and that teenagers could confuse fiction with reality, Ex-Human limited its product to adults. It also bars chatbots that represent minors.

Moderation Versus Creativity: The team underestimated real-time moderation. A vampire character or a murder-mystery roleplay involves dark themes, so the system has to block unsafe content without shutting down legitimate fiction.

Platform Beyond the App: Ex-Human serves more than 60 B2B clients, mostly in entertainment. Games use it to power NPCs that feel alive, and IP holders can turn their characters into interactive experiences for fans.

q: What is Ex-Human and what does it build?
a: Ex-Human is a platform where consumers and businesses create and customize empathetic AI characters, including their backstory, speaking style, accent, looks and behavior. Artem Rodichev says "The main idea here is to build a non-boring version of ChatGPT." [03:17] Its consumer app is called Botify AI.

q: Why did Artem Rodichev leave Replika to start Ex-Human?
a: After seven years as head of AI at Replika, Artem saw limits in offering a single, hard-to-customize companion and wanted its kind of technology to serve many products and use cases. His motivation was "to build the whole ecosystem to scale empathetic AI." [06:17]

q: Can AI companions help with loneliness and social anxiety?
a: Artem says user feedback shows some people use companions to feel less lonely, reduce social anxiety and become less afraid of talking with others. He describes isolated users who "can train and practice their social skills with these companions in no judgment environment." [13:24]

q: Why is Ex-Human's companion product only for adults?
a: Artem says the team did not understand all the consequences of such powerful empathetic characters, which users were telling very private things. They also saw that "teenagers, they could not understand where is reality" [12:02] versus fiction, and that teens could discuss unsafe topics.

q: What are the biggest challenges in scaling a multimodal AI companion platform?
a: Artem points to replying within a couple of seconds, generating text, voice, images and video in real time, and keeping GPU costs and subscription prices reasonable. Growth also forces frequent architecture changes, and as he puts it, "we need to continuously rebuild what we built previously." [16:46]

s11-bonus-the-autonomous-retail-bottleneck-removing-machine-friction-and-deploying-smart-sensor-fusion-for-loss-free-unattended-operations-with-keren-fanan-ceo-of-myop

Plug In UI Without Redeploys: MyOp lets teams plug external UI components, built with AI, design tools or outside developers, into live production logic while keeping them isolated and manageable at runtime, without reopening the core codebase.

A Gaming-Industry Superpower: As a VP of product in gaming, Fanan could ship production changes in days or even hours. Those firms relied on costly, custom in-house tools, and MyOp aims to bring that control to everyone.

A Focused, Ugly MVP: In three to four months, MyOp had a first library and a very basic dashboard working with a known design partner, whose pains shaped the focus. Two of that partner's developers took it into production.

Developers Don't Read Either: The team assumed developers would learn through docs and tutorials. Feedback showed users didn't understand what to do, so MyOp redid onboarding to guide them in-product while still allowing self-exploration.

Don't Overlook Red Flags: Fanan says a couple of bad hires taught her that wanting someone to join badly can hide warning signs. On a tiny team, each person can change the atmosphere and the company's DNA.

q: What is MyOp and how does it work?
a: MyOp is a development platform for front-end developers that helps companies ship UI and UX faster. Keren Fanan explains that "we let teams plug external UI pieces, which is technically external UI components, directly into live production logic" [03:02], while keeping them isolated and manageable at runtime.

q: Where did the idea for MyOp come from?
a: All three co-founders had felt the pain of long development and deploy cycles from different angles. Fanan also saw in the gaming industry what direct control over parts of production could do, saying "And that was like an unbelievable superpower" [05:36].

q: How long did it take to build the MyOp MVP?
a: It took about three to four months to get a very basic version working with the first design partner. It included the first version of the core library and, as Fanan described it, "a very basic version of our dashboard with probably the ugliest UI you've ever seen" [08:34].

q: Why did MyOp redo its developer onboarding?
a: The team had assumed developers liked to figure things out themselves through documentation and tutorials. Fanan said they "started getting a lot of feedback from people trying our system that they literally don't" [12:07] understand what to do, so they set out to make next steps clear within the product.

q: What hiring mistake did Keren Fanan learn from at MyOp?
a: Fanan said the team made a couple of bad hires, which matters enormously when a company is very small. She explained, "And you want someone to join so badly that sometimes you overlook probably some of the red flags that you see." [21:10]

s11-e6-the-death-of-the-legacy-landing-page-rebuilding-a-no-code-pioneer-for-the-agentic-ai-and-multi-armed-bandit-era-with-michael-sacca-ceo-of-leadpages

Beyond the Landing Page: About six months in, Michael Sacca's team decided the real problem Leadpages solves is optimization, and began moving it from a landing page builder toward a conversion rate optimization tool.
Identifying Anonymous Visitors: Audience insights surfaces about 60 demographic and firmographic data points on anonymous visits, helping customers spot personas their messaging misses.

Blunt Messaging Wins: Labels like "lead insights" confused people. Testing for opens, clicks and trials showed that plainly describing the feature worked better, and a free beta built conviction before pricing it.
One Owner per Funnel Stage: To break down silos, marketing took acquisition, a new RevOps team took conversion and product took retention. RevOps got its own growth PM, PMM and engineering access.

Milestones Over Scrum: Product and engineering skip Agile, Scrum and Waterfall. People estimate their own tasks, which roll into milestones and an end date, and delays shift later dates in a no-fault system.

q: What does Leadpages do?
a: Michael Sacca describes Leadpages as a MarTech company with a landing page builder focused on helping companies iterate on paid ad campaigns. He said marketing teams can change their "messaging, iterate without having to use any engineering resources, and then A-B test and" [03:08] optimize their way to better performance.

q: What is Leadpages audience insights?
a: Audience insights lets customers identify anonymous traffic visiting their site, so they can see who is arriving but perhaps not converting. Sacca explained that "there's about 60 different demographic and firmographic data points that we can get from an anonymous visit." [06:14]

q: How did Leadpages find the right messaging for its new data feature?
a: Sacca's team tested messaging with its own customers and some external paid advertising, looking for email opens, clicks and trials. They found that the more blunt they were about what the product did, "the easier it was for our audience to understand." [08:53]

q: How did Michael Sacca restructure teams at Leadpages to reduce silos?
a: Sacca gave marketing ownership of traffic and acquisition, a new RevOps team ownership of conversion, and product ownership of retention. A lesson he brought from Dribbble was that "having ownership is one of the most powerful things that we can create as leaders" [10:40].

q: Does Leadpages use Agile or Scrum for product and engineering?
a: No, Sacca said the team uses a simple milestone system in which the people doing each task decide how long it will take. His reasoning is that "people are more accountable to their own deadlines than they are to my deadlines." [14:35]

s11-bonus-the-real-time-generative-video-race-breaking-the-speed-barrier-and-shipping-ltx-foundation-models-to-millions-of-creators-with-ofir-bibi-vp-of-research-at-lightricks

Generative AI as the Engine: Rather than only adding generative features to existing apps, Lightricks built LTX Studio around generative AI for storytelling. Ofir calls it a very big shift from B2C to B2B, and the company later built its own video model, LTX Video.

Patching Models Has Limits: The team wrapped weak base models in pre- and post-processing pipelines. Errors compounded, fail cases surfaced with millions of users and deadlines slipped, so they got buy-in to fine-tune and train models to fix root causes.

Split Research and Engineering Roles: Ofir first hired for people who could do both, but found them rare, slow to train and prone to losing focus. He split the work into researchers and engineers who speak the language and can bring prototype algorithms onto devices.

Hire for Quality Obsession: Ofir asks candidates about the work they feel most connected to, then dives deep into the details, effort and untried ideas. He looks for people obsessed with making what they build work as well as possible.

A Demo That Beat Apple's Camera: A three-person team pulled many frames through video APIs and combined them for cleaner photos. When Lightricks' CEO compared the still-crashing demo with the iPhone's stock camera, an Apple executive conceded its HDR looked better.

q: What is Lightricks and what is its vision?
a: Lightricks is a company founded in 2012 whose first app was the portrait editor Facetune, and which has since built products including LTX Studio and the LTX Video model. Ofir Bibi explained, "Our vision in the company is bridging the gap between imagination and creation." [04:41]

q: Why did Lightricks build LTX Studio?
a: Ofir Bibi said large foundation models could suddenly handle many problems the team had been building separate technology to solve. Instead of only adding those abilities to current products, they decided to "build a new type of product that is using generative AI as its engine" [07:14], aimed at helping people tell and create their stories.

q: What mistake did the Lightricks research team make when building on generative models like Stable Diffusion?
a: According to Ofir Bibi, the team assumed it could turn strong proofs of concept into production features by patching around existing models, which led to shaky pipelines, lower quality and missed deadlines. The root problem was that "the base models were just not good enough" [29:20], and the answer was deeper research, fine-tuning and more training.

q: How did Ofir Bibi build the Lightricks research team?
a: Ofir Bibi initially tried hiring people who could be both researchers and engineers, but found that profile very rare and slow to train. He recalled realizing, "I need to split the responsibilities and hire for two different roles" [22:17], while looking for people in both who cared deeply about quality.

q: How did Lightricks' early mobile camera compare with the iPhone's stock camera?
a: Ofir Bibi told the story of CEO Zev demonstrating the still-crashing MVP to an Apple executive and comparing it side by side with the stock camera. As Bibi heard it, "the Apple executive was mumbling curses around the fact that our HDR looked better than theirs" [15:11].

s11-e5-the-public-internet-bottleneck-rebuilding-the-physical-routing-layer-for-high-performance-blockchains-with-austin-federa-co-founder-of-doublezero

Leased Wavelengths, Not New Cables: DoubleZero isn't laying fiber yet. It and its contributors mostly lease channels on existing lines, isolating traffic from the public internet for very low latency and jitter.

Twenty Contributors as the Benchmark: Austin argues that with only 20 tier one ISPs, reaching 20 independent network contributors would let DoubleZero credibly claim it is as decentralized as the public internet.

Multicast Emerged as a Draw: The team expected FPGA offloading of validator tasks to be the biggest use case. It is powerful for networks like Solana, but multicast has become one of the most exciting areas.

Senior Hires Ship Faster: The roughly 20-person team has basically no juniors, with at least eight years of experience each. Many engineers came from high-performance networking with no crypto background.

Underestimating the Banking Hurdle: Even after raising $28 million, DoubleZero struggled for months to get a solid banking relationship. Austin says recent regulatory clarity has changed that landscape.

q: What is DoubleZero?
a: DoubleZero is a project building a physical fiber network for high-performance systems, with blockchain as its first major product-market fit. Austin Federa describes it as "creating an alternative to the public internet for high performance distributed systems" [03:02].

q: How does DoubleZero reduce latency and jitter compared with the public internet?
a: Austin explains that DoubleZero and its contributors mostly lease individual channels on existing fiber lines instead of laying new cables. These links are low latency, and "they have extremely little jitter, because we're basically isolating all of our traffic" [07:35] from public internet traffic.

q: How decentralized does a network like DoubleZero need to be?
a: Austin points to the number of top-level internet providers as the benchmark, saying "there's only 20 tier one ISPs. So if we can get 20 network contributors," [08:29] the project can make a very credible argument that it is as decentralized as the public internet. Running the network through multiple independent contributors, rather than one company, is one of its main innovations.

q: Why does DoubleZero use FPGAs?
a: FPGAs let DoubleZero offload common tasks from systems such as blockchain validators. Austin says of these chips that "you can reprogram them on the fly. And they're not as fast as dedicated hardware" [10:51], but they are far faster than software.

q: What is Austin Federa's advice on hiring at a startup?
a: Austin warns that experience at a breakout company doesn't necessarily make someone top talent, and urges founders to check several references. Because former employers rarely give openly negative reviews, he says "a non-strong endorsement is a anti-endorsement nowadays" [26:58].

s11-bonus-the-forgotten-password-paradox-why-service-accounts-ntlm-flaws-and-over-privileged-ai-agents-are-the-real-ground-zero-for-nation-state-breaches-with-tim-eades-co-founder-ceo-of-anetac

Validate Before Building: Before starting Anetac, the team interviewed 35 security executives about identity vulnerabilities across human and non-human accounts: how big the problem was, what regulators said, and why no one had tackled it.

Discovery as the Superpower: Anetac focused on discovery and its efficacy, covering where a non-human account sits, how old its credentials are and what it chains to. That context guides the right treatment plans.

Design for the Operator: The product took about 14 months to reach what the team called MVP, iterating from PowerPoint to Figma with customers. Eades warns founders not to lose sight of the economic buyer, technical buyer and operator.

Two-Track Roadmap: User groups and customers help rank usability and workflow features. Strategic bets follow market trends, including Anetac's belief that identity vulnerability management will overtake application vulnerability management in an agentic world.

Scaling Through Partners: Anetac's go-to-market priority is recruiting and enabling partners, such as pen testers, red teams, virtual CISOs and MSSPs. Eades says it has something like 35 or 40 of them worldwide.

q: How did Anetac get started?
a: Tim Eades and his team first interviewed 35 security executives about identity vulnerabilities, then he turned to former colleagues about starting a company. One Sunday during a Liverpool game, as Eades put it, "I downloaded a Microsoft PowerPoint template and literally created a deck" [03:18], then did the financials and sent it to investors.

q: What does Anetac look at when discovering non-human accounts?
a: Eades says discovery has to provide context, looking at "not just where it is and what it sits and how old are the credentials" [06:36]. It also traces the account's chain, such as a service account connecting to an application, then Lambda, then GitHub, so the right corrective action can be taken.

q: How long did it take to build Anetac's MVP?
a: Eades describes a long period of iterating on the interface with customers, moving from PowerPoint graphics to Figma and through the design process. He said the product's development period was "probably 14 months before we really called it MVP" [05:23].

q: How do AI agents shape Anetac's product roadmap?
a: Eades sees agents as identities and expects an agentic architecture to change where vulnerability management matters. He believes that "applications fade away, and the identity vulnerability management will take over" [09:24], so that is where Anetac puts its strategic investment.

q: How should a startup handle competing feature requests?
a: Eades advises knowing your superpower, being very good at it and staying focused when people push requirements in different areas. In his words, "startups die of indigestion before they die of starvation" [06:05].

s11-e4-transforming-dormant-media-libraries-into-rights-aware-fact-checked-ai-intelligence-with-brooke-hartley-moy-co-founder-ceo-of-infactory-ai

Turning Archives Into Queryable Data: Infactory helps large enterprises turn complex assets like news archives, space telemetry and football footage into structured, queryable data that can power AI agents, co-pilots and internal tools.

Core Tech Over Polish: Co-founder Ken built the original MVP in about six weeks. The team accepted a clunky, unintuitive interface so it could focus on core capabilities and query performance, which showed customers and investors its view of AI infrastructure.

Two Lenses on the Roadmap: Felipe made fast adjustments from early customer feedback, while Brooke focused on what large enterprises would need six months to a year out. She called that mix a bit of a superpower.

Saying No to RAG Revenue: Infactory turned down requests to support RAG applications despite having the skills to build them. The work could have brought early revenue, but it sat outside the core tech and wasn't sustainable for the business.

Fix Forward After Regression: A massive regression, maybe within 24 hours of a planned public developer launch, forced the team to scrap its launch plans. They chose to fix what was broken instead of rolling back, and recovered faster than Brooke expected.

q: What does Infactory do?
a: Infactory is a data platform that works primarily with large enterprises in regulated industries and media, turning complex data into structured, queryable data. Brooke Hartley Moy said it lets them "turn what is otherwise an underutilized asset into something that could power things like AI agents" [03:13].

q: How long did it take to build the Infactory MVP?
a: Brooke Hartley Moy said co-founder Ken largely built it, with some help from ChatGPT's coding assistance rather than tools like Cursor, which the team now uses. She put the timeline for "the original MVP within about six weeks" [06:11].

q: Why did Infactory turn down RAG projects?
a: Brooke Hartley Moy said the team is well-versed in retrieval augmented generation, "but we also believe that it's not the right solution" [16:41] for many of the use cases customers bring to Infactory. Those projects were also not at the heart of what its core technology is trying to achieve.

q: How are AI agents changing the way media companies think about their content?
a: Brooke Hartley Moy said media companies once focused on search and natural language questions over their archives, but now expect much more access to come through agents. She explained that they want "their data assets for agents to be the main access point, not an actual like human referral traffic" [23:11].

q: What advice does Brooke Hartley Moy have for new founders?
a: Brooke Hartley Moy advises founders to just do it, listening to customer feedback while largely ignoring everyone else's doubts. On viability, she said "The only person that can tell you whether or not this is actually viable is like one, the customer base" [27:40], with the second test being your own motivation.

s11-bonus-p2-the-radical-transparency-framework-eliminating-middle-management-and-running-an-18-year-product-studio-as-a-pure-meritocracy-with-yaroslav-lazor-sergiy-korolyov-co-founders-of-railsware

Craft Alone Didn't Drive Growth: Revenue stayed flat for many years while engineer-led management focused on craft. Growth began when the team decided to push itself to be more commercially successful.

Recruiting Unlocked Scale: Railsware first hired for new roles ad hoc, figuring out interviews on the fly. Building a dedicated recruitment team, and searching beyond Ukraine for engineers, helped it grow.

The $80,000 Calendly Miss: Railsware had borrowed money to invest in clients, then stopped before taking Calendly equity. The founders say that $80,000 stake would now be worth $250 million, and they use it to size later problems.

Studio of Independent Products: Railsware now acts as a mother company for three of its own products, two joint ventures and a consultancy, with increasingly independent teams. The plan is to build at least one billion-dollar business among them.

Validate Before Polishing Pixels: Find out who you're building for by talking to people, even if they reject you. Then check your ideal customer profile, reachable market and realistic conversion rates to see whether revenue could plateau.

q: Why is Railsware's consultancy model hard to scale?
a: Sergiy Korolyov explains that quality software needs very good engineers, and clients used to typical outsourcing shops often start the conversation with rates rather than seeking a technical partner. As he put it, "comparing to the bigger outsourcing shops, which has thousands of people, our model is still unscalable" [05:05].

q: Why didn't Railsware invest in Calendly?
a: Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov say earlier client investments had gone badly, and trying to recover them was tiring and painful, so they declined equity in Calendly. In the founders' words, "we said, let's pull the plug on investments. It just doesn't make sense." [12:13].

q: How did Railsware scale its team?
a: Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov describe searching for talent in countries such as Romania, Spain, Portugal and Brazil, and later creating a team to run the hiring process. As the co-founders put it, "Building a recruitment team was the key point for us" [08:42].

q: What problem is Railsware's Coupler trying to solve?
a: According to Yaroslav Lazor and Sergiy Korolyov, many companies don't understand their P&Ls, marketing or sales numbers, and joining data often requires an expert. The goal is an easy analytics platform with dashboards, reports and AI communication, and as the co-founders said, "Coupler is aimed to bring light into this fog of the data." [18:06].

q: Should a first-time founder hire a CTO right away?
a: Sergiy Korolyov would probably advise working with a product studio first to start the product and validate the idea, then deciding whether to hire a CTO. He has often seen the mistake "that people just think that they need to hire CTO without having any understanding what this role is" [27:36].

s11-bonus-p1-the-radical-transparency-framework-eliminating-middle-management-and-running-an-18-year-product-studio-as-a-pure-meritocracy-with-yaroslav-lazor-sergiy-korolyov-co-founders-of-railsware

Build From Your Own Pain: Mailtrap came from Railsware's own risk of emailing real customers from staging copies. It traps the emails an app sends from development and staging environments in an inbox.

A Three-Day Checklist Product: Railsware built a checklist tool in three days by storing each checklist as text in a Jira field. It reached 700 users in six months and became a million-dollar business, with half a developer adding complexity over time.
Test Demand Before Building: Mailtrap added an Automations menu item leading to a 20-question alpha signup form. More than 400 replies arrived in two weeks, showing which features users wanted most.

Learn the Role Before Hiring: The founders first play a new role, such as product manager, to learn which details matter. Then they seek a cornerstone hire who is better at it than they are and can build the team.

Trial Days Test Collaboration: Candidates spend a half or full day on a real task with two Railsware people, so both sides can see how they work together. Railsware says it hires about one in 200 applicants.

q: How did Mailtrap get started?
a: Mailtrap solved Railsware's own problem: copies of production data in staging could lead to emails reaching real customers. As one of the Railsware co-founders described the idea, "Let's make a trap of an inbox that will show" [06:46] all the emails an app sends from development and staging.

q: How did Railsware build a checklist product in three days?
a: One of the Railsware co-founders explained that the team "hosted the whole checklist inside of a field in Jira" [07:12], using a text representation that rendered as a working checklist. The product came from the company's own need, reached 700 users in six months and later became a million-dollar business.

q: How does Railsware validate and prioritize new product features?
a: For marketing automation in Mailtrap, the team added a menu item that opened an alpha signup form before deciding which features to start with. One of the Railsware co-founders reported that "in two weeks, we collected more than 400 replies" [11:01], which let the most popular features rise to the top.

q: How do Railsware's founders hire for roles they don't know well?
a: Sergiy Korolov explained that the founders first play the role themselves to understand which details need attention. Then, as he put it, "you start to search for the person who is better in those details than you" [17:06], ideally a cornerstone leader who can build a team.

q: What is Railsware's "everything is product" concept?
a: Railsware treats internal departments and major functions as products, with their own users, developers and product managers. One of the co-founders said that for every department or big function "that we build, we treat as a product" [23:45], and described how this approach shaped a smoother, more automated recruitment experience.

s11-e3-the-4-rs-framework-moving-ai-demos-into-production-to-cure-legacy-healthcare-payer-inefficiencies-with-rob-duffy-cto-of-healthedge

Platformize What Already Works: Duffy ranks four approaches, with scaling a tool that already works for one team as best. Building from scratch is the worst, because you lack a good frame of reference for requirements and scalability concerns.

Feature Parity Is Not a Goal: Consolidating four or five tools means some features won't carry over. Duffy says to decide that early, and pick what's best for the whole business even if a team's current tool suits it locally.

Treat Internal Teams as Customers: Platform roadmaps come from collaborative planning with dependent teams, including their needs over the next 12 to 18 months. Roadmap items should speed up or remove work for those internal customers.

The Scaling Paradox: Companies usually decide to build a platform when systems already aren't scaling. The effort spent coping with that can be the biggest barrier to building or adopting the fix, so teams have to carve out time for it.

Mandates Don't Drive Adoption: As a technical project manager at Amazon, Duffy tried to push technology with a mandate and no one adopted it. He learned to understand teams' problems and earn a place on their roadmap.

q: What does HealthEdge do for health insurance payers?
a: HealthEdge provides software as a service that includes a core administrative processing system for adjudicating claims, a payment integrity product and a care management platform. Rob Duffy explained that with claims processing, the aim is to reach a point "where no human has to touch that information" [04:15].

q: What is a minimum viable platform?
a: For Rob Duffy, it is not a first iteration built from scratch but something proven that can be scaled to more teams. He described it as "a product or a tool that is already working for one team." [08:34]

q: How do you handle feature parity when consolidating tools into one platform?
a: Duffy advises deciding early that missing features won't slow down platform adoption, even though some engineers will find that hard to accept. As he put it, the team needs a "trade-off earlier on around feature parity is not a goal." [10:40]

q: How should a platform team build its roadmap?
a: Duffy recommends collaborative planning with the teams that depend on the platform and treating them as real customers. At HealthEdge, he said, "everything on our roadmap should in some way be speeding up or removing some work for our customers." [12:54]

q: Why don't top-down mandates work for platform adoption?
a: Duffy learned this at Amazon, where leaning on a mandate from his boss made him ineffective and no one adopted the software. He said that once you try to use a mandate, "it loses all of its power" [19:18], so you need to influence across organizational boundaries and collaborate.

s11-bonus-why-vibe-coding-fails-at-scale-and-how-no-code-ecosystems-unlocked-1b-in-user-revenue-with-emmanuel-straschnov-co-founder-ceo-of-bubble
Three Years to an MVP: Bubble had no launch event or waitlist. Emmanuel defines its MVP as the roughly three years it took until users could build a working app without talking to the founders.

Two Founders, Five Years: Emmanuel and Josh built everything themselves, which kept a complex product's UX consistent. It also made hiring harder, and Emmanuel isn't sure staying a duo that long was right.
Rewrites Come With Scale: Bubble rewrote its backend maybe three to four times, moving through Cloudant, Firebase and Elasticsearch to Postgres. The lesson: favor proven technologies over fancy ones.
The Cost of No Limits: Bubble didn't cap workflow actions, data types or fields. That sets it apart, but apps with 2,000 columns on one data type strain the interface and backend.
Visual Editing Meets AI: Emmanuel argues vibe coding leaves non-coders facing code. Bubble is pairing its visual editor with conversational AI, so users can build and fix apps in natural language.

q: What is Bubble and how does it make money?
a: Bubble is a web-based editor for building applications without code, paired with a platform that hosts them. Emmanuel Straschnov explained that rather than selling access to the editor, "what we sell is more the hosting site" [03:21].

q: How is Bubble different from vibe coding tools?
a: Emmanuel argues that a non-coder can get code from a vibe coding tool, "but you're going to have to look at the code" [23:08]. Bubble's approach is to combine a visual interface that is easier to learn and manipulate with AI and natural language.

q: How long did it take to build Bubble's MVP?
a: Emmanuel defines the MVP as the point where users could build a working application without talking to the founders. Of reaching that milestone, he said, "I would say it took us about three years to get there" [06:04].

q: What scaling challenges did Bubble face?
a: Emmanuel said hard technical limits forced major rework, and a traffic surge from Product Hunt caused crashes for several days. On the rework, he recalled, "I think we had to rewrite our backend maybe three to four times" [14:42].

q: What would Emmanuel Straschnov do differently in building Bubble?
a: Emmanuel said he probably wouldn't repeat the decision to leave the platform so open-ended, though he opposes removing those capabilities now. His lesson is that "It's much easier to start a little bit stricter and remove limits" [21:29] than to do the reverse.

s11-bonus-the-epistemic-podcast-shift-destroying-dashboard-fragmentation-and-injecting-multi-platform-orchestration-with-clayton-gentry-co-founder-cto-of-podstock

Start Narrow, Then Broaden: Podstock began with Megaphone logs, a campaign tracking dashboard and delivery forecasting. Louder demand for cross-platform analytics led to a "light pivot" that put forecasting in a holding pattern.

Manual Matching Informed Automation: Clayton matched thousands of YouTube videos to RSS audio by hand. Patterns like YouTube publishing eight hours after the audio helped shape the automated system, with humans still handling edge cases.

Delete the Over-Engineered Pipeline: Clayton wrote a custom Python service to replicate Postgres data into BigQuery, then deleted it for BigQuery federated queries, which he calls 100 times simpler and less error prone.

Fit Features to Deadlines: Borrowing from Shape Up, Clayton and co-founder Michael shape a pitch, decide what to leave out, set a deadline and "scope hammer" the feature to fit. Appetite is measured in weeks of engineering.

Stay Lean, Hire for Portfolio: The bootstrapped team avoids hiring too fast. Clayton weighs portfolios and meaningful Elixir community contributions, since a technical interview alone isn't a sufficient signal.

q: What is Podstock and what problem does it solve?
a: Podstock, co-founded by CTO Clayton Gentry, brings together analytics from podcast hosting platforms, YouTube, Spotify and other channels, with tools for campaign planning, tracking, audience insight and custom reporting. Gentry says it helps podcast companies grow revenue "and streamline their ad operations by aggregating and centralizing your podcast analytics" [03:48].

q: What was the first version of Podstock?
a: Clayton Gentry says the MVP supported only Megaphone, using its raw download and impression logs, and took roughly 90 days to build with Phoenix LiveView. As he described it, "It was essentially a campaign tracking dashboard" [07:30], with basic order delivery forecasting added.

q: How does Podstock decide what to build on its roadmap?
a: Clayton Gentry and co-founder Michael fuel roadmap discussions with customer and prospect conversations, then shape a pitch that defines what is in and out of a feature. They set a deadline and cut scope to meet it, and as Gentry put it, "We don't fit the timeline around the feature" [15:22].

q: What engineering mistake did Podstock learn from?
a: Clayton Gentry built a bespoke service to decode Postgres write-ahead logs and load the data into BigQuery, then replaced that chain with BigQuery federated queries. While fighting an obscure bug, he recalls telling himself, "dude, you're building a podcast analytics startup" [23:39].

q: Why do things that don't scale in an early startup?
a: Clayton Gentry matched YouTube videos to RSS audio manually and even built an admin UI to support the work, which revealed patterns that later informed automation. He explained that "when you do things manually, you really learn the ins and outs of the data" [18:26].

s11-bonus-the-weekend-prototype-pivot-transitioning-from-fintech-devops-to-advancing-ai-research-infrastructure-with-david-asamu-co-founder-of-nesla

Weekend Hackathon Origins: Nesla grew out of a weekend hackathon David Asamu hosted with friends while working at a fintech company. The group experimented with available AI tools to solve one of their own problems.

Local-First Document Chat: DocsChat, Nesla's first MVP, lets users index sources such as Google Docs and ask questions across them, using local LLMs like Llama so data doesn't have to be shipped elsewhere.

Balancing Research and Products: With limited time and resources, the team weighs effort against value, pairing long-term research with quicker products that can build on its own or others' existing research.
Underestimated GPU Costs: The team didn't project the cost of GPU time for training and experiments well enough. It is now looking at grants, startup programs and free cloud access for researchers.
Ownership Drives a Tiny Team: Nesla's five people largely choose what to work on based on their interests, so Asamu looks for vision alignment and, above all, motivated people who take ownership.

q: What is Nesla and what does it do?
a: Nesla is an AI research lab co-founded by David Asamu that publishes research and also looks for ways to apply it to everyday problems. As Asamu put it, "We try to bridge the gap between research and real world change." [02:46]

q: What is DocsChat, Nesla's first product?
a: David Asamu describes DocsChat as a tool for chatting with your documents wherever they are hosted, such as Google Docs, by indexing them and asking questions across them. Privacy shaped the design, and he stressed that "the important stuff is that it's running locally" [05:01].

q: How does Nesla decide which AI research and products to work on?
a: Asamu says choosing projects has been the biggest challenge, so the team balances long-term research against short-term products while reviewing its resource constraints. He said it is important to consider "the effort to value ratio in terms of what we are doing as well." [06:20]

q: How does a small, self-funded AI lab deal with limited compute?
a: David Asamu says access to GPUs and money to keep running are real challenges for Nesla, which is currently relying on friends and family. He also sees an upside to the constraint: "that's also an advantage because it gets you to be creative in how" [11:12] you solve problems efficiently.

q: What mistake did the Nesla team make early on?
a: Asamu says the team didn't project the cost of its AI experiments well enough, particularly the GPU time needed for training. In his words, they "underestimated how much all of this will cost to actually even get started and keep everything" [14:10] running.

s11-e2-the-4x-faster-indexer-scaling-rust-based-search-to-millions-of-documents-without-infrastructure-bloat-with-clement-kero-renault-co-founder-cto-of-meilisearch

Hackathon-Born Search Engine: Meilisearch began in November 2018 as search for an e-commerce site. A Rust build on RocksDB and Roaring Bitmaps, modeled on Algolia's API and experience, went on to win a Louis Vuitton hackathon.

Roadmap Tied to Paying Users: Kero calls hiring product managers the best decision. Priority goes to customers who index millions of documents, need low-latency search and will pay, while the engine stays available and open to pull requests.

Sharding Beyond Replication: The engine went from handling about 2 million documents around 2020 to over 500 million. Sharding splits content across smaller machines, avoiding the multiplied large servers that replication requires.

Disk-Based Vectors with Arroy: The team ported the C++ base of Spotify's Annoy library to Rust as Arroy, storing vectors in LMDB for durability. A working version took about two months, and memory use is still being refined.

Blameless Response to Failure: A completely broken version shipped one day before Christmas, forcing a rushed fix that took about a week. The team punished no one and instead analyzed what happened to avoid repeating it.

q: What is Meilisearch and what is it used for?
a: Meilisearch is a search engine for the data you provide it, such as an e-commerce site, marketplace or SaaS application, rather than public web data. Clément Renault explained that you "just plug Meilisearch and it will be able to provide a search bar on your website" [02:58].

q: How did Meilisearch get started?
a: Renault and co-founders Quentin and Thomas set out to build a good search engine for an e-commerce website, then won a Louis Vuitton hackathon and went on to work for the company. In Renault's words, "This hackathon like created Meilisearch." [04:03]

q: How does Meilisearch scale to hundreds of millions of documents?
a: Renault said the team long focused on scaling a single instance and has more recently moved to sharding content across machines, which allows smaller servers and faster indexing. On capacity, he said that "with a new engine, we are capable to handle like more than 500 millions without sweat" [09:56].

q: How does Meilisearch store vectors for semantic and hybrid search?
a: The team built Arroy, a Rust vector store based on Spotify's C++ Annoy library, and keeps its contents in LMDB alongside the documents for durability. Renault said they set out "to find a good solution for Meilisearch to store vectors on disk and not in RAM" [11:19].

q: What is the Ask route that Meilisearch is planning?
a: It is a planned feature that lets people ask questions through a search bar on a website they own, with Renault aiming for instant answers instead of a wait of several seconds. Renault described it this way: "It will be a route on Meilisearch to ask Meilisearch about stuff." [13:27]

Transcripts Came First: Metacast's first beta skipped playlists and focused on transcripts, letting listeners read ahead, search, jump to sections, and bookmark or share clips.

Table Stakes Reshaped the Roadmap: Users loved the transcripts but needed playlists, speed selection and other standard features before switching. Metacast had that chunk of work done by October 2024.
Flexible Foundations Early On: The team invested early in a flexible data model and an API-based, mostly serverless architecture to keep costs and maintenance low for a team of two or three.
Bots Sent Costs Spiraling: Opening the podcast catalog to the web drew bots, with traffic around 300,000 requests a day. Performance held, and a re-engineering later cut costs 50 to 70x.
Small but Engaged Audience: Arnab reports about 800 monthly active users, steadily growing, with about 100 paying. Many of those payers regularly share praise, bug reports and feature requests.

q: What can you do with podcast transcripts in Metacast?
a: Arnab Deka explains that listeners can read ahead of the audio, jump to different sections, and bookmark or share specific clips. As he put it, "You could search for different snippets inside that using the transcript." [08:36]

q: What technology was used to build the Metacast app?
a: Arnab and his co-founder Ilya chose Flutter so they could avoid building iOS and Android separately before knowing whether the idea was worth pursuing. Arnab said, "So we decided to do a quick prototype in Flutter, which is a open source framework," [05:28].

q: How did Metacast reduce its infrastructure costs after bot traffic?
a: Publishing the podcast catalog on the web brought heavy bot traffic, and the original system had not been built with caching in mind. Arnab said the team did a big re-engineering, and "we cut down the cost like 50 to 70x recently." [16:25]

q: What mistake did the Metacast founders make early on?
a: Arnab says they made transcripts the primary focus before learning that users also expected standard podcast app features. He reflected, "I feel like we could have built 80% of the stuff we built into transcripts in half the time" [18:46].

q: What advice does Arnab Deka have for young startup founders?
a: Arnab advises validating that the problem matters to real people, then deciding whether your life, family, time and finances allow you to commit for years. He noted, "Because I feel like startups are more like marathons." [25:44]

s11-e1-the-7-year-revenue-drought-surviving-near-zero-growth-to-build-a-15b-cloud-analytics-juggernaut-with-rob-woollen-co-founder-cto-of-sigma-computing

Seven and a Half Years: Rob Woollen says Sigma spent about seven and a half years reaching product market fit with essentially zero revenue, then went from zero to over $100 million in revenue in the last three and a half.

Rebuilding a Working Interface: In 2020, Woollen and his co-founder chose to rebuild the whole interface despite having customers. Vision helped align the team, and early adopters of the new version, including larger deals, built momentum.

Parity Versus Strategic Bets: Sigma balanced closing gaps with business intelligence rivals against reserving capacity for bets like letting users change data, something competitors weren't doing and deals didn't yet hinge on.

Test Hypotheses Sooner: The team spent almost two years building its own interface, programming language and database. Woollen admits he kept believing next month would fix it, when they could have validated ideas earlier.

Hire for Product Sense: Beyond programming talent, Woollen looks for people who empathize with users, enjoy iterating and will rebuild their own work. Sigma's edge, he says, is its interface rather than any one feature.

q: What is Sigma Computing and what does it do?
a: Sigma is data analysis software for building dashboards, reports and applications on top of a company's centralized data. Co-founder and CTO Rob Woollen describes it as "something that looks like a spreadsheet, but works on very large scale data." [02:59]

q: How long did it take Sigma to reach product market fit?
a: Rob Woollen says it took about seven and a half years of an almost 11-year journey, all spent on the same problem of helping non-programmers work with large-scale data. He describes that stretch as "getting to product market fit and getting MVP and having essentially zero revenue." [04:49]

q: Why did Sigma rebuild its interface in 2020?
a: Woollen and his co-founder believed a new interface could be far better than the one that was roughly working, even though it meant discarding work and convincing the team. Woollen says proof came from "early customers that adopted this new interface we had built that were much more successful." [06:37]

q: How does Sigma decide what to build on its roadmap?
a: Woollen says the team balances features needed to compete in an established market against strategic work that could make the product much better or handle cases existing tools couldn't. The goal is to close gaps while still being able to "reserve capacity for building things we think are strategically innovative or important." [09:19]

q: What mistake did Sigma make on the way to product market fit?
a: Woollen points to assuming that what they had built would eventually become the right thing, including an almost two-year effort to build the whole stack. As Woollen put it, "we could test them and we could validate some of these hypotheses earlier" [15:11].

s10-bonus-optimizing-remote-workplace-engagement-replacing-flat-video-grids-and-enhancing-virtual-collaboration-with-real-time-spatial-audio-ecosystems-with-erik-braund-founder-ceo-of-katmai-tech

Built Without Third-Party Engines: Katmai chose not to build on platforms like Roblox, Unreal or Unity, to control its tech and product. The team wrote it in TypeScript, with 3D tooling, and had to optimize heavily because early versions could overheat or black out computers.

The Office Built Itself: A scattered team added sound zones, desks, screen shares and lockable doors so they could work together inside their own technology. That almost accidentally became the virtual office product.

Polish Over Moving Fast: Katmai spent much of 2024 smoothing rough edges and drew the line at version one of its virtual office in February 2025. Erik felt a concept some people need help grasping would get few second chances.

Starbucks Forced Rapid Scale: A loyalty program launch meant compressing rich 3D environments for mobile and adding fraud detection, anti-phishing and more pen tests. The team scaled to millions of people, and the work led to a separate loyalty experiences product.

Surveys Can Mislead: Katmai temporarily removed its old chat when rolling out in-meeting chat, since most survey respondents said they didn't use it much. Angry emails followed, and restoring it took a proper development process.

q: What problem with video conferencing is Katmai trying to solve?
a: Erik Braund saw that traditional video calls suit planned meetings but not the lifelike connection of being with people. He said "video conferencing as we know it is like solid for scheduling a" [04:11] meeting in the future with people you had the foresight to invite, and Katmai's immersive video conferencing aims for something more natural.

q: How do sound zones work in Katmai's virtual office?
a: Erik explained, "we have these things called sound zones where you can cross a line and now you're in a new sound zone." [10:35] Users can also close and lock a door to make that zone private.

q: Why didn't Katmai build on Unity, Unreal or Roblox?
a: Erik said the team knew those options existed but decided against building on a third party. In his words, "we just chose not to because we wanted to control our own destiny and have more" [07:33] control over the tech and the product.

q: How did Katmai scale its 3D experiences for Starbucks?
a: A launch to the Starbucks loyalty program meant supporting many mobile users on cell connections, along with added security and fraud protections. Erik said, "We had to basically figure out how to compress these rich 3D environments and these networked experiences" [20:17]. He reported that the team successfully scaled to millions of people.

q: What mistake caused users to be unable to connect to Katmai?
a: While migrating infrastructure to bring down AWS costs, the team missed a piece used for audio and video connections. Erik recalled, "we forgot to migrate our turn servers when we did all of this" [23:52], which led to a day of emails from users who couldn't connect before the team rolled back and fixed it.

s10-e30-the-qr-code-data-shift-connecting-physical-interactions-with-digital-marketing-fabrics-and-scaling-contactless-engagement-with-ravi-pratap-maddimsetty-co-founder-cto-of-uniqode

Reuse What Already Works: The QR code MVP took about 90 days because it reused the Bluetooth beacon backend, with its short URLs and redirection. Ravi resisted full UI or microservices rewrites until the demand hypothesis was tested.

The 40-Minute Welcome Email: An automated three-line email asked new users why they signed up. Ravi prioritized the problems raised in replies, aiming to convert more 14-day trial users into paying customers.

Everyone Takes Support Shifts: Engineers and designers rotated through support one week at a time, so the people writing features saw how customers used them and dealt with the tickets their bugs created.

One Platform, Many Segments: Uniqode kept its self-serve, product-led focus while adding enterprise features. Self-serve users and brands like Nestle and Marriott share one version of the software, with feature access set by plan.

Don't Penalize Early Adopters: Raising prices on existing customers after adding features led to complaints and cancellations. The team reversed the increase and refocused on adding value and on newer customers.

q: How did Uniqode start, and why did it move from Bluetooth beacons to QR codes?
a: Ravi Pratap Maddimsetty says the company, then called BeaconStack, set out to connect smartphones to the physical world using Bluetooth beacons, NFC, GPS and QR codes. As he recalled, "the funny thing is the QR codes just took off" [04:30], so the team focused on QR codes and later rebranded as Uniqode.

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Uniqode's QR code product?
a: Ravi said the team started in January and had the product out by about mid-March, building a QR code interface on top of the existing beacon platform's Python and Django backend. In his words, "We took about 90 days to build the first MVP" [07:03].

q: How did Uniqode decide what to build next in its early days?
a: Ravi tracked signup, activation and purchase metrics, and prioritized the objections trial users raised, while the team decided for itself how to implement each feature. His reasoning was that "if I solve these users' problems, I know I'm going to get them to become a paying customer" [12:49].

q: What pricing mistake did Uniqode make with existing customers?
a: Ravi explained that the company raised plan prices on earlier customers after rolling out many enhancements, which led to complaints and cancellations, and the increase was reversed. He concluded that "raising prices on a user base that's been loyal to you" [24:35] was a mistake they should have avoided.

q: Will QR codes replace barcodes on product packaging?
a: Ravi believes so, and says Uniqode is helping businesses make that transition, noting that GS1 has recommended the change by 2027 under what he called Sunrise 2027. As he put it, "we think barcodes will get replaced with QR codes" [27:43].

Two Teams, Shared Responsibility: Engineering is measured on shipping features and security on reducing risk. Jit aims to serve both, including a portal where team leaders own and see the security of their team's code.
Closing Isn't the Finish Line: An early mistake was moving on to the next deal too soon. Jit realigned resources and mindset to keep enterprise customers close, happy and getting value.

Agents for AppSec Teams: With AI coding tools swamping security teams, Jit is reimagining its product so practitioners have agents running recurring workflows and ad hoc tasks, aiming for at least 10x productivity.

a: Jit is a company focused on helping developers build security into the software development lifecycle, catching issues before they reach production. Shai Horovitz explained that the team found a way to "take about 10 different scanners, 10 different controls, build them into a GitHub application" [05:28].

q: Why did Jit move from product-led growth to enterprise sales?
a: The original assumption was that developers would be the buyers and largely serve themselves, but Shai's look at the product and talks with customers pointed elsewhere. He concluded that "what we built is an enterprise level product that was a much better fit to be sold" [07:03] through an enterprise sales motion.

q: Why is Jit bringing agentic AI into application security?
a: Shai said customers began describing engineering teams producing far more code with copilots and vibe coding platforms. As he relayed their message, "look, we're swamped in a way that we've never been swamped" [17:25], which sent Jit on a strategy journey to reimagine the product.

q: What does Shai Horovitz look for when hiring at Jit?
a: Shai looks for people who are humble, work well in teams and are extremely ambitious, with a history of handling setbacks and working hard. He said, "Before we look at experience and skills, I look at culture and what are these people bringing to the table" [11:03].

q: What mistake did Jit make with enterprise customers?
a: Shai said the team would think a deal was already won and move on to the next one amid competing priorities. "It took us time to understand that enterprise customers need a different type of process and require us to stay very close to them" [15:47], he said, and the company later realigned to fix it.

the-gene-simmons-of-data-protection-are-you-ready-for-the-genai-data-frontier

Old Controls Won't Cover GenAI: Anthony Cammarano says a major misconception is that existing security and GDPR compliance are enough. Models can still leak sensitive data through training memorization or exfiltration at inference.

Three Sources of New Risk: GenAI widens exposure through an explosion of users, machines and agents, data flowing into training, retrieval and tool calls, and unstructured data whose governance is very immature.

Protect Data at the Source: Keep data protected from where it originates and reveal it only through authorization. Anthony says this automatically mitigates 80 to 90% of the vulnerabilities he discussed.

Agents Expand the Attack Surface: Poisoning, prompt injection and jailbreaks aren't limited to training data or prompts. Untrusted content at the end of a tool an agent trusts, via MCP or A2A, can manipulate the system.

Start With Visibility: Audit and monitor what goes into and out of models, then classify sensitive data, add content and safety guardrails, and check inputs for malicious intent. NIST and OWASP offer useful frameworks.

q: What is the biggest misconception about GenAI data security?
a: Anthony Cammarano says it often comes down to organizations believing their current practices are enough. He described the mindset as "I don't need to do anything, right? And what I have today and what I do today can and will cover" [02:30] what GenAI brings.

q: Why is unstructured data a security risk for GenAI?
a: Large language models are largely built on unstructured data, which lacks the catalogs, owners and schemas that companies wrap around structured data. According to Anthony, "the governance structure around unstructured data is very immature, very loosely defined" [11:44].

q: What is a data-centric approach to GenAI security?
a: It protects the data itself rather than relying on the data stores that hold it, with authorization as the only point where it is revealed. Anthony explained that "if you take a data-centric view to protection, then your data is always protected" [15:31].

q: What is a prompt injection attack?
a: Anthony describes it as a prompt crafted to fool or evade a model's safeguards so it reveals something sensitive or unauthorized. He compared it to an earlier threat: "many years ago of when websites were connected to databases and we had this SQL injection attack" [19:14].

q: How can organizations stay ahead of GenAI security threats?
a: Anthony advises starting with auditing and monitoring, then adding data classification, safety guardrails and defenses against malicious prompts. The guiding principle, he said, is that "you do have to accept that old controls will not work, that data is becoming much more dynamic" [23:49].

Merchant of Record Model: Paddle technically resells its customers' software and takes on transaction liability, so it can handle global tax calculation, filing and remittance, plus subscription renewal compliance and fraud.

Slicing the Invoicing MVP: To move upmarket, Paddle built invoicing around the most common use case. It left recurring invoices out of the first slice, accepting some manual work for customers to get feedback sooner.

Five Levers for Prioritization: Paddle's product managers weigh roadmap work by its impact on acquisition, monetization, retention, cost and risk, using data to get a directional read on each project's value.
A Grueling Replatform: Rebuilding the core billing components as Paddle Billing took a lot of people probably 12 to 18 months. Lovell says it unlocked new functionality and faster product velocity.
Depth Over Breadth: Lovell reflects that shifting resources too soon left a product in an MVP state too long, causing customer friction. He also says too many strategic priorities cost teams focus.

q: What does it mean for Paddle to be a merchant of record?
a: Lucas Lovell explains that Paddle resells its customers' software and takes on liability for each transaction, which lets it handle tax compliance, subscription renewal compliance and fraud. In his words, "what this means is that we are technically reselling your products" [02:59].

q: How did Paddle scope the MVP of its invoicing product?
a: Lovell's team focused on the use case most customers needed instead of covering many invoicing models, and accepted that customers would do some manual work for recurring invoices. "So an example of that was we didn't build in recurring invoice capability." [08:52]

q: How does Paddle prioritize its product roadmap?
a: Lovell says the team stays customer-led and quantifies how each project will affect the business, whether it wins new customers or meets a new regulation. He sums up the framework as "acquisition, monetization, retention, cost, and risk as the five ways" [12:13] product helps Paddle move forward.

q: Why did Paddle rebuild its billing platform?
a: Lovell expected a modern foundation to unlock functionality the old monolithic product, Paddle Classic, constrained, and to raise product velocity, and he says both proved true. Of the resulting Paddle Billing work, he said, "we didn't just rebuild Paddle, we redesigned Paddle for the modern software company." [18:28]

q: What is the future direction of Paddle's product?
a: Lovell wants Paddle to move from operational partner to growth partner, using levers such as checkout conversion, local payment methods, pricing experiments and AI where it makes sense. As he put it, "the future for Paddle is about how do we turn payments into a growth lever?" [22:18]

s10-bonus-the-de-googled-workspace-movement-decentralizing-enterprise-tech-with-private-open-source-productivity-suites-with-david-young-founder-ceo-of-federated-computer

A Linux Distribution for Cloud: Federated Computer combines existing open-source building blocks, including Nextcloud, Baserow and Jitsi, and adds the glue: single sign-on, one place to manage users, and integrated storage.

Flat Price Per Company: Young says the average business spends $300 to $400 per employee per month on SaaS. Federated's best tier, with video conferencing for up to 500 users, is $120 per company per month.

Connect Tools, Don't Bloat Them: When ListMonk users wanted more, the team didn't cram CRM features into the mailing list tool. It connected ListMonk to EspoCRM, treating each product as part of one distribution.

Scale Means Right-Sizing: Young's lesson from running Joyent is that the key to scale is getting as small as possible. Federated focuses on serving small businesses, such as a 10-person company, well while spending as little as possible.

Fix Hiring Mistakes Quickly: Young says hires who don't work out are more on him than on them, often because he got lazy in vetting. Once it's clear a hire was a mistake, the sooner you cut ties, the better.

q: What is Federated Computer?
a: Federated Computer, founded by David Young, bundles open-source SaaS tools for businesses and handles the IT work of keeping them running. Young explained that "we provide customers with all the open source SaaS software they need" [03:57].

q: How much does Federated Computer cost?
a: David Young says the best tier includes video conferencing for up to 500 users, groupware, online documents, spreadsheets and a no-code database. He described it as "so many different solutions for $120 per domain, meaning per company per month" [04:21].

q: How was the first version of Federated Computer built?
a: David Young's team started with pre-built open-source projects and mapped each one's capabilities and gaps to work out what glue they had to invent. On the tooling, he said, "We did most of this using system tools, so Bash, Go, these sorts of languages" [07:17]. The company launched in 2022.

q: How does Federated Computer keep customer data private?
a: David Young says each customer's setup is entirely private, with nothing shared between customers. In his words, "Every one of our customers gets their own install." [05:01]

q: What does David Young say about scaling a tech product?
a: Young argues that very few projects need massive scale, and that right-sizing makes it easier to understand the tools and hire for the problem. As he put it, "the key to scale is not getting big. It's figuring out how to get as small as possible." [16:00]
