Compliance Is Not Security: Iwona Rajca warns that equating the two is a dangerous mindset. Other red flags include poor visibility into who can access what data, database admins who can see everything, and missing multi-factor authentication.

Attackers Now Scale Through Services: Ransomware-as-a-service sells installation packages, guides and even support lines. Supply chain attacks hit one vendor to reach many businesses, as with MOVEit, which compromised over 2,000 companies.

Simplicity Shrinks the Attack Surface: Disjointed and monolithic systems are harder to understand, audit, test and monitor. Rajca points to modularity and platform-agnostic data protection that gives one central view of access and use.

Make Stolen Data Meaningless: Protegrity replaces original data with substitutes such as tokens across the environment, then unprotects it only when used, through automation and role-based access controls. An intruder sees only nonsense.

Repeatable Pipelines for Data Sharing: Security fears and manual, DIY processes hold back data sharing. Protegrity is working with clients to productize anonymization that prevents re-identification while keeping the impact on analytical value minimal.

q: What are the signs that a company's cybersecurity approach is outdated?
a: Iwona Rajca looks for a lack of control and visibility over data access, such as separate identity systems across platforms, all-seeing database admins, or no multi-factor authentication. The bigger red flag is treating compliance as security, because as Rajca put it, "Security is not a checkbox exercise." [03:36]

q: What is a supply chain attack?
a: Rajca describes it as an attack on your third-party software provider, business partner or other vendor, with examples including MOVEit, a Snowflake-centric attack and Finastra. She explained that "the intention is that they try to hack one system to get to many businesses." [05:20]

q: What does security through simplicity mean?
a: Rajca calls it a principle rather than a blueprint, based on the idea that complicated environments have a wider attack surface. In her words, the concept says "you should move towards simpler systems." [08:14] She names modularization, including microservices, as a big part of it.

q: How can companies secure data without blocking its use?
a: Rajca says successful companies shift "their mindset from perceiving security as a blocker to perceiving it as an enabler." [11:27] Protegrity's approach is to protect data across the entire environment and reverse it to its original form only when it is being used, based on role-based access controls.

q: Why aren't more businesses sharing and monetizing their data?
a: Rajca cites security concerns and past failures, such as a New York City taxi trip data set that was allegedly anonymized but reverse engineered. She also said data sharing efforts are often DIY: "These processes struggle with the fact they're very manual and it's hard to repeat them." [14:17]

s10-e28-replacing-legacy-lms-silos-and-driving-student-engagement-with-institutional-communication-networks-with-kavitta-ghai-co-founder-ceo-of-nectir

Open Source Got Them Started: With no technical experience, the founders built Nectir Chat on open source code. Schools paid for implementation support, engagement expertise and integration with the LMS and other campus tools.

A Crash That Built Trust: About 20,000 UCSB students hit Nectir at once as remote classes began, and it kept crashing for a week. Strong customer service helped, and UCSB signed a 10-year contract a year later.

Pivoting While Still Selling: Nectir Chat was selling, but the founders saw AI as a better answer. With limited runway they built Nectir AI, which matched six years of the first product's revenue in six months.

The Rule of Four: A feature goes on the roadmap once four separate customers ask about it in sales and discovery calls. The team also weighs whether users have enough AI literacy to use it, and its effect on critical thinking.

Measured Student Outcomes: Ghai reports that the first campus-wide deployment found a 20% GPA increase for Nectir AI users versus non-users, 13% higher final scores and a 36% rise in intrinsic motivation to learn.

q: How did Nectir get started?
a: Kavitta Ghai and co-founder Jordan started Nectir as UC Santa Barbara undergrads after a class Slack group showed her how technology could improve the classroom. When the university said Slack wasn't built for schools, Ghai asked what would work, saying "If you had a magic wand and you actually could make a platform like this that scales across the entire campus" [05:16].

q: Why did Nectir pivot from a chat tool to AI infrastructure for higher education?
a: Nectir Chat was selling, but Ghai and her co-founder concluded AI could better deliver 24/7 personalized student support, and Stanford GSB had asked for a platform built around AI teaching assistants. Ghai recalled realizing that "there's a better solution that we could be building today to solve this problem" [12:13].

q: What happened when UCSB moved to remote learning on Nectir?
a: Ghai said the platform had never been pressure tested for thousands of simultaneous users, and it crashed repeatedly for a week. As she described it, "literally 20,000 students got online onto Nectir Chat all at once" [22:38].

q: How does Nectir decide which features to build next?
a: Ghai's team uses what she calls the rule of four to judge market viability, while also checking that customers understand AI well enough to use the feature. She explained that "if in sales and discovery calls, we hear four separate customers ask about" [16:23] the same feature, it goes on the product roadmap.

q: Does Nectir AI improve student outcomes?
a: Ghai cited a published study of the first campus-wide deployment, saying "we found a 20% increase in the GPA in students that use Nectir AI" [26:11] compared with those who did not. She also reported gains in final scores and motivation, and said the study led to statewide research with the California Community College system.

s10-bonus-the-cicd-performance-shift-accelerating-build-pipelines-and-eliminating-developer-idle-time-with-darko-fabijan-co-founder-cto-of-semaphore
A Deliberately Narrow MVP: Semaphore first supported only Ruby on Rails and focused on running tests fast, with no deployment phase. The focus amazed some users but turned others away.

Speed Created the Aha Moment: Users picked a repo, Semaphore analyzed its setup, and a first pipeline quickly turned green. Bare metal hardware instead of AWS made it fast, and the company remains bootstrapped.
Rewriting for Bigger Customers: Around 2016, growing customers outgrew the product. Semaphore rebuilt it from scratch, taking about two and a half years to get the new version into users' hands.
Too Many Juniors, Too Fast: Hiring many out-of-college developers to boost velocity overwhelmed the team and forced a major course correction. Darko says the lost speed cost market opportunities.
Start a Playbook on Day One: Darko advises founders to record each new challenge and how they handled it, in a markdown file or Google document, so the team can reuse the answer next time.

q: What is Semaphore and who is it for?
a: Semaphore is a continuous delivery tool that Darko Fabijan says helps teams ship code faster, mainly high-velocity product teams. He described a typical CTO's demand as "I want sub four minutes, a feedback loop for my engineers when they push the code" [03:18].

q: How was the first version of Semaphore built?
a: Darko said it took roughly nine months to reach beta and about a year to reach general availability, with a strong focus on the Ruby on Rails community. For speed, he explained, "we relied on bare metal hardware, we didn't use AWS" [05:24].

q: Why did Semaphore rewrite its product from scratch?
a: Customers had grown, some to around 200 people, and could no longer model their processes in the product. Darko called a rewrite an anti-pattern, but said "we reinvented Semaphore from scratch to eliminate all the limitations" [12:33].

q: Why did Semaphore release an open source Community Edition?

q: What hiring mistake did Semaphore make while scaling its tech team?
a: Darko said the company chose to hire more out-of-college developers in place of fewer senior people, believing it could support them and move faster. As he put it, "we overwhelmed the team with too many junior-ish people" [10:30], which required a major course correction.

the-gene-simmons-of-data-protection-fortifying-your-data-defenses

Breaches Fuel Convincing Scams: Clyde Williamson warns that stolen personal details power phone scams, such as a fake police officer who knows about your grandchild at college and asks for money for a supposed medical emergency.

PCI Shows Rules Work: Credit card theft dropped dramatically after PCI, while US PII theft continued largely unabated. Williamson expects the US to eventually enforce privacy rules, forcing unprepared organizations to catch up.

Removing Names Isn't Anonymity: Williamson cites research showing gender, date of birth and zip code can identify about 87% of people in the US. He advises bringing in privacy expertise, such as a chief privacy officer.

Analyze Without Exposing Identities: Tokenization swaps real values for consistent substitutes, so records can still be matched. Differential privacy and synthetic data support large-scale analytics; homomorphic encryption is still too slow.

Limit Access by Role: Giving each role only the data its job needs shrinks the damage when someone clicks a phishing link. At a retailer, isolating card data and using tokens elsewhere also narrowed the security team's focus.

q: Why does consumer data privacy matter if my information has already been breached?
a: Clyde Williamson says each compromise still adds risk, because scammers use personal details to pose as people such as police officers in a fake emergency. A victim may pay because, as he put it, "they have information that makes them sound like they know what they're doing" [04:40].

q: Is data anonymous if you remove names and addresses?
a: Not necessarily, according to Williamson, who cites research that re-identified people using only gender, date of birth and zip code. He said, "Just those three pieces of information is enough to identify about 87%" [10:38] of people in the United States.

q: How can businesses analyze customer data without exposing personal information?
a: Williamson points to tokenization and other pseudonymization, where "you can substitute the real value with a fake value that's consistent" [08:55]. This lets teams match the same customer across tables and run many kinds of analytics without exposing the real name.

q: What is differential privacy and when is it useful?
a: Williamson explains it with coin flips that determine whether a query gets the true answer or a slight fib, so no single record can be trusted as real. It doesn't suit every analysis, but across tens of thousands of people, "this differential privacy allows me to get really highly accurate analytical data" [15:28].

q: How can companies limit the damage from a phishing attack?
a: Williamson recommends restricting sensitive data to what each role needs to do its job. A clicked link can still infect a system, but "you've limited the exposure down to the bare minimum of what that person might be able to" [18:09] get into.

s10-e27-the-nearshore-engineering-era-sourcing-elite-latin-american-tech-talent-and-eliminating-time-zone-fragmentation-with-gino-ferrand-founder-ceo-of-teclaio

s10-e26-p2-the-physical-ai-revolution-translating-complex-sensor-telemetry-into-real-world-insights-with-ivan-poupyrev-nick-gillian-co-founders-of-archetype-ai

One Model, Many Sensors: Archetype designed Newton to fuse cameras, radar, lidar and time series sensors, even 100 cameras across a city or factory. Customer demand decides which sensor types come first.

Products Must Not Fail: Ivan contrasts proving a technology works with proving a product does not fail, in development, deployment and use. Focusing on particular sensors first limits those failure modes.

Lenses Over Agents: Ivan says people rejected agents for AI meant to amplify human abilities. Archetype's "lens" metaphor proved sticky: users can focus, direct and stack lenses, and quickly grasp what they can and can't do.

Blame Process, Not People: The founders want a no-blame culture that still finds out why things fail. If an engineer's config change breaks production, the fix is better tests, procedures or QA, leaving a safety net for big risks.

An Early Physical AI Bet: Archetype bet on physical AI before VLMs arrived, when even connecting a camera to a foundation model was hard to explain. A very small team has since trained Newton and tested it on real customer problems.

q: What is Archetype AI's Newton model?
a: Newton is Archetype's foundation model for the physical world, built to take in many types of sensors or many instances of the same sensor. Nick Gillian explained that customers "can plug in cameras and radar sensors and time series sensors and lidars all into one holistic model" [02:08].

q: Why does Archetype AI use lenses instead of AI agents?
a: Ivan Poupyrev said that for AI meant to amplify human capabilities, "agents just doesn't work really well there because agents are just autonomy" [08:04]. Archetype instead uses the metaphor of a lens, a new way to see the world that users can focus, direct and stack.

q: What is the difference between building a technology and building a product?
a: According to Ivan Poupyrev, building a technology is about proving it can work, while a product has a different goal: "It's to prove that technology does not fail." [04:06] He pointed to failures during development, deployment and use, which Archetype limits by initially focusing on particular sensors.

q: What is the future vision for Archetype AI and Newton?
a: Ivan Poupyrev described a new kind of computer, where an AI model is the central computing unit and people program it in human language. As he put it, "we see Newton emerge as a general-purpose computing" [16:16] platform.

q: What advice do Archetype AI's co-founders give young entrepreneurs?
a: Ivan Poupyrev advises pairing a big, scalable idea with an MVP you can ship and put in front of customers quickly. Nick Gillian urges founders with real expertise to trust their gut and make a bet, warning that "if you definitely follow the herd, then you're always going to be second" [27:38].

the-gene-simmons-of-data-protection-kiss-keep-it-simple-stupid-a-data-security-dilemma

Protect the Data Itself: James Rice's KISS method embeds protection into the data through de-identification, so it travels with the data at rest, in transit and in use. Defense in depth still matters.

Spend Versus Breaches: Rice cites about $180 billion in 2023 cybersecurity spend, while compromises rose 70% to 80%. Much of that money guards apps, networks and cloud, which he calls "envelope security."

Fit-for-Purpose Protection: Match the technique to the business need. A token can stand in for a Social Security number and be reversed if needed, while anonymization turns a birth date into an age range and discards the original.

Shrinking Compliance Scope: By de-identifying credit cards, a major credit reporting agency took many systems out of PCI DSS scope. Rice puts the savings on audit, compliance and other security at $40 million to $60 million.

Start With One Use Case: Don't boil the ocean. Pick a high-value use case, discover and classify sensitive data, segment it by risk and consumption needs, then choose anonymization, masking or tokenization.

q: What is the KISS method in data security?
a: KISS stands for Keep It Simple, Stupid, and James Rice of Protegrity applies it by attaching protection to the data itself, for example by replacing sensitive values with tokens. As Rice put it, "data protection should mean protecting the data, not everything around the data" [04:43].

q: Why do traditional cybersecurity defenses fail to stop data breaches?
a: James Rice argues that spending goes to applications, access rights, infrastructure, networks and cloud, leaving the data exposed if an attacker gets through. Of those controls, he said, "what are those things not protecting they're not protecting the data itself" [07:19].

q: What is the difference between pseudonymization and anonymization?
a: James Rice explains that anonymization throws information away, such as turning a date of birth into an age range that can't be reversed. Pseudonymization keeps a way back to the original: in Rice's words, "you're able to actually replace that information with a token" [14:08].

q: Does data tokenization and de-identification affect performance?
a: Yes, James Rice says there is a performance trade-off, and that Protegrity offers several integration methods to address it, including protocol-level intercepts, APIs or SDKs, and database agents. Of customer pushback, Rice said, "Data protection is hard, and there is a performance trade-off" [20:18].

q: How should a company get started with data-centric security?
a: James Rice advises beginning by "architecting and prioritizing around a use case" [20:48], ideally one where data protection delivers the most business value. From there, he suggests discovering and classifying sensitive data, segmenting it by risk and consumption, and choosing a fit-for-purpose protection method.

s10-e26-p1-the-physical-ai-revolution-translating-complex-sensor-telemetry-into-real-world-insights-with-ivan-poupyrev-nick-gillian-co-founders-of-archetype-ai

Generalization Beats One-Off Models: Narrow models needed fresh data whenever the task, environment or device changed. Archetype's Newton foundation model aims to generalize across tasks and fuse multiple sensor types.

Lenses Steer the Model: Instead of back-and-forth chat, users apply lenses that focus Newton on areas like safety, security or productivity as it continuously analyzes live sensor data. Multiple lenses can run in parallel on one model.

Customer Research Shaped the MVP: Talks with hundreds of companies surfaced three use cases: reading physical measurements like temperature and vibration, understanding human behavior, and connecting the two.

A Model Isn't a Solution: Physical-world companies can't simply download a model and run it. Newton is wrapped in a platform that handles sensor connections, data management, authentication and real-time data.

Hire for No Playbook: The distributed team, close to 25 people, looks for hands-on hires who cope with ambiguity, accept changes in direction and aren't afraid to fail, as long as they learn why they failed.

q: What problem is Archetype AI solving with physical AI?
a: Ivan Poupyrev explained that traditional sensor models had to be trained on exact data for exact tasks, and small changes meant starting over. For most people building with sensors, "the cost of data collection to build a robust system is just insurmountable" [08:20]. Archetype's Newton model is meant to generalize across tasks and sensors.

q: What are lenses in Archetype AI's Newton platform?
a: Lenses are a third interaction model, alongside assistants and agents, that guides Newton toward what a user cares about while it analyzes sensor data. Nick Gillian contrasted this with repeatedly asking a chatbot about a package, saying you just want to say, "notify me when FedEx comes to the door" [14:27].

q: How did Ivan Poupyrev and Nick Gillian start working together?
a: A member of Ivan's team at Google had used Nick's open source Gesture Recognition Toolkit, and Ivan called to recruit him to a top secret project in 2014. Ivan had been skeptical of AI, but recalled, "Nick joined the team and he's converted me" [05:35].

q: How does Archetype AI decide what goes on the Newton roadmap?
a: Nick Gillian said the team carefully chooses pilot customers and uses their problems, sensors and requirements to decide which features to accelerate. The aim is technology that scales, and as Nick put it, "we're not just building one-off bespoke solutions for each domain or each sensor type" [20:24].

q: What does Archetype AI look for when hiring?
a: Ivan Poupyrev described wanting people who are hands-on, can work without a playbook and can handle changes in direction. Failure is accepted but must be understood: "It's okay to fail, but it's not okay not to know why you fail" [23:12].

s10-bonus-the-workplace-play-shift-combating-hybrid-remote-loneliness-and-engineering-high-engagement-slack-game-networks-with-quinn-li-oshea-founder-ceo-of-braid

Polish Matters for Consumer Signal: The first app took a week of Figma design before being built in React Native. Quinn Li argues that a janky-looking consumer product biases users and muddies the signal on whether it works.

q: What is Braid and what does it do?
a: Braid, founded by Quinn Li O'Shea, uses games to help coworkers build rapport and connection, with games currently embedded in Slack. Quinn Li describes it this way: "Braid is an employee engagement platform that's focused on bringing people" [02:37] together at work through play.

q: How did Braid build and measure its first MVP?

q: How does Braid decide who to hire?
a: Quinn Li favors a paid contract-to-hire trial that shows whether communication is good and working together feels energizing. As Quinn Li put it, "There's nothing like just working on a project together for a week or two to see," [09:22] whether it is going to work out.

q: What advice does Quinn Li O'Shea have for early-stage founders?

s10-e25-modernizing-blue-chip-alternative-assets-and-scaling-digital-portfolio-management-with-alberto-simon-co-founder-chief-product-officer-of-masterworks

Test Demand and Angle First: The first MVP was a landing page with email sign-up, meant to learn whether people cared and which pitch worked: art fanatics and democratized ownership, or alternative-asset diversification.

Control Over Quick Setup: The team skipped WordPress for Node.js, React and GraphQL. It took longer to launch the first page, but gave them design freedom and avoided a later migration to a proper front-end stack.

An Amazon-Style Investing Funnel: While awaiting SEC and FINRA approval, the team had users complete steps like KYC/AML details, payment setup via Plaid and Dwolla, and a custom agreement, aiming to leave them one button press from investing.

Phone Calls Helped Close Investors: Interest faded when real money was required, so Masterworks tested interns on the phones and moved to a membership funnel where prospects had to talk with the team about their goals.

Art Focus and Crypto Detours: Leading with the art brought heavy high-res images, slow performance and weak sales closing. An early crypto component, later dropped, also delayed the product they ultimately moved forward with.

q: What is Masterworks and how does it work?
a: Masterworks, co-founded by Alberto Simon, lets people buy fractional shares in paintings and get their cut of the profits when a work is sold. Simon described the idea as "Allowing people to invest fractionally into multi-million dollar paintings" [04:38].

q: What did the first Masterworks MVP look like?
a: Alberto Simon said the first version was built to gauge interest and learn which marketing angle would work: "So that included a landing page, a page where people could sign up and give us their email." [05:45]. The first technology MVP followed, with share reservations, a transaction ledger and an internal admin tool.

q: Why did Masterworks build its own front end instead of using WordPress?
a: The team wanted full control over designs and chose Node.js, React and GraphQL, even though the first page took longer to launch. Simon said they quickly realized "that our product isn't totally easy to fit into a box." [08:05].

q: Why does Masterworks have investors talk to someone before investing?
a: Alberto Simon said many people showed interest but stopped responding when it was time to pay, and art was something they didn't truly understand. The team tested phone sales and found that "when it comes to money, people still seem to have some comfort" [12:09] with talking to someone.

q: What early mistake did Masterworks make with its product?
a: Simon said, "One of the first early mistakes we made was focusing a lot of the product on the art angle" [17:34]. Large high-resolution images slowed the site, and the art-centered approach also hurt the ability to close sales.

s10-bonus-the-decentralized-data-engine-monetizing-enterprise-ai-datasets-and-regulating-model-training-access-with-don-gossen-co-founder-ceo-of-nevermined
Pricing Mistakes Sank AI Builders: Charging too little left builders covering power users' costs, while charging too much drove churn among lighter users. Some simply shut their products down.
Metered Costs Become Credits: Users acquire an agent's credits, and each tool burns a set amount through smart contracts. In Don's example, a GPT-4 request costs 400 of a user's 1,000 credits.
Hiding the Crypto: Users can register with Gmail or GitHub and pay by card through Stripe. A non-custodial MPC wallet is still created behind the scenes, and crypto users can pay in USDC.

Payments Emerged From Provenance: Nevermined began by tracking where data and algorithms come from and how they're used. Demo audiences kept seeing a payments use, and in fall 2022 the team dove into payments.

Focus Over Shiny Opportunities: Don says overemphasizing NFTs diverted attention from the core proposition, hurting productivity, go-to-market and maybe branding. His lesson: adapt to the market, but hold your conviction.

q: What is Nevermined building?
a: Nevermined is building payments infrastructure that lets AI agents pay and get paid, with a focus on AI-to-AI interactions. Don Gossen summed up the ambition as "We're building the PayPal of AI." [05:57]

q: Why aren't traditional payment tools like Stripe enough for AI agents?
a: Don Gossen argues that agents are dynamic, and the cost of serving one request can differ by an order of magnitude or more from another, depending on the model used. In his words, "Existing payment solutions like Stripe, for example, they're designed around pricing" [03:04] of SKUs.

q: How does Nevermined's credit system price AI agent usage?
a: Users acquire an agent's tokens, or credits, which are burned according to the tool the agent selects, with redemption handled by smart contracts. Don describes a system that hooks into the agent's observability "and takes the metered cost of running that agent service" [05:48] and turns it into a settlement cost for the user.

q: Do you need a crypto wallet to use Nevermined?
a: No, users can sign up with social logins and pay with a credit or debit card through a Stripe integration. Don explained that "that registration function still results in a wallet that's created, but it's a non-custodial wallet." [14:14]

q: What mistake did Nevermined make with its focus?
a: Don Gossen said the distraction hurt the team's productive capacity and go-to-market, and maybe its branding. The misstep was "putting too much emphasis on the non-fungibility of an asset like NFTs" [24:48], which pulled attention from the core proposition.

s10-e24-the-causal-ai-shift-providing-deterministic-context-to-ai-agents-and-automating-cloud-reliability-with-shmuel-kliger-founder-of-causely

Root Cause Over Alert Floods: One problem can degrade a flood of services and send teams into a war room. Causely aims to have software name the root cause behind those latency and error-rate symptoms instead.

Causality Meets Topology: Built on patents Kliger developed years ago, Causely combines causal knowledge of how problems propagate with environment topology, mapping possible root causes to their symptoms and searching that map in real time.

OpenTelemetry's Costly Paradigm Shift: Kliger welcomes applications reporting on themselves instead of management tools reaching out to discover them. The catch is a flood of traces and logs, so the value lies in extracting what matters.

A Hand-Picked Founding Team: Kliger waited to start Causely until the people he wanted were available. All engineers but one previously worked with him at Turbonomic, some going back to Smarts, his first company.

Trust Gates Automation: Causely starts with troubleshooting, with remediation and prevention as goals. Kliger says success depends on earning users' trust to let software act, a journey that took a few years at Turbonomic.

q: How does Causely find the root cause of service degradation?
a: Shmuel Kliger explains that Causely uses OpenTelemetry data to discover services, dependencies and data flows, then combines that topology with built-in causality knowledge to map root causes to symptoms. The system can then "use that mapping in real time to do searches to pinpoint root causes" [09:59].

q: How does Causely work with OpenTelemetry?
a: Causely consumes OpenTelemetry traces and logs to discover the environment, monitor latency and error rates, and infer root causes. Kliger says the huge data volume is the challenge, noting that "this data is important, but more important is how do I extract from" [16:22] it what matters.

q: What is on the Causely product roadmap?
a: Kliger describes adding analytics that remediate problems and predict and prevent bad states, working alongside today's root cause analysis. He also plans to widen coverage to other cloud services and instrumentation, explaining that "The other dimension is what I call the adjacency dimension." [12:23]

q: What mistake did Shmuel Kliger make while scaling Turbonomic?
a: Kliger says that as Turbonomic grew to 700 people, only a handful deeply understood and shared his conviction, when he would have wanted something like 10% of the company. He says he did not ensure there was a critical mass of people "that has the conviction and the belief that I had in the power of the technology" [22:16].

q: What advice does Shmuel Kliger give young entrepreneurs?
a: Kliger urges founders to start with strong conviction: "Have the right convictions. And if you have the right convictions, don't let" [27:32] others tell you that you're wrong. He admits his approach is controversial, since he builds technology out of conviction first and then finds the right problem to solve with it.

s10-bonus-the-agentic-pm-shift-replacing-product-requirements-documents-with-code-ready-task-architectures-with-tyler-wells-co-founder-cto-of-braingrid

Born From a Shrinking Team: As headcount fell at Propel, Tyler's team leaned on Cursor to keep shipping. He estimates code completion and light chat gave a 2-3x boost before they dug into unleashing the agent.
Rules as Agent Guardrails: Without rules, agents can wander. If you don't say you use Jest, one might introduce Mocha. BrainGrid began by helping developers discover, install and use these rules.
Small Team, Different Next Hire: BrainGrid is three people and wants to stay small. Tyler expects the next hire to be in go-to-market or DevRel rather than another developer.

Specs Written for Agents: Tyler foresees humans and AI co-writing far more detailed specs, then agents working with senior engineers to break them into chunks for coding tools. He expects Linear and Jira to largely fade.

q: What is BrainGrid?
a: BrainGrid is a developer platform that Tyler Wells says aims to unleash agentic coding through rules, planning and implementation, while managing the artifacts agents need. The team also builds the product with its own workflow, and Tyler said, "We're using that same flow as we're building the platform for BrainGrid to build BrainGrid." [05:11]

q: Why do AI coding agents need rules?

q: Will AI agents replace tools like Linear and Jira?
a: Tyler Wells expects the traditional handoff from product manager to engineering to task tickets to change, with agents helping write detailed specifications and break them into consumable chunks. He predicted, "I see things like Linear and Jira largely starting to go away" [15:32].

q: How is BrainGrid approaching hiring and team size?
a: At the time of the interview, the team was Tyler Wells, a co-founder from Propel and a front-end developer in Colombia. Tyler said, "we want to keep the team as small as possible for as long as possible." [09:25]

q: What startup mistake did Tyler Wells learn from at Propel?
a: Tyler says Propel made a big bet on customer-facing analytics and took longer than it needed to realize the market was not going to appear. He believes they should have "had our exit criteria well-defined to say, hey, this experiment is working, keep going," [13:34] or else stopped and pivoted.

s10-e23-from-the-netscape-era-to-the-multicloud-era-building-a-15-year-infrastructure-moat-and-designing-remote-first-culture-with-anthony-eden-founder-ceo-of-dnsimple

Start With a Bare-Bones MVP: DNSimple went from first code in April 2010 to launch that July, using Ruby on Rails, PowerDNS and one hired design template applied to plain forms. Unnecessary screens were stripped out to keep it simple.

Shoestring Infrastructure First: With no outside investment, early name servers ran in unicast on shared VPSs costing about $10 to $15 a month. Performance was poor, and within a couple of years DNSimple moved to Anycast and leased hardware.

Attacks Drive DNS Scaling: A major 2014 denial of service attack overwhelmed protective hardware and got DNSimple blacklisted in a data center. It built similar A and B side setups across data centers and used Anycast to add capacity gradually.

Customers Shaped the Roadmap: Eden built for his own needs, quizzed engineers at Ruby events and took customer ideas, including one that led to the alias record. Planning stayed short term and focused strictly on DNS and domains.

Slow Growth by Design: DNSimple never felt the need to chase funding and now has 25 team members. Eden says steady growth let him spend time with his kids, though he waited too long to bring in a fractional CFO.

q: Why did Anthony Eden start DNSimple?
a: Anthony Eden was frustrated with managing DNS at GoDaddy, so he and his brother built an alternative, later adding domain registration and certificates. He recalled, "The DNS part was really bad. And I said, why am I still using this?" [03:47].

q: How was the first version of DNSimple built?
a: The first version used Ruby on Rails, was deployed to Heroku as Eden recalls, and ran PowerDNS name servers on virtual private servers, with a REST API following shortly after. Eden, who says he is not a designer, hired somebody "to build just one template and I just applied that to pretty much everything" [05:37].

q: How did a DDoS attack affect DNSimple?
a: In 2014, a major denial of service attack overwhelmed even the managed hardware DNSimple had put in place for protection, and the company was blacklisted in one of its data centers. Eden said, "So it was to the point of where we actually lost network." [12:24].

q: Is DNSimple venture funded or bootstrapped?
a: DNSimple was bootstrapped with no outside investment at the start, and Anthony Eden says the business never felt the need to chase funding to reach the next step. Of that healthy pace, he said "that's something that was by design. It was a choice made to follow a path of slow and steady" [15:43].

q: What advice does Anthony Eden give young entrepreneurs?

s10-bonus-optimizing-software-delivery-intelligence-integrating-signals-across-git-and-jira-to-audit-ai-token-efficiency-and-dora-metrics-with-andrew-lau-co-founder-ceo-of-jellyfish

Services Before Product: Jellyfish offered early partners free help with forecasts, budgets and slides in exchange for access to tools like Jira and GitHub. Manual work became custom code, then the MVP, over a couple of years.

Objections Became the Roadmap: With about 10 alphas, the team started cold calling to sell. The "no" and "maybe if" answers became roadmap items, prioritized by cost, market, company size, persona and problem space.

Makers Before Scalers: The first 10 hires were technical, filling gaps in DevOps, data science, UI and Postgres on a Django stack. Lau looked first for good people and communicators who could work through arguments together.

Don't Scale Prematurely: Lau warns that building for unseen scale costs time and can create liabilities. The trade-off is accepting later scale walls, such as a customer with more Git repos than engineers, and paying for them in time, money and grumpiness.

Start Marketing Earlier: Despite vowing not to under-market again, the founders didn't get going until around 2020. Lau says they could have started in 2018, talking about the challenges of leading teams before the product was ready.

q: What does Jellyfish do?
a: Jellyfish, co-founded by CEO Andrew Lau, serves engineering leaders ranging from team leads and managers to CTOs. In Lau's words, "We build tools to help engineering leaders lead their teams." [02:47] That includes helping make sure projects are resourced and delivered on time and that team members are supported.

q: How did Jellyfish build its MVP?
a: Andrew Lau and his co-founders went back to people they had interviewed and offered hands-on help in exchange for access to their digital tools. He recalled telling them, "And we'll do it for free and we'll do it with you" [05:49]. Work done by hand was gradually automated and tested with others who had similar problems.

q: When should a startup build for scale?
a: Andrew Lau advises against optimizing for scale that may never arrive, saying, "I hate the concept of building for scale before you see it." [11:34] He adds that founders must then expect to hit scale walls later and be ready to pay for that trade-off.

q: What mistake did Jellyfish's founders make early on?
a: Andrew Lau says the founders waited too long to market the company, which he attributes partly to engineer introversion. As he put it, "I think we started too late with kind of marketing, blogging, telling our story," [15:30]. q: How are AI coding assistants changing engineering leadership?

Calls Became the Roadmap: Annoyed by helping people over chat, Josh got customers on calls and sometimes offered to build a fix that weekend if they bought. That feedback loop still heavily shapes the roadmap.

q: How was the first version of Referral Rock built?
a: Josh built it on the .NET stack he already knew and reused earlier code for templated, multi-tenant websites. He turned survey answers from interested businesses into resource files so he could "populate those sites without building an admin interface" [07:21].

q: What scaling problem did Referral Rock run into early on?

Designed to Deprecate Itself: Focused pairs, writes tests and teaches customers new skills. A win is a customer going from five developers to zero and steering on their own, not growing from two developers to ten.

Holding Firm on Price: Austin refused substantial discounts offered against promises of more work. It slowed growth dramatically and turned sales into teaching why two developers at $220 an hour can beat eight at $80.

Hire for Patient Communication: Focused looks for "unintimidating and unintimidated" people. Interviews center on whether candidates can explain highly technical things without making someone feel stupid.

Polish Before Selling a Service: A poorly planned design kickoff with longtime customer Lettuce damaged trust. Focused owned the mistake, gave designers time to retrospect, and re-engaged Lettuce on design.

q: What does it mean for a software consultancy to be designed to deprecate itself?

q: What was the first version of Focused?

q: How did Focused handle pressure to discount its pricing?

q: What mistake did Focused make when launching design services?

s10-bonus-the-education-first-fintech-shift-using-ai-decision-engines-to-simplify-investing-for-everyday-earners-with-jason-schappert-co-founder-ceo-of-moola

Born from Near Failure: Schappert's aviation test-prep business ended in an eight-figure exit, but he says it nearly went broke twice. The budgeting system and spreadsheets he built to recover became the basis for Moola.

Investing First, Banking Later: Moola's self-funded MVP took nine months and launched with investing and IRAs. Trying to build banking and investing at once, and adding people to do it, burned more cash than necessary.

Revenue Levers Drive Roadmap: Long, regulated onboarding and high acquisition costs make each customer valuable. Moola plans debit cards, envelope-style "pockets," high-yield savings, HSAs and 529s to deliver more value.
Scale the Right Users: Adding 100,000 users who each deposit only $5 would lose money once KYC, AWS and other costs are counted. Schappert wants the right metrics and customers before scaling.

Personalized Money Decisions: Moola's direction is using language models with a member's banking data to weigh choices like rent or phone plans, including opportunity costs such as moving expenses and a longer commute.

q: What is Moola and why was it created?
a: Moola is a fintech company founded by Jason Schappert that grew out of the money struggles he faced while running his aviation business. His wife urged him to add technology to the system he had built, and Schappert described the goal as "taking the system that we know works and applying it to the masses" [04:02].

q: What did Moola's MVP include?
a: After nine months of work, Moola's MVP focused on investing, including IRAs and what Schappert calls the Moola Meter, which he described as more machine learning than AI, with a large language model included. Banking features were left for later, and as Schappert put it, "So we launched just the investing" [05:51] side first.

q: How does Moola plan to use AI to personalize financial advice?
a: Schappert described using a large language model with banking data to analyze a member's situation, such as whether moving to cheaper rent really saves money after moving costs and commute. He said the aim is "to get that granular and that involved in your financial" [24:06] situation to help people make informed decisions.

q: How should a founder decide when an MVP is ready to launch?
a: Schappert advises finding a balance between releasing a buggy product and never launching because you are chasing every bug. His guiding philosophy is "You don't have to get it right. You just have to get it going." [05:10].

q: What does Jason Schappert look for when hiring?
a: Schappert hires for culture fit and personality, with exceptions where credentials are required, and says breaking that rule always hurt him. Schappert explained, "I've always used this phrase as we are looking for scrappy people" [10:35], meaning people willing to put in the effort, including during demanding sprints.

Compliance Was the First Wedge: At Wayfair, Tameem's team handled audit demands while deploying 600 to 700 times a day. RapDev's first offering used ServiceNow to help regulated firms in areas like banking, pharma and insurance ship code faster.

Own the Scope Miss: Burned by consultants who ran out of hours or demanded change orders, Tameem built RapDev on the opposite rule: if a project's scope or hours are missed, that is on RapDev, not the customer.

Scrutinize Fixed-Fee Deals: A roughly six-week Datadog migration with shifting scope and legal threats dragged past a year, and RapDev offered the money back to get out. It now closely examines scope before taking fixed-fee work.

q: How can highly regulated companies deploy code faster with ServiceNow?
a: Tameem Hourani's team used ServiceNow to automate QA testing, validation and cross-checking so audit requirements would not hold back releases. He said what worked early on "was helping those customers accelerate their audit requirements" [07:00], first in banking and later in pharma and insurance.

q: Why did RapDev start building Datadog plugins?
a: Tameem Hourani saw that regulated customers such as banks had legacy technology that Datadog wasn't focused on but that they still needed to monitor. The pitch was that "we can build a product for Datadog that will allow you to monitor Solaris and HP-UX and all this legacy tech" [09:15].

q: How does RapDev scale a services business without raising funding?
a: Tameem Hourani said the company leans on technology rather than just headcount, and reuses code across its niche engagements. "We've automated most of our business processes through tech" [13:19], he noted, including work such as invoicing, closing the books and recruiting.

q: What did Tameem Hourani learn about fixed-fee consulting contracts?
a: A project for a well-known sporting company, which he did not name, kept changing scope and stretched from about six weeks to more than a year under a fixed fee. Hourani said, "we've never did any more fixed fee without really scrutinizing the scope of the project" [17:42].

s10-bonus-leveraging-kernel-level-ebpf-to-eliminate-sampling-blind-spots-and-track-ai-pipelines-with-shahar-azulay-co-founder-ceo-of-groundcover

Data Stays With Customers: Groundcover has run its databases and entire data plane in customers' environments since day one, which lets it stop pricing by data volume. Shahar sees this as a harder differentiator to copy than eBPF.

A Sensor-First MVP: Within the first three months, Groundcover was installed in a big company. The MVP was mostly an eBPF sensor and a few simple dashboards, with no logs yet, but it worked out of the box and was enough to close the first customer.

Broad Platform Over Niche: Expecting to rip and replace incumbents, the team built log management, infrastructure monitoring and APM very early. A niche eBPF tracing tool, Shahar argues, would never have won organizational buy-in.

Self-Serve for Technical Buyers: DevOps and R&D buyers want to try products before talking to sales. Documented self-install and a live playground keep later sales talks shorter and focused on use cases and migration.

Explain What Feels Obvious: Bring your own cloud felt so intuitive to the founders that they didn't explain or simplify its benefits. It took a few months to a year to fix, and users then responded much better.

q: What is Groundcover and how does it use eBPF for observability?
a: Groundcover is an observability platform for cloud native environments that competes with platforms such as Datadog, Dynatrace and Grafana Cloud. Shahar Azulay describes eBPF as "a technology that allows us to basically turn on the light" [03:22], so teams start getting data without changing their code or environment.

q: Why did Groundcover choose bring your own cloud instead of SaaS?
a: Shahar says the founders felt that starting as SaaS would create technical debt they could never reverse, so the data plane has run in the customer's environment from day one. He acknowledged, "That's a very unorthodox choice for a startup in the SaaS era" [07:50].

q: What did Groundcover's MVP look like?
a: According to Shahar, it was mostly a first eBPF sensor with a few simple dashboards, and it did not yet collect logs or really help users troubleshoot and correlate data. Still, after the first three months, "we already installed Groundcover in a big company" [05:22].

q: Why did Groundcover build a full observability platform instead of a niche tool?
a: Shahar explains that observability is a mature, noisy market, so the team needed logs, infrastructure monitoring and APM to have a chance of displacing existing tools. They had an "early understanding that it's gonna be a rip and replace motion rather than" [09:41] a product living alongside an incumbent as a complement.

q: What mistake did Shahar Azulay make with Groundcover's bring your own cloud approach?
a: Shahar says the approach felt so intuitive that the team did not simplify it or spell out its benefits for users. He described it as a mistake "of not trying to explain that vision to the user" [15:33], and said people reacted much better once the team did.

SME Payments in One Place: Mamo helps small and medium-sized businesses collect payments from customers and pay vendors and suppliers, offering what Imad describes as SME banking style services.

s10-e19-generative-remixes-scaling-social-music-creation-tools-and-unlocking-fair-artist-monetization-with-simmi-singh-coo-chief-product-officer-of-hook-music

Remix Demand Without Tools: Singh says 40% of music on TikTok is remixed. Hook lets everyday people take a 30-second snippet from a catalog, apply genre filters or mash up songs, add video and share it.

Granular Controls for Rights Holders: Hook's enterprise side lets labels and publishers set which parts of a catalog can be mashed up or remixed into certain genres, applying a lesson from getting music partners onto streaming.

A Deliberately Narrow MVP: Hook targeted remixers making sped-up, slowed-down and simple-effect versions. The core set added a few genre filters and mashups, and the studio dropped users straight in rather than walking them through steps.

Scale Foundations in Stages: Hook wanted DDEX-standard content ingestion from day one because major labels would require it, but took a crawl, walk, run approach. Some early tech choices had to be reworked six to nine months after launch.

Fixed Deadlines Caused Burnout: Singh admits pushing a two-month timeline too hard, leading to mistakes and an unhappy team. Team retros surfaced unrealistic expectations, and she went to leadership to find timeline flexibility.

q: What is Hook Music?
a: Hook is a short-form music remix app where users pick a snippet of a song, apply genre filters or create mashups, add video and share the result. Simmi Singh, its COO and Chief Product Officer, said "The whole idea about Hook was to make music expression simple and easy." [04:23]

q: How does Hook give music labels and publishers control over remixes?
a: Hook has an enterprise product that lets rights holders ingest licensed content and decide how it can be used, such as which parts of a catalog are open to mashups or certain genres. Singh explained that "with hook we're building like very granular permissions around" [06:25] the catalog.

q: How does Hook make mashups faster than traditional tools?
a: Singh said making a mashup manually means listening to many songs and matching beats, which can take hours. Hook's algorithm recommends songs, and parts of songs, that would work together, and as she put it, "We're basically making a mashup within like seconds." [09:43]

q: What mistake did Simmi Singh make while building Hook?
a: Singh treated the timeline as fixed without fully accounting for scope, and pushed back on the team's feedback more than she needed to. She recalled that "they were getting burnt out I could see it there were a lot more mistakes" [26:30], which led her to seek flexibility from leadership.

q: What advice does Simmi Singh have for founders who just shipped a product?
a: Singh advises talking to real customers and users to avoid getting stuck in your own bubble, and taking care of yourself through balance. She highlighted that "people who came and didn't use it, I think are the most important cohorts to listen to" [36:52].

Engineering the Founding Team: Nikita designed Neon's founding DNA around its architecture, calling Postgres committers and contributors. Co-founders Stas and Heikki brought Postgres internals experience and community credibility.

Building in Public Paid Off: The first version took about 12 months. The site leaked to Hacker News before launch, and a public Rust repo that repeatedly hit GitHub trending helped drive stars and market-fit signal.

A Three-Part Master Plan: Build separated storage and compute, win developers through self-serve, then add enterprise sales. Neon passed $5M ARR but is rethinking the sales force to pursue the Gen AI and agentic opportunity.

Outages Forced a Leadership Upgrade: Exponential usage brought repeated outages and risked burning out key people. Nikita responded by hiring a professional staff team, and says the service is now super stable.

Remote as a Talent Edge: Though he'd prefer everyone in an office, Nikita says being fully distributed gives Neon asymmetric access to Postgres and systems talent. Neon also hires and fires faster than SingleStore did.

q: What is Neon and how is its Postgres architecture different?
a: Nikita Shamgunov says Neon began as an open source alternative to AWS Aurora, with one global multi-tenant storage system and Postgres compute running in virtual machines that attach to it. q: How did Neon find early product-market fit?
a: Neon built in public, kept its code open source and made the technology very easy to try, while a free tier fed user feedback. Nikita explained that if you do this, "your market fit signal is a lot more clear than otherwise." [09:59]

q: How did Neon handle outages as it scaled?
a: Nikita Shamgunov says rapid growth led to one outage after another, and he responded by building out a staff team, including heads of engineering, product, marketing and finance. Describing the start of the trouble, he said, "So 12 months ago, all hell broke loose" [18:46].

q: How does Nikita Shamgunov think about building a startup team?
a: Nikita looks for an asymmetric advantage in finding talent, which at Neon comes from being fully distributed. He applies one principle at every stage of the company, saying "the team you build is the company you build" [06:37].

q: What is the future of Neon in the age of AI agents?
a: Nikita believes there will be a billion developers and that each person will have agents doing digital work, all needing a database and other services. He said the "future of Neon is more of a serverless agentic platform and not just a Postgres database" [23:16].

minting-unicorns-blockchain-ai-and-dubai-with-mohammad-albalooshi-ceo-difc-innovation-hub

Licenses Built for Startups: The DIFC innovation license is 90% subsidized and allows 100% foreign ownership with no restriction on capital repatriation or foreign talent. Joining the Innovation Hub does require being on the ground.

Four Things Startups Need: Albalooshi names market access, capital, regulatory support and talent. The hub addresses them with accelerators, a regulatory sandbox, tailored licenses, its own investments and efforts to draw VCs and family offices.

Jobs as a Core KPI: Winning leadership support meant arguing that subsidizing startups early would pay off long term. Creating next-generation jobs is one of Albalooshi's main KPIs, and he cites Tabby, valued at $1.5 billion, as the ecosystem's first unicorn in 2024.

q: What is the DIFC Innovation Hub?
a: It is the startup ecosystem within the Dubai International Financial Center, which has its own legal and regulatory framework based on English common law. Mohammad Albalooshi describes it as "the largest startup ecosystem in the Middle East and North" [02:44] African region, with more than a thousand fintech and innovation companies.

q: How does the DIFC Innovation Hub support fintech and AI startups?
a: It offers tailored licenses, a regulatory sandbox, co-working spaces, accelerator programs and investment support. Mohammad Albalooshi sums up what startups need: "It would be access to market, access to capital, regulatory support, and access to talent." [10:45]

q: What is the Dubai AI Campus and what are its goals?
a: It is a dedicated ecosystem for artificial intelligence companies, with AI-specific licenses and tools provided by partners such as NVIDIA, AWS and Microsoft. Mohammad Albalooshi said, "our aim is that we want to attract 500 companies" [09:06], referring to AI companies by 2028, along with more than 3,000 AI jobs.

q: How much does the DIFC innovation license subsidize early-stage startups?
a: Mohammad Albalooshi explains that for the DIFC innovation license, "it's 90% subsidized because our thesis is that" [16:51] early-stage founders should find it as easy as possible to launch their ideas. q: Do founders need to be in Dubai to join the DIFC Innovation Hub?
a: Yes, Mohammad Albalooshi says the hub is a physical community, so license holders have to be on the ground. For founders abroad looking to enter the market, he says the accelerator programs "are the perfect platform for global startups" [15:35], and events like the Dubai Fintech Summit offer a way to get a pulse of the market.

s10-e18-replacing-complex-iac-plumbing-with-visual-internal-developer-platforms-with-cory-odaniel-co-founder-ceo-of-massdriver

Ops Builds, Developers Diagram: Operations teams publish OpenTofu or Helm modules with compliance rules built in. Developers diagram the architecture they need, while Massdriver handles provisioning and compliance scanning behind the scenes.

Bring Your Own Modules: Engineers liked the prebuilt version but didn't control the cloud, and ops teams blocked it. After about 15 people asked to upload their own modules, Massdriver repositioned as a tool for ops teams to cut DevOps red tape.

Interviews Flip the Power: Candidates pick an open source issue in Elixir or Go and arrive as the subject matter expert, with the interviewer acting as the new hire. Cory skips whiteboard and algorithm tests and usually sends offers the same day.

Scaling Down After Scaling Up: Early momentum led Massdriver to grow to about 11 people, which added coordination overhead and slowed the team. Cory now hires only when there is a job nobody on the team can learn or make time for.

Let the Crowd Sell: A screen left unmounted at KubeCon faced the aisle, drawing groups who debated the demo and convinced each other. Borrowing their language at reInvent, without changing the demo, the team hit 20 times its sales call goal.

q: What is Massdriver and how does it work?
a: Massdriver is a platform where operations teams publish infrastructure modules, such as OpenTofu and Helm, that carry their company's compliance rules and non-negotiables. As Cory O'Daniel explains it, "and then developers just diagram the cloud architectures they need." [04:44]

q: What problem is Massdriver trying to solve?
a: Cory O'Daniel saw in professional services that clients were often left with a large gap in understanding how their cloud systems worked. In his words, "There's not a ton of engineers that have deep cloud experience, right?" [02:54] Massdriver lets developers get infrastructure without learning ops tools, while ops teams keep using the tooling they know.

q: How did Massdriver find its real customer?
a: Cory O'Daniel says the team first sold prebuilt modules to engineers, but ops teams blocked adoption and revenue maxed out around half a million dollars. After repeated requests from ops teams, the team changed course: "oh maybe we should just let people upload their own modules to it" [14:47].

q: How does Massdriver interview software engineers?
a: Candidates choose an open issue, bug or annoyance in an Elixir or Go open source project, research it, and then work on it live with the team. Cory O'Daniel tells them, "You are now the subject matter expert coming in and it is my first day on the job." [22:53]

q: Can a startup delay its first operations hire?
a: Cory O'Daniel says many early Massdriver customers had no ops team, and the aim was to postpone that hire until it was truly needed. He explains that "one of our goals in our business was allow you to push that out and make that first hire" [33:19] a better experience, with a relatively debt-free environment waiting for that person.

5da9ce4f-a2d8-4cf6-8eb9-39cff018dbcd
s10-bonus-the-voice-native-crm-frontier-eliminating-cold-leads-and-automating-outbound-pipelines-with-no-code-ai-agents-with-torrey-leonard-co-founder-ceo-of-thoughtly

Zapier for Call Center Agents: Thoughtly's AI agents handle inbound and outbound calls, trained on a company's script and internal information, with integrations that act before, during and after each call.

Build the Request Venn Diagram: Rather than building customer asks one by one, Torrey mapped how they overlapped. That shaped the integration roadmap and revealed a common need to act before, during or after a call.

From Browser Meetings to Phones: The MVP paired a basic Google Meet-style call tool Torrey built himself with a React Flow decision-tree builder. Customers asking for phone calls pushed it toward AI phone agents.

The $5,000 Walk-Away Offer: After detailing how hard the job would be, Torrey offered a founding engineer candidate a $5,000 Visa gift card to decline. The engineer joined anyway, signaling real dedication.

Event Booths Fell Flat: Thoughtly spent tens of thousands, maybe up to $100,000, on contact center events with little return. Sending two people just to attend and network cost under $1,000 and worked far better.

q: What is Thoughtly and what does it do?
a: Thoughtly builds AI agents that handle inbound and outbound phone calls, connecting a company's software to actions before, during and after calls. Co-founder and CEO Torrey Leonard summed it up this way: "Think of us as like a Zapier for call center agents." [02:49]

q: How was the first version of Thoughtly built?
a: Torrey Leonard built a basic Google Meet-style calling tool and a decision-tree agent builder, using React Flow with a Next.js front end. He said "React Flow is what the MVP initially used" [06:07], and the team was still using it at the time of the interview.

q: How did Thoughtly decide which features and integrations to build first?
a: Torrey compared every customer request to find where they overlapped, so each piece of work could solve problems for as many customers as possible. In his words, "the best thing to do is just build this Venn diagram" [08:02] instead of building each request one at a time.

q: How does Thoughtly handle many phone calls at the same time?
a: Torrey explained that simultaneous callers each get their own call, so scaling comes down to infrastructure and vendor reliability. As he put it, "that is what we're selling is infinite scalability" [14:04], and a larger engineering team was brought on to move the system from Google Cloud Run to Kubernetes.

q: What advice does Torrey Leonard have for early-stage founders?
a: He advises confirming that people need the product and getting paying customers before leaving school or a job, or chasing investment. His benchmark: "if you can get a hundred complete strangers to pay for" [24:48] it at $10 or more each, that tells you something.

minting-unicorns-blockchain-ai-and-dubai-with-dr-marwan-al-zarouni-ceo-of-ai

AI as a Tool for Happiness: Dr. Marwan says Dubai wants AI to augment jobs and daily life rather than replace people, removing mundane tasks so citizens, residents and tourists have more time for what they love.

Verifying Process, Not Just Results: Circular Protocol puts the process behind a result on the blockchain. In a surgical robot example, vetted data and code let teams trace a problem to where it arose and who wrote the code.

Pay for Delivered Compute: DePIN spreads AI workloads across distributed nodes, letting users shop globally for price. With smart contracts, a training run that produces no result doesn't have to be paid for.

Blockchain Belongs in the Background: AI agents can use programmable money to shop, pay and negotiate without human interaction. Dr. Marwan expects AI to be what people see, with blockchain enabling it behind the scenes.

PropTech Needs Shared Standards: Real estate is a major D33 innovation area, but Dr. Marwan says ownership transfer laws and red tape hold it back, and agreement on real world asset and tokenization standards is needed to move forward.

q: How does Dubai plan to use AI in everyday life?
a: Dr. Marwan Al Zarouni says AI is an underlying theme of the Dubai Economic Agenda 2033, known as D33, and is meant to remove friction and mundane tasks. As he put it, "We want to use AI as a tool, as a catalyst to enhance people's life, not to replace jobs" [03:48].

q: What is Circular Protocol and how does it help AI?
a: Circular Protocol is a project Dr. Marwan has worked with closely that uses blockchain to verify how a result was reached, which he says matters in areas like drug approval and medical trials. He explained that it "does not only verify the end result, but also the process that was used to get to that end result." [07:01]

q: How can DePIN help with the cost of AI compute?
a: Dr. Marwan describes DePIN, or decentralized physical infrastructure, as a way to distribute AI workloads across many compute nodes and shop for the best price worldwide. He also pointed to a smart contract feature where "if no result is generated from the training, you don't have to pay" [09:46].

q: Why hasn't blockchain taken center stage like AI?
a: Dr. Marwan argues that blockchain is an enabler for digital-first technologies, handling things like payments while AI is what people actually see. In his words, "it's a technology that belongs in the background." [12:04]

q: How is Dubai addressing AI ethics and data privacy?
a: Dr. Marwan says Dubai took up AI ethics early, bringing big tech, social and human capital entities, and digital government bodies together, with a focus on transparency, bias, privacy and synthetic data. Recalling the Smart Dubai era, he said "we had something called the Dubai Ethics Committee" [14:03].

s10-e17-the-code-aware-dast-era-scaling-runtime-security-at-the-speed-of-ai-coding-assistants-with-joni-klippert-co-founder-ceo-of-stackhawk

Usability Over a Better Scanner: StackHawk's MVP took an open source DAST scanner and made it opinionated, with Docker deployment, a few lines of YAML and clearer output. Scans could be completed in around seven to 10 minutes.

Scanning Next to the Code: The scanner runs on the client side via Docker or CLI, so thousands of attacks don't cross the internet. Scans run faster, and StackHawk avoids scaling and managing scan runners itself.
Test the API at Source: StackHawk focused on deep API testing because one route can serve 2,000 pages. It launched with REST and SOAP, then added GraphQL and gRPC testing.
Shift Sales Motion Sooner: As enterprise interest grew, StackHawk kept spending heavily on inbound demand gen suited to SMBs. Klippert says she would have built up enterprise sales bench faster.
Mapping the Attack Surface: Klippert says mid-market companies easily have 1,000 or 2,000 repositories, and StackHawk sees about 30 to 50% containing APIs or applications that need testing.

q: Why did Joni Klippert start StackHawk?
a: Klippert was researching why security lagged behind DevOps and first looked at pen testing as a service, saying "I just thought it's so intellectually dishonest to have a human being" [05:29] attack an app and hand over a PDF. After talking to 50 CISOs and VPs of engineering, she learned that automating Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) was what they wanted.

q: How was the first version of StackHawk built?
a: Joni Klippert and her team started with an open source DAST scanner and focused on making it usable for software engineers, with Docker and later CLI deployment, YAML configuration and organized results. As she explained, "what we decided is, okay, the world doesn't need a better scanner" [08:37].

q: Why does StackHawk focus on API security testing?
a: Klippert says legacy DAST tools expected browser-based applications and didn't really understand how modern applications are built. Testing and fixing at the API route has wide impact "because that one API route could serve 2,000 pages on a website" [11:50].

q: Why does the StackHawk scanner run on the customer's side?
a: Joni Klippert explained that running the scanner close to the code base avoids sending thousands of attacks across the internet, so "that round trip time is really fast and it makes the scanning capability really fast" [17:33]. It also means StackHawk doesn't have to scale and manage scan runners for customers, while results still stream back to its SaaS platform.

q: How does StackHawk plan to use AI?
a: Klippert said the roadmap is AI heavy, using code base introspection to get APIs and applications under test quickly and reduce manual work such as filling out YAML files and identifying authentication mechanisms. In her words, "when you introspect the code base and use AI, it is so much faster" [24:10].

fc86dffb-89cb-4fbb-a4e2-4b5d4d0dfa66
s10-bonus-utilizing-group-photo-interactivity-and-visual-memory-scrapbooks-to-drive-lifetime-campus-engagement-with-eric-leebow-founder-ceo-of-freezecrowd

Picture Books Sparked the Idea: Camp group photos and a Lehigh freshman picture book listing interests led Leebow to imagine connecting campus communities through photos, even picturing bubble chats inside them.

Cutting to the Core Product: After a 2009 launch was shut down, FreezeCrowd brought in a new developer team, recoded, dropped ideas like study guides and refocused on group photos. It was up and running in 2011.

Features Must Matter to Members: Leebow separates focus areas from nice-to-haves and wants, prioritizing features that make a difference in members' lives. The released mobile app was headed back to the drawing board.

Multi-School Launch Complicated Scaling: Starting at many schools at once made early scaling harder, and Leebow suggests one school might have been easier. Students from over a thousand colleges and universities have since joined.
Hire for Complementary Skills: Leebow, the creative mind behind FreezeCrowd, advises founders to find people whose skills differ from their own, such as a technical builder to pair with a promoter.

q: What is FreezeCrowd and what problem does it solve?
a: FreezeCrowd is a platform from founder Eric Leebow that connects college students and alumni with their campus communities, using group photos as a social element. Leebow describes it as a place where "you have this platform where you can break the ice and connect with people" [05:09].

q: How did Eric Leebow come up with the idea for FreezeCrowd?
a: Leebow drew on camp group photos and his freshman picture book at Lehigh University, which listed interests such as video games and basketball next to his name. He recalls thinking, "there's got to be a way to connect these people with these keywords and interests" [03:19].

q: What happened to the first version of FreezeCrowd?
a: Leebow says something was launched in 2009, but "they had to shut it down because it wasn't working perfectly" [05:40]. He found a new developer team, recoded parts of the product and focused on group photos, and the platform was up and running in 2011.

q: How does FreezeCrowd decide which features to build?
a: Leebow asks whether a feature is something to focus on, a nice-to-have or simply a want. He says that with too many features, "you have to prioritize on the features that actually mean something to the" [09:32] members.

q: What scaling challenges has FreezeCrowd faced?
a: Leebow explains that "we started at multiple schools and that made it challenging for us to scale right away" [12:24]. He mentions campus representatives, word of mouth and friends joining as ways the platform can grow.

s10-e16-the-meta-layer-workspace-consolidation-of-fragmented-tech-stacks-and-the-zendesk-acquisition-with-mihri-minaz-co-founder-of-beams

Ship Local, Track Everything: The first Beams Mac app, built in Swift in a couple of weeks, had no real backend beyond a version check. It used Apple's local calendar data, tracked feature usage and was shared as a Google Drive link.

Onboarding as User Research: Beams onboarded 300 people over video calls, asking questions and watching where they didn't click. The team paired that with usage tracking and public feature requests to shape the roadmap.

Over-Engineering Was the Risk: With a very experienced team, Mihri saw over-building as the scaling danger. Rejecting the idea that early code should last five years helped them move fast, though they later had to work on cloud provider independence.

Meetings Lacked a Budget Owner: Calendar insights proved very hard to monetize because no one in a company owns meetings. Managers' concerns about AI adoption and costs led Beams to track which tools, like ChatGPT or Copilot, people actually use.

Responsibility for Possible Misuse: Mihri notes Beams could be seen as a monitoring tool. She wants only data useful for cost-cutting to reach management, and sees preventing its use in performance evaluations as the builder's responsibility.

q: What is Beams and how does it help companies cut SaaS costs?
a: Beams is a work intelligence platform that integrates with tools such as calendars, Slack, email and G Suite to show how teams spend time and which tools they use. Mihri Minaz explained that "this helps companies to reduce their SaaS costs because they can see underutilized tools" [03:17], as well as overlapping ones.

q: How was the first version of Beams built?
a: Mihri Minaz said the team built a native Mac app in Swift and released it in a couple of weeks by sharing a Google Drive link. The first version had no real backend, and as Mihri put it, it "just had the version check endpoint so everything was local" [06:20], apart from usage tracking.

q: Why did Beams expand from calendar insights to tool usage insights?
a: Mihri Minaz said that when the team approached company owners and managers, "what we noticed is this is very hard to monetize in this market" [19:05]. Managers' priorities were adopting AI tools and reducing costs, so Beams focused on showing whether people actually use the tools their company pays for.

q: How does Beams decide what to build next?
a: Mihri Minaz described combining usage data, user conversations, public feature requests and the vision of being the meta layer of work tools. Windows and Microsoft support were deliberately held back because, in Mihri's words, "our target group or market entry is for G Suite environment" [11:27].

q: Could a work tool usage tracker like Beams be misused for employee monitoring?
a: Mihri Minaz acknowledged that Beams could be considered a monitoring tool and raised the risk of its data being used for performance evaluations. Mihri's view is that builders must work to prevent this: "You should know that what you build can be misused." [22:57]

s10-bonus-the-high-concurrency-crisis-why-page-caching-fails-modern-membership-sites-and-crushing-the-wordpress-success-wall-with-wes-tatters-managing-director-of-rapyd-cloud
Dynamic Sites Defeat Caching: On BuddyBoss community sites, each user's activity feed is unique, so caching and CDN techniques that benefit static sites start to fall apart.

Concurrency Needs Speed and Cores: Rapyd Cloud pairs fast CPUs with multi-core scaling, running on AWS with AMD Zen 4 at launch and Virtuozzo containerization, all hidden behind a WordPress-focused dashboard.

Security Below the Plugin Layer: Instead of asking customers to stack security plugins, Rapyd runs real-time, server-level malware protection inside the virtualized container, with no configuration needed.
Looking Beyond BuddyBoss: Planned as BuddyBoss Hosted, Rapyd became a separate brand as LearnDash, Lifter LMS and even BuddyBoss competitors' users showed the same scaling problems.

Developers on the Support Desk: Rapyd sought support staff with PHP, WordPress and plugin experience. Wes says they respond in 45 seconds on average, around the clock, and help with site problems too.

q: Why does page caching fail on WordPress membership and community sites?
a: Wes Tatters explains that on community sites like those built with BuddyBoss, each user sees a unique experience based on their profile, choices and groups. As he put it, "in a dynamic environment you can't use any of those caching technologies." [03:38]

q: How can a WordPress site handle more concurrent users?
a: According to Wes, concurrency is how many customers can visit a site at the same time, and it calls for the fastest possible CPU plus the ability to scale across multiple cores. In his words, "Every time we add a CPU core, we expand the number of users" [07:39].

q: What technology is Rapyd Cloud built on?
a: Wes describes AWS as the underlying engine, Virtuozzo as the middleware, and a user-friendly React dashboard that hides the complexity from customers. Speaking about Virtuozzo, he said, "It sits on top of AWS and allows us to do very high performance containerization" [09:32].

q: How does Rapyd Cloud secure WordPress sites without security plugins?
a: Wes says Rapyd worked with security partners to run real-time, server-level malware and vulnerability protection that customers don't need to configure. He explained that "instead of putting our security inside WordPress, we put our security" [13:36] inside the server itself.

q: Can you host multiple sites in one Rapyd Cloud container?
a: Wes says the MVP couldn't do this, because Rapyd chose early on that it "would run a system with a single container, single site." [23:34] After customer requests, a multi-site container option was in development at the time of the interview, targeted for the end of Q1, while the isolated single-site product will still be sold.

s10-bonus-the-data-driven-gtm-engine-transitioning-from-traditional-sales-to-product-led-growth-and-agentic-analytics-with-thomas-hansen-president-of-amplitude

Analytics at the Platform Core: Since joining in summer 2022, Hansen has helped move Amplitude beyond core product analytics to a platform with experimentation, session replay, guides and surveys, a CDP and more around it.

Session Replay Before RBAC: Amplitude delayed role-based access control by a quarter or two to ship session replay, a tough call because many of its nearly 3,500 enterprise customers were asking for RBAC.

Customers Weigh Heavily on Roadmap: The voice of the customer gets an overweighted say. Product management holds interlocks with sales and sales engineering to surface opportunities, then debates priorities.

Scaling to Trillions of Events: Event volumes have gone from millions to trillions for very large customers. That takes ongoing engineering investment to keep performance up and stop cost of goods sold from rising in step with volume.
Trust From Day One: Hansen gives his team trust up front instead of making them earn it, sets expectations, holds people accountable and treats work as rapid experiments to tweak or stop.

q: What does Amplitude do?
a: Thomas Hansen describes Amplitude as a digital analytics platform that helps companies build better products and better monetize their customers. It does this, in his words, "by providing clear insights into their customers' behavior so they can take action" [02:58].

q: Why did Amplitude prioritize session replay over role-based access control?
a: Hansen says customers were really looking for session replay, so data governance work such as RBAC slipped by a quarter or two, even though many customers wanted it too. He recalled "realizing we had to do that a little bit later to prioritize session replay earlier" [06:50], and says both are now done.

q: How does Amplitude decide what to build next?
a: Hansen says product management holds interlocks with the go-to-market organization, gathering input from sellers and sales engineers before discussing priorities. He credits the three co-founders for the principle that "the voice of the customer in Amplitude has an overweighted input onto our roadmap" [07:40].

q: How does Amplitude approach scalability?
