a: Hansen points to building a team that can take the business from roughly $300 million in revenue to a billion and beyond, and a product that performs at trillions of events. He also stresses investing so that "cost of goods sold are not scaling proportionally with the event volume" [12:54].

q: How does Thomas Hansen build and lead teams?
a: Hansen believes in empowering people, holding them accountable and building a diverse team whose strengths complement each other. He gives trust from the start rather than waiting for it to be earned, saying "trust has to be the foundation of everything" [09:14].

s10-bonus-moving-beyond-scratch-built-apps-and-using-ai-to-assemble-enterprise-software-from-pre-validated-modules-with-anand-kulkarni-founder-ceo-of-crowdbotics

Requirements as Common Currency: Crowdbotics uses AI to reverse engineer codebases into natural language requirements that people and machines can both read. Those requirements can then be turned back into new code.
A Marketplace Built for Data: Crowdbotics ran an open development marketplace, gathering links between requirements and libraries. Getting the data it needed took about five years.

Familiar Tools Beat New Ones: Anand spent a week trying to learn serverless while building the MVP, then chose Django, which he knew well. Vue was harder to undo, with most of the front end later moved to React.

One Metric Guides the Roadmap: For requirements capture, the team aims to be the most accurate tool on the market. Candidate work is ranked using data and customer input, based on its likely impact on that metric.

Killing the Low-Code Editor: Crowdbotics built a visual drag-and-drop editor that customers didn't care about. Anand says sunk cost delayed shutting it down, and the lesson was that focus drives scale.

q: What does Crowdbotics do?
a: Anand Kulkarni describes Crowdbotics as a modernization company that uses AI to turn codebases into human-readable requirements, which can then be turned back into code. His core insight is that "in the LLM era, human written requirements give you this common currency" [03:29] between machines and people.

q: How did Crowdbotics get the data to train its AI?
a: The company ran an open development marketplace that matched customers needing software with development teams, while capturing how requirements mapped to libraries. Anand explained that "the best way to get that kind of data is specifically by running your own development marketplace" [05:35].

q: What tech stack did Crowdbotics use, and how has it changed?
a: The early platform used Python and Django with Vue on the front end, and the company has since moved most of that front end to React and runs its AI on Azure and Azure OpenAI. Anand said of leaving Vue, "that's one that was painful to walk back from, no question" [09:50].

q: How does Crowdbotics approach scalability?
a: Anand sees scalability as a problem that returns as ambitions grow, and says there were times the team had to scramble to meet spikes in demand. Having learned from that, he said, "We generally like to build for and test for substantially more scale than we currently have" [15:24].

q: What advice does Anand Kulkarni have for new entrepreneurs?
a: Anand advises founders to know who they are solving a problem for, stay focused on that person, and get the product in front of customers. As he put it, "you convincing a customer is what turns it into a business" [22:30].

dec9104b-df3d-4a1e-befb-d0209dc87111
s10-e15-merging-code-first-end-to-end-testing-with-modern-synthetics-and-agentic-root-cause-analysis-with-hannes-lenke-co-founder-ceo-of-checkly

Testing in Production, Continuously: Checkly runs customers' automated test scripts, including Playwright tests, against live production systems from 20 data centers worldwide to check that websites, APIs and services work.

Don't Let Traction Delay Vision: Early paying customers pulled focus from monitoring as code. The first iteration drew no users, and it took a whole year to get a command line interface version to market.

Small Releases, Fast Feedback: Checkly finds likely early adopters, ships them a minimal feature set behind a feature flag and interviews them. A cycle should take four weeks, sometimes eight, and may send the team back to the drawing board.

Four Voices Shape the Roadmap: Checkly weighs customer requests, including a public roadmap with upvotes, sales feedback, engineering needs like technical debt and scaling, and its own vision, aiming to give each 25% of team capacity.

Hiring With Radical Transparency: The remote-first team of 45 people in 14 countries publishes its hiring playbook and salary ranges. Lenke still interviews every candidate, looking for culture fit, hunger and whether they will up-level the team.

q: What is Checkly and what does monitoring as code mean?
a: Checkly is a synthetic monitoring platform that continuously runs automated tests against production to check that websites, APIs and services work. Describing the monitoring as code approach, Hannes Lenke said "we allow our customers to use real code from within their code repositories" [03:23].

q: How did Checkly get started?
a: After selling his mobile testing startup to Sauce Labs, Hannes Lenke saw a need for a developer-focused tool that used end-to-end tests to monitor production. He found Tim, who later became a co-founder, nearby in Berlin, "creating a side project called Checkly back then" [05:03].

q: What did the first version of Checkly look like?
a: Hannes Lenke explained that "the first version was a very simple version" [06:09], hosted on Heroku with a Postgres database and a simple UI. It monitored APIs and later websites using Puppeteer, and Tim's openness about the project on Twitter attracted the first users.

q: What mistake did Checkly make with monitoring as code?
a: Early paying customers arrived before Checkly supported monitoring as code, so the team focused on their problems instead of the larger vision. Reflecting on it, Hannes Lenke said the "mistake was to not pushing the vision hard enough" [16:31].

q: How does Checkly plan to help developers resolve incidents faster?
a: Hannes Lenke said the next product evolution goes beyond waking developers when a service is down, pointing to causes such as a slow database. The goal is to "tell you where the problem actually comes from, help you to remediate the issue faster" [17:15].

6c1fbdec-6dbe-42b6-bd57-a7e332e65bc4
s10-bonus-the-value-pricing-revolution-overthrowing-the-hourly-hamster-wheel-and-maximizing-profits-for-solo-consultants-with-jonathan-stark-author-of-hourly-billing-is-nuts

Hourly Billing Rewards Junior Developers: Managing about 10 developers, Stark saw that a low-salaried junior could earn far more profit than the firm's best, fastest developer. He traced it to billing by the hour and went solo on January 1, 2006.

Offer Three Options: Borrowing from Alan Weiss's Value-Based Fees, Stark advises putting good, better and best options in proposals. Clients weigh how to work with you, and new value pricers leave less money on the table.
Value First, Scope Last: Don't try to scope a project in the sales meeting. Learn the value, set prices based on it, then decide scope from the desired outcome and the price the client chooses.

Scale by Raising Your Altitude: Stark describes three tiers of client work: maintenance, implementation and deciding what comes next. To scale without hiring, move toward strategic advisory work, selling your brains rather than your hands.
Ruthless Simplicity: Stark sets a yearly theme, works from 15 or 20 recurring daily to-dos and skips nice-to-haves. His Ditching Hourly podcast has no intro music, ads or routine editing.

q: Why did Jonathan Stark stop billing by the hour?
a: While managing developers at a FileMaker consulting firm, Stark noticed that hourly billing made a junior developer far more profitable than a highly skilled one. He said that after puzzling over it, "I finally realized it was because we were billing by the hour" [04:25]. He then went solo to work out an alternative without risking his colleagues' livelihoods.

q: How do you control scope creep on a fixed-price software project?
a: Stark's answer includes a sales-meeting "why conversation" and a mind shift he calls "scope last," where scope is decided after value and price. As he put it, "you do not try and do not even try to scope the project in the sales meeting" [09:41].

q: How can a solo consultant scale without hiring a team?
a: Stark recommends shifting from implementation toward strategic work that helps clients decide what to do next. He explained, "My approach to scaling for myself and the people I work with is to increase the altitude of involvement with your clients." [14:02]

q: What is the hourly trap?
a: Stark describes people who need more money but feel they can't raise their rates, work any more or easily hire help. Of that bind, he said, "So they're trapped in this, I call it the hourly trap." [19:43]

q: How is Jonathan Stark using AI to spread his value pricing advice?
a: Stark has experimented with training an AI on about a thousand hours of recorded community Q&A sessions dating back to 2017, and it points users to the source of each answer. He described it as an "AI bot thing that can do a really good job answering" [25:07], though he noted it isn't perfect.

s10-e14-the-empathetic-engineering-culture-scaling-high-performance-tech-teams-and-mitigating-security-risks-without-dev-burnout-with-eric-muller-vp-of-engineering-ciso-at-presence

Minimum Lovable Over Minimum Viable: Eric prefers a "minimum lovable product" because viability means different things to engineering, product and design. A first release should make clients smile and feel proud.

Challenge Mid-Project Scope Creep: When a new feature threatens delivery, Eric asks whether its champion wants to tell their CEO the project is late because of it. Many then agree it can wait for version two.

Hire for Life Beyond Code: Beyond technical and problem-solving skills, Eric wants people who can talk with clients. He's encouraged by outside interests, like cooking or meditation, that help developers recharge and avoid burnout.

DevOps Is Hardest to Scale: Client projects need DevOps expertise but rarely full-time for their whole length. That makes it hard to keep specialists busy, and outside hired guns aren't guaranteed to be available again.

Owning Mistakes Relieves Pressure: With an overcommitted release due that day, Eric told the team they clearly weren't going to launch and took the blame. The team relaxed, found the problem and launched.

q: What is a minimum lovable product?
a: Eric Müller favors the idea over a minimum viable product because teams can disagree on what viable means. As he put it, "Someone once said it's not minimum viable product, but minimum lovable product." [04:40] He says it should be something clients feel proud to put into the market.

q: How do you push back on scope creep without derailing a project?
a: Eric first sets realistic version-one priorities early, while everyone is still optimistic. When a feature creeps in later, he tells its champion, "that's a great idea, but I'm concerned about its delivery." [07:52] He then asks whether they want to tell their CEO the project is late because of that feature.

q: How can engineering leaders hire developers who are less likely to burn out?
a: Eric Müller looks beyond technical skill to what candidates do away from programming, such as cooking, jogging or meditating. He asks, "What are the things that they do to recharge their batteries so they stay in love with" [13:11] being a programmer.

q: Why is DevOps so hard to scale in a digital product consultancy?
a: Eric explains that client projects need DevOps people, but not full-time for the entire engagement, while several projects may start at once. He said, "DevOps is just the hardest area to manage, to scale, to keep those people engaged," [16:47] and he thinks it gets easier only once a company reaches a certain size.

q: How should an engineering leader respond when the team is going to miss a deadline?
a: Eric Müller says the leader made the commitments and has to own the outcome. In his words, "When you own it, that takes the pressure off of the team." [19:46] That gives the team a chance to fix the problem, though he notes not every mistake ends happily.

s10-bonus-co-sourcing-evolution-moving-beyond-traditional-outsourcing-to-build-fully-integrated-high-velocity-engineering-squads-with-andrey-kudievskiy-founder-ceo-of-distillery

Sell a Ready-Made Squad: Andrey defines Distillery's MVP as a team of three to five people who have already worked together and can submit production-ready code within the first few days, instead of hires trickling in one at a time.

Enterprise Over Startup Thrills: Distillery leans toward mid-market and enterprise clients. The work can be less exciting and use older tech, but it offers a steadier stream, while startups can die and leave unpaid bills.

Hire Leaders Without Sacrificing Quality: Distillery first looks to promote from within, then hires outside. It has brought in outside field CTOs to interview department leads when its own individual contributors might not be able to judge leadership.

Breaking the $10M Ceiling: Distillery was stuck at $10 million in revenue until Andrey built an advisory board and then a board of directors, and brought in leaders including a head of finance and chief revenue officer, removing himself from many decisions.

Diversify Your Cash Reserves: When Silicon Valley Bank failed, 80% of Distillery's cash reserves were inaccessible days before payroll. Andrey's fix: keep reserves at a large bank and spread funds across more than one place.

q: What does Distillery do?
a: Distillery began as a database development and mobile app company and now helps other businesses with engineering talent based in Mexico and Argentina. Andrey Kudievskiy explained that "we actually transitioned and transformed ourselves into AI-enabled staff augmentation" [03:27].

q: Why did Distillery open nearshore engineering locations in Latin America?
a: Andrey credits advisor and former client Joel Milner with convincing him to open locations there so engineers could work as if they sat next to clients. As Andrey put it, "in Latin America, in Mexico, in Argentina, because it's the same time zone." [30:32]

q: How can a founder break through a revenue growth plateau?
a: Andrey says Distillery got past its $10 million plateau after he sought outside help, built a board and brought in management. He warns that if founders can't check their ego and hire people better than they are, "then your growth will be limited to how high can you jump." [19:15]

q: What did Distillery learn from the Silicon Valley Bank collapse?
a: Andrey called relying on one bank a preventable mistake, after most of the company's reserves became inaccessible with payroll approaching. His advice was direct: "First, keep the money in just two different locations." [22:07] Distillery has since moved to one of the top four banks and he recommends keeping reserves with a larger institution.

q: How is generative AI affecting software engineering jobs, according to Distillery's CEO?
a: Andrey Kudievskiy sees some functions, such as parts of quality assurance, needing far less time than before. Still, he argued that "there is no need for less engineers." [25:08] What is needed, he said, are engineers who have adapted to using generative AI.

minting-unicorns-blockchain-ai-and-dubai-with-sonia-gokhale-venturesouq

From Global to Regional: VentureSouq's early portfolio spanned the US, Europe and India. As government funding and startup visas strengthened the local ecosystem, it shifted focus to MENA, where most of its investments now are.

Thematic Funds Over Generalist: VentureSouq launched what Sonia calls the region's first fintech fund, was nearing the close of a second, and planned a climate fund next, concentrating its expertise and networks on one sector at a time.

Lessons Borrowed From LATAM: LATAM resembles MENA: countries united by culture and language, but fintechs must be regulated in each one. VentureSouq uses what it saw in LATAM companies to help MENA portfolio companies.
Why Tabby Is Thriving: Sonia credits the regional buy now, pay later company's success to low default rates, high GDP per capita and founders who know retail. A recent raise valued it as a unicorn.

The Case for US Investors: Global investors tend to fill a later-stage gap in the region. With the dirham and riyal fixed to the US dollar, Sonia says they can get emerging market type returns without FX risk.

q: What is VentureSouq and what does it invest in?
a: Sonia Gokhale, a co-founder, explains that "VentureSouq is an early stage tech VC based in Dubai." [03:15] It began with a global portfolio, now invests mostly in MENA, and is building thematic funds, starting with fintech and then climate.

q: Why did VentureSouq choose to focus on fintech?
a: Sonia says the portfolio was already heavily fintech and the partners are very finance focused. She also sees it as foundational, noting that "FinTech is one of the first things that you need to build that infrastructure" [09:12].

q: How do Dubai regulators work with fintech startups?
a: According to Sonia, founders can get access to regulators, explain what they are building and collaborate on an approach. She says regulators "will build regulations with the companies as opposed to putting it down upon them." [08:09]

q: Why is buy now, pay later company Tabby doing well in the region?
a: Sonia points to the local market, where people have a different attitude toward debt and GDP per capita is among the world's highest. As she put it, "you have very low default rates in this region, which is fantastic for a buy now, pay later company." [15:22]

q: What advice is there for a US startup considering expanding to Dubai?
a: Sonia advises learning how the market differs from the US, including price sensitivity, understanding regulation and getting in front of the right funders. She said, "I think it's really important to understand the market, especially your market that you're addressing." [16:21]

s10-e13-the-scale-to-30-billion-era-re-architecting-postgres-and-managing-viral-traffic-surges-for-the-worlds-largest-gaming-community-with-josh-levine-cto-of-chesscom

Surges Forced Deep Re-Architecture: COVID lockdowns drove a 4x traffic spike, and The Queen's Gambit brought another. Before Josh joined, the team sharded databases, moved to application-layer joins and added bigger hardware.

The Modular Monolith: With no time to fully decompose its PHP monolith, Chess.com routed certain paths to separate Kubernetes node pools, so an overloaded area wouldn't take down the rest of the site.

Work Streams Create Visibility: Developers each had 60 to 70 assigned Jira tickets. Grouping features into work streams, with a tech lead and PM and Notion specs mapped one-to-one to Jira Epics, clarified priorities.
Engine Analysis Grew Up: Game analysis began on eight Stockfish engine nodes regardless of demand. Josh thinks it now has 9,300 cores, and it can dynamically spill into the cloud.
Test Scale Gradually: After a year of performance tuning, a homepage banner dared users to crash the server, and they did. Josh says a feature flag or a percentage rollout would have been wiser.

q: How did Chess.com handle the traffic surge during COVID and The Queen's Gambit?
a: Josh Levine explains that before he joined, lockdowns and then the Netflix series each drove traffic up 4x. The team had to shard databases "and switch to application layer joins and get new hardware" [18:41].

q: What is Chess.com's modular monolith approach?
a: Josh says the team used Cloudflare and other routing tools to send certain paths to dedicated resource pools in Kubernetes, isolating failures from the rest of the site. The reason was practical: "We didn't have time to decompose all the different services," [21:45].

q: What technology and databases does Chess.com run on?
a: Josh describes a PHP monolith using Symfony, alongside a Java server for live chess, with some services since moved out of the monolith. On the data side, he mentions a "monolith with vertically partitioned MySQL databases. I think there's like 21 clusters." [14:58]

q: What happened when Chess.com dared users to crash its server?
a: After shipping a lot of performance tuning, the team ran a homepage banner inviting people to try crashing the server by playing live chess, and it crashed. Josh admits, "We were a bit brazen. But yeah, we crashed the server largely due to hubris, our own hubris." [27:13]

q: How does Josh Levine approach building engineering teams?
a: Josh puts caring for people first, with reliable cadences where they can share knowledge, find support and raise frustrations. As he puts it, "I would say relationships lead to knowledge leads to projects is the main approach that I took to building team." [17:06]

s10-bonus-eliminating-it-works-on-my-machine-complexities-with-open-source-package-management-and-devbox-with-daniel-loreto-founder-ceo-of-jetify

Born From Platform Team Déjà Vu: As head of engineering at Virta Health, Daniel built a platform team and saw companies recreating the same internal tooling. That spend didn't differentiate the business, so he set out to productize it.

Why Docker Wasn't Enough: Jetify first used a Docker container per project, but cache busts could mean 20-minute rebuilds, and Mac virtualization drained resources. The team wrapped Nix in an easier interface and open sourced it.
Where Open Source Ends: Jetify tries to open source features for individual developers. Features needed at organizational scale, such as administration and security compliance, tend to be paid.

Open Source Fixed Feedback: An early proprietary Kubernetes deployment product needed deep integration, so users couldn't easily try it. Going open source and building a Discord community got Jetify the user feedback it lacked.

Scale What Users Depend On: Jetify stays scrappy when testing whether a new feature or use case is valuable. It invests in polish, reliability and scalability once customers are starting to depend on it.

q: What is Devbox by Jetify?
a: Devbox is Jetify's open source tool for creating reproducible developer environments that teammates can recreate exactly. Daniel Loreto says it "lets you define a developer environment, define all the tools that you need for a particular project" [02:50]. A complementary offering, DevSpaces, can start those same environments in the cloud.

q: Why did Jetify build Devbox on Nix instead of relying on Docker?
a: The team first worked inside Docker containers, but found rebuilds slow and resource usage heavy, particularly on Macs. Daniel Loreto recalled that after a small change, "all of a sudden you found yourself waiting 20 minutes because the entire container was rebuilding" [07:12]. They found Nix could create reproducible environments, then wrapped it to improve the user experience.

q: How does Jetify decide which features are open source and which are paid?
a: Daniel Loreto explains that "those features that are for the individual developer, we try to make those open source" [09:53]. Features needed as an organization grows, such as administering a large team or handling security compliance, tend to be paid.

q: How does Jetify's AI end-to-end testing product work?
a: It uses Jetify's developer environments to set up a reproducible instance of the application being tested. Daniel Loreto says that on top of that, "we have an AI agent that just walks through every screen" [03:57], automatically generating integration tests and running them. At the time of the interview, it was in private beta.

q: What mistake did Jetify make with its first product?
a: Jetify's first product, for deploying to Kubernetes, was strictly proprietary SaaS and required deep integration with customers' technology, which made it hard to try and get feedback on. Daniel Loreto says one of the "best decisions we ever made, in my opinion, for the company is to go open source" [11:49]. The company also set up a developer community on Discord.

minting-unicorns-blockchain-ai-and-dubai-with-raakin-iqbal-nucleus-ai

Enhancing Models, Not Building Them: Nucleus AI isn't creating its own LLM or action model. It enhances a traditional neural network approach, offered as a neural network as a service that learns the relationships between a customer's data points.

Airport Pilot Shows Nuance: In a Dubai Airport demo, an engine linked to a 10-page document went beyond listing food options for a traveler whose mother had mobility problems. It suggested nearby gates where options were concentrated.

Tackling Stacked Regulations: A pilot with Dubai Blockchain Center aims to hold context across VARA, central bank and other rules, so token launch and blockchain company applications fit them and approvals move faster.

Software First Toward AGI: Raakin says Nucleus is nowhere close to AGI, partly due to hardware and energy limits. The plan is to advance the software now and be ahead when someone solves the hardware problem.

Dubai for Global-Ready Products: Raakin advises startups built to be global from day one to consider Dubai, citing its geographic reach, streamlined regulation, stakeholder support and access to resources.

q: What is Nucleus AI and what does it offer?
a: Nucleus AI is a company, co-founded by CEO Raakin Iqbal, that aims to help SMEs and ministries get more out of their data while working toward AGI. Raakin explained that "our offering is like a neural network as a service" [04:12], where customers add their information and the AI learns how the data points relate.

q: What does pre-AGI mean, and is Nucleus AI building its own LLM?
a: Raakin uses pre-AGI to describe enhancing today's AI tools as steps toward AGI, such as pursuing an infinite context window and agents that can understand large chunks of data. He was clear about the approach: "So we're not recreating or creating our own LLM or action model." [04:33]

q: How did Nucleus AI perform against ChatGPT in the Dubai Airport pilot?
a: Raakin asked about Terminal 3 food options for his mother, who has mobility problems, and the Nucleus engine recommended gates where several options were close together. He called it a small breakthrough because "it understood that human nuance of the conversation" [07:56].

q: Why do AI chatbots struggle with complex regulatory work?
a: Raakin says large, evolving rule stacks from bodies like VARA and the central bank can overlap or leave gaps, and chatbots lose context as conversations go on, which leads to hallucinations. In his words, you typically "start to lose context off of any conversation on the third or fourth message onwards" [14:32].

q: Should AI startups expand to Dubai?
a: Raakin recommends it for companies trying to enter the international market, pointing to the city's geographic access, resources and support. As he put it, "If your product has global scalability, meaning you're built with keeping being global and day one" [24:28], then Dubai is a place to go.

s10-e12-the-60-layer-deep-threat-why-ai-generated-exploits-require-agentic-supply-chain-security-and-self-healing-code-with-nick-mistry-svp-ciso-of-lineaje

Crawling to the Nth Level: Lineaje's crawlers recursively map every component and transitive dependency, capturing source code risks, metadata and contributor data. Integrity attestation then checks each component against a known good source to detect potential tampering.

Risk Data Wasn't Enough: Mistry says the first mistake was only highlighting risks. Overwhelmed customers needed help acting, so Lineaje added remediation recommendations, integrations with existing tools and a summary dashboard.

Fixes That Don't Break Builds: Lineaje analyzes the full stack to find a compatible plan that removes the most risk without breaking software, which may mean an older package version. Incompatible fixes get Jira instructions so teams can plan them.

Forking Unmaintained Open Source: Mistry says about 52% have no fix available. For unmaintained components, Lineaje will fork and fix the code, then contribute it back to the community or provide it to customers through a private repo.

Adapting to Restricted Clouds: Lineaje was built as multi-tenant SaaS for public cloud, but early adopters included critical infrastructure, government and Defense. The team adapted it for semi-private environments that are air-gapped or contained.

q: What led to the creation of Lineaje?
a: Nick Mistry had lived through several software supply chain incidents, and Log4Shell pushed him over the edge. He described "the realization that we actually did not know what was in our software" [05:44], then spent six months researching before collaborating with co-founder Javed Hassan on the idea.

q: How does Lineaje identify software supply chain dependencies?
a: Mistry explained that the team "built this concept called crawlers that basically will crawl your software, identify all its components" [03:39]. The crawlers then work recursively through each component's dependencies down to the nth level, identifying risks and capturing metadata and contributor data along the way.

q: Why is fixing open source vulnerabilities so difficult for development teams?
a: According to Mistry, "we found that many updates to your software will break your software" [10:50], which makes remediation painful to implement. Lineaje responds by separating compatible fixes that can be automated from incompatible ones that teams need to plan for.

q: What happens when an unmaintained open source component has no fix?
a: Mistry said that if a component is not maintained, "we will fork branch it and contribute it back either to the community" [13:38], provided a community exists to absorb it. Otherwise, Lineaje provides the fixed version to its customers through a private repo.

q: What is next for Lineaje?
a: Mistry described Lineaje Gold Source, aimed at giving developers open source with a 99.5% guarantee of being free of at least critical and high vulnerabilities, with Lineaje addressing the remainder. The goal is to end the cycle of scanning, patching and breaking, and he asked, "why can't we just solve this for everybody from the beginning?" [22:02]

s10-bonus-the-80-coverage-guarantee-overcoming-the-flaky-test-bottleneck-and-scaling-multi-agent-ai-testing-with-jon-perl-co-founder-ceo-of-qa-wolf

Ship Over Research: After about nine months building a reinforcement learning agent to automate QA, co-founder Laura said she'd take another job unless they shipped. The team built an open source Puppeteer test-creation tool in one month.

Cut Scope to Learn Faster: The ideal MVP would have written test scripts live as users clicked through a site. QA Wolf instead generated the script after recording ended, trimming UX to hit its one-month deadline.

Solve the Problem Behind Requests: Users got stuck automating tests or struggled to install an NPM package. That led to a browser-based product for creating and running tests, which Jon likens to Figma for QA engineering.

Sell the Outcome: A prospect asked QA Wolf to do the testing for them. Jon feared it wouldn't scale but went along with his co-founders, and managed test coverage became the path to product-market fit.

Defer Scaling Until It Hurts: A messy run system crashed after revenue climbed from zero to a million in months. The team rebuilt it on Kubernetes, but Jon believes building for scale up front might have cost them a product people would pay for.

q: What does QA Wolf do?
a: QA Wolf delivers automated testing as a service so companies can ship faster and keep bugs out of production. As Jon Perl put it, "we provide automated test coverage as a service for companies" [02:41].

q: What was QA Wolf's first MVP?
a: After months of AI research, Jon Perl's team built an open source tool on Puppeteer in one month. Jon said its purpose was "to make it really easy to create automated tests" [05:46].

q: How did QA Wolf find product-market fit?
a: A prospective customer liked the tooling but had no time to use it and asked QA Wolf to do the work. Jon Perl said what got them to product-market fit "was not just selling a technology, but selling the outcome of having" [15:44] their automated coverage managed for them.

q: How should early-stage startups think about scalability?
a: Jon Perl recalls that QA Wolf's first run system worked for a few hundred users but later had to be completely rebuilt. He considers that a worthwhile trade-off and recommends "deprioritizing scalability until you have a real problem there" [12:59].

q: What advice does Jon Perl give technical founders?
a: Jon Perl tells technical founders not to be afraid of shipping, even though they will always want to make the product better. His advice is to "get it out there, try and sell it and learn from the market." [19:27]

s10-e11-the-end-of-data-decryption-processing-sensitive-ai-and-web3-workflows-on-encrypted-data-with-fully-homomorphic-encryption-with-nigel-smart-chief-academic-officer-at-zama

Two MVPs, Two Audiences: Zama first built a Rust library implementing TFHE for developers, plus a Python-based system that lets data scientists turn PyTorch-like programs into encrypted versions. Open source, webinars and meetups helped draw people in.

Encrypted Smart Contracts: Built on the Rust library, the FHEVM extends Ethereum so Solidity developers can manipulate encrypted values on-chain. Smart notes this could remove a barrier for banks that can't put customer data in the clear on a blockchain.

Decryption Needs Key Management: Encrypted results eventually have to be read by someone, so Zama built key management that gives authorized parties access. It uses multi-party computation, an area Smart had worked on at Unbound.

Attacking Slowness on Many Fronts: FHE is far slower than normal encryption, so Zama works on the math, implementation, compilers, GPUs and FPGA or ASIC accelerators. It also partners with hardware vendors and with Google on its HEIR compiler.

Abandon Dead Ends Quickly: With a huge design space, some pieces of math and cryptography don't dovetail. Smart says the challenge is spotting a dead end fast, then deciding whether to keep pushing or turn back and try another path.

q: What is fully homomorphic encryption?
a: It is encryption that supports both additions and multiplications on data while it stays encrypted, which Nigel Smart explains is enough to compute anything. As Smart put it, "Homomorphic encryption allows you to do computation on encrypted data." [10:26]

q: What was Zama's first product?
a: Smart describes two initial MVPs: a Rust library implementing TFHE and a Python-based system for machine learning and AI work. He said, "One was a Rust library to enable developers to build on Rust, and another which was to enable more data scientists to build applications." [07:37]

q: What is Zama's FHEVM?
a: The FHEVM lets developers write Solidity smart contracts that work with encrypted values on a blockchain. Smart describes it as "the FHEVM, which is the addition to Ethereum, which takes Ethereum and allows you to write" [12:08] such contracts.

q: Is fully homomorphic encryption slow, and how is Zama speeding it up?
a: Yes, Nigel Smart says of homomorphic encryption, "It's really slow in comparison to normal encryption methods." [17:17] Zama is working on better algorithms, implementations and compilers, along with GPU, FPGA and eventually ASIC acceleration.

q: What is Zama's long-term vision, and what is HTTPZ?
a: Smart wants data to stay encrypted all the time, even while it is being processed, so that data breaches and privacy are no longer worries. Comparing it to the web's move from HTTP to HTTPS, he said, "So in some sense, we're trying to create something like HTTPZ," [23:45].

s10-bonus-the-real-time-voice-and-video-boom-eradicating-gpu-cold-starts-and-serverless-latency-for-interactive-ai-with-michael-louis-co-founder-ceo-of-cerebrium

Born from Production Pain: Michael Louis found productionizing machine learning at his e-commerce company painful, yet it transformed operations. After Walmart acquired it in 2021, he and his lead engineer set out to make AI applications easier to build.

Three GPU Problems to Solve: Cerebrium targets costly GPUs with serverless pay-for-use compute, avoids the year-long commitments cloud providers push, and speeds cloud iteration with caching that gets pushed code live in about nine seconds.

Test Value, Not Integrations: The MVP, an e-commerce inventory forecasting tool built in under two months, used UI templates and manual work. Users sent Excel sheets and the team ran forecasts behind the scenes to learn whether the tool was valuable.

Unit Economics at Scale: A client running 250 concurrent GPUs pushed the early platform and Amazon's quota limits. Louis learned infrastructure must also pay for itself, mixing spot, reserved and on-demand instances across cloud providers.

The Feature Engine Trap: Chasing requests like WebSockets and batching pulled focus from cold starts, then about 12 seconds. As customers moved to production that wasn't good enough, and those who had asked for the features ended up churning.

q: What is Cerebrium and why was it built?
a: Cerebrium is a serverless infrastructure platform that helps businesses build, deploy and scale AI applications. Michael Louis was motivated by his struggle with machine learning at his previous e-commerce company, saying "it was honestly probably the worst experience I had in my entire software career" [03:26].

q: Why are cold starts such a hard problem for serverless GPU applications?
a: Michael Louis explains that AI models carry huge payloads: "We're talking gigabytes of dependencies, model weights." [05:01]. Serverless means customers pay only for the compute time they use, but loading those models extremely quickly is a tough engineering challenge that he says Cerebrium solved.

q: How did Cerebrium build its MVP?
a: The first version was an inventory forecasting application for e-commerce companies that took just under two months, using UI templates and a lot of manual work behind the scenes. Michael Louis said the real question being tested was "are they getting value from this tool?" [07:59].

q: What was a major mistake Cerebrium made as an early infrastructure startup?
a: Michael Louis says the team became a feature engine to onboard customers and stopped pushing on core strengths like cold start times. Six months later they saw that customers "who asked for those very features ended up churning just because our cold starts weren't" [16:28] improving.

q: How did Cerebrium handle scaling GPU infrastructure in the early days?
a: Michael Louis recalls one client running 250 concurrent GPUs before the platform was ready, which repeatedly hit Amazon's quota limits. He admits that "what we did in the early days is we just threw resources at the problem" [12:12], an approach he doesn't recommend, and the team has since worked on scalability and unit economics.

s10-bonus-the-open-source-design-revolution-breaking-the-figma-monopoly-with-browser-native-svg-and-code-first-collaboration-with-pablo-ruiz-muzquiz-co-founder-ceo-of-penpot

Built for Their Own Workflow: Kaleidos began incubating Penpot in 2018 to ease handoff friction between its designers and developers. It worked so well internally that the team opened it to everyone as open source.

Functional Code, Browser Stack: Penpot uses PostgreSQL and Clojure, chosen partly because vector design applies many mathematical transformations live. Going all in on the browser stack helped the team deliver a beta in about a year.

The Browser Rendering Pivot: The team bet that browsers rendering SVG through the DOM would keep up with massive design projects. Pablo says browsers are not up to the task, so they announced a tech pivot.

Premature KPIs Backfired: Penpot measured itself against a future goal, big teams creating multiple projects. For at least a year the metric looked broken, causing waste and bad decisions until they chose measures they could act on now.
Community as the Moat: Pablo sees an active community, not just an open-source license, as Penpot's moat. The team recently set a goal of four active outside contributors for every core team member.

q: What is Penpot and who is it for?
a: Penpot is a web-based, real-time collaboration suite for designing and prototyping user interfaces, created by Kaleidos. Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz stresses that it targets developers as well as designers, saying the team set out to "build a superior tool for design prototyping that really brings both" [04:10] into one workflow.

q: What technology was Penpot built with?
a: Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz says the team used PostgreSQL for the database and Clojure, which runs on the JVM and lets work move between backend and frontend. Because design objects undergo many live mathematical transformations, he said, "it made a total sense that we would use a functional programming language" [06:37].

q: What scaling problems has Penpot faced with SVG rendering in the browser?
a: The team expected browsers rendering SVG through the DOM to keep performing as design projects grew very large, and later announced a tech pivot. Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz put it bluntly: "The reality is that browsers are not up to the task and they don't plan to be." [15:37]

q: How does Penpot decide what goes on its roadmap?
a: Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz describes a mix of feature parity, the team's own vision for designer-developer collaboration, and community feedback at carefully chosen moments. The roadmap is public and shows who is working on what, and as he explained, "The roadmap is actually where we are working." [10:36]

q: What mistake did the Penpot team make with KPIs?
a: Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz says they adopted aspirational KPIs too early, judging the present against how big teams would eventually create multiple projects. The lesson was that "We need to look at other things that we can act upon today and see a shift next month." [19:57]

s10-e10-the-universal-cart-breakthrough-overcoming-retail-fragmentation-to-build-the-ultimate-cross-platform-online-shopping-wishlist-with-william-neill-co-founder-of-basket

Two-Week MVP, Focused on Saving: Basket's first build, in native code, tested one thing: sharing a link from the browser into a mobile app. The save had to be seamless so shoppers stayed in their flow.

Flutter Over Conventional Advice: Facing the cost and upkeep of native apps for a tiny team, Basket chose Flutter despite being told React was the only way to go. William says they're happy with the decision.

Analytics Overturned Early Assumptions: The team expected homeware shoppers but found fast fashion and a much younger, heavily female audience. That forced changes to the app's aesthetic and how it presented content.

Fresh Product Data Is Foundational: Capturing metadata on the device goes stale, with some major sites changing product data daily. Basket moved the work server side and plugged into major product feeds where it could.

Hire for Attitude, Not Just Talent: After fairly high early turnover, William looks for talented people who believe in the product and can work through hard coding walls. The team now includes about five engineers, a designer and a product manager.

q: What is Basket and what does it do?
a: William Neill, Co-Founder of Basket, describes it this way: "Basket is a smart wishlisting tool. So it allows you to save things" [02:44]. Users can organize items into collections, share them with friends and family, use gifting features and get price drop and back-in-stock notifications.

q: How did the idea for Basket come about?
a: It grew out of Kinderlist, a tool for creating children's wish lists that co-founder Lex started and William later joined. When COVID hit, William says, "People started to use our tool for a whole bunch of other stuff" [05:06], including paint and furniture, which pointed to a broader opportunity.

q: Why did Basket build its app with Flutter instead of native code?
a: The two-week MVP was native, but William says the team "Decided that actually going the native route was going to be both costly and also fairly" [07:46] high maintenance for a tiny team. They chose Flutter, even though agencies were telling them React was the only way to go, partly because its community was growing.

q: Why is keeping product data up to date so hard for a wishlist app?
a: William explains that capturing metadata on the device when someone shares a link is easy, but "The problem with that is that it goes out of date pretty quick." [15:31] Basket also had to work out how to match the same product saved by different people, which led it to server-side processing and major product feeds.

q: What product mistake did Basket's team learn from?
a: William points to "building out features without validating the use case or the analytics behind supporting that" [18:16]. He says time and momentum were lost on features that should have stayed small, quick bets the team could learn from.

s10-bonus-the-non-deterministic-gaming-frontier-using-generative-ai-to-create-endless-replayability-and-walk-to-earn-rewards-with-rohith-varanasi-co-founder-of-block-party

Walking Powers the Game: Block Party players connect HealthKit, where one step equals one energy, then use it to buy real-world buildings. Items of varying rarity, found in drops scattered around the world, upgrade those buildings.

Generative AI as Core Mechanic: Rohith contrasts Block Party with games whose assets must exist before a player acts. Here, generative AI makes each action produce a unique visual and experience, aiming for infinite replayability.

Text Alone Wasn't Fun: A rough alpha with generative text but no generative visuals flopped with close friends. Flux from Black Forest Labs then offered image generation fast and cheap enough to work inside a gameplay loop.

Ingesting 175 Million Buildings: Covering the continental US plus parts of Canada and Mexico meant loading about 175 million buildings into Postgres. Batches of 10,000 would have taken forever, so the team used AWS Glue.

Hire In-House Design Earlier: Rohith's regret from the past couple of years is not having an in-house designer, despite good part-time and agency help. He would bring that resource on much earlier if he could start over.

q: What is Block Party and how do you earn rewards by walking?
a: Block Party is a mobile game that Rohith Varanasi describes as turning the world into a giant human Monopoly, where steps become energy for buying real-world buildings in the game. As Rohith put it, "You connect your HealthKit, you walk around, and you earn in-game currency for just walking." [03:02]

q: How does Block Party use generative AI for endless replayability?
a: Rohith Varanasi says games until now have been somewhat deterministic because everything a player sees has to be pre-computed. Block Party instead generates unique outcomes from player actions, and he explained, "we're using Gen AI as a core mechanic." [03:52]

q: Why was Flux important to building Block Party?
a: Rohith Varanasi says the first iteration without generative visuals was lackluster and did not retain players, and the release of Flux by Black Forest Labs came at the right time. He described it as a "state-of-the-art image gen model that's fast enough and cheap enough to work in a gameplay" [07:25] loop.

q: What tech stack does Block Party use, and can it scale?
a: Rohith Varanasi says the app is native Swift on iOS only, with an Elixir and Phoenix backend hosted on Render and a Postgres database. He points to Elixir's built-in networking and message passing between nodes, saying, "I think choosing Elixir set us up for scalability." [11:35]

q: What advice does Rohith Varanasi have for first-time founders?
a: Rohith advises founders to strap in, because startup life is a roller coaster that social media celebrations don't fully show. He also cautions that for first-time founders, "it's very easy to just tie your identity" [18:09] to what they're building, which can turn toxic if taken too far.

s10-e8-asset-light-logistics-strategy-orchestrating-an-independent-fulfillment-network-via-multi-carrier-software-and-network-apis-with-jason-harbert-co-founder-cto-of-flowspace

Asset-Light Fulfillment Network: Flowspace owns and operates none of its warehouses. It partners with professional 3PLs that use its software as their warehouse management system, while brands use it to manage orders and inventory.

Placement Drives Shipping Savings: Flowspace studies sales data, say the last few years, to advise how many fulfillment centers a brand needs, where they go and what to stock in each. Shipping from nearby can mean $4 ground delivery in one day.

Ruthlessly Small MVPs: The team trimmed projects to something buildable in about two weeks that delivered some customer value, then followed up if people used it. Code quality and high test coverage stayed non-negotiable.

Roadmap Swim Lanes: Harbert likes reserving roughly 70% of engineering capacity for features, 20% for engineering initiatives and maybe 10% for support, so unglamorous work like database upgrades never competes with shiny features.

Get One Paying Customer First: A Y Combinator mentor rejected the founders' diagram of a billion-dollar Flowspace and asked if even one person had paid. Harbert's lesson: win one customer, learn from them and build from there.

q: What is Flowspace and how does its fulfillment network work?
a: Jason Harbert describes Flowspace as an e-commerce and retail fulfillment platform that helps brands optimize and orchestrate fulfillment, using a network of partner 3PLs that run on its software. Harbert said the company does not "operate any of the facilities that kind of comprise our network" [04:24].

q: How did Flowspace get started?
a: The idea came from a conversation over a beer between Harbert and his co-founder Ben, who had run warehousing logistics at The Honest Company and once had trucks of diapers with nowhere to go. Harbert recalled that Ben "had no idea what warehouse space was available" [05:15].

q: What did the first Flowspace MVP look like?
a: Harbert built a prototype with Ruby on Rails and JavaScript that let users find and book warehouse space, create orders, and receive and ship pallets. He said it "was very Airbnb-ish where you could go and find warehouses and book space" [07:03], and it helped the founders start signing up warehouses.

q: How can a startup balance new features against technical work on its roadmap?
a: Jason Harbert likes to split engineering capacity into swim lanes for features, engineering initiatives and support, so necessary technical work isn't competing with business requests. As Harbert put it, "take, say, 70% of that and say, all right, I'm going to reserve this amount for feature development" [11:06].

q: What advice does Jason Harbert give early-stage founders?
a: Harbert advises very young companies to focus on building and talking to customers, to be willing to pivot, and to avoid busy work. He shared how a Y Combinator mentor told the founders to "get one person to pay for your product" [27:16] before describing what it would become.

the-haunted-house-of-apis-a-portal-to-the-beyond-with-allison-averill

Don't Over-Trust Third-Party APIs: Developers often trust vendor APIs more than user input. A compromised data feed can open your app to attacks like SQL injection, so validate and sanitize what comes in.

LLM Output Is a Wild Card: LLMs are non-deterministic, so the same prompt can yield very different responses. Validate and sanitize their output before it feeds other parts of your app, especially anything that executes code.
Visibility Comes First: Keep an inventory of every third-party API and where it connects. Averill says people are often shocked by how many Traceable discovers that security teams may not have seen.

Monitor to Size the Blast Radius: Watching inputs and outputs of third-party APIs lets you check whether a vendor's breach has reached your app or touched sensitive data, even when your own controls are configured properly.

Automate Security to Keep Speed: Instead of spreadsheets developers must keep current, tools can discover APIs, monitor their security posture and alert on sensitive data flows or broken authentication. People still have to fix the issues.

q: How do third-party APIs introduce security risk into applications?
a: Allison Averill points to unsafe consumption of APIs, where a compromised third-party data stream can expose your app to attacks such as SQL injection. She warns that "Developers tend to trust third-party APIs more than they would trust user input" [07:03], so data from them should be validated and sanitized.

q: How are generative AI APIs different from other third-party APIs?
a: Averill describes them as a subcategory of third-party APIs, so the same risks apply, but large language models are non-deterministic. In her words, you can "prompt a model with the same prompt twice and get two totally different responses." [11:46]

q: What is prompt injection and why does it matter for apps that use LLMs?
a: Averill explains that prompt injection means crafting a "really clever prompt to get the model to potentially reveal something it's not supposed" [12:40] to, or to act against its instructions. The risk grows when an app feeds that output into other components, for example if malicious code goes undetected before it executes.

q: What can the 2018 Facebook breach teach developers about third-party API risk?
a: Averill says an insecure first-party API configuration at Facebook meant that "it potentially exposed the access tokens of up to 50 million Facebook users." [15:37] Because other apps used Facebook sign-in, she advises knowing where such APIs are used and monitoring for unusual logins, though she doesn't know how many real breaches resulted.

q: How can teams move fast and still secure their API integrations?
a: Averill says the key is automation rather than manually maintained lists of integrations. As she put it, "We now have tools that can go and automatically discover all of your APIs" [22:27], and those tools can also monitor security posture and send alerts.

the-haunted-house-of-apis-phantom-threats-with-adam-arellano

Attackers Log In, Not Break In: Adam says attackers mostly use stolen, valid credentials, then use botnets to pull eight to ten records at a time. The activity looks like normal traffic, unlike a huge, obvious data dump.

Unknown APIs Are Phantom Threats: Some companies don't know they have APIs affecting their security. Even sophisticated ones may not know how many they have, what crosses them, who can see it, or how they're vulnerable.

Business Logic Opens the Door: Adam notes most OWASP API Top 10 issues stem from poor business logic. With broken object level authorization (BOLA), a user cleared to fetch one thing can move laterally and grab others.

Scraped Data Fuels Automated Scams: Adam ties fake CEO emails to data scraped through APIs, including LinkedIn's former API. At one company he worked at, users who replied bought gift cards and lost $4,000 or $5,000.

Watch Movement Beyond the Door: Knowing who enters an API isn't enough. Teams need ongoing visibility into lateral movement and patterns, such as repeated login probes that reveal valid email addresses, so they can block the offending device or IP.

q: What are phantom threats in API security?
a: Adam Arellano describes them as dangers you aren't aware of or can't see directly, and for some businesses the APIs themselves qualify. As Adam put it, "some companies is a phantom threat because they're not even aware that they have APIs that affect" [03:30] their security.

q: How do botnets exploit APIs without being detected?
a: Adam explains that attackers avoid pulling an entire database at once, which would be easy to spot, and instead use automated botnets to take small amounts over time. He says they steal "eight, nine, 10 records at a time that look like normal traffic using a valid credential" [05:52].

q: What is broken object level authorization (BOLA)?
a: According to Adam, BOLA happens when "you haven't thought to restrict which objects you have authorization to." [11:47] He compares it to a grocery store that checks what you want at the door but never checks what you actually grab once inside.

q: How can scraped API data lead to CEO impersonation scams?
a: Adam says attackers can combine scraped contact details with a public job change and the CEO's name to send emails that appear to come from your new boss. Describing a case where users bought gift cards, Adam said that until the card numbers were shared, "everything behind that was automated, not a single person involved." [09:54]

q: How can teams detect and stop hidden API threats?
a: Adam, a technology advisor at Traceable who acknowledges his bias, says teams need to see how users move within APIs, not only who comes in and out. In his words, what "really needs to happen is you have full-time visibility of what's going on, not just in and" [13:28] out of the store.

s10-e8-from-cisco-meraki-and-splunk-to-fixing-privilege-sprawl-why-treating-identity-as-a-static-one-time-login-invites-cloud-catastrophe-with-shashwat-sehgal-co-founder-ceo-of-p0-security

Access Beyond Human Users: P0 Security aims to secure and govern cloud access for every kind of identity, including engineers, contractors, sales engineers, workloads and service accounts, across the lifecycle.

First Deployment Within Months: Starting in late 2022, the team had its first customer deployment by February 2023 and closed that contract by March or April, then sought similar customers and made the MVP work in their environments.

Roadmap Mapped by Segment: Sehgal's team speaks with five to ten customers and prospects weekly, then maps the product gaps between its current best-fit segment and the broader market, revisiting the roadmap regularly.

Scale Without Boiling the Ocean: P0 laid architectural foundations meant to reach hundreds of thousands of identities, but did not over-optimize performance while early customers had roughly 100 to 300 engineers.

Question the Feature Request: A customer may ask for a feature because they haven't considered other ways to solve the underlying problem. Sehgal relies on MVPs and tight customer-to-R&D feedback loops to catch misdiagnoses early.

q: What does P0 Security do?
a: P0 Security focuses on securing cloud access, with a mission of abstracting security away from developers. Co-founder and CEO Shashwat Sehgal says the company aims to "help secure access to a company's crown jewels in the cloud" [05:46], no matter who is trying to access them.

q: Why are non-human identities a cloud security challenge?
a: Sehgal says the number of entities that can take action in the cloud has exploded over the last few years. It is no longer only employees, because "increasingly it's also workloads, service accounts, quote-unquote non-human identities" [03:30].

q: How did P0 Security build its MVP and win early customers?
a: Sehgal says the first deployable version reached a customer within about three months, and that deployment became a closed contract. From there the approach was, in his words, "let's find another customer that looks like the last customer we closed" [00:25] and make the MVP work for their environment.

q: How did P0 Security approach scalability?
a: Sehgal says the team laid architectural foundations intended to scale to tens of thousands of employees and hundreds of thousands or more workloads and machine identities. He also cautions that with smaller early customers, "it's also important to not boil the ocean" [13:23].

q: What does Shashwat Sehgal look for when hiring a startup team?
a: Sehgal looks for intellectual curiosity, high integrity and a willingness to take extreme ownership. On curiosity, he says "you have to go one step beyond and hire not just smart, but also curious or flexible people" [10:26].

the-haunted-house-of-apis-the-haunted-web-of-apis-with-richard-bird

Sprawl Starts as Operations: Bird says API sprawl is an operational problem that turns into a security one when APIs are built without authentication or safeguards, or carry private data they shouldn't.

Breaches Are Repeating: Citing a new API security report, Bird says 57% of organizations they talked to had an API breach in the last two years. Of those, 73% had at least three and 41% had five or more.
The 70% Blind Spot: Bird cites estimates that only about 30% of large-enterprise API traffic crosses web application firewalls and CDNs. The unseen 70% is where the creepy crawlers live.

Changed APIs Can Slip Through: In two major breaches, live APIs were pulled, fixed and returned to production without lifecycle controls. Developers forgot to restore encryption, and tens of millions of records were taken.
Platform Over Point Solutions: Admit the problem, test your current tools, then adopt a platform that ranks API risk, compares normal behavior with abuse and moves toward surgical runtime protection.

q: What is API sprawl and why is it a security risk?
a: Richard Bird describes API sprawl as APIs multiplying across an organization without consistent standards, oversight or controls. As he put it, "API sprawl is not a security problem. API sprawl is an operational problem." [04:23] It becomes a security problem when an attacker finds an exploitable API in that mess and uses it as a pathway.

q: Why do security teams lose track of APIs?
a: Bird explains that security teams historically had no responsibility for APIs, and API creation belongs to DevOps rather than security. He also points to a lack of governance, saying "nobody's in charge of APIs, right? On the operational side, API ownership is fractioned" [07:46].

q: What are the creepy crawlers in an API ecosystem?
a: For Bird, they are APIs exchanging information with little oversight, often outside the channels that web application firewalls and CDNs can see. He summed it up this way: "the creepy crawlers are really all the things that you don't know about in your" [10:36] environment that involve APIs.

q: How can an API that was already in production cause a major data breach?
a: Bird cites breaches at a large mobile carrier and a healthcare services organization, where APIs were taken out of production, changed and put back without lifecycle management. He said that "in both of those cases the developers forgot to reinstate encryption on" [12:19] the affected APIs, which bad actors then found and used to exfiltrate customer records.

q: How should organizations secure their APIs as they scale?
a: Bird advises first admitting there is an API security problem, then evaluating whether current tools can really stop API breaches, and then looking at API security platforms. He urges teams to "recognize that this is a holistic effort, not a point solution." [17:17]

the-haunted-house-of-apis-the-dark-corners-of-apis-with-katie-paxton-fear

Forgotten APIs Become Open Doors: APIs are everywhere, and knowledge of them fades as people leave. Katie Paxton-Fear says that after maybe two to three years, there may be nobody left who knows a given API exists.

Developer Autonomy Breeds Unknown APIs: Developers often spin up APIs for convenience or possible future use, without guidelines or documentation. Katie installed software that was never bought, and its API was still up years after she left.

Start With an Inventory: Without budget or maturity for dedicated tools, dig through GitHub commit history, server files, cloud environments and running pods, and ask developers what APIs exist. Fuzzing word lists and API management tools can help.

Decommissioning Takes More Than Switch-Off: Teams need to track what developers deploy, where and how, so it can be properly retired when they leave. A poor relationship between development and security teams is another common mistake.

Plan for the APIs You Miss: Even with continuous monitoring, you won't find every API. Katie advises having an API incident response plan, so the team can focus instead of panicking when a hidden API is attacked.

q: How do APIs end up unknown or forgotten inside a company?
a: Katie Paxton-Fear explains that developers often work autonomously, creating APIs for convenience or future use that never get documented or decommissioned. Knowledge also leaves with people, as she describes: "The answer is the last developer who worked on it leaves the company" [05:53].

q: Why are shadow and undocumented APIs attractive targets for attackers?
a: Katie says you can't protect an API you don't know exists, while attackers are highly motivated to find it. For them it is a payday, and in her words, "That is a way in, not even a backdoor, right? It is just a nice entryway," [10:19].

q: How can an organization start discovering unknown APIs without a big budget?
a: Katie suggests gathering information from GitHub commit history, files on servers, cloud environments, running pods and developers themselves. Her advice to some companies she has worked with "has been run an inventory." [11:22]

q: What mistakes lead to unknown APIs being overlooked?
a: Katie points to missing decommissioning processes, adversarial relationships between development and security teams, and a lack of API security tools, inventory and incident response planning. She warns that if your process for "decommissioning things is switch off, you are not going to catch everything." [13:40]

q: Can API security tools find every hidden API?
a: No. Katie says solutions like Traceable, where she works, can help with intelligence and continuous monitoring, but some APIs will still be missed. As she puts it, "get them all. And what you need when that happens is a plan" [12:43].

04ece806-80e1-4cc3-b48c-39cbfbd8cfbf
the-haunted-house-of-apis-the-witchs-brew-with-jayesh-ahire

Three Buckets of API Risk: Jayesh groups OWASP API risks into access control (such as BOLA and broken function level authorization), data privacy (excessive data exposure) and inventory management (knowing which APIs you have).

Retire Old API Versions: A major Australian telecom shipped a newer, better-secured API but left the old public one accessible. An attacker used it to get sensitive data, including passport details, on millions of users.

Context Beats Black-Box Testing: SAST reads code without context, and traditional DAST attacks from outside, which brings false positives. API security testing aims to replicate business logic abuse across APIs and third parties.

Gate Every Development Stage: Build security into API design, use SAST while developing, secure infrastructure-as-code at deployment, and run continuous automated tests on staging so issues are fixed before production.

Match Tools to Maturity: Early-stage teams can start with developer security awareness, a SAST tool like SonarQube and a DAST tool like ZAP. Mature organizations also need API inventory, posture management, design standards and contextual testing.

q: What are the most common OWASP API security vulnerabilities?
a: Jayesh Ahire groups them into access control, data privacy and inventory management, and calls access control the most prominent and most exploited in recent years. Describing that category, he said "sometimes you just left the door open and that door can be exploited by attackers" [03:12].

q: How is API security testing different from traditional SAST and DAST?
a: Jayesh explains that SAST looks only at code without context, while DAST has traditionally been an outside, black-box attack that can produce false positives. API testing has to cover interactions between APIs and third parties, and as he put it, "It needs way more insight into the business logic of the application." [07:52].

q: How can an old or retired API lead to a data breach?
a: Jayesh described an Australian telecom that released a more secure API version but never retired the old public one, which an attacker then exploited to access data on millions of users. He pointed to inventory management, citing the "older version of the API, which was accessible even after it was supposed to be" [10:46] retired.

q: How do you build an effective API security testing framework?
a: Jayesh recommends making testing native to the development life cycle, with security gates at design, development and deployment, plus continuous automated testing on staging. He warns that security is "always an afterthought, and to address that problem, make sure that when you design your APIs" [14:03] you consider security practices.

q: What API security testing tools should an early-stage company use?
a: Jayesh suggests helping developers understand security, then starting with a SAST tool and a DAST tool, while noting DAST can produce false positives. His advice is to begin with "something lightweight open source like SonarQube, ZAP. But as you mature, keep looking for better tools" [19:48], such as Traceable, where he runs product management.

s10-bonus-overcoming-the-75-failure-rate-with-rigid-process-mapping-and-strategic-co-sourcing-architecture-with-elkhan-shabanov-ceo-of-digicode-americas

Partner, Not Body Shop: Digicode aims to go beyond supplying developers by advising clients on strategy. For Elkhan, the first sign of a successful relationship is when conversations shift from technology goals to business goals.

Delivery Managers Unlock Scale: One role blends project, program, product and people management with delivery, plus real authority. New hires shadow an experienced delivery manager until they are ready to run on their own.

Marketing Before Sales: Referrals could no longer support goals tied to 30-35% yearly growth, so Digicode built a sales team before a marketing team. The effort failed, and they restarted with marketing strategy and brand awareness.

Resilience Through Crisis: COVID forced an office-based company to adopt remote work, which prepared it for Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Elkhan says clients never complained that projects had slowed or stopped.

Rethink the Technical Co-Founder: Elkhan advises business founders with tech-based ideas to pay for the work instead of hunting for a technical co-founder, whose limits can steer the company and whose equity can be costly to unwind.

q: What does Digicode do?
a: Elkhan Shabanov describes Digicode as 400-plus developers helping companies achieve business and technology goals, with an aim of being a partner and advisor rather than just a software vendor. He says a good sign is that "It is much better to have a discussion with the client about business than about technology." [08:03]

q: How did Digicode scale its software services business?
a: Elkhan credits an internal role called delivery manager, which combines project, program, product and people management with responsibility for delivery. He says the company wanted someone with "a lot of responsibility but at the same time with authority who can be that lens" [12:15] for client communication.

q: What mistake did Digicode make when building a sales team?
a: When referrals and partners' personal networks were no longer enough to meet growth goals, the company tried hiring salespeople first. Elkhan said, "I think that was a big mistake because we started building a sales team before we built a marketing team." [16:59]

q: How did Digicode keep operating during the war in Ukraine?
a: Elkhan explains that the remote work methods adopted during COVID were already in place when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and the team also had solutions ready when power and internet were later affected. In his words, "That helped us to continue operation without interruption." [15:05]

q: Do non-technical founders need a technical co-founder?
a: Elkhan advises business founders against searching for one, because the search can take a long time and the company can become hostage to that person's limits. His advice is to "stop looking for the technology co-founder. Because more times than not," [26:31] it takes very long, and he says it is better to pay someone to do the job.

s10-e7-the-tablet-graveyard-consolidating-third-party-delivery-chaos-into-a-unified-pos-architecture-with-vishal-agarwal-founder-ceo-of-checkmate

A Pivot Born From Tablets: Checkmate began as a check-splitting app. After about 18 months, a restaurant showed Vishal two POS stations and nine delivery tablets, and 22 or 24 of roughly 50 leads quickly said yes to a fix.

Email Parsing as the MVP: The first version scraped third-party order confirmation emails and pushed the data into POS systems through existing API integrations. It was built in days, with a Ruby on Rails backend, Heroku and a database server.

Customers Drive the Roadmap: Checkmate chose to prioritize what existing customers need to grow revenue over features that win new ones. Five Guys' request for menu management led to a customer portal when the company had no user interface.

Surviving Weekend Order Peaks: Servers once crashed every Friday and Saturday evening, when delivery demand peaked. Checkmate worked through queuing and scaling mechanisms, hired specialists and moved from Heroku to AWS for more control and flexibility.

Confusion Is a Product Flaw: Vishal recalls being rude to a client who struggled with the system. He later apologized, fixed the problem and gave them his number, concluding that a customer's confusion reflects a shortcoming in the solution.

q: What problem led to the creation of Checkmate?
a: Vishal Agarwal was pitching a check-splitting app when a restaurant showed him a bigger problem with delivery tablets. He recalled that "there was two pos stations and nine different tablets" [03:42], so Checkmate set out to integrate third-party delivery platforms into restaurant POS systems.

q: How did Vishal Agarwal validate demand for Checkmate's delivery integration?
a: Before the solution was built, Vishal contacted about 50 leads he had been talking to for the original check-splitting product and asked whether they were interested. As he put it, "I think 22 or 24 of them replied within 48 hours." [04:43]

q: How was the first version of Checkmate built?
a: Vishal's CTO built an email parser that pulled order details from delivery platforms' confirmation emails and sent them to POS systems through an API. Vishal said they "stood up the solution with Heroku and a database server" [06:46], with a Ruby on Rails backend.

q: What scaling challenges did Checkmate face as order volume grew?
a: Vishal said the product was not built for scale and the team had to fight hard as orders grew. "There were days, Noah, where every Friday and Saturday evening, our servers would crash." [15:18] The company later migrated from Heroku to AWS and hired specialists.

q: How does Checkmate decide what to build next?
a: Vishal explained that the roadmap comes from talking to customers, with a deliberate focus on what existing customers need to grow their revenue. "The most important thing to build for us is what do the customers need?" [09:48]

bfbfee55-1d79-40f1-b6c1-30b4e1922fdf
s10-bonus-the-real-time-language-breakthrough-eliminating-call-center-friction-and-building-future-proof-llm-infrastructure-with-heiki-riesenkampf-founder-of-commonbase

Prove It With Off-the-Shelf APIs: The first Commonbase version chained transcription, translation and speech generation, using Twilio, Deepgram, Llama on Groq and ElevenLabs to show simple real-time speech translation was possible.

Simplify the First Prototype: Heiki built the MVP in Replit to stay scrappy and collaborative. In hindsight, he would have preferred connecting two browser sessions rather than adding the complication of Twilio phone calls.

Attack Latency With 80/20: Customers always ask about latency. Commonbase improved it and stabilized its infrastructure by cutting networking time and API hops between providers and its servers, without over-engineering.

Two Lines, One Month: Translation delay grew as calls got longer. After a month of debugging, removing two lines that built an audio buffer fixed it. Heiki's lesson: rubber duck bugs with a fresh set of eyes sooner.

Own Models, Rented GPUs: Commonbase is fine-tuning its own models and aims to build an end-to-end speech-to-speech model, while relying on cloud providers for GPUs as long as possible instead of building a cluster.

q: What is Commonbase?
a: Commonbase is a universal speech translator founded by Heiki Riesenkampf to connect people across language and cultural barriers. Heiki describes the mission simply: "We help people speak any language in real time" [02:43]. The idea draws on his own experience as an immigrant adjusting to different languages and cultures.

q: How does Commonbase's real-time speech translation work?
a: Heiki Riesenkampf explained that the initial pipeline transcribes speech into text, then the next step is to "translate the text into another language, and turn the translated text into speech again." [04:27] The early stack used Twilio for phone calls plus third-party services for transcription, translation and speech generation. The team is now fine-tuning its own models for the same pipeline.

q: How can you reduce latency in real-time speech translation?
a: Heiki Riesenkampf's team applied 80/20 analysis to find improvements that did not require too much engineering effort. In his words, they were "trying to reduce the total number of API hops that we need to do" [13:18], along with cutting networking time.

q: What caused the growing translation delay on longer Commonbase calls?
a: An early feature built up an audio buffer of raw call audio so the file could be saved when the call ended. After a month of debugging, Heiki Riesenkampf said, "I just removed two lines of code" [15:03], and the delay disappeared. He believes describing the bug to another engineer would have surfaced it much more easily.

q: Should a machine learning startup build its own GPU cluster?
a: Heiki Riesenkampf thinks it is a waste of time for most machine learning companies, saying, "I don't want to build my own GPU cluster." [11:02] He argues that unless you are training an LLM that costs $10 million or more, you are much better off relying on someone else's infrastructure.

s10-e6-the-shadow-identity-crisis-intercepting-critical-saas-vulnerabilities-and-generative-ai-data-leaks-at-the-point-of-decision-with-guy-guzner-co-founder-ceo-of-savvy-security

Fix Identity Gaps Through Automation: Savvy finds a company's SaaS identities, exposes weak or compromised credentials, reused passwords and gaps in MFA or single sign-on, then helps remediate them through automation.

Build the Enterprise MVP Carefully: The MVP took a little over a year, with microservices, a Go backend, GraphQL and CI/CD. Guy says enterprise vendors don't get many chances with customers, and the architecture has hardly changed since.
Design Around Unit Economics: After costly scaling at Fireglass, Savvy pushed CPU-intensive work to a browser extension on customer machines and stayed out of the data path, capturing only metadata.

Deployment UX Can Block Sales: An extension sign-in pop-up led customers to refuse rollout. The team created Pathfinder, which learns a user's identity from signals and can then authenticate silently in the background.
