Choose a Few Things: Early on, Savvy tried to win every customer and built many features in parallel. Guy would now rule some things off the table from the start and do just a few really well.

q: What does Savvy Security do?
a: Savvy Security is a SaaS security company focused on identity, which Guy Guzner describes as a gateway to applications and data now that there is no longer a perimeter. In his words, "it helps customers find all of their different SaaS identities" [03:06], then find where they are being misused and remediate those gaps through automation.

q: What is Savvy Security's zero touch integration?
a: It is a patent-pending technology that integrates with SaaS applications without an administrator having to create and maintain the integration. Guzner explained that Savvy is "using our browser extension footprint to become not just passive in collecting data, but also active in generating requests into the application backend" [12:50], reusing the trust a user has already established.

q: How did Savvy Security design its product to scale?
a: Guy Guzner's team combined a cloud service with a browser extension that handles much of the CPU-intensive processing on the customer's machine. They also avoided sitting in the data path to escape expensive bandwidth costs, building it so "that we just need to be in the control path of the traffic" [11:54].

q: What mistake did Savvy Security make with enterprise deployment?
a: The team underestimated deployment complexity: authenticating the browser extension created a credentials pop-up that customers would not roll out to 30,000 users. Guzner admitted that "we realized that we were naive" [14:06], and the fix led to a feature called Pathfinder that learns identities automatically.

q: What does Guy Guzner look for when building a startup team?
a: Guzner started Savvy with three co-founders, and many early hires had also worked with the team at previous companies. He said the lesson is never "to be blinded by talent and never compromise fit to the team and personality" [09:22], since people with the right attitude can be taught.

s10-bonus-the-founders-for-hire-evolution-moving-past-the-agencies-to-build-early-stage-products-with-custom-venture-studios-with-rob-grazioli-managing-partner-of-bread

Founders for Hire: Bread works with early-stage founders on product, design, engineering, sales motion and go-to-market, operating less like a vendor and more like a partner helping them reach or follow a raise.

Run the Company Like Product: Bread works in six-week cycles, keeps no backlog and makes small to mid-sized bets. It tests growth ideas, such as serving larger legacy businesses, the way it would test a feature.

Automate to Stay Small: Internal tools for staffing, budgeting and forecasting build the reports so operators can focus on decisions. The goal is to scale quality without adding overhead or middle management.
Hire People Who Climb Ladders: Rob looks for experienced, versatile people, such as full stack engineers or designers who code, who can move quickly between the big picture and the details.

A Near-Bankruptcy Lesson: Around 2013, a flimsy book of business, likely R&D overspending and a lost key account left payroll short. Founders skipped their pay, split the team, took on debt and clawed back to profit.

q: What does Bread do for early-stage founders?
a: Bread, where Rob Grazioli is a managing partner, helps founders shape their product, refine sales and go-to-market, and handle design and engineering. Rob describes the model as "less like a vendor and more like a partner or even like a venture fund" [04:12].

q: How does Bread approach product development?
a: Rob Grazioli says Bread works in six-week cycles, avoids backlogs and treats work as small to mid-sized bets, such as validating a feature or design. In his words, "You try to do the smallest thing you possibly can that achieves the outcome" [05:04].

q: What does Rob Grazioli look for when hiring?
a: Rob favors experienced, flexible people who can both see the big picture and solve specific problems, which often means full stack engineers or designers who can code. He loves "people who know when to climb up and when to climb down" [11:12] the ladder between those views.

q: How can a services business scale without adding middle management?
a: Rob Grazioli says Bread first asks why it needs to scale, automates work like reporting, and explores other revenue, including an experimental PE-like function for buying and growing small software products. He explains, "We also don't want to create a middle management layer in our business or for our clients" [12:50].

q: What was Rob Grazioli's biggest mistake as a business owner?
a: At his first services company, Rounded, the team let a bill-paying account end, expecting another project that did not arrive. Rob recalls, "we didn't have enough money to pay our people" [16:40], and calls it a foundational learning experience.

s10-e5-eliminating-emotion-driven-retail-losses-with-data-reprocessing-algorithmic-trading-engines-with-sebastian-raffaele-co-founder-cto-of-minotaur

Webhooks Turned Alerts Into Trades: Minotaur began with Pine Script strategies on TradingView. Instead of waking at 2 a.m. to act on an alert, the team used webhook signals to send the trade straight to the exchange.

Great Backtests, Lost Money: A strategy that looked amazing on past Bitcoin data lost the few thousand dollars put on it live. The team then hired developers and built an in-house backtester covering gaps they saw in TradingView's.

Cover the Downside First: Running the algorithms aggressively was a mistake. Dialing them back significantly and adding a model to cover downside risk is where Raffaele says the product started excelling.

Referrals as a Product Signal: Customers seemed happy, but referrals weren't coming. Raffaele treated that as a problem with the product itself, not something to blame elsewhere, and developed it further.
Scaling on the Wrong Numbers: Twice, scaling too fast set the self-funded company back, including scaling based on revenue. It had to drop ad spend and now balances paid and organic marketing.

q: What is Minotaur Trading Systems?
a: Sebastian Raffaele, co-founder and CTO, describes Minotaur as an on-ramp for people seeking consistency when trading cryptocurrency through automation. He is clear about its limits: "It's not going to make you rich overnight." [05:31]

q: Why do manual retail traders tend to lose money in crypto?
a: Raffaele points to emotion, fear of missing out and an edge held over retail traders, which he compares to a casino's. As he put it, "that little spread they have over you allows them to win almost always" [03:55].

q: How did Minotaur build its first automated trading system?
a: Raffaele learned basic Pine Script, developed strategies on TradingView and attached webhook signals to its chart alerts. The signal would "fire off the exact same trade to the exchange and have the exchange execute that for you." [08:35]

q: Why can TradingView backtests differ from live trading results?
a: Raffaele praises TradingView but says liquidity and inaccuracies in historical candle data can distort its backtests, citing issues "with their backtesting system that does not allow you to see things clearly" [11:28]. When Minotaur re-ran a promising strategy on its own in-house system, it was basically losing all the time.

q: What did Sebastian Raffaele learn about risk in algorithmic trading?
a: Raffaele learned that pushing an automated system for fast monthly returns carries the same danger as pushing too hard manually. His rule is to cover the downside, and he says the "downside and the upside will take care of itself." [23:40]

9c6923bc-1e08-45db-a7e5-bfef938bb9a2
s10-e4-open-banking-infra-replacing-insecure-credential-sharing-with-safe-open-brokerage-apis-for-millions-of-retail-accounts-with-brendan-wood-co-founder-ceo-of-snaptrade

Pivot From Your Own Pain: Passiv was spending roughly 80% of its engineering budget on broker integrations. When other fintechs asked to use them and cold calls drew strong demand, the team shifted focus to selling them as SnapTrade.

Speed Over a Clean Rebuild: SnapTrade's MVP took three to four months by adding a new authentication front end to Passiv's existing API. It validated demand quickly but left technical debt the team is still dealing with.

Depth Before Broker Coverage: Customers showed that reliability and features like on-demand account sync and order placement mattered more than supporting every broker. SnapTrade focused on doing a few major ones well.

Passiv as Customer Number One: To beat the chicken-and-egg problem between brokers and apps, Passiv justified early integrations and broker relationships. Opening them to other apps then helped attract bigger names on both sides.

Radical Candor With Brokers: SnapTrade tells brokers early what it is doing, even when that risks threats or shutdown demands. Wood says most are supportive, and that long-term success depends on their backing and trust.

q: What is SnapTrade?
a: SnapTrade is a unified trading API that lets people connect their stock trading accounts to third-party apps for things like portfolio analysis or tax planning. Co-founder and CEO Brendan Wood explained, "we think of ourselves like Plaid, but for trading specifically." [02:36]

q: Why did the Passiv team pivot to building SnapTrade?
a: Brendan Wood said broker integrations were consuming so much effort that it was hard to focus on Passiv's own product quality. "We were spending probably 80% of our engineering budget on integrations." [04:05] Other fintech founders were also asking to use those integrations.

q: How was the SnapTrade MVP built so quickly?
a: Brendan Wood said it took roughly three to four months because many integrations already existed in-house. The team was essentially using its "existing API and adding a new authentication front end to it to allow other applications" [06:26] to use the same backend.

q: How does SnapTrade work with stockbrokers?
a: SnapTrade partners with brokers, which Brendan Wood says provide custody, compliance and execution, and he believes the product won't work in the long run without their support. "We're radically candid with financial institutions about what we do." [19:29]

q: How does SnapTrade hire engineers and other team members?
a: After a few bad hires, Brendan Wood changed the process: candidates who seem competent in interviews do a well-paid, one-week contract trial working on practical problems. As he put it, "the way that we do things now is we don't give people coding tests." [13:04]

s10-bonus-whats-new-with-swob-with-alex-florio

Tinder, But for Jobs: Swob lets job seekers set a location, job type and industries, then swipe right to apply or left to pass. Alex Florio's own frustrating job search, while he was using Tinder, inspired it.
Job Supply Came First: Users liked the app but found few jobs in smaller towns. Swob made supply priority one and now lists over 7.5 million jobs across North America.
Beyond the Application: Swob is adding educational content on resumes, employer etiquette and interview prep, because candidates often miss out on opportunities over avoidable mistakes.

Built on Employer Pain Points: Employers said other sites sent paid-for applicants who weren't local. Swob built local hiring features, and one small U.S. automotive company made a hire within two days of posting.
Moving Employers to Freemium: Swob is revamping its employer side, shifting from monthly or annual subscriptions to free job posting, with an option to boost listings for more visibility.

q: What is Swob and how does the job app work?
a: Swob is a job app built to simplify the job search, where users swipe right to apply and left to pass, on mobile or desktop. Alex Florio summed it up: "if you think Tinder, but for jobs, so you put in your location" [02:16].

q: How many jobs are available on Swob?
a: Florio says growing the number of jobs was the top priority, especially after feedback that some areas had few listings. According to him, "there's over seven and a half million jobs across the platform in North America" [03:32].

q: Why is Swob adding educational content for job seekers?
a: Florio says many people, especially younger ones, struggle with resumes, employer communication and interview prep. The aim is that users are not just finding openings, "but you're actually landing those opportunities as well" [09:43].

q: How does Swob help employers find local candidates?
a: Employers told the team that other job sites brought them applicants from out of town or out of the country, so Swob developed features for hiring locally. Florio shared the story of a small U.S. automotive company that had been struggling to find candidates: "And literally within two days, they made a hire." [16:52]

q: Is it free to post a job on Swob?
a: Florio says Swob is revamping its employer side, moving from monthly or annual subscriptions to a freemium model. Under that model employers "can go and post their jobs for free" [18:15], with the option to boost a posting to make it more visible.

s10-e3-the-trillion-user-scalability-crisis-re-architecting-bitcoins-layer-2-for-instant-enterprise-grade-global-liquidity-with-kevin-hurley-co-founder-cto-of-lightspark

Simplifying Wasn't Enough: Lightspark's first product took about a year and wrapped LND nodes in a simpler interface and SDK. Customers still struggled with channels and inbound liquidity, so the team abstracted channels away entirely.

One Node Per Customer: Lightspark began by running a full LND node for each customer, which kept the stack simple. Hurley knew an AWS pod per customer wouldn't scale, but wanted to prove the product before optimizing.

Capital First, Efficiency Later: Early on, Lightspark overcapitalized its nodes so customer payments would route under any usage pattern. Seeing how funds actually flow now lets it stay well connected while locking up far less money.

UMA Links Currencies and Countries: Universal Money Addresses extend LNURL with human-readable addresses. A sender can pay in U.S. dollars and the recipient get Mexican pesos, with Lightning and Bitcoin as the transparent glue.

Hire Collaborators, Stay Lean: Lightspark looks first for good, collaborative people, not those out to win every argument. It typically hires only when it feels some pain and has a clear plan for the new person.

q: Why is Lightspark built on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network?
a: Kevin Hurley says many on the team came from Facebook, where they worked on Diem, and carried over the mission of an open, global protocol for money. As Hurley put it, "we realized that you really need something truly neutral" [03:27] and decentralized as a settlement network for global payments.

q: What was wrong with the first version of Lightspark?
a: It ran LND on AWS behind a simpler interface, but customers, including longtime crypto players, still had a hard time with core Lightning concepts such as channels. Hurley said, "What we found was that even trying to simplify it, it was still too complex." [04:58] The team went back to the drawing board and abstracted channels away.

q: What is Universal Money Address (UMA)?
a: Hurley describes UMA as an extension of LNURL that uses human-readable addresses and lets people send from any currency to any other, connecting existing banking rails with Lightning. In his words, "Lightning and Bitcoin is just the transparent glue that kind of meshes those" [11:22] things together.

q: How did Lightspark manage Lightning liquidity early on?
a: Until the team understood the network and customer usage patterns, it put extra capital into its nodes so transactions could be routed reliably. Hurley explained that "we really just overcapitalized our nodes initially." [07:13] He says Lightspark can now use capital far more efficiently.

q: Was Lightspark built to scale from day one?
a: Not infinitely: Kevin Hurley says the company is chasing scale a bit and aims to support anticipated customer levels plus a buffer. His view is that "You don't want to over-engineer things from the beginning" [14:46] before seeing some product-market fit, while also avoiding a redesign every time customers are added.

s10-bonus-whats-new-with-turso-with-pekka-enberg
SQLite for Production: Turso adds features such as replication to SQLite for modern workloads. It also offers remote access, turning the in-process library into something similar to Postgres.

Database Per Tenant: Turso is lightweight enough to run lots of databases, such as one per user. Pekka says this helps with scaling, privacy and data isolation, though multi-tenancy was still being readied for production.

Waiting on Vector Search: Turso first sat out the vector database wave to watch the market. About six months later, seeing the Postgres community step up, the team decided this important workload was almost existential.

On-Device RAG: Vector search in SQLite lets retrieval happen on the device, cutting latency and keeping private data local. Pekka expects strong retrieval can take smaller, on-device models pretty far.

React Native First: Turso began its mobile SDK work with React Native, building on its popular JavaScript SDK. Pekka expects native iOS and Android support will both be needed, with Flutter and others depending on demand.

q: What is Turso and how does it relate to SQLite?
a: Turso's tagline is "SQLite for production," and it builds features onto SQLite for modern workloads such as serverless and mobile. Pekka Enberg explained that SQLite worked well for the team, "but it was just missing some features like replication, which we needed at the time" [02:49].

q: Why use a database-per-tenant architecture?
a: Pekka says separate databases help with scaling, and also with privacy and keeping data isolated, from the backend all the way to mobile devices. In his words, it resonates "because now you can have these databases which are isolated from each other" [07:17].

q: Why did Turso add vector search to SQLite?
a: Vector search supports retrieval augmented generation, which retrieves relevant data for large language models. Pekka said the team initially waited, but after seeing the Postgres community move, "we started thinking this kind of becomes like an existential thing" [11:24].

q: What are the benefits of on-device vector search?
a: Pekka Enberg points to lower latency and better privacy, since searching and model-related processing can happen within the device itself. Speaking about private information, he said, "It doesn't necessarily have to leave the device" [10:25].

q: How does Turso decide which mobile SDKs to support?
a: Turso started with React Native because its JavaScript SDK is by far its most popular, and Pekka expects to need both native Android and iOS as well. For Flutter and other frameworks, he said, "I think for us, it's just going to be demand based" [15:49].

s10-e2-securing-intellectual-property-minimizing-exit-risks-and-navigating-regulatory-scrutiny-in-the-sdlc-with-matt-van-itallie-founder-ceo-of-sema

Executive Visibility for Code: The idea for Sema came from a 2013 C-suite meeting where sales and marketing had executive dashboards, while the CTO relied on spreadsheets and qualitative assessment to explain engineering.

Fewer Features, Built Fully: Sema's first product went too broad with partial versions of many things. When it wasn't growing enough, the team lopped off a big chunk and rebuilt on a smaller, firmer core.

Faster Second MVP: After about two years of research and roughly eight months to the first MVP, Sema built its GenAI code detection MVP in three months with a hyper-focused team and pared-down requirements.
Hand-Build Before Scaling: New code scan modules are built by hand from a CSV, usually for a month or two. This saves engineering time and tests whether it's the right thing before solving for scale.
Only Payment Means Yes: Matt warns that praise like "I'd love it" is still a no until someone pays. Sema shows wireframes and proofs of concept early and presses customers on why a problem matters.

q: What inspired the creation of Sema?
a: Matt Van Itallie was in a C-suite meeting in 2013 where sales and marketing had tools giving executives insight, but code had nothing comparable. As Matt put it, "everybody had an executive dashboard, thanks to code, except" [03:27]. That led him to ask whether code could be built to help understand code and coders.

q: What is Sema's codebase health score?
a: It is a 1 to 100 score of non-functional requirements, built after many years of collecting data, that gives boards, CTOs and the C-suite a common language for investing in code. Matt explains, "If you're a 30, your codebase is a lot riskier" [19:28] than a codebase scoring 70.

q: How does Sema approach GenAI-generated code?
a: Sema built a product that helps engineering teams manage how much of their code base is GenAI, human, or a mix. Matt says keeping a human in the loop is one way to make GenAI code safe, and stresses, "This isn't about automating away engineering jobs." [20:19]

q: How does Sema test new features before engineering them to scale?
a: When building a new code scan module, the team first creates it manually, which saves engineering time and checks that they are building the right thing. Matt described the process: "We run the analytics, produce a CSV, and build it by hand" [15:17].

q: What mistake did Sema make with its first product?
a: Matt Van Itallie says the first iteration went too broad, with partial versions of many things. His lesson was that "what we should have done is build full versions of fewer things." [08:21]

s10-bonus-from-employee-8-at-stripe-to-challenging-the-triopoly-of-aws-azure-and-gcp-fixing-the-broken-cloud-native-developer-experience-with-anurag-goel-founder-ceo-of-render

Abstracting Repeated Infrastructure Work: Anurag saw that his Kubernetes setups looked much the same, as did most companies' work on AWS. Render offers autoscaling, private networking and persistent storage without customers writing YAML or opening an AWS account.

Rewriting Python in Go: Anurag built the first version in Python in about a couple of weeks. After benchmarking it against a Go implementation on resource use and latency, he rewrote everything in Go over January.

Pull Out the Real Problem: Daily customer feedback has been the biggest influence on Render's roadmap. When users propose solutions, the team's job is to uncover the underlying problem and solve it in the way that makes the most sense.

Scale So Users Never Leave: Render hit bottlenecks whenever Pete Buttigieg, whose campaign it hosted, gave a debate-stage closing statement. It now serves over 50 billion requests a month and aims to keep customers from outgrowing it and rebuilding on AWS.

Marketing Should Have Come Sooner: Render more than doubled revenue in the past year on organic growth, with the free tier as its only marketing. Anurag wishes he had built a mature marketing team earlier, saying the company is leaving money on the table.

q: What is Render and how is it different from running Kubernetes on AWS?
a: Render is an all-in-one platform that Anurag Goel built to remove the undifferentiated complexity and cost of running your own Kubernetes infrastructure on a large public cloud. He says that as a customer, "you never have to think about writing a single line of YAML or even opening an AWS account" [05:02].

q: Why did Anurag Goel start Render after leaving Stripe?
a: Anurag set out to find an ambitious problem by building things in many different domains and putting them into production. In the process, he explained, "I realized that every Kubernetes setup I had looked pretty much the same" [03:19], and saw that this work was both undifferentiated and too complex for what it delivered.

q: What programming language is Render built with?
a: Anurag wrote the first version in Python, his preferred language, then rebuilt it in Go after benchmarking showed better resource utilization, speed and latency. As he put it, "And Render has been a Go shop ever since" [07:55].

q: Can Render scale as an application grows?
a: Anurag says Render serves over 50 billion requests a month, and many applications on it have grown to hundreds of thousands or millions of users. He noted that "it's much, much harder to build something that scales with you over the very long term" [13:25] than something that just helps you get started.

q: What advice does Anurag Goel give to startup founders?
a: Anurag advises founders to be incredibly excited about their product and domain, drawing on expertise, personal experience or learning about customers. He warns that "if there isn't enough of a founder market fit, then you're not going to succeed" [20:46], or at least not to the level you would want.

s10-e1-the-api-to-agent-translation-layer-building-governing-and-securing-mcp-servers-for-the-ai-ecosystem-with-sagar-batchu-co-founder-ceo-of-speakeasy

Right Product, Wrong Phasing: Speakeasy first built developer portal components for API onboarding, but selling them meant catching companies the week they launched an API. The team pivoted to SDKs, which every API could benefit from right away.

Self-Hosting Slowed Early Reach: Making the first product self-hostable from day one added technical debt and extra work. Sagar calls it a mistake, since the priority should have been getting it to as many customers as quickly as possible.

Great Defaults, Then Control: Deterministic config plus some LLM help on the OpenAPI spec gets customers to a 90 to 95% great SDK out of the box. Knobs and configs then let them make the last-mile decisions.

Contract-to-Hire Early Engineers: Facing a tough 2022 hiring market, Speakeasy had contractors work for four to six weeks as an interview. The first five or six engineers joined this way, and all proved a great fit.

Recovering From a Docs Detour: After committing customers to a docs product it couldn't deliver, Speakeasy partnered with other companies, took on support work and committed to an integration so those customers weren't left hanging.

q: What is Speakeasy and what does it do?
a: Speakeasy is a platform for distributing APIs to customers and supporting both onboarding and long-term usage. Co-founder and CEO Sagar Batchu describes it this way: "Speakeasy is a platform that really helps you take your API to market." [02:48]

q: Why did Speakeasy pivot from developer portals to SDKs?
a: Sagar Batchu explains that scaling the portal product required catching companies right as they were about to launch an API, a tough go-to-market problem. Of the original product, he said "I don't think it was the wrong product," [07:03] but he believes the phasing was wrong, so the team turned to SDKs.

q: How does Speakeasy balance SDK defaults with customization?
a: Speakeasy combines deterministic config with LLM assistance on the OpenAPI spec to produce strong out-of-the-box SDKs. Sagar says that from there "it's really important to invert control at that point" [16:15] so customers can tune the SDK for their end users.

q: How did Speakeasy hire its first engineers?
a: Sagar Batchu's team worked with contractors for four to six weeks under a contract-to-hire policy. In his words, "we use that contract work as an interview to come on full time." [13:29]

q: What is next for Speakeasy's API platform?
a: Sagar sees the API lifecycle as three phases: "It's build, it's test, and it's run." [20:53] Having made inroads on building and distribution, Speakeasy plans to address testing next and is exploring with customers what running APIs on the edge could look like.

s9-e35-eliminating-blind-spots-in-overseas-manufacturing-and-scaling-digital-quality-control-with-prince-ghosh-co-founder-ceo-of-factored-quality

Spreadsheet-First MVP: Factored Quality began with Doris Dev's services team running QC from a spreadsheet. The first benchmark was swapping in its own software with no drop in service quality, then optimizing efficiency underneath.

Software Plus Inspector Network: The product pairs a quality management system with QC services delivered through thousands of third-party inspectors who audit factories, inspect goods in production and test products in development.

Quality Is Not the Variable: Prince frames product decisions as a triangle of quality, scope and timeline. A customer commitment may fix scope or timeline, but he doesn't like quality to ever be what gives, because craft becomes part of company identity.

Two-Way Roadmapping: The roadmap blends the founders' top-down vision with bottom-up customer requests. Vision alone can ignore buying budgets, while requests alone can leave a startup beholden to its largest customers instead of building for future ones.

White Glove as an Edge: While big companies face pressure to automate customer success with AI and agents, Factored Quality offers boutique, human support. Prince says it is a major reason brands sign on and stay.

q: What is Factored Quality?
a: Co-founder and CEO Prince Ghosh describes it this way: "Factored Quality is a digital platform for consumer goods brands to run quality control" [02:47]. It combines quality management software with QC services performed by a network of third-party inspectors at factories around the world.

q: Why do consumer brands struggle with quality control in overseas manufacturing?
a: Prince Ghosh explains that brands often start with one factory and add many more across multiple countries as they grow. As supply chains get more complex, "it became harder and harder for the people on the brand side to actually know what was happening" [05:22] on their factory floors.

q: How was the Factored Quality MVP built?
a: Prince Ghosh says the first version used Doris Dev's services team, "running quality as a service, and using a spreadsheet and kind of building an internal" [07:11] operating system driven purely by that spreadsheet. The team then built software around each part of it.

q: Should an early-stage startup optimize for scale?
a: Prince Ghosh warns against it: "optimizing for scale early on is one of the most surefire ways to kill a company" [15:41]. He sees doing things that don't scale as a startup's advantage over incumbents, though eventually you have to find ways to "pseudo scale" them.

q: How does Factored Quality respond when it makes a mistake with a customer?
a: Prince Ghosh says the team has had inspections fall short of its standards during rapid growth, and that the response starts by "first just being truly honest and transparent" [21:03]. The team then helps the customer rectify the impact and puts a process or automation in place to avoid a repeat.

Instant Calls Over Scheduling: Owwll connects people through private, paid one-on-one audio calls without sharing phone numbers. Hill is betting on instant availability to cut out DMs, scheduling, cancellations and no-shows, though it means changing user habits.

Supply Was the Easy Part: With real money live, many wanted to be paid experts but few wanted to pay to call them. Owwll added a 10-call minimum before experts could change their price, and later began charging for expert accounts, which helped retention.

Fixing the Missed Call Problem: A notification-based call system left about 40-50% of calls missed. Overhauling it so phones ring like a regular call, even in sleep mode, brought missed calls down to the low teens.

Control Through the Back Office: With developers overseas, Hill wanted a custom back office to track calls, revenue and refunds in real time, approve experts, and deactivate accounts quickly when scams or reports come in.

Growth Through Established Communities: Rather than winning one referral at a time, Owwll features partner groups on its home screen. With South Florida Tech Hub, that means Tech Tuesdays, when members are listed at the top and encouraged to call each other.

q: What is the Owwll app?
a: Founder Jason R. Hill describes it this way: "Owwll is a platform that allows professionals to instantly connect through one-on-one audio calls" [02:38]. Users browse categories and call available experts at a set price through a secure in-app call, without exchanging phone numbers.

q: What technology was used to build Owwll?
a: Hill says the app was built on React Native, explaining, "So that way you could go on Android and Apple simultaneously." [07:30]. It also uses Agora for the one-on-one audio calls, Stripe for payments and a custom-designed back office.

q: What is the hardest part of building a two-sided marketplace app?
a: For Hill, attracting experts was easy, but demand was not once real money was involved. As he put it, "nobody actually wanted to pay to talk to the experts." [13:05] He also found that experts relied on Owwll itself to drive callers to them.

q: How did Owwll reduce its missed call rate?
a: Hill's team overhauled the calling mechanism so a phone rings like a regular call, even in sleep mode, after user education failed to solve the problem. He said "that was the best thing that we updated" [23:20], with missed calls now in the low teens.

q: What advice does Jason R. Hill give founders about raising money?

s9-e30-the-infrastructure-as-code-rebellion-overthrowing-terraform-blockades-and-launching-figma-style-devops-models-with-adam-jacob-creator-of-chef-and-founder-ceo-of-system-initiative

Infrastructure as Data: System Initiative models infrastructure as digital twins on a hypergraph of reactive functions. Change an application's port and the load balancer pool that depends on it reconfigures automatically.

Inference Hit Its Limits: An early MVP inferred infrastructure from a few constraints, such as needing a server to run Postgres. Because infrastructure choices are so specific, users ended up playing whack-a-mole to get what they already wanted.

Ambition Over Early Off-Ramps: The team had working, delightful Kubernetes configuration generation that wasn't very programmable. They kept building the more powerful platform instead, part of a five-year effort.

Stop Optimizing the Old Engine: Jacob split the team between a Postgres-based engine and its successor. When an onboarded customer quickly found the old one too slow, everyone moved to the new engine.

Teams Like Pro Sports: Jacob rejects factory metaphors for software. He treats engineers as expert athletes to train, drill and coach, then places them on teams based on their strengths and weaknesses.

q: What is System Initiative and how is it different from Terraform-style tooling?
a: System Initiative is Adam Jacob's attempt to rebuild how DevOps work gets done, replacing a stack of glued-together tools with a more multiplayer, real-time experience. Jacob says it "transforms all that stuff up into data" [04:06] rather than code, then models it on a hypergraph of functions.

q: Why didn't System Initiative's first MVP, which inferred infrastructure, work out?
a: The early version let users specify a few constraints and inferred the rest, but infrastructure usually depends on very specific choices and configuration. Jacob explained that "you wind up kind of playing whack-a-mole with the constraints" [07:15] to get the result you already know you want.

q: Why did System Initiative shift its focus from Kubernetes to AWS?
a: Jacob's team started by modeling Kubernetes, but found that despite complaints, people were largely fine with it, saying "the market kind of still was a little in love with it" [09:55]. AWS tooling was easier to focus on and drew more discontent from users.

q: What was the hardest scaling challenge in building System Initiative?
a: Jacob points to recalculating a large in-memory graph, where one property change can affect hundreds or thousands of others and still needs to feel close to real time. Traditional databases weren't quite the right fit, so the team did a lot of work "basically designing our own in memory database" [17:58].

q: What mistake did Adam Jacob make while building System Initiative's reactive engine?
a: Jacob had one group optimize the old Postgres-based engine for early customers while another built its replacement. He said "the customer feedback we learned was that it was too slow" [22:40], so he moved everyone to the new engine.

Just-in-Time Access as MVP: Rather than first gathering all the context needed for scalable access, Opal started with time-based, role-specific access synced to on-call schedules, a major pain point for engineers who need into a failing production system.

Saying No Early: Opal turned down certain integrations and very complicated workflows, focusing on just-in-time access, actionable least privilege and reporting on mission-critical systems, even when customers had thousands of applications to cover.

Trust Shapes the Roadmap: As a security company first, Opal prioritized hybrid environment support, role-based access control within its own product and native hyperscaler integrations for mission-critical production systems.

Know Your One-Way Doors: Opal accepted some early tech debt to reach milestones, but would not compromise on a flexible data model or on architecture behind its core strengths: reliability, accuracy, speed and data.

q: What is Opal Security?

q: Why did Umaimah Khan start Opal Security?
a: Khan kept seeing access management go wrong everywhere and got frustrated with legacy tools she felt were built to check compliance boxes, so she took a sabbatical to work on the problem full time. She described access management as "this incredibly messy, fragmented like issue, like at every scale" [03:30].

q: What was Opal Security's MVP?
a: Khan said the MVP centered on just-in-time access, starting with syncing access to on-call schedules. She framed the question as "how do you just patch through access that's very time-based, that's very role-specific for a period of time" [06:30].

q: How did Opal Security approach scalability and technical debt?
a: Khan said scale was in mind from day one, with a flexible data model worth the investment, while other choices were made case by case. The areas where the team would not compromise architecturally follow from the product itself: "Our core strengths are reliability, accuracy, speed and data." [15:32]

q: What is the future of access management according to Umaimah Khan?

s9-bonus-riding-the-36k-star-black-swan-how-an-impromptu-open-source-fork-saved-the-devops-ecosystem-from-proprietary-lock-in-with-omry-hay-co-founder-cto-of-env0

The Pivot to the Data Store: Axiom began by building event tooling, then saw that users couldn't get its value without storing all their events. The throwaway demo store, EventDB, built to ease onboarding, pointed to the real product.

A Novel Architecture, Underestimated: The new data store relied on object storage and serverless queries. The team repurposed the old API and front end, taking on tech debt, though the store took long enough that they could have rebuilt both.

Finding the Edges of AWS: Data reached S3, but bandwidth between S3 and Lambda kept limiting query speed, and adding Lambdas raised cost concerns. Talking with the S3 and Lambda teams helped Axiom work around the limits.

Feedback Before Long-Term Roadmaps: After the beta cloud launch, the team spent about a couple of quarters working through user feedback. It still avoids overdefining roadmaps, planning by quarter and blending its vision with near-term customer needs.

Hiring From Long-Built Trust: Axiom's core team met on IRC and has known each other for over 15 years, working together at Canonical and Xamarin. New hires are judged on self-motivation and their ability to fill the team's gaps.

q: What is Axiom and what is it used for?
a: Axiom is an event store that takes in events such as logs and traces, stores them and makes them immediately queryable for log analysis, tracing, product analytics and more. Co-founder and CEO Neil Jagdish Patel said, "Axiom is a event store essentially and when you have logs or trace events" [02:50].

q: Why did Axiom pivot to building its own data store?
a: Early users liked the event tooling but said they couldn't afford to keep enough data to make it viable, while also asking about the demo store inside the product. Neil Jagdish Patel recalled that "the penny dropped and we quickly realized that's the thing we should be" [06:56] working on first.

q: What technical challenges did Axiom face with S3 and AWS Lambda?
a: The team could get data into S3 but couldn't query it fast enough, and adding more Lambdas raised cost concerns. Neil Jagdish Patel said "there were problems like the bandwidth between S3 and Lambda. We were getting caught" [09:03] on that constantly.

q: Do you need to define a schema before sending data to Axiom?
a: No, Neil Jagdish Patel said users can send webhooks, trace data or other events without describing them first. In his words, "you can just send it over to Axiom. We don't force you to tell us" [21:17] what you're sending.

q: What mistake did Axiom's founders make early on?
a: Neil Jagdish Patel said they didn't get the initial product to people who could give feedback or advice quickly enough, and the team now shares features as early as possible. He believes "we could have reduced the time to this version of Axiom" [19:55] by maybe even a few years.

s9-bonus-from-13-years-of-bootstrapping-to-defying-the-tech-winter-stripping-away-the-flat-29-fee-monopoly-by-owning-the-full-payment-stack-with-nic-beique-of-helcim

Own the Stack for Pricing: To undercut the typical 2.9% rate, Helcim built many systems in-house, including fraud management and settlements. Third-party tools were faster to ship but gave away too much of the economics.
A Three-Year Waterfall MVP: A processor can't launch without fraud, settlement, encryption and other core systems, so agile was hard. A build first estimated at 18 months took three years.
Paying Down Launch Debt: After the 2020 launch, Helcim moved from on-prem servers to GCP and Kubernetes, refactored to about 30% Golang and 70% PHP, and adopted a Vue front end.

Hiring Juniors in Calgary: With little experienced talent locally, Helcim hired graduates who were builders and grinders. Engineering grew to about 50 people in their first or second job, bringing fearlessness but also avoidable landmines.

Too Much Built In-House: Wary of security vulnerabilities, the team resisted frameworks and libraries too long. It learned that open source can catch problems faster, and a bug bounty program started early helped it improve.

q: What is Helcim and who is it for?
a: Helcim is a payments company that lets businesses accept primarily credit cards, as well as ACH, with a focus on affordable pricing and customer service. Nic Beique says that "we like to call ourselves a grown-up square" [02:48], serving traditional businesses such as dentists, accountants, wholesalers and automotive.

q: Why is it so hard to build a payment processor from scratch?
a: Nic Beique compares it to an iceberg: payment tools sit above the water, while fraud, KYC/AML, settlement and other systems sit underneath. As he explained, "the problem with it is that you can't launch without one of these systems" [04:55].

q: Why did Helcim build its own fraud and settlement systems?
a: Nic Beique says pricing was central, and paying many third-party providers per call would have made it hard to compete. The team decided early that "we're going to have to go build a lot of these things ourselves" [07:31], including Helcim Defender for risk and EQ, a double-entry accounting, settlement and reconciliation system.

q: What scaling problems did Helcim run into after launch?
a: Helcim had to leave its on-prem setup for the cloud and rework parts of its architecture as it grew. Nic Beique admitted, "I think we made probably the biggest pitfall was around microservices" [14:13], noting that the original architecture had no event streams.

q: What advice does Nic Beique have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Nic Beique advises founders to embrace and double down on their drive rather than get distracted by naysayers. They should still listen to feedback, but in his words, "nobody's going to know your business and your vision as much as you do" [23:44].

s9-e25-the-incident-response-revolution-overthrowing-war-room-chaos-and-automating-slack-native-sre-workflows-with-jj-tang-co-founder-ceo-of-rootly

Too Specific for Other Companies: The tool JJ Tang's team built at Instacart didn't work elsewhere because every company runs its own incident process. A more generic product that fit more use cases solved it.
Slack Bot as the Wedge: Rootly skipped replacing PagerDuty at first and shipped a simple Slack bot for collaboration. Pitching an all-in-one platform had intimidated enterprise buyers.

Shared Slack Channels Offset Bugs: The early platform was quite buggy, so Rootly opened a shared Slack channel with every customer and often fixed issues within the hour, deepening those partnerships.

Managers Must Be Operators: Engineering leaders take a coding exercise and the business development lead must be confident cold calling. Rootly learned that great resumes could mean copy-pasted playbooks.
Multi-Cloud for On-Call Reliability: Tang's team once saw multi-cloud as overkill, but building on-call paging changed that. Rootly now runs on GCP as well as AWS for redundancy.

q: What is Rootly and what problem does it solve?
a: Rootly is an incident management and on-call platform, mostly for engineers, that covers paging, collaboration, postmortems, timelines and metrics. JJ Tang saw the problem at Instacart, where, in his words, "we were mostly just pinging each other on Slack and pinging the most senior engineer" [03:58].

q: What did Rootly's first MVP look like?
a: JJ Tang explained that rather than trying to replace PagerDuty from the start, Rootly targeted its collaboration gaps. As he put it, "our MVP is strictly just going to be this very simple bot that we built on Slack" [06:36].

q: How did Rootly handle bugs while shipping quickly in the early days?
a: JJ Tang said speed was the most important thing, even though the early platform was quite buggy. To tighten the feedback loop, the team decided for every customer, "We have to have a shared Slack channel with them." [09:56]

q: Why did Rootly move to a multi-cloud infrastructure?
a: Customers wanted Rootly to build an alternative to legacy paging tools, and Tang's team realized reliability would be critical to that product. "We had to make sure reliability scaled better than anything else on the market." [20:16] Rootly went from running only on AWS to also running on GCP.

q: How does Rootly use generative AI in incident management?
a: JJ Tang described AI features that surface related past incidents with step-by-step guidance, build charts from natural language requests and show common questions asked during an incident. The aim is a faster reliability loop, because "shortening the loop is your defensible advantage as a product" [13:43].

s9-e24-the-data-streaming-renaissance-bypassing-jvm-bloat-and-squeezing-10x-performance-from-modern-hardware-engines-with-alex-gallego-founder-ceo-of-redpanda-data

Design for the Real Hardware: Gallego asked what he would do differently if software were built for multi-core CPUs, high-bandwidth memory and fast NVMe devices. He saw a large gap between that hardware's potential and Apache Kafka, then the state of the art.

Controversial Early Technical Bets: Redpanda chose C++ when startups weren't using it, adopted a thread-per-core architecture and wrote its own drivers. Gallego tested on two data center machines bought off Craigslist to get close to the metal.

Customers Pulled the Roadmap: Early users ran the free software in production, then asked for transactions, a UI, connectors, tiered storage and audit logging. With one or two exceptions, development has been driven by customer demand.
Hire for Intensity: Gallego values people who latch on to a problem and take it to the finish line. The first 100 employees of the roughly 200-person company came strictly through friends of friends.

Make Core Values Explicit Early: After an early, well-known hire turned out to be racist and was quickly fired, Gallego saw the culture had to be defined and filtered for. The values: being a good human, customer obsession and winning as a team.

q: What is Redpanda?
a: Redpanda is a data streaming platform that is fully compatible with the Kafka API protocol, built to be mission-critical software. As founder and CEO Alex Gallego put it, "Redpanda is this native C++ single binary." [05:02]

q: How was the first version of Redpanda built?
a: Alex Gallego started writing the code after leaving Akamai in 2019, and bought two data center machines with enterprise NVMe devices and 25 gigabit networking cards. He chose physical hardware over renting in the cloud because "I wanted to see how far I can push down, how close to the metal I could push down." [06:02]

q: How does Redpanda decide what to build next?
a: Early adopters told the team which capabilities they needed in order to add more use cases, such as transactions, connectors and multi-AZ support. Gallego said that apart from one or two features where Redpanda pushed the market forward, "it has been all customer demand" [10:38].

q: What mistake did Alex Gallego learn from while building Redpanda's culture?
a: Gallego said the top mistake, corrected early on, was not having clarity on the company's core values, which surfaced after hiring a famous computer scientist who was racist. The person was fired, and Gallego concluded, "we have to define what the culture is explicitly." [16:53]

q: What is the future vision for Redpanda?
a: Gallego wants to change how data-intensive applications are built with a tool that covers both bounded and unbounded data while staying cost-effective and easy to use. He said "the future is about continuing to lower the bar for" [19:59] people to adopt streaming technologies, in both cost and complexity.

s9-bonus-the-bootstrapped-alm-blueprint-reaching-20m-arr-with-zero-venture-capital-and-automating-risk-aware-quality-assurance-with-adam-sandman-founder-ceo-of-inflectra

MVP Versus Sellable Product: Adam Sandman built the first version in about seven months of evenings and nights. It went live in February, but the first sale waited until September, after self-service reporting and customization were added.

Replace the Heavy Incumbent: The MVP reimagined market leader Test Director as a lighter web app with requirements, test and bug tracking. Customers could install it on a server without being experienced IT admins.

Roadmap From Three Signals: Inflectra weighed needs shared by several paying customers, competitor research and loss analysis on prospects who didn't buy. A UX redesign also helped after people liked the functionality but not the UI.

Protect White-Label Deals: Inflectra white-labeled an automation tool after losing deals to bundled rivals. When the maker went out of business, a contract clause gave Inflectra the IP, and it hired the development team.
Values Shape the Team: Inflectra hires for cultural fit first, then finds a role. Salespeople are salaried rather than on commission, so the team works together to close deals.

q: What does Inflectra do?
a: Inflectra offers a software platform to help teams plan, manage, build and test software, typically for medium to large companies in mission-critical industries. Adam Sandman rejects the idea that speed has to cost quality, saying "What we believe is that that's a false trade-off." [03:09]

q: How long did it take Inflectra to get its first sale?

q: How should founders handle feature requests from people who haven't bought yet?
a: Sandman found that many early requests came from people who still didn't buy, which made the feedback non-actionable. He advises separating what people will pay for from what merely sounds good, warning that "you're going to be sabotaged by good ideas that" [09:39] no one wants to pay for.

q: How did Inflectra add its Rapise test automation tool?
a: Inflectra first white-labeled another company's tool because it was losing deals to competitors that bundled test management with automation. When that company went out of business, Sandman said the IP "reverted to us. We had the rights to build and maintain it." [17:21]

q: How does Adam Sandman see generative AI changing software quality?
a: Sandman believes AI can speed up every part of the software development life cycle, but used poorly it could produce buggier, less reliable software. Of generative AI, he said "It is the next major evolution and maybe revolution in technology." [30:16]

s9-e23-the-120m-war-chest-shift-overthrowing-legacy-payment-bottlenecks-and-accelerating-the-path-to-fintech-unicorn-status-with-vlad-sadovskiy-founder-ceo-of-netevia

Banking Through Gig Workers: Netevia was built on channel sales, with a reseller community selling payments and digital banking on their own schedules. Vlad says the company is on the cusp of creating 1,000 salespeople who are bankers from home.

Customers Wanted a Primary Bank: The team expected small businesses to keep their big-bank accounts and add Netevia for virtual cards and debit cash back. Instead, users wanted it as their main account, forcing rapid feature builds driven by customer feedback.

Compliance Is the Scaling Challenge: Vlad says banking as a service is hard less because of technology than regulatory oversight, KYC and KYB requirements, and the work of presenting use cases to the partner bank.

Plaid Needed Extra Safeguards: In the first week, a user connected 24 bank accounts that weren't really his and tried to move money. Netevia added identity verification for account connections to stop people from using stolen usernames and passwords.

Rewards Help Keep Money Inside: Users moved funds out to Cash App and Zelle, while Netevia's income depends largely on in-app spending. Limited-time rewards encouraged people to keep money on the platform, though Vlad says the challenge isn't fully solved.

q: What is Netevia and how is it different from other fintech companies?
a: Netevia, founded by Vlad Sadovskiy, combines payments and digital banking, focuses on small businesses, and sells through a reseller community of gig workers. Vlad describes the goal as "being able to create a community of digital bankers that work around the country" [03:51].

q: What did Netevia learn from launching its first banking product?
a: Vlad Sadovskiy's team started with a simple set of features, including a card, an account, bill pay and cash back, expecting businesses to keep their existing banks too. He found that "the first thing that happened is people wanted to use this as a main bank account" [06:58], so the team had to add features quickly.

q: What fraud problem did Netevia run into with its Plaid integration?
a: Vlad Sadovskiy says that in the product's first week, a user began trying to transfer money from accounts that didn't belong to him. "Before we knew it, he had 24 different bank accounts connected to our bank account" [11:48], which led Netevia to build additional identity verification.

q: How does Netevia encourage customers to keep money on its platform?
a: Vlad Sadovskiy explains that users often tried to move money straight out to Cash App and Zelle accounts. In response, "we've introduced limited rewards to solve the problem" [13:49], and people would rather keep their money in place while waiting for a reward.

q: What advice does Vlad Sadovskiy give young entrepreneurs?
a: Vlad's first piece of advice is to be passionate, and he looks at whether an idea provides a niche solution to a specific problem. Even for ideas he considers too early or ambitious, he says, "I would definitely tell them to pitch the idea as many times as they can" [18:13].

s9-bonus-from-film-tech-to-architecting-a-bitcoin-backed-bretton-woods-system-overthrowing-custodial-bridging-risks-with-sasha-mitchell-head-of-bel2-founder-of-elacity

Swaps Without Bridging: BeL2's MVP lets Bitcoin holders swap BTC for USDT offered on an EVM layer 2. A zero-knowledge proof of the Bitcoin transfer tells the smart contract to release the USDT, with no bridging or locking up of Bitcoin.

Bitcoin as Backing Gold: Mitchell envisions decentralized loans against Bitcoin and even self-issued stablecoins backed by it, with Bitcoin acting like gold behind a stable currency people can actually use.

Oracle First, Relayers Next: BeL2's first service, the Bitcoin Oracle, feeds Bitcoin data into smart contracts. Relayers are meant to add smarter, time-based functions, such as making sure a loan is repaid so the Bitcoin can be returned.

Hiring for Bespoke Skills: Cairo, used for BeL2's zero-knowledge work, is still a niche language. Mitchell says forming the engineering team was manageable largely thanks to experience, connections and at least five years of trust-building.

Communicate the Pivot: Moving into BeL2 meant budget cuts, and a defunded team took the news to the community, causing upset. Mitchell says the pivot wasn't the mistake; the way it was communicated was.

q: What is BeL2 (Bitcoin Elastos Layer 2)?
a: BeL2 is a protocol that lets Bitcoin communicate with other blockchains and trigger smart contracts without changing Bitcoin itself. Sasha Mitchell explains that "what BeL2 does is it makes Bitcoin a financial hub" [05:44].

q: How does BeL2 swap Bitcoin for USDT without a bridge?
a: A Bitcoin holder sends BTC to the seller's Bitcoin wallet, and a zero-knowledge proof of that payment is passed to the smart contract holding the USDT, which then releases it. Mitchell sums it up: "So what's happened here is there's been no bridging." [08:38]

q: Why are blockchain bridges considered a security risk?
a: Mitchell explains that bridging typically locks an asset on one side and mints or releases something on the other, which creates an attack vector. In his words, "when we see these big blow ups that happen in blockchain, where these big hacks happen, in most cases, they were these bridges." [09:03]

q: What mistake did Sasha Mitchell's team make when pivoting to BeL2?
a: Budgets for other Elastos technologies were cut to make BeL2 happen, and one defunded team told the community, which created hysteria and upset. Mitchell says the pivot itself was successful, but "it certainly was a mistake in the way in which we communicated" [24:36].

q: How does Elacity change digital rights management for creators?
a: Elacity, which Mitchell founded, has smart contracts check a user's decentralized identity for a token with viewing rights and issue the decryption key, replacing a centralized license server. Mitchell says this means "a creator can now get 95, if not 100% of their income" [33:10], compared with roughly 50 to 60% today.

s9-e22-from-meeting-his-co-founder-on-tinder-to-leading-a-yc-startup-in-a-war-zone-scaling-an-on-demand-creative-marketplace-under-fire-with-roman-sevast-co-founder-president-of-awesomic
Validate Before You Code: Awesomic launched with only a landing page describing the idea and got three customers within two weeks. Only then did the team start building the product.

A Three-Day MVP: Roman built the first version in about three days, using bought modules and open source packages where possible and refusing to over-engineer, even if the code wasn't up to corporate standards.
Balancing Both Marketplace Sides: Scaling means balancing talent and customers. Awesomic once lacked designers; now thousands apply every month and the focus is mostly on acquiring customers.
Stay Default Alive: After an early high-interest loan, Roman wanted no more cash gaps. Drawing on Paul Graham and Y Combinator, Awesomic kept a bootstrap approach even after raising millions.
Conferences Didn't Pay Off: An early trip to a tech conference used up all their money and produced zero sales. Later visits to major events in Europe and the US didn't work for them either.

q: What is Awesomic and how does it work?
a: Awesomic matches companies with design and software engineering talent through a tool that works much like a project management app, where customers simply create tasks. Roman Sevast explained, "It's basically AI project manager which, inside our tool, decides who works on which task" [03:46].

q: How did Awesomic validate its idea and build its MVP?
a: The founders first put up a landing page and got three customers within two weeks, then built the product. Roman said, "To develop the first version of Awesomic, it took around three days." [07:35]

q: How did Awesomic decide what to build without a roadmap?
a: Roman said the team freestyled for four years and is only now developing a multi-quarter roadmap. Their approach was to "just listen to our users, talking with them like every week." [08:56] They implemented requests when those matched other customers' pains.

q: How did Awesomic respond when the war started in Ukraine?
a: Roman said the company moved to help relocate its Ukrainian talents and their families and pets, then set up new offices in safer cities. As he described it, "within three days, we relocated from dangerous city to safest area, around 300 people." [15:23]

q: What advice does Roman Sevast give young entrepreneurs?
a: Roman advises doing everything much faster, because years pass quickly, and never giving up. On testing ideas, he said to "spend one month, figure out this idea is not working," [23:05] and then move to the next one rather than spending three years to reach the same result.

s9-bonus-the-metadata-breakthrough-bypassing-legacy-tree-walks-and-scaling-real-time-ai-dataset-ingestion-with-bjorn-kolbeck-co-founder-ceo-of-quobyte

Storage MVPs Are Full Products: Björn says storage leaves no corners to cut. Building on lessons from the XtreemFS research project, Quobyte still took about two and a half years from its late 2013 start to reach a launch customer's production environment.

Test Like Production From Day One: Soon after the internal prototype, an engineer built a distributed platform that rolls the master branch onto a cluster and hammers it with homegrown and industry tools like FIO. Björn calls early testing probably the key decision.

Design Out Central Bottlenecks: Quobyte uses quorum replication, with leader election handled peer-to-peer by the nodes sharing the data. The algorithm, part of Björn's PhD work, let the system scale to thousands of data nodes.

Use Cases Shaped The Roadmap: Quobyte started with OpenStack and virtual machines, then added applications one by one. Each exposed undocumented file system behavior, while larger clusters, such as 250 nodes, brought different problems.

Paying Down Technical Debt: Quobyte spent two years cleaning up debt, even pushing back features customers were waiting for. Björn says the painful stretch paid off in greater agility for building new features.

q: What is Quobyte?
a: Quobyte is both the company and its product, a software-based parallel file system for large-scale storage of tens to hundreds of petabytes. Björn Kolbeck, its co-founder and CEO, said of it, "We like to call it the world's easiest parallel file system" [02:54].

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Quobyte?
a: It took about two and a half years, starting in late 2013, to deliver a version a launch customer could use in production. Björn Kolbeck explained that in storage, "your minimum viable product is actually a full product" [05:29].

q: How do you test a distributed file system for reliability?
a: Björn Kolbeck said unit testing is a must but not enough on its own. Quobyte built automated testing on a production-like cluster to catch regressions, and he advised that "you have to use standard file system benchmark tools to regularly test the system" [07:04].

q: Can scalability be added to a storage system later?
a: Björn Kolbeck argues that scale and resiliency have to be designed into the architecture and algorithms from the ground up. If you don't develop your "concepts with scale and resiliency in mind, you can't add it later on" [12:07].

q: What advice does Björn Kolbeck have for technical founders?
a: Björn Kolbeck urges founders to learn and value marketing and to understand their customers by talking with them directly. Reflecting on his own mistake, he said, "If they're like me and our technical founder, don't underestimate marketing and sales." [18:54]
