s9-e21-the-synthetic-audio-frontier-overthrowing-the-uncanny-valley-and-engineering-ethical-human-parity-ai-voices-with-matt-hocking-co-founder-executive-chairman-of-wellsaid-labs

Voices Trained From Real People: WellSaid Labs trains lifelike AI voices from real voice talent using its own proprietary models, so users can type a script, audition a virtual voice actor and render a recording.

Design Around Model Imperfections: The early MVP was slow and had anomalies, so the team let users render multiple clips at once and gave them basic tools to correct mispronunciations, which seeded later research on respellings.

Quality Over Voice Quantity: Customers weren't asking for 100,000 voices. They wanted quality, consistency and collaboration, especially content teams that constantly update and republish scripts, so those features led the roadmap.

Make It Work Before Scaling: The core model went through seven or eight versions, re-architected, rebuilt and retrained, before reaching customers. Enterprise needs like availability, reliability and trust became a bigger focus later.

Tell Your Story Louder: WellSaid avoided making claims ahead of reality, but Matt says that, as a mistake, they could have done more to capture people's imagination and draw interest by telling their story more loudly.

q: What does WellSaid Labs do?
a: WellSaid Labs creates AI voices that people can use to produce content and product experiences on demand and at scale. Matt Hocking explains that the company trains "lifelike synthetic voices or AI voices from the voices of real people" [02:50].

q: How did WellSaid Labs get started?
a: Matt Hocking met his co-founder Michael after joining AI2 as an entrepreneur in residence in 2018, while Matt was also working on a voice-centric healthcare experience that needed manual recordings. Seeing Michael's deep learning research, Matt said "it set off a lot of alarm bells for me" [03:42] about how much time it could save.

q: How did WellSaid Labs handle the limitations of its first AI voice model?
a: The team built the product to work around slow rendering and pronunciation problems, including multi-clip rendering and quick correction tools. According to Matt Hocking, they chose to "build a product experience that worked with those imperfections" [05:48].

q: How did WellSaid Labs decide what to build on its product roadmap?
a: The team first addressed the technical limitations that surfaced with early users, then listened as different customer profiles emerged, particularly teams of content creators with ongoing workflows. Matt Hocking recalls, "Our customer was asking for consistency and our customer was asking for collaboration." [08:57]

q: How does WellSaid Labs approach ethical AI voice technology?
a: Matt Hocking says the team considered early on how people should be allowed to use the technology and how to protect people from possible harm. He contrasts their partnerships with voice talent with "trying to just take any type of data" [17:51] off the internet to train models, and says he would make the same choice again.

s9-bonus-whats-new-with-alice-technologies-rene-morkos-founder-ceo
Optioneering for Construction Schedules: ALICE applies AI to scheduling, generating millions of ways to build a project so teams can test added cranes, crews or overtime, or resequence around delays.
Setup Time Was the Barrier: ALICE Pro's 3D, constraint-based approach took weeks to set up. Clients liked it but already had P6 schedules and didn't want to rebuild a model from scratch.
ALICE Core Works on Existing Schedules: It ingests Oracle Primavera P6 and most other scheduling formats, starts generating value within minutes, and cuts setup time by 100x.

3D Logic in a 2D World: The 18-month challenge was applying constraints like materials, equipment, crane radii and calendars to task-based schedules. René says part of that problem had never been solved.
Faster Setup Changes Rollouts: A data center company went from trying ALICE on one or two more projects to saying it could roll out on 10, with setup now taking 30 minutes to four hours per project.

q: What does ALICE Technologies do?
a: ALICE Technologies, founded by René Morkos, applies AI to construction scheduling through what he calls an optioneering platform. He describes it as "An ability to simulate or generate millions of different ways to build a project." [01:17]

q: What is ALICE Core and which schedule files does it work with?
a: ALICE Core applies ALICE's optimization algorithms directly to existing schedules, so users can reschedule, resequence, shuffle resources and add crews or cranes. René says it can ingest an "Oracle Primavera P6 file or almost any other scheduling format." [02:59]

q: How long does it take to set up ALICE Core compared with ALICE Pro?
a: René explains that setting up the 3D-based ALICE Pro took on the order of weeks, while the new approach is 100x faster. Speaking about a data center customer, he said, "Literally, setup time is 30 minutes to four hours for every project." [14:34]

q: Why was it so hard to apply AI optimization to existing construction schedules?
a: René compares ALICE Pro's constraint-based world to a 3D object and task-based tools like P6 or Microsoft Project to a 2D drawing. The 18 months of work, he says, went into "figuring out how to do these constraint-based, or to use my analogy, 3D transformations inside" [06:04] that task-based world.

q: What new features are coming to ALICE?
a: René highlights selective resequencing, selective objectives such as minimizing time or cost, and scheduling on top of 2D PDF drawings, all expected within a few months of the interview. On the first, he said, "The first is the ability to selectively reschedule." [15:28]

s9-e20-investor-attraction-blueprint-overthrowing-legacy-outreach-and-engineering-founder-first-public-relations-engine-with-michael-hummel-co-founder-ceo-of-establish

Three Pillars of Investability: Establish works on narrative (including media and influencer signals), traction, and access to its investor network. Hummel says its average client gets around 62 investor meetings.

Benchmark Traction Against Funded Peers: Study similar companies that closed a round, ideally in the last 12 months, and ask founders what got them funded. Those metrics can become the first milestone you pitch to investors.

Niching Down After an Audit: After working with nearly a thousand companies, the team asked which clients it enjoyed most and which were happiest. The answer was early-stage startups, so it went all in and stopped accepting its old kinds of clients.
Go Slow to Go Fast: Expanding beyond PR meant building untested systems and proving they worked before pushing growth. One of the company's core values is to be fast, but thoughtful.

Guard the Hiring Bar: Hummel says failed hires typically come down to culture fit, not competency, and that a director hire was given too long to adjust. Multiple leaders now interview each candidate before any offer.

q: What does Establish do for startups raising capital?
a: Establish, led by Michael Hummel, helps early-stage startups raise capital by working on their narrative, building traction and connecting them with investors. Hummel frames these as three pillars, saying "There's three things that any startup needs" [03:21] to become desirable to investors.

q: Why did Establish shift from a general PR firm to focusing on early-stage startups?
a: Michael Hummel's team audited which clients they liked working with most and which were happiest. He found that "it really just kept coming back to these early stage companies" [09:03], especially those that got media coverage, raised money and kept working with the firm.

q: How can a startup figure out what traction investors want to see?
a: Michael Hummel suggests looking at similar companies that recently closed a round and, if possible, talking with their founders. The goal is to learn what they "did they actually do in order to get funded?" [04:58] and aim for those metrics as a first milestone.

q: What does Michael Hummel look for when hiring?
a: Hummel looks for relevant background, but cares most about culture fit and genuine passion for the startup ecosystem. He explained that "every single person that has not worked out for us, it's typically due to the culture fit issue." [12:28]

q: What advice does Michael Hummel give first-time founders?
a: Michael Hummel tells founders, "This is going to be way harder and way longer than you think," [22:09] but says it is infinitely worth it. He also urges them not to let ego stop them from getting outside help and learning what has already worked.

s9-bonus-demystifying-unit-8200s-cyber-warfare-dominance-and-launching-a-new-cloud-efficiency-engine-with-alon-arvatz-author-of-the-battle-for-your-computer-ceo-of-pointfive

Integrate Before Building an MVP: PointFive spent two to three months on a "Minimum Integratable Product," connecting to customer environments and producing reports manually for feedback before developing its detection engine.
Let the ICP Filter Feedback: PointFive targeted enterprises with very big engineering teams from day one, so even consistent feedback from smaller organizations was taken with a grain of salt.

Aim at Engineers, Not Finance: In a crowded cloud cost market, PointFive focused on platform engineering teams, giving engineers deeper technical context and driving action on savings rather than mainly reporting spend.

Buy Before Build to Scale: After IntSights taught Alon the pain of ignoring scale, PointFive leaned further toward it, using an outside vendor for single sign-on and managed databases to avoid DevOps and maintenance work.

Skip Noncritical NDA Redlines: PointFive measured its pre-POC process and found that not redlining NDAs, unless something was critical, saved a month with enterprise customers and helped land first logos faster.

q: What does PointFive do for cloud cost optimization?
a: PointFive, where Alon Arvatz is co-founder and CEO, helps enterprises cut cloud costs by working mainly with platform engineering teams and the FinOps people within them. Alon described the focus as "more driving action across the engineer organization to become more cost efficient and optimize their infrastructure" [10:09].

q: What is a Minimum Integratable Product (MIP)?
a: It is the step PointFive took before its MVP: integrate with a customer's environment, work with the data manually and produce reports to get feedback. Alon Arvatz recalled the team asking, "Why don't we start with something that is even more basic" [06:19].

q: Why did Alon Arvatz move from cybersecurity to cloud cost management?
a: Alon Arvatz and his team saw the challenge of managing cloud costs at large scale, especially at Rapid7, and found other enterprises shared the problem. They saw a sizable market that matched their belief in frugality, and Alon said "we just decided to drop our cybersecurity experience" [05:19].

q: How can an early-stage startup speed up enterprise POCs?
a: Alon Arvatz said PointFive's process before a POC took too long, partly because the team sent NDA redlines back and forth. After measuring the difference, he reported, "we learned that just the fact that we didn't add red lines to an NDA saved us one month on the POC" [19:35].

q: What is Alon Arvatz's book The Battle for Your Computer about?
a: The book tells the story of the Israeli cybersecurity industry, and Alon Arvatz also sees it as an act of gratitude toward the ecosystem that supported him. A publishing contact first steered him toward his personal experience, but Alon said "I pulled it more towards talking and telling the story of the" [23:31] industry.

s9-e19-the-event-native-api-revolution-unifying-synchronous-rest-and-asynchronous-kafka-pipelines-with-linus-hakansson-chief-product-officer-at-gravitee

Event-Native API Management: Gravitee brings REST, SOAP and GraphQL APIs together with Kafka, MQTT, WebSockets and Webhooks, so teams can document, secure and govern synchronous and event-driven APIs with the same tools.

From Monthly Plans to Themes: Gravitee moved from month-to-month, customer-driven planning to a company mission and product themes, then tracked how much engineering time went to work outside that mission and tried to shrink it.

Trading Quick Wins for Differentiation: Gravitee limited some customer feature requests to invest in what would set it apart. It still made exceptions for strategic deals and had to explain internally why it was drifting from the plan.

Hunger Over Startup Pedigree: Gravitee hires for eagerness to learn and a drive to win more than prior startup experience. Those high standards slowed hiring and a planned 200-person headcount by the end of 2022 didn't happen, but it never had to lay people off.

Federation Across Vendors: Gravitee is working to be the central place for discovery and subscriptions for APIs running on third-party gateways like Amazon, Azure, Apigee and MuleSoft, and for events from brokers such as Confluent or Solace.

q: What does Gravitee do?
a: Gravitee provides an API platform covering needs such as security, documentation, rate limiting, discovery and monetization. As Linus Håkansson put it, "we basically help organizations to secure and manage and productize those APIs across the entire lifecycle" [03:13].

q: What is event-native API management?
a: It is Gravitee's term for managing event-driven APIs, such as Kafka and MQTT, alongside traditional REST and SOAP APIs. Linus Håkansson said the market had lacked "unified tooling to address all of those APIs in the same place" [21:03].

q: How does Gravitee build its product roadmap?
a: Gravitee starts with its company mission, derives high-level product strategy themes from it, and then works backwards with product managers and the CTO. Linus Håkansson explained that the team ensured it "delivered a roadmap that could be connected to one of those three themes effectively" [11:17].

q: What is API federation in Gravitee?
a: Federation is a concept Gravitee is working on for APIs that run on other vendors' systems rather than on the Gravitee gateway. Linus Håkansson said those systems can run the data portion while "Gravitee will be the central point for discovery, subscription management" [22:28], and maybe even analytics.

q: How is Gravitee using AI for API documentation?
a: Linus Håkansson said Gravitee is working on AI tooling for organizations that may not have readily available API documentation, using generative AI to add examples and context. He explained that "Gravitee can automatically generate documentation for your APIs based on the actual traffic that we are observing" [25:01].

s9-bonus-doing-the-work-of-a-whole-devops-team-with-just-two-people-erin-marie-jesus-maria-of-msquared

Paint-Dab Roadmapping: MSquared treats its roadmap as a canvas. It tries ideas, such as putting its lightweight digital asset manager in front of two clients, then builds toward whichever draws the most user interest.
A Band, Not a Headcount: Erin Marie and Jesus Maria are the core team, bringing in friends as "roadies" for milestones. Staying small and fully remote cuts overhead and avoids scaling into layoffs.

Hiring Creative Roadies: They favor creative people skilled in software but without computer science backgrounds, who know Golang and APIs, like moving between projects and can laugh. Liking the movie Airplane is a criterion.

Client Branches, Not SaaS: Client-specific features live in separate branches without disrupting the core code base. Customers can self-host or have MSquared host, and Erin prefers per-user licensing over a SaaS model.

The Business Learning Curve: As cloud engineers, they found payroll, insurance and taxes a three-year learning curve. They researched heavily and leaned on friends, including accountants and lawyers, in their collective.

q: What does MSquared do?
a: MSquared began during the pandemic as an idea to help small businesses build platforms, and a year in, Lionsgate called needing its services. Erin Marie described it this way: "M2 is a platform engineering company that is helping Lionsgate be the leader in the digital media supply chain management." [03:25]

q: What is mCloud Plus?
a: mCloud Plus was MSquared's first MVP, a Terraform-based, cookie-cutter way to spin up VPCs, availability zones, storage and, if needed, EC2 instances on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure. Jesus Maria said the technique "can pretty much deliver you an entire cloud within like probably 15 minutes." [06:47]

q: How does mCapture handle media metadata?
a: mCapture acts as a lightweight metadata backbone that can tag content, pull information from sources such as IMDB and deliver it to other systems like Salesforce. Jesus Maria explained that "a customer or a client or a production house can select the type of data that they want" [08:46] to store.

q: How can a two-person team scale a platform engineering business?
a: Erin Marie and Jesus Maria scale through a collective, bringing in friends from the industry to push a milestone and then roll off. Erin Marie said, "We prefer to keep us small and lean, and that helps with reducing that overhead cost." [17:38]

q: Does MSquared sell its products as SaaS?
a: MSquared is steering away from the SaaS model, and its modular products can be hosted by the customer or by MSquared. Erin Marie said, "We're not looking for a SaaS model, but more of a licensing per user." [27:16]

s9-e18-the-era-of-physical-ai-engineering-deep-learning-computer-vision-and-real-time-risk-action-at-scale-with-jai-ranganathan-chief-product-officer-at-motive

Simple Camera, Data First: Motive's first camera skipped onboard AI. Telematics flagged hard braking, acceleration or swerves, and the uploaded video was analyzed in the cloud and became training data.
Precision and Recall Together: Rather than give up one for the other, Motive strives for 99.5% of in-cab alerts to be correct while capturing over 90% of the events that actually happen on the road.

Platform Over Big Accounts: Motive walked away from some early large customers to build common capabilities like distraction detection, accepting less presence among the biggest fleets for its first few years.

Scaling the Engineering Organization: Jai says the hardest scaling problem has been getting 600 developers across computer vision, embedded and backend to work on one platform, isolated enough to progress.
Explainability Beats Sophistication: An accurate telematics-based driver score failed because drivers couldn't understand why they were penalized. Motive had to drop it and revamp it.

q: How did Motive get started?
a: Jai Ranganathan explains that founder and CEO Shoaib built a free app to track hours of service ahead of a regulation requiring electronic tracking for long-haul commercial vehicles. When the rule took effect, the app served as a growth funnel, "which allowed him to quickly bring a lot of trucks onto our platform" [03:49].

q: How did Motive collect training data for its AI dashcams?
a: Jai says the first camera recorded continuously, and telematics signals such as a hard brake or swerve triggered a video upload to the cloud for analysis. Of those uploads, he said "this became the basis for our training data that allowed us to" [06:48] evolve the products over time.

q: How accurate does Motive want its in-cab safety alerts to be?
a: Jai says the team refuses to trade away either precision or recall, and also aims to capture over 90% of events on the road. The precision goal he described is that "99.5% of our events, when you hear an alert in the cab, it's going to be correct" [07:52].

q: Why did Motive's early driver scoring model fail?
a: Jai says the telematics-based model was sophisticated and accurate, but gave drivers no context for why they were rated poorly, which led to bad conversations between customers and drivers. In his words, poor explainability "led to a product that was frankly unusable for the purpose it was built to serve" [17:04].

q: What has been Motive's biggest scaling challenge?
a: Jai says system performance and very large accounts have been less difficult than coordinating a large engineering workforce across hardware and software. The goal is bringing 600 developers "to one platform and having them all be effective and sufficiently isolated that they can make" [14:26] progress while still delivering an integrated solution, a battle he says is ongoing.

s9-bonus-from-wall-street-institutional-research-to-coaching-top-tier-fortune-100-executives-mastering-the-s-curve-of-growth-with-amy-frame-and-whitney-johnson-co-founders-of-disruption-advisors

The S-Curve Maps Growth: Growth moves through launch point, sweet spot and mastery. Naming your stage helps normalize early overwhelm, and signals at mastery when to take on a new challenge or jump to a new curve.

From Speaking to Scalable Services: The early business was 80% speaking. By 2019 it had flipped toward coaching and offsites, and the S-curve tool is meant to help scale those services with data on how people are growing.

Let People Place Themselves: The tool now asks people to name three major things they're trying to get done and where they are on each S-curve. Their own view is the great predictor of their longevity, not where others think they are.
Bootstrapping as a Chosen Constraint: The founders traded faster growth for control, treating limited resources as a forcing function to think clearly about what to do next and how to fund it.

Specs Must Survive Translation: Without tech backgrounds, the founders learned that product ideas need specific, pressure-tested writing for developers. Several times they took two steps back when the written spec didn't match what was imagined.

q: What is the S-curve of growth framework?
a: It is the foundational framework at Disruption Advisors, with three stages: launch point, sweet spot and mastery. Whitney Johnson said their big insight was that "the S-curve could help us understand" [06:04] how people learn, grow and change.

q: How does the S-curve Insight tool assess where someone is?
a: Whitney Johnson explained that it evolved from calculating a person's position to asking about the three major S-curves they are on. The idea is to "let them tell you where they think they are" [16:21], which she called a powerful unlock.

q: Why did Disruption Advisors choose to bootstrap?
a: Whitney Johnson said external capital can speed up growth but also means giving up some ownership and control. She noted the founders felt that "by bootstrapping, it was going to force us to really think very clearly" [23:37] about their next moves.

q: What does Disruption Advisors look for when hiring?
a: The firm looks for people who take initiative, want to do the work and collaborate, and it tries them out by working together as contractors. Whitney Johnson said "we don't necessarily go out and look for the most qualified on paper person" [20:38].

q: What did the founders learn from using their own tool on their team?
a: Team members indicated their personal time wasn't respected, and digging in revealed that missed podcast deadlines routinely had one person up at 3 a.m. to upload episodes. Whitney Johnson said that when they got curious, they realized "we've got a system that's" [29:54] not working.

s9-e17-bypassing-documentation-friction-implementing-developer-learning-engines-and-30x-engagement-video-frameworks-with-jake-ward-co-founder-ceo-of-data-protocol

Research Before Building: Jake Ward spent under two years running developer workshops worldwide, meeting a little under 2,000 developers. They said they wanted to build cool things, go fast, avoid breakage and stay out of trouble.

The Dumpster Fire MVP: A paid design firm delivered three animated courses with robotic voiceovers, prompting a potential buyer to ask where the money went. The team reshot the same scripts as video in a WeWork and rebuilt the interface.

Designed for Developers: A CLI terminal-style interface signals the platform is built for developers and keeps their hands on the keyboard. Users can pin notes to accounts that track progress without collecting first or last names.

Users Scale, Content Doesn't: Data Protocol built for audience growth, then attacked inefficiencies in scripting, post-production, design and hosting. Customers get engagement, proficiency and sentiment metrics on dashboards, not hand-built reports.

Plan for Goliath Customers: Large partners brought 90-day payment cycles and weeks of extra edits that could sink a small startup. Ward advises deciding upfront how far you will go, white glove or otherwise, and having a contingency plan.

q: What is Data Protocol?
a: Jake Ward, co-founder and CEO, explained that "data protocol is a platform that enables companies to better support their software developer" [02:52] audiences and internal workforce. It turns the kind of information found in dev docs and API guidance into short-form, on-demand video built for developers.

q: Why does Data Protocol use video instead of traditional developer documentation?
a: Ward says 85% of working software developers "say that they would prefer to get information through video" [03:44] rather than traditional dev docs or blog posts. He also argues that developer relations and advocacy teams often struggle to connect with their developer partners, and Data Protocol aims to fill that gap.

q: How was the Data Protocol MVP and beta built?
a: After a disappointing first version, Ward said, "Four months later, we were ready with those same scripts." [09:00] The team shot them as video in a Washington, D.C. WeWork, added post-production and took the beta to about 500 developers, whose positive response helped the company raise money.

q: How does Data Protocol approach scalability?
a: Ward described "the unique challenge of a double-sided market in which both sides don't scale" [16:17], then clarified that content doesn't scale but users do. The team focused on making content production and hosting more efficient and on giving customers metrics through dashboards.

q: What founder mistake does Jake Ward warn against?
a: Ward admits he was not fully committed and did not have his hands on the wheel for nine months in the company's early days. His lesson is that "there's no such thing as a halfway founder" [21:36], so founders need to care about everything from the outset.

s9-bonus-the-dorm-room-to-20m-supply-chain-shift-overthrowing-distribution-dinosaurs-and-automating-healthcare-procurement-with-luka-yancopoulos-co-founder-ceo-of-grapevine
Overbuilding the First Product: After getting funding, Grapevine took almost a year to launch. Luká estimates about 60% of that MVP was features today's primary users wouldn't ultimately use.

Narrowing the Target Market: Grapevine moved from a broad healthcare audience to businesses under 1,000 employees in specialties like dermatology, ambulatory surgery and oncology, which revealed clearer patterns in customer needs.

Everyone Makes Cold Calls: For about three months after launch, everyone from the CEO to data management staff cold called for product feedback. The team also watched session replays to see how people actually used the app.

Unscalable First, Fix Later: Manual processes and technical shortcuts helped Grapevine move faster. When usage doubled three months in a row in late 2023, memory leaks and overloaded servers forced the team to bottleneck users.

Eliminating Supply Shopping: Grapevine puts offerings from a practice's suppliers on one screen and can introduce lower-priced upstream vendors. The long-term goal is for doctors and nurses to never have to shop for supplies.

q: What is Grapevine and how does it work?
a: Grapevine is a medical supply purchasing platform where healthcare businesses link their existing suppliers so it can read their historic spend and vendors' current offerings. Luká Yancopoulos described it as "a one-of-a-kind shopping center built exclusively for that one healthcare business" [19:05].

q: Why was Grapevine started?
a: Luká began building it while still in college, after people he and his co-founders cared about became frontline workers during the COVID pandemic. He called it "an emotional response, really, to protect people that we cared about and provide value" [03:07].

q: What mistake did Grapevine make with its MVP?
a: Luká said the team was overconfident about its understanding of the market and built many features that primary users wouldn't end up using. As he put it, "we definitely overbuilt our MVP. After getting funding, it took us almost a year" [16:28] to launch.

q: How did Grapevine get early customer feedback?
a: The whole company called potential users to pitch the concept and ask what they needed, while session replays showed how people used the app. Luká said, "We had everyone cold calling basically for the first three months after launching the product" [09:32].

q: What scaling problems did Grapevine run into?
a: Near the end of 2023, platform usage doubled three months in a row and the team had to bottleneck users. Luká recalled, "We had memory leaks. Our servers couldn't handle the operations that we were asking them to handle." [13:38]

s9-e16-bypassing-kong-and-azure-apm-implementing-global-edge-rate-limiting-and-decentralized-api-key-governance-with-james-perkins-co-founder-ceo-of-unkey

Keys Before Gateways: Unlike platforms that lead with a gateway, Unkey started with creating, managing and revoking API keys, so solo developers and small startups could offer a user-facing API without learning gateway intricacies.

MVP in Under Two Weeks: First commit was June 9 and launch was June 21, 2023, using familiar tools: Next.js, Clerk, Upstash, Tinybird, PlanetScale and a TypeScript API. Pricing and the first paying customer followed in July.

Limited-Use Keys for AI: As developers built token-based AI products, Unkey added keys capped at a set number of uses. The key stops working at the limit, so teams don't have to build usage enforcement themselves.
Rewrites Have Customer Costs: The API moved from TypeScript to Go, forcing early users to recreate their keys. A later return to TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers was seamless, with no mass reissue.

Betting on Underdog Hires: Unkey's first hire was a junior engineer with no production experience, chosen for work ethic. He exposed how much knowledge was undocumented and lived only in the founders' heads.

q: How did Unkey get started?
a: James Perkins says his co-founder Andreas pitched a small joint marketing project between Clerk, where James worked, and Upstash, where Andreas worked. James saw more in it, recalling, "I sat there and thought, this is actually much bigger problem than most people realize." [04:21]

q: How can API keys limit usage for AI products?
a: James Perkins explains that Unkey lets developers set how many times a key can be used, which suits products selling a fixed number of generations. As he put it, "we introduced something called limited use keys," [09:39] and the key stops working once it hits its limit.

q: Can Unkey handle sudden spikes in API traffic?
a: James Perkins says scalability was a top priority from the start, and the system stayed solid when one customer jumped from about 30,000 requests a day. He recalled that "one of our customers threw something like 3 million requests in a day through the system." [14:11]

q: What would James Perkins do differently when building Unkey's API?
a: James points to the API, which went from TypeScript to Go and later back to TypeScript. The first switch was painful for early users, and he said "we actually had to tell people to, you need to go and recreate all of" [22:14] the keys produced in the original MVP.

q: What is on Unkey's roadmap?
a: James Perkins describes a globally distributed gateway, along with tools such as SDK and documentation generation. He said, "What we want to bring is a one to two click gateway that will allow you to protect an entire API" [18:38] or an entire web app.

s9-bonus-the-scale-stage-architecture-blueprint-overthrowing-devops-debt-and-scaling-high-velocity-engineering-organizations-with-zach-goldberg-author-of-the-startup-ctos-handbook

Listen Before Changing Things: An outside hire has technical background but lacks organizational context. Zach's early Gruntwork days are about mapping where things stand, building a roadmap and not blowing everything up on day one.

Plan Across Three Horizons: Zach splits planning into the next sprint, the quarter or year, and a one-to-five-year strategy. Near-term work is maybe 50-70% customer-focused, with room for developer experience, debt and tooling.

Beware the Distributed Monolith: At GrowFlow, a strangler pattern effort to retire an older .NET codebase produced services that couldn't deploy independently. The team stopped investing in one coupled service and upgraded the monolith instead.

Guardrails for Many Teams: Gruntwork helps enterprises enforce consistent security and compliance, such as requiring approvals before a developer can create a storage bucket open to the world, even across 25 teams with differing needs.

Hire for the Role's Temperament: Beyond skills and remote fit, Zach weighs natural tendencies. Some roles need a detail-oriented checklist follower, while others need someone who will tear up the checklist and keep improving it.

q: What does Gruntwork do?
a: Gruntwork is a B2B DevOps and infrastructure company whose DevOps Foundations product helps enterprises improve their operating procedures, security and compliance for cloud infrastructure. Zach Goldberg, its CTO, explained that "Gruntwork provides tools, processes, and a bit of professional services to" [03:36] help organizations get on top of those problems.

q: How can enterprises keep cloud security consistent across many development teams?
a: Zach Goldberg describes putting processes in place so that risky actions, like opening a storage bucket to the world, require approvals, and only certain IAM roles can do certain things. The challenge he poses is, "How do you create a sense of consistency and standards that enforce compliance and security" [15:43] when product teams have different needs, cadences and cultures.

q: What should a new CTO do first when joining a company?
a: Zach says someone hired from outside should focus on learning the organization and its people, then make changes collaboratively over the first couple of months. In his words, it means "trying to put the pieces together, so to speak, and not rock the boat." [07:51]

q: How should engineering leaders balance customer features against tech debt and developer experience?
a: Zach suggests the short-term roadmap be maybe 50 to 70% customer-focused, while still investing in developer experience, debt and tooling so engineers aren't fighting their tools. "But I'm a huge believer in investing in the team itself." [10:01]

q: What is a distributed monolith and why is it a problem?
a: It is a system with multiple services that are tightly coupled and can't be deployed independently, which Zach calls the worst of both worlds. Describing a modernization effort at GrowFlow, Zach said, "we made the mistake of accidentally creating a distributed monolith." [19:41]

s9-e15-scaling-from-an-internal-hackathon-project-to-a-multi-million-dollar-global-knowledge-layer-with-saravana-kumar-founder-ceo-of-kovaico-document360

Hackathon Before the Real Build: After spotting a market gap, Saravana had about 35 engineers stop other work for a two-week hackathon. The team scrapped that validation build, reused bits of it, and began V1 in January 2018.

A Deliberately Narrow V1: Document360's first version handled only public-facing knowledge bases, focused on publishing articles and making search very good. Private and mixed knowledge bases, SSO and enterprise security came later.

Let Votes Steer the Roadmap: Customers and trial users submit requests at feedback.document360.com, which had some 1,400 waiting. Saravana recently told the team to build anything with 100 or more votes without further debate.

Design for 100,000 Users: From day one, the team was told to imagine at least 100,000 people using each feature. Document360 runs fully on Microsoft Azure platform services, including serverless functions, with no VMs.
Hire Your Direct Reports First: If starting over, Saravana would first hire five strong direct reports who could run the business and build their own teams, because "A players hire A players."

q: What is Document360?
a: Saravana Kumar explains that "Document360 at a very high level, it's a self-service knowledge base." [02:42] It is a platform companies use to build their own knowledge bases, and it is one of four products under parent company Kovai.co.

q: What gap in the knowledge base market did Document360 set out to fill?
a: Saravana saw customer support suites at one end and complicated legacy tools at the other, with nothing in the middle. Of the support suites, he said "for them the knowledge base is only a small module in a bigger ecosystem" [04:54], so they miss features a typical mid-sized company needs.

q: How was the first version of Document360 built?
a: Saravana documented what a modern knowledge base should look like, then paused other work for a team hackathon, recalling that "we did a two weeks hackathon" [05:57] to validate the idea. The team then scrapped that build, kept some pieces, and took about six months to produce a stable V1.

q: How does Document360 decide what to build next?
a: Early on, the team weighed customer requests and built the must-haves for the product's stage, and users can now submit and vote on ideas on a feedback site. Saravana said, "Only two weeks ago I told the team, blindly go and implement everything that got more" [08:47] than 100 votes.

q: What advice does Saravana Kumar have for young founders?
a: Saravana advises being persistent and choosing a problem big enough to hold your interest for years. He suggests founders ask themselves, "Can you live with this problem for seven years?" [21:23]

s9-bonus-from-inventing-the-100b-stablecoin-tether-to-formatting-internet-identity-overthrowing-centralized-profiles-with-craig-sellars-co-founder-of-tether-ceo-of-self

You Are the Non-Fungible Token: Sellars co-founded Tether in 2014, then built an early NFT platform. That work taught him that each person is unique and the most valuable asset, which led to Self and its focus on owning identity assets.

A Protocol Plus an App: Self pairs MDIP (Multidimensional Identity Protocol), an open source community standard, with an application for interacting with a network of digital identities. The blockchain component is optional.

Scale Without Overloading Chains: Self balances scalability with decentralization. Putting all data on blockchains is too slow and expensive, so Sellars points to tools like IPFS and Peerbit, with scale designed in from day one.

Vet Third-Party Tools Early: Assuming some third-party tech was ready for prime time cost the team months of spinning their wheels, mostly in year one. They cycled through alternatives and had to build some tools internally.

Define Requirements Sooner: Early experimentation skipped robust requirements. Sellars would have defined them about 24 months ago instead of 12, making documentation and answering third-party integrators easier.

q: What is Self and what is the Multidimensional Identity Protocol (MDIP)?
a: Craig Sellars describes Self as two things: MDIP, an open source community standard, and the Self application that lets individuals interact with a growing network of digital identities. Of the protocol, Sellars said, "The goal is to set the standard for the internet of identity as we call it." [03:35]

q: Does Self's decentralized identity system require a blockchain?
a: No, Sellars says the blockchain piece can be left out, although the team's toolkit includes Bitcoin, its derivatives and EVM-style chains alongside libP2P and IPFS. As Sellars put it, the blockchain "component is actually optional. We're taking what we can from that technology" [04:21].

q: What is the digital genome in digital identity?
a: It is Sellars's term for the collection of valuable attributes and information that make up a person's identity, with the user deciding who gets to see it. Sellars described it as "in essence, the atoms and molecules that make up your identity" [12:38].

q: How is Self designed to scale to billions of digital identities?
a: Sellars favors simple rules and balances scalability against decentralization, keeping from putting all data on blockchains and pointing to technologies like IPFS and Peerbit for fast peer-to-peer communication. He argues scale must be planned before first deployment: "Because you can't really build in scalability after the fact." [10:09]

q: What lesson did Craig Sellars learn while building Self?
a: Sellars said the team assumed certain third-party technology was ready when it was not, which cost them months, mostly in the first year. His advice from that experience: the lesson "learned is make sure you're doing your due diligence on the tools you expect to use" [11:59].

s9-e14-the-doordash-for-home-services-overthrowing-legacy-service-friction-and-engineering-on-demand-residential-maintenance-infrastructure-with-mike-bifulco-co-founder-cto-of-craftwork

Paint a Room First: The MVP tested whether anyone would hire them to paint a room. The founders learned to paint from a master painter, then tracked their first month or two of work almost entirely on a spreadsheet.

Employees, Not a Marketplace: Craftwork directly employs its 30-plus painters, guaranteeing them work and offering healthcare benefits, unlike the per-job, often under-the-table arrangements Mike describes as common in painting.

Price by Room Size Buckets: Instead of measuring exact surface area, Craftwork groups rooms into size ranges, such as 0-200 or 200-400 square feet. This avoids tape measures and drawings and simplifies the customer's experience.

Self-Serve Estimates Backfired: An instantly updating online estimator left customers toggling line items instead of submitting. Replacing it with a simple contact form and fast human follow-up filled the top of the funnel much better.

Prove One Market First: Craftwork wants painting to work well in Charlotte before expanding, while asking how each new feature would look in 2, 10 or 100 markets. Moving into other home services may never happen.

q: What is Craftwork and how is it different from a painting marketplace?
a: Craftwork is a tech-connected home painting company based in Charlotte, North Carolina, which Mike Bifulco likens to a DoorDash experience for getting your home painted. Its painters are employees rather than contractors matched through a platform: as Mike put it, "a marketplace or something like that, we hire and employ painters." [06:06]

q: What was Craftwork's MVP?
a: According to Mike Bifulco, "the MVP for Craftwork was, can we get someone to hire us to paint a room in their home?" [06:50] The founders learned to paint from their master painter, Omar, and the tech side began by moving from a spreadsheet to a website where people could contact them.

q: How does Craftwork price a painting project without measuring every room?
a: The team built its initial pricing model from paint coverage data, material costs and the time needed to paint rooms of different sizes and shapes. Rather than using exact square footage, Mike Bifulco explained that "we kind of bucket rooms based on their general size." [10:48]

q: Why did Craftwork remove its online self-serve estimate tool?
a: Customers could build their own estimate and watch the price update, but many kept adjusting line items and never submitted the project. Mike Bifulco said "the telemetry showed us customers would pull this thing up and have essentially decision paralysis" [23:31], so the team tried a simple contact form, which worked much better.

q: Will Craftwork expand into plumbing, electrical or other home services?

s9-e9-the-connectivity-as-code-paradigm-bypassing-legacy-vpn-subnet-chaos-and-eliminating-public-attack-surfaces-with-ryo-koyama-co-founder-ceo-of-remoteit

Born From Home Camera Security: Ryo Koyama and co-founder Mike Johnson didn't want to open their home networks through port forwarding to view cameras, so they built a secure way to reach their equipment from anywhere.

Small, Portable Code in C: Expecting the product to become horizontal, the team built much of the technology in C. That kept the code small, efficient and portable across environments.

Cellular Networks Broke Old VPNs: Most cellular networks use CGNAT with no public IP addresses, so VPNs that industrial users relied on stopped working. Remote.it went on to serve industrial IoT, network gear, surveillance and cloud.
Owning the Go-to-Market: Letting a very large telecom reseller drive the market was a mistake, since its focus was subscriber retention. Walking away to pursue chosen markets directly was the fix.

q: What is Remote.it and what does connectivity as code mean?
a: Remote.it is built on technology that Ryo Koyama calls connectivity as code, which automates the manual work of configuring, securing and maintaining network connections. Koyama says the product itself fits the no-code movement: "Think of it as no code for connectivity." [04:24]

q: Why was Remote.it created?
a: Koyama and co-founder Mike Johnson were installing network surveillance equipment at home and ran into port forwarding, which opens a network to the internet. Koyama recalled, "we thought we don't really want to expose ourselves to the Internet." [05:00]

q: Why do traditional VPNs break on cellular networks?
a: Koyama explains that most cellular networks use CGNAT, so devices on them don't have public IP addresses. When industrial users moved to cellular, he said, things like VPNs "all of a sudden broke and no one understood why." [09:17]

q: How did Remote.it approach scalability?
a: Koyama says the team always believed private connectivity should work everywhere, the way DNS does for the public internet. He said that if it didn't scale "like DNS, it's not going to work. q: What was the biggest mistake Ryo Koyama's team made at Remote.it?

q: Why was the Mosquitto MQTT broker created?

q: How does Mosquitto's performance compare with other MQTT brokers?
a: Roger Light says Mosquitto does well in single-instance comparisons, although horizontal clustering was not yet available at the time of the interview. q: What design decision does Roger Light regret in Mosquitto?

q: Where is Eclipse Mosquitto used in the real world?

Don't Hire Ahead of Commitments: In late 2019, with triple-digit growth and big commitments expected, BILT began hiring early. COVID shifted those companies' priorities, forcing personnel cuts and teaching Henderson more patience.

Do Disruptive Work First: Customer interviews and dogfooding shaped the roadmap into themes and epics. The team prioritized core structures, interfaces and a stable API surface before building out features, working in two-week sprints.

q: What does Craig McLuckie look for when hiring?

Hacked-Together First MVP: Pancoast scraped friends' Mint data into Google Sheets with a Chrome plugin, asked questions via Google Forms, and sent recommendations by email and text.

Positive Texts Over Push Notifications: The Beans engages users by text, with positive, proactive messages, because people living paycheck to paycheck often expect app badges and push alerts to mean bad news.

Pivot to Employer-Paid Distribution: Launched direct-to-consumer in January 2020, The Beans couldn't raise that March. Partners like schools offered to pay for staff access, and the company officially pivoted to B2B in 2022.

q: How does The Beans use automation to reduce financial stress?

s9-bonus-the-edge-computing-architecture-blueprint-breaking-server-latency-and-scaling-developer-first-feature-flags-with-jonathan-norris-co-founder-cto-of-devcycle-taplytics

Follow the Daily Users: Taplytics was built around A/B testing for marketing and product people, but its most passionate daily users were developers using feature flags. That, plus mobile no-code headwinds, led to DevCycle.

Greenfield Over a Reskin: Rather than reskin Taplytics, the team rebuilt on Cloudflare Workers and moved server SDK business logic into customers' own servers, avoiding the cost and strain of scaling a centralized AWS cluster under spiky traffic.

Generate SDKs, Then Share Logic: Early cloud SDKs were generated from an OpenAPI spec, with about a week of cleanup each. For a longer-term solution, DevCycle compiled AssemblyScript to WebAssembly to share logic across languages and edge workers.

The Cost of On-Prem: A large FANG on-premise deal pulled resources into a software fork, stalled the core business and slowed releases from continuous deployment to every two months. Norris says he'd probably decide differently.

Hire People Who Push: Norris favors self-motivated hires, often intermediate engineers ready for more runway, and weighs communication and teamwork over technical ability, especially for remote teams.

q: Why did DevCycle rebuild from scratch instead of reskinning Taplytics?
a: Jonathan Norris says the main reason was architectural: serving huge request volumes from a large centralized AWS deployment was costly and hard to scale, especially with spiky mobile traffic. He explained that "we learned over the years that serving 10s or 100s of billions of" [06:22] HTTP requests every month had taught the team those limits.

q: How does DevCycle keep feature flag latency low?
a: Jonathan Norris says DevCycle uses Cloudflare Workers at the edge and puts decisioning logic into open source SDKs that customers run in their own servers or products. He said there is no easier way to get low latency "than to get rid of the network call" [22:17].

q: How does DevCycle support SDKs in many programming languages without rewriting its logic?
a: After first generating cloud SDKs from an OpenAPI spec, the team wrote shared logic in AssemblyScript, a subset of TypeScript, that runs in SDKs for languages like Java, Go and Python. Norris said "the solution we actually went down, was investing in what's called WebAssembly" [13:45].

q: How does DevCycle organize feature flags for engineering teams?
a: Instead of one giant list of flags, DevCycle's top organizational layer is the feature a team is working on, with its flags, targeting and environments visible underneath. Jonathan Norris said they wanted to "remodel how feature flags are organized to better match how teams actually like small teams actually write and develop software" [09:03].

q: What is OpenFeature and why does DevCycle support it?
a: Jonathan Norris describes OpenFeature as an open, platform-agnostic standard for interfacing with feature flags that addresses vendor lock-in, and he recommends it for teams with internal flagging tools. As he put it, "you can use that interface once and then change providers later" [28:09].

s9-e5-the-identity-workflow-revolution-engineering-drag-and-drop-authentication-and-shattering-the-build-vs-buy-tax-with-gilad-shriki-co-founder-of-descope

Buy Infrastructure to Move Fast: Descope used AWS, Cloudflare and SaaS tools for databases, Kubernetes and log management, and launched in less than a year. Gilad notes that a large seed round made this approach possible.

No Compromise on Scale or Security: Descope sits in front of customers' applications, so if it goes down, they do too. High availability, redundancy and no single point of failure were part of the design from day one.

Feedback Drives the Roadmap: The team interviewed what Gilad thinks was over 150 customers before starting, then used design partners and analyzed prospect, developer and conference conversations to shape priorities.

Qualify Requests Before Prioritizing: Gilad recalls prioritizing a customer request that ultimately went unused, adding noise and displacing other work. The team uses post-mortems and retrospectives to learn from misses like this.

q: What is Descope and what does it do?
a: Descope is an authentication and authorization platform for web and app developers, and Gilad Shriki says it also handles customer identity and access management. He summed up the pitch this way: "So instead of coding and building their own mechanisms, use our service." [03:00]

q: How did Descope build its MVP so quickly?
a: Gilad Shriki says the team relied on ready-made, best-of-breed services such as AWS, Cloudflare and SaaS tools rather than building that infrastructure itself, and launched in less than a year. In his words, "Early on, we decided we need to be fast." [05:45]

q: How does Descope approach scalability and reliability for authentication?
a: Gilad says security and scalability were core to the design from day one, along with high availability and redundancy. Explaining the stakes for customers, he said, "We ask them to trust us. If we're down, they're down." [13:24]

q: Why is Descope pushing passkeys?
a: Gilad Shriki says Descope already supports passkeys and is creating education to help app developers use them. The company is pushing hard on them for B2C "because we believe it's the best of both worlds," [18:32] meaning security and user experience.

q: Can developers use Descope without talking to a sales or support team?
a: Yes, and Gilad is especially proud of this because the founders' previous company relied on very high-touch enterprise deployments. He said, "We have a lot of developers joining the product, starting a project, launching a system without even talking to us." [14:43]

s9-bonus-squeezing-maximum-conversion-from-130000-ab-tests-and-killing-the-competitor-copying-fallacy-with-sahil-patel-ceo-of-spiralyze

Crowdsource Your Test Ideas: Spiralyze scrapes A/B tests across the web, finds patterns in winners and predicts which will likely win for a client. The industry average is that only 11% of tests beat the control.

Organize Around Winning Elements: Spiralyze sorts its test patterns by the distinct element being tested, such as product screenshots or social proof, and ruled out organizing them by industry vertical or call to action.

Let Sales Pitches Steer Roadmaps: Without a large user base, the team showed features in sales pitches, even from staging, to see what created excitement. Wynter sessions with target buyers added early, specific feedback.

Get Counseling Before You Need It: Sahil says every founder's journey has more valleys than peaks. He advises working on yourself and your relationship early, a lesson he learned the hard way.

q: What does Spiralyze do?
a: Sahil Patel describes Spiralyze as a conversion rate optimization company that combines a SaaS prediction product with a service that builds and runs tests for clients. In his words, "We find patterns in what winning tests are, and then we run those winning tests." [03:03]

q: Why do A/B testing programs lose momentum?
a: Sahil says early tests often deliver big lifts from low-hanging fruit, but winning gets much harder after that, and each test takes effort to design and build. Teams also struggle for ideas: "you run out of good ideas to test pretty soon." [07:52]

q: Do product screenshots improve B2B SaaS conversion rates?
a: According to Sahil, Spiralyze found that screenshots generally beat showing nothing or generic stock images, because B2B buyers are buying the product. He said that "when you show a screenshot, you get generally a much higher conversion rate" [10:49].

q: How did Spiralyze build its early product roadmap?
a: Sahil explained that the team lacked a large user base, so it looked to sales conversations for leading signals and worked in short sprints. As he put it, "we show it in the sales pitch and see where it created excitement" [14:30].

q: What mistake did Spiralyze make when demoing its product?
a: Sahil said the team assumed that showing the product was enough to create a wow moment, but a collection of screens didn't land with prospects. His lesson: "If you show it without a story to tell, the narrative, it doesn't connect" [25:29].

s9-bonus-the-expedia-of-insurtech-overthrowing-health-insurance-jargon-and-engineering-ai-powered-personalized-enrollment-rails-with-ariel-dominguez-irena-tigranyan-co-founders-of-healthbird

Cutting the All-in-One Vision: HealthBird shelved a plan to integrate EHRs and doctors nationwide, which required contracts with every provider it targeted. It focused first on everyday items like ID cards, plans and billing, and launched without Rx.

Enrollment Before Everything Else: The team put marketing and engineering behind web enrollment, where users enter a zip code to see qualifying plans, costs and doctors. After about 19 iterations, by Irena's estimate, they moved on to the app.

q: How long did it take to build the first version of HealthBird?

q: What went wrong when HealthBird first launched?

q: How should early-stage startups think about scalability, according to HealthBird's founders?

s9-e4-the-cicd-optimization-blueprint-bypassing-bloated-dev-pipelines-and-slashing-cloud-expenses-with-predictive-test-selection-with-ayal-regev-co-founder-cto-of-redefinedev

Run Only Necessary Tests: Redefine optimizes customers' CI pipelines by running only the tests needed for a developer's changes, aiming for much faster feedback while saving the organization resources.

From MVP to Lovable Product: Ayal targets a "minimum lovable product" customers don't want to uninstall. That takes real value plus onboarding good enough that users don't tire out before they see it.

Narrow the Integration Funnel: Supporting four to six testing framework integrations too early stalled the roadmap. Redefine dropped some, focused on one or two, and planned to expand again after product-market fit.

Bring in Experts Sooner: A team mostly from cybersecurity had blind spots in data processing and hosting. Familiar regular databases didn't fit, and learning on the fly led to patches on patches until experts joined.

Scale One Stage at a Time: Redefine runs on every customer CI run, handling up to millions of requests a day. The team spots looming bottlenecks and adapts to the next scale, going zero to one, one to 10, then 10 to 100.

q: What is Redefine and how does it optimize CI pipelines?
a: Redefine, where Ayal Regev is Co-Founder and CTO, is a CI optimization platform built to give developers faster feedback while saving organizational resources. Ayal said it "optimizes the testing process to allow organizations to move quickly" [04:56], running only the tests needed for each change.

q: What is the difference between an MVP and a minimum lovable product?
a: For Ayal Regev, a working product isn't enough, because customers have to love it to the point that they don't want to uninstall it. He said he has "come to look at the MVP as more of an MLP, a minimum lovable product" [06:03], where onboarding matters as well as the core value.

q: How should an early-stage developer tool startup choose which integrations to support?
a: Ayal Regev said Redefine expanded its supported testing frameworks too early, then dropped some to focus on its product roadmap. His advice is that "you should really define the funnel of your customers based on the tech stack" [08:41] you support, then go find those customers.

q: What technical mistake did Redefine make with data processing?
a: Ayal Regev explained that the team started with the kind of regular databases they already knew and tried to learn on the fly instead of bringing in experts. In his words, "we realized early on that it wasn't a good fit for the problem that we're facing" [20:42], and they have since brought in experts to prepare for bigger scale.

q: What is the future vision for Redefine as AI writes more code?
a: Ayal Regev wants to close the loop between writing code quickly with tools like ChatGPT or Copilot Chat and getting it to production. He noted that today "you still have to wait all this time" [22:50], and the goal is to make that process instantaneous for Redefine customers.

s9-bonus-the-immigration-risk-fabric-bypassing-legal-friction-with-data-driven-onboarding-maps-and-global-mobility-engines-with-leonardo-shapiro-founder-ceo-of-not-alien

Many Movers Lack a Destination: Leonardo says 51% of a 900 million person market are unhappy where they are but don't know where to go. The MVP set out to assess eligibility for immigration programs worldwide.

Survey Over Chatbot: Not Alien chose a long, visual yes-or-no survey instead of an interviewing chatbot, going all in on design so users would feel comfortable sharing personal information. Leonardo reports 80% completion.
Simple Tech Beat Hype: The team spent about a month testing large language models before its CTO pushed for a simpler approach. The problem was then resolved in three days.
Users Want Hand-Holding: The original plan was survey, interview, then a lawyer match. Feedback showed users wanted the whole process project-managed, Trello-style, and even filed for them.

Hire People Who Feel It: Leonardo keeps a list of past colleagues he connected with to invite to future companies. He also wanted the core team to be immigrants who understand the user's pain firsthand.

q: What is Not Alien and how does it work?

q: Why did Not Alien use a survey instead of an AI chatbot for immigration eligibility?
a: Leonardo's team felt that users needed a rich, comfortable experience built on trust before disclosing personal details, so they invested heavily in graphical design. q: What mistake did Not Alien make with generative AI?
a: Leonardo says the team tested pretty much every LLM engine, partly because it was the hype and they assumed people would expect it. q: What does Leonardo Shapiro look for when building a startup team?
