q: What advice does Leonardo Shapiro give young entrepreneurs?
a: Leonardo warns that emotional attachment leads to confirmation bias, and says to seek feedback from people who aren't emotionally invested in you. His advice: "Make sure that you don't get too emotionally attached with what you're building." [22:20]

s9-bonus-the-dataops-democratization-blueprint-overthrowing-airflow-infrastructure-overhead-and-scaling-serverless-data-orchestration-with-blake-burch-founder-ceo-of-shipyard

Spun Out of an Agency: Shipyard began as Forklift, an internal PMG tool for moving data between warehouses and automating code. In 2020 it was split off, which meant decoupling it from internal business logic and databases.

Function Before Polish: The early product had no drag-and-drop UI or prebuilt templates. Users strung tasks together through forms and wrote their own code, as long as it ran automatically and produced logs.

Roadmap Driven by Lost Sales: Repeated reasons for "no" on sales calls, plus user and data engineer feedback, set priorities. That led to visual workflow connections and well over 150 low-code templates.
A Costly AI Experiment: Words to workflows took three to six months but was never released. Users still had to fill in inputs and fix steps, so it saved maybe 30 seconds over drag and drop.

Narrow the Use Case: In hindsight, Blake would focus early on one use case, such as reporting automation or reverse ETL, or even one industry. A broad workflow platform makes it harder for new users to see what they can do.

q: What is Shipyard and what does it do?
a: Shipyard is a data workflow platform that helps teams move, automate and act on data, for example sending data from Snowflake to email or Google Drive. Blake Burch said it "allows teams to be able to easily move and automate their data" [02:28] without the technical skills that typically requires.

q: How did Shipyard get started?
a: It spun out of Forklift, an internal tool at the digital advertising agency where Blake Burch ran data teams. Blake said that if you ask his co-founder Eric, it was "a way for us to stop bugging him to host scripts elsewhere." [03:53]

q: How does Shipyard decide what to build next?
a: Blake Burch said the roadmap was prioritized around sales calls, active users and others in the data space. It was set "based on the types of external conversations that we were having." [08:35]

q: How does Shipyard handle scaling for customer workflows?
a: Workflows run on Shipyard's infrastructure, so customers don't have to set it up or scale it, and the team designed for many simultaneous jobs from the beginning. As Blake put it, "That's on us to figure out. And so it's been baked into our kind of core philosophy" [11:46].

q: What happened with Shipyard's words to workflows AI feature?
a: The feature turned a plain-language description into workflow tasks, but users still had to fill in details and sometimes reorder steps, so it was never released. Blake Burch said they were "effectively only saving clients maybe 30 seconds of time" [15:08].

s9-e3-embedded-lending-infrastructure-and-navigating-emerging-market-api-scaling-with-reinis-simanovskis-co-founder-cpo-of-finfra

Pivot to Embedded Lending: Reinis and his co-founders moved to Indonesia for consumer lending, saw its potential narrowing, and pivoted to embedded lending infrastructure, where they saw no one seriously operating and hoped for an early mover advantage.

A Three-Month First Integration: Finfra's MVP was its first live embedded loan product. Reusing the consumer lending backend, built in a low-code environment, plus a custom API layer, the team launched it in three months.

Sales-Driven Development Has a Price: Building for each new client gave fast feedback and suited a tight runway, but created technical debt and inconsistent integrations. Finfra is now standardizing partner APIs and loan product setups.

Commitment Before Integration Work: After a month of work on a bank integration that never launched because the contract wasn't signed, Finfra began readjusting sales to require some commitment to a commercial agreement first.

Faster Onboarding for Partners: Finfra now manages seven partners and has gone from a three-month onboarding to as little as a week for some, with the aim of eventually onboarding partners within a day.

q: What does Finfra do?
a: Finfra provides infrastructure that lets other businesses add lending to their core product, including regulatory cover, loan management, servicing and introductions to capital providers. Reinis Simanovskis said Finfra works with founders and managers to "help them integrate lending as a value-add service" [03:32].

q: How does Finfra's embedded lending model work if it is not a bank?
a: Reinis explained that platforms such as construction material websites or supply chain platforms act as distribution channels, while a regional credit fund or bank supplies the capital for mostly business loans. As he described it, Finfra will "operate on a P2P lending basis. We're going to connect the platforms" [05:21] with those lenders.

q: How did Finfra decide what to build in its early days?
a: Reinis said the team took a sales-driven approach, developing what each new client in the pipeline needed. In his words, "Whatever we see from what we have in the sales pipeline, that's going to be what we're developing" [06:44]. Later, the roadmap shifted to researching demand and market size across ideal customer profiles.

q: What are the downsides of building custom integrations for each fintech partner?
a: According to Reinis, customizing for each partner was not built for scale, and Finfra is now standardizing its APIs and loan product setups. He said the approach "creates lots of technical debt, creates a lot of inconsistencies between different integrations" [06:56], though he does not regret the trade-off.

q: What would Reinis Simanovskis do differently as a founder?
a: He somewhat regrets turning down a small investment, with advice and resources, from more experienced European lending entrepreneurs who wanted a substantial stake in his earlier consumer lending business. Reinis said it could have saved a lot of time, noting that "It's a huge value in the startup world as time to market is everything." [20:30]

43b1bfc1-b634-47e2-8756-9eabcfa47aac
s9-bonus-programmatic-venture-finance-and-algorithmic-cash-management-with-raven-jiang-co-founder-cto-of-arc
Manual Money Movement at MVP: Arc's first revenue-based financing product focused on onboarding and data aggregation. Sending out cash and collecting payments was going to be done manually at first.

Customer Needs Sparked New Products: Some revenue-generating, bootstrapped customers lacked a real corporate bank account. A checking feature meant to speed access to cash advances grew into a separate offering.

Credible Paths Over Early Scale: Arc chose tools with proven scaling records but skipped building scalable implementations upfront. Knowing it was a B2B company, not Facebook-scale, made some design decisions easier.

A Missing Await Broke Services: Raven's observability code stopped some serverless functions from completing, hitting several backend services. The team traced the subtle bug and planned recovery, including replaying missing event messages.

Hire for Startup Problems: Early hiring across the company leaned toward big-company credibility, which led to some cultural mismatch. Raven advises finding people suited to the problems a startup actually needs to solve.

q: What is Arc and what does it offer startups?
a: Arc offers cash management, treasury and financing services to software businesses, often startups around the Series A to B range. Co-founder and CTO Raven Jiang describes it as "a full-service B2B fintech platform" [02:38], which started out focused mainly on revenue-based financing.

q: How long did it take to build Arc's MVP?
a: The MVP was an onboarding flow with third-party integrations and a light loan management system on the back end. Raven Jiang said "it probably took less than a month to get that initial product in front of the first live customer" [04:45].

q: What tech stack is Arc built on?
a: Raven Jiang said "The app continues to be actually built on a fully TypeScript front-end, back-end with PostgreSQL" [04:52]. The goal was a fast, type-safe and relatively standard environment where people could be productive and keep product velocity high.

q: How did Arc approach scalability in its early product?
a: Raven Jiang said the team adopted proven technologies and frameworks but did not put extra effort into scalable implementations right away. In his words, "as long as the credible migration path exists, I think we were happy" [11:14].

q: What would Raven Jiang do differently when hiring at an early-stage startup?
a: Raven Jiang said some early hires across the company were optimized for credibility, and big-company working styles did not always fit. His advice is to "think about the problems that you actually need to solve and find people that you think would be good at solving those problems" [18:31].

s9-bonus-shattering-the-network-telemetry-silo-with-avi-freedman-of-kentik

Keep It All, Ask Anything: Existing appliances rolled network traffic up into metric streams. Kentik built its own multi-tenant column store so users could keep all the data, query it fast and handle its huge cardinality.

Validate With People in Pain: The MVP's interface was crude, yet prospects who had lived the problem mostly asked what it cost and when they could try it. That gave the team confidence to raise venture capital.

Bare Metal Over Cloud: Freedman judged that running always-on infrastructure in the cloud couldn't support a good business. Kentik runs net-booted bare metal with containers and, mostly, its own orchestration system.

Shortcuts With a Shelf Life: Kentik used Postgres to parse SQL and combine results from its distributed system. It carried the company for eight years, but the team is now gradually moving work out of it for efficiency.

Bootstrap to Shape DNA: Large early customers meant onboarding got less focus. Freedman would bootstrap longer, not to keep more equity, but to force the company to make discovery and onboarding easier.

q: What does Kentik do?
a: Kentik is a SaaS platform that takes network telemetry, including traffic data, metrics, synthetic tests and routing protocols, from physical and virtual infrastructure. Co-founder and CEO Avi Freedman describes it as a company that "helps people who run the infrastructure that connects us all to make it fast and secure" [02:31].

q: Why did Kentik build its own database for network traffic data?
a: Avi Freedman had seen traffic data overwhelm time series and relational databases, largely because of its enormous cardinality. Rather than aggregating the data away, he said, "our challenge was how can we keep it all and do fast querying over it all" [07:18], which led to a multi-tenant column store.

q: Why does Kentik run on bare metal instead of the cloud?
a: Freedman made efficiency a priority from the start because he wanted to build a good business. As he put it, "I knew from the very beginning, running always on infrastructure in cloud is a sucker's bet" [12:42].

q: How did Kentik validate its first MVP?
a: Freedman's team showed a rough early version to service providers, web companies and enterprise infrastructure teams who understood the difficulty firsthand. Freedman said, "We went to people that were living the problem" [08:08], and their eagerness to try it gave the team confidence to raise capital.

q: What would Avi Freedman do differently if he started Kentik again?
a: Freedman would bootstrap longer, while still aiming to build a larger, enduring technology company. He explained that "bootstrapping a little longer can help influence the DNA in ways that are harder to do once you're at a larger scale" [24:10].

s9-e2-the-embedded-payroll-fabric-bypassing-legacy-monoliths-with-developer-first-fintech-apis-and-multi-state-compliance-rails-with-juan-barroso-co-founder-cto-of-salsa
Two MVPs, One Thrown Away: Juan built a six-to-eight-week MVP for product discovery, then raised money, hired a team and rebuilt it. The second version ran its first paycheck in five to six months.

Manual Back Office First: Salsa focused on customer-facing APIs and experience, leaving most tax operations manual at launch and tracking compliance to-dos in Notion tables. It was painful, but Juan thinks it paid off.

Boulders Plus Iteration: Quarterly planning splits investment between a few big foundational features, guided by sales conversations, and improvements to existing features, guided by customer feedback.

Reactive Was a Mistake: Juan says Java Reactive looked good on paper but the ecosystem wasn't mature enough. The team built utilities to ease the pain and is working toward moving off it, noting Kotlin coroutines scale fine.

Outbound Improves Customer Fit: Salsa first relied on inbound interest, then became far more active in outbound to find its ideal customer profile and better control the quality of customers it was getting.

q: What is Salsa and who is it for?
a: Salsa offers APIs, web components and other building blocks that let software platforms create payroll products to sell to their own business customers. Juan Barroso explains, "we build payroll infrastructure to make it easy for developers to build their own payroll products" [02:34].

q: Why did Juan Barroso start Salsa?
a: After years of building payroll engines, including horizontal payroll at QuickBooks, Juan saw that one solution could not fit everyone. As he put it, "There was always somebody that was not really happy" [03:55], which led to the idea of infrastructure that lets developers tailor the experience.

q: How was Salsa's first product built?
a: Juan built the discovery MVP with Kotlin, Spring and Netflix's DGS framework for GraphQL, and the rebuilt version kept that approach on AWS, with React for components and internal tooling. Of the original MVP, Juan said, "We threw away the MVP, so we did a second one" [05:24].

q: How long does it take to launch payroll with Salsa?
a: Juan says customers can now launch with a very small engineering effort, which reflects the company's early vision of making payroll easy to integrate and fast to launch. According to Juan, customers can launch "in four, six weeks with one engineer" [12:13].

q: How does Salsa approach scalability?
a: Juan thinks about it in two dimensions: product abstractions that can grow into new use cases and countries, and transactional scale in the cloud on AWS. Juan's guideline is, "I like to be one order of magnitude ahead of what we have today" [11:00].

b0bf4682-cacf-45eb-bbb5-68a57111c37e
s9-bonus-data-centric-ai-blueprint-bypassing-privacy-walls-and-scaling-high-fidelity-synthetic-data-pipelines-with-fabiana-clemente-co-founder-cdo-of-ydata

Data Access Sparked YData: As a data scientist, Clemente once waited about six months for data access because of privacy, regulation and security concerns. That frustration led her and her co-founders to build development tools for data scientists.

Synthetic Data First: The roughly three-month MVP tackled data access by generating synthetic data meant to keep the original's value without re-identification risk. It used Scikit-learn, PyTorch and Dask connectors, with a basic UI and little customization.

Trust Needs a Quality Report: Users kept asking how good YData's synthetic data was. Answering that with an easy-to-interpret quality report became an early roadmap priority, followed by interviews with data scientists about other data preparation pains.

Don't Silo Research and Product: Splitting engineering from data science slowed integration and development, even though both worked on one product. YData reorganized so the teams could collaborate almost in real time.

Async Has Limits: After moving to the US, Clemente cut synchronous time with the team in Europe and let the leads self-organize. Product vision and priorities became misaligned, showing that strong technical people still need close product alignment.

q: What problem led Fabiana Clemente to start YData?
a: Clemente struggled to access and process data while working as a data scientist, with privacy, regulation and security concerns in the way. As she recalled, "it took me like six months just to get access to the data" [03:47].

q: How does YData use synthetic data to get around privacy barriers?
a: YData's first product created synthetic datasets that data scientists could use without the re-identification issues tied to people or customers. Clemente described it as "a model that could be used to generate data that would have the same data value as the original data" [05:46].

q: What tools were used to build YData's first MVP?
a: Clemente said "The backend, we used a lot of Scikit-learn," [06:37] along with PyTorch to build the model. The team also developed connectors with Dask to pull data from a source, synthesize it and send the synthetic data to a destination.

q: How did YData build trust in the quality of its synthetic data?
a: Customers repeatedly asked how good the synthetic data was, so the team made a clear, interpretable quality report a roadmap priority. Clemente explained that "in order for people to use this technology, they would need to have some kind of trust on it." [07:43]

q: What advice does Fabiana Clemente have for new entrepreneurs?
a: Clemente says building the product, though a big effort, is easier than building the team and culture. Her advice is that "You should really invest in people," [21:57] and not let customers, investors and the roadmap crowd that out.

s9-bonus-the-death-of-localhost-engineering-dev-container-orchestration-and-terraform-powered-cloud-workspaces-with-kyle-carberry-co-founder-cto-of-coder
Consumer First, Then Enterprise: Coder began as a consumer platform that took a little under a year to build. The company pivoted to enterprise, and none of that first product's code exists today.

Abstract Every Custom Request: A Skydio contact's request for a "Slack me" command alert became a general OAuth and CLI capability, so integrations such as 1Password and Okta can benefit many more customers.

Simplicity Built for Scale: Coder ships as a single static binary without CGO, built for portability and easy deployment. Kyle says its architecture supports organizations of up to roughly 50,000 engineers.
Know Your Strengths: Kyle calls trying to manage an engineering team a big early mistake. His team told him he wasn't a good manager, and he would rather write code and focus on quality.

Slow Hiring During Hypergrowth: After code-server became a fast-growing GitHub project, Kyle learned that popularity makes for bad filtering. Everyone wants to join a perceived rocket ship, so true intent is harder to judge.

q: What is Coder and who is it for?
a: Coder is a self-hosted remote development platform that gives developers a ready-to-code environment with one click, aimed particularly at large enterprises. Kyle Carberry says it started from the idea that "10 years from now, people probably won't be coding on their laptops." [02:56]

q: How is Coder built to scale and deploy easily?
a: Kyle Carberry says Coder was tailored to the scale of large engineering organizations and kept very simple, as a single, isolated service. In his words, "We packed it as like a single static binary" [09:53], primarily for portability and ease of deployment.

q: How did Coder decide what to build on its product roadmap?
a: Kyle Carberry says some choices were driven by vision, especially what the team turned down, but many came from enterprise customers asking for features they would pay for. Describing the response to those requests, he said, "And we were like, we'll design something abstract" [06:05].

q: What is the future of Coder and cloud development environments?
a: Kyle Carberry sees three phases: moving organizations' development environments to the cloud, enhancing them with added tools, and eventually letting developers control the whole loop themselves. The first involves "replacing that local laptop that's maybe not as efficient as it needs to be" [13:23] inside an organization.

q: What hiring advice does Kyle Carberry give founders whose product is taking off?
a: Kyle Carberry advises being very cautious, and says a company's hottest stretch is maybe when he would slow hiring the most. He explains that he isn't calling applicants bad people: "It's just to say that people will mold themselves for the right opportunity." [17:48]

s9-e1-from-turning-down-a-competitor-to-powering-roblox-and-gamestop-scaling-a-global-edge-network-without-wall-street-capital-with-matt-levine-of-cachefly

Betting on Anycast: Skeptics told Matt that Anycast couldn't handle content or long-lived connections. After a friends-and-family beta of a year and a half to two years, CacheFly showed a CDN could be built on it.

Self-Serve as the Equalizer: When Matt saw buying CDN as an enterprise-only process, CacheFly let customers sign up by credit card, with plans from $15.99 to $99. In its first three to four years, it probably had 3,000 to 4,000 customers.
Count the Silent Users: Early roadmaps came from tickets and customer feedback. Matt learned that each complaint likely represents 10x to 100x more people with the same problem who simply leave.

A Second Run at Self-Service: A pay-as-you-go launch swamped support with inexperienced users, and Matt wanted it off. When self-onboarding returned, the team automated features once switched on manually for enterprise customers.

Cache Misses Matter Most: Matt says customer libraries have long been too big for CDNs to fully cache, yet bake-offs focus on cache hits. He expects CacheFly's delivery focus to be on cache miss performance.

q: What does CacheFly do?
a: CacheFly is a content delivery network that helps customers deliver web content faster by caching copies of files in cities around the world. Matt Levine explained, "We basically offload people's typically media files, but it can be anything" [02:31].

q: How was the first version of CacheFly's CDN built?
a: Matt's first CDN ran in two locations, Palo Alto and New Jersey, using lighttpd on FreeBSD and a custom load balancer, with files pushed out to each site. As Matt described it, "The MVP was really just distributed web servers, syncing files between them" [10:40].

q: Can you build a CDN using Anycast?
a: Matt Levine set out to test this even though people said Anycast was meant for short-lived things and would break with content delivery. After building and running it in a friends-and-family beta, he reported, "And it turns out you can build a CDN on Anycast" [05:10].

q: How did CacheFly handle traffic growth during COVID?
a: Traffic surged while supply chain gaps, shipping delays and restricted data center access made adding hardware difficult, so the team turned to used equipment. Matt said, "We became a logistics company for two months, trying to figure out that part of scalability" [18:57].

q: Should a startup build on cloud infrastructure?
a: Matt Levine advises building on cloud while you are small, but planning from the start for how to move off it fully or into a hybrid setup to control costs. In his words, "you need a plan to get off of it as soon as you hit traction" [28:38].

s8-bonus-from-the-tech-behind-toy-story-to-a-global-workforce-os-overcoming-engineering-bottlenecks-and-flatlining-infra-costs-with-alex-yarotsky-of-hubstaff

Speed First, Pay Later: Hubstaff's founders used a PaaS to skip DevOps and outpace competitors. It later meant performance work and a migration to their own AWS infrastructure, which Alex says was well worth it.

Roadmaps Change With Scale: As a startup, Hubstaff ranked ideas by request volume and could copy competitors. As a market leader in the scale-up phase, it leans on event analytics, FullStory journeys, heat maps and user feedback.

Measuring Features With TARS: Each new feature gets a defined target audience within Hubstaff's users, then is tracked for adoption, retention and satisfaction, because people may keep using a feature they hate.
Hire for Two Qualities: Hubstaff looks for engineers who are diligent and open-minded. If interviews confirm both, years of experience and familiarity with the tech stack don't matter.
Don't Delay Parting Ways: Alex says they spent too long absorbing work from people who didn't scale with the company. Offer help, but if it doesn't work, part ways so they can find a better fit.

q: How was the first version of Hubstaff built?
a: Alex Yarotsky, who joined later, recalls that the MVP took less than six months and offered basic time tracking with simple project and task management. It used a custom C++ framework for Linux, Windows and Mac OS, plus a web dashboard, and Alex noted that "it's not just a web app, it's web app plus desktop app" [03:59].

q: How does Hubstaff handle scalability and performance issues?
a: Alex says the product "wasn't really built with the scale in mind, so we had to address it along the way" [12:08]. The team watches monitoring and APM tools daily to spot spikes and bottlenecks, and two engineers are on call around the clock each week.

q: What is the TARS framework Hubstaff uses for new features?
a: Alex describes TARS as target audience, adopted, retained and satisfied, applied to each feature to guide how it is built and adjusted. Satisfaction is measured separately because, as he put it, "retention does not mean satisfaction, right?" [09:54].

q: What does Hubstaff look for when hiring engineers?
a: Alex Yarotsky says the company looks for two qualities in candidates: "They're diligent and they're open-minded." [11:06]. Years of experience and prior work with Hubstaff's tech stack matter far less to them than those traits.

q: Is Hubstaff big brother software for monitoring employees?
a: Alex acknowledges the industry has that reputation and says Hubstaff is taking a different route, with tools that help employees and managers improve. In his words, "We don't want to be associated with this negativity behind being" [16:27] a big brother.

s8-bonus-the-1-trillion-flag-architecture-decoupling-deployments-from-releases-and-mastering-in-memory-edge-evaluation-with-pato-echague-co-founder-cto-of-splitio

Decouple Push From Release: Split lets engineers put code in production without releasing it, test it with a few people, then roll out to the team, the company and the outside world. Mistakes can be taken back without a full rollback.

The First Kill Switch: A front-end engineer who had never released software broke the website while trying the early internal tool. He clicked the kill button on his flag, and the site came back up in 30 seconds.

Enterprise First, by Design: Split chose early to appeal to enterprises, which meant heavy work on security certification. Meeting the demands of major banks, such as a 300-item list, prepared the team for later customers' security questions.

Mission-Critical From the Start: If feature flags can't be served, customers' applications don't behave as intended. That put focus on flag delivery speed, CDNs, latency, observability and the deployment pipeline, with few people and 24-7 support.

Empower Teams Earlier: Pato says his biggest mistake was leaning in with his own opinions as a technical founder. In hindsight, he would let teams make their own calls, make mistakes, recover and build scar tissue.

q: What is Split and what does a feature management platform do?
a: Split is a feature management platform that uses feature flags and experimentation to help engineering teams move faster and improve delivery quality. Pato Echagüe explains that by separating a push from a release, "engineers can have an extra look in production before things get released" [02:48].

q: What problem led to the creation of Split?
a: Pato says the three founders met at a small startup called RelateIQ, where shipping code kept causing new breakage and morale suffered. As he recalled, "every time we pushed something, we broke something else" [03:08]. A feature flagging tool let them push to production without releasing right away.

q: How does a feature flag kill switch help when a release breaks production?
a: A kill switch lets someone turn off the flagged code without a full rollback, then restore it once the software is fixed. Describing an engineer whose code broke the website, Pato said, "click the kill button. 30 seconds, the site came back up." [00:19]

q: Why did Split decide to sell to enterprise customers early?
a: Pato says the founders weighed a bottom-up developer play against going enterprise first, and recalled, "We made a decision early on that we wanted to appeal to enterprise." [08:03] That required significant time on security certification and on being clear with procurement and security teams.

q: What does Pato Echagüe look for when hiring early startup employees?
a: Pato looks for cues of greatness by asking candidates how they solved problems and what decisions they made along the way. If they remember the details, he said, "it means that they were actually in the trenches, like tinkering, trying to solve a really hard problem." [09:28]

s8-e30-the-modernization-factory-overcoming-a-15-trillion-technical-debt-and-automating-monolith-to-microservice-extraction-with-moti-rafalin-co-founder-ceo-of-vfunction
Technology Risk Before Market: vFunction raised a relatively large seed round and built for three and a half years before going to market. Some of the world's largest banks then used it.

From One-Time to Recurring: Early large deals were one-off modernization projects. Splitting the platform into an architectural observability manager and a refactoring engine add-on opened a recurring revenue model and a bigger market.

Break Monoliths in Code: The team first tried splitting applications at runtime, then found it more or less impossible. They also learned customers wanted engineering velocity, so they shifted to code-level extraction for developers and architects.
No Pre-Hiring in Sales: vFunction started small in sales and adds reps only as existing ones hit quota. Moti would rather miss opportunities than risk missed quotas, low morale and departures.
Debrief Without Blame: Moti brought briefing and debriefing from the Israeli Air Force. The aim is improving as a team, so people feel safe sharing mistakes, never pointing fingers.

q: Why isn't lift and shift enough for cloud modernization?
a: Moti Rafalin argues that enterprises have to modernize legacy applications to use what the cloud offers. As he put it, "if you only lift and shift or you just move applications as is to the cloud" [04:32], you won't get the maximum value.

q: How does vFunction turn a monolith into microservices?
a: Moti explains that vFunction uses a "combination of dynamic analysis and static analysis" [06:01], along with data science and machine learning, to understand an application's architecture. It then identifies domains you may want to decompose, and an automation piece extracts that code into microservices.

q: What is architectural observability?
a: Moti describes it as observing an application's architecture on an ongoing basis, with alerts when there is drift, added complexity or cross-domain pollution. It applies before and after modernization because, as he said, "you don't want to fight that war a second time" [08:34].

q: What mistake did vFunction make in its early product thesis?
a: The team initially thought it could break applications apart at runtime so companies could use cloud capabilities without modernizing them. Moti said they learned that engineering velocity was the real driver, and that "you need to really break it at the code level and not in runtime" [15:28].

q: How does Moti Rafalin approach scaling an enterprise sales team?
a: Moti grows the team based on business results, starting small and building infrastructure so each salesperson can meet or beat quota before more are hired. He acknowledges that many VCs may disagree, but says, "I'd rather miss some opportunities than pre-hire." [12:47]

s8-bonus-the-acquisition-playbook-productizing-devops-infrastructure-and-scaling-a-247-cloud-operations-engine-with-shaun-ritchie-ceo-of-nclouds

Acquire Instead of Starting Cold: Shaun wanted to build people through a services company, but earning certifications and credentials takes significant time. He bought a smaller, AWS-focused firm with engineering talent to scale.

The Company as MVP: Shaun looked at about four or five companies before choosing nClouds, which fit his criteria: AWS focus, a history with Silicon Valley startups and scaling organizations, and strong market fundamentals.

Services Don't Blitzscale: A services business grows linearly on gross margin, so Shaun's plan pairs better sales and marketing with step-function growth through acquisitions, such as CloudNexa, which almost doubled the company's size.

Career Paths Beyond Management: With people as the product, Shaun focuses on training and career paths. Engineers who want to be deep experts rather than managers shouldn't be limited in advancement or earning potential.

Lead, Don't Just Listen: After the acquisition, Shaun came in to listen and learn without shaking things up. He found people were craving leadership, and says direction, goals and priorities should be set as quickly as possible.

q: What does nClouds do?
a: nClouds is a cloud engineering services company and a top-tier AWS partner serving customers throughout North America. CEO Shaun Ritchie said of the team's role, "We really work as extensions to our customers" [02:39].

q: Why did Shaun Ritchie acquire a services company instead of founding one?
a: Shaun wanted to focus on building people and saw buying a smaller services organization as the fastest route. Building one from scratch means gaining certifications and, as he put it, "credentials and all that kind of stuff takes a significant amount of time." [03:44]

q: What mistake did Shaun Ritchie make after taking over nClouds?
a: Shaun led with listening and learning and held back from making immediate changes, underestimating how much direction the team wanted. He said, "What I underestimated was that people needed leadership more than they needed an outlet to be listened to." [17:15]

q: How do you scale a cloud services company?
a: According to Shaun, you can't blitzscale services; you grow through better sales and marketing, more customer value and acquisitions. He explained, "But a services organization, you have to grow linearly because it's based on a gross margin," [14:08].

q: How does Shaun Ritchie approach integrating an acquired company?
a: With CloudNexa, Shaun wants to combine the best of both organizations and leave behind less effective practices and structures. Borrowing the improv rule of "yes and," he said that in any integration, "everybody throughout the organization has to say yes and." [20:35]

s8-bonus-the-death-of-the-crashing-spreadsheet-engineering-predictive-ai-ingestion-and-asset-intelligence-rails-with-arunabh-dastidar-co-founder-ceo-of-realsage

Born From Crashing Spreadsheets: Arunabh was a director of asset management handling over $1 billion in real estate when his Excel files crashed during a $130 million repackaging deal. He went back to engineering and built RealSage with two co-founders.

Validate Before Building: The team spoke to dozens of people and found real estate data stuck in functional and technology silos, then pulled into Excel for quarterly meetings. The MVP reached its first beta customers within six months.

AI-Powered Data Ingestion: Users can drag and drop existing Excel files, and RealSage maps them to database columns, validates the data and flags ERP errors. Arunabh says this removes 80% of analyst and data engineering time.

From Hindsight to Foresight: AI models spanning 35 use cases suggest actions, such as moving a building's marketing budget from one channel to another. The asset owner or manager stays at the wheel while the system nudges decisions.

Mistakes Without Punishment: When miscommunication nearly sank a major distribution partnership, the team regrouped over a weekend and Arunabh joined a candid call with the other side. The contract was signed two days later.

q: What is RealSage and what does it do?
a: RealSage uses data science and AI to help asset owners and managers make decisions on pricing, budget reallocation, refinancing and more. Co-founder and CEO Arunabh Dastidar describes it this way: "RealSage as a company essentially is a decision support system for asset owners and managers." [02:32]

q: What problem led Arunabh Dastidar to start RealSage?
a: Arunabh was taking a Friday evening call on a $130 million repackaging deal when his spreadsheets failed him. He recalled, "We had to close and my Excels were crashing." [04:06]

q: How does RealSage handle messy real estate data?
a: Arunabh explained that the company's data is often unstructured or full of holes and errors, and cleaning it delays any business intelligence. He said, "we use AI to auto map, auto spread data, validate the data" [10:10], with error reporting during ingestion.

q: Was RealSage built to scale from the beginning?
a: Yes, Arunabh said the team chose modular, microservices-driven infrastructure from day one, despite the effort it takes to maintain at an early stage. In his words, "We are a team of engineers. We have built this scale in mind" [13:56].

q: What advice does Arunabh Dastidar give to young entrepreneurs?
a: Arunabh advises founders to persevere, pivot and fail fast, even after the early excitement has faded. He also urges them to be "in love with the problem and not the solution." [22:48]

s8-e29-the-16-million-host-blueprint-treating-operating-systems-like-sql-tables-and-engineering-open-source-endpoint-security-with-zach-wasserman-co-founder-cto-of-fleet

SQL Instead of Scripts: osquery uses SQLite virtual tables hooked to OS APIs and the file system, so users can query and join device data with a little SQL instead of writing Python, PowerShell or Bash.

One API for Everyone: Fleet's React single-page app uses the same APIs customers get. Zach says this slows shipping somewhat, but anything clickable in the UI can be done by API, and the app doubles as a reference implementation.

Persisting Before eBay: About a year or more in, with sales not working, the founders weighed pivoting but stuck with the idea. eBay later helped reveal what the product needed to be enterprise ready.

Subsetting as a Differentiator: Tonic's patented subsetting shrinks a database, such as 10 terabytes of production data down to a one-gigabyte test set. Andrew estimates around 40% of customers use it.

Refinement Hurt Expansion: Tonic perhaps over-invested in polishing existing features instead of adding capabilities. Customers renewed, but the customer success team had little to upsell, which hurt net dollar retention.

q: What does Tonic.ai do?
a: Andrew Colombi explains that Tonic analyzes your database and creates another one based on it, so teams can test without using sensitive production data. In his words, "We make fake data and we make it for test and development purposes." [02:47] Customers also use it for things like sales demos.

q: How did the idea for Tonic.ai come about?
a: While at Palantir, Andrew built fake data for projects where the real data was too sensitive to share, and found it took far more work than expected while proving useful to others. He summed up the combination as "it's harder than you think and more valuable than you think." [05:11]

q: How did Tonic first copy a database schema?
a: Andrew says the very first version took a shortcut to get the job done right away: "just scrape the schema, use some regexes," [09:35] and hope for the best. It eventually mangled a customer's schema in a critical bug, and the team has matured the process since.

q: Was Tonic.ai built to scale from day one?
a: No, Andrew says the founders focused first on making the product work and sell, and later began addressing scalability in certain areas. Performance also hinges on the customer's own technology, because "the scalability of our platform, depends on your source database." [15:21] Tonic uses a very different architecture for Databricks to take advantage of its scalability.

q: What mistake did Tonic.ai make with its product roadmap?
a: Andrew believes the team perhaps focused too much on refining existing features rather than expanding capabilities, leaving little to upsell at renewal time. He described the reaction as "the features are all the same. They're just all a lot better." [18:22]

s8-bonus-the-code-dependency-revolution-solving-open-source-burnout-and-engineering-the-tearank-protocol-with-max-howell-creator-of-homebrew-founder-of-tea

Rewarding the Whole Dependency Tree: Tea uses package manager data to attribute value across open source, including deeply buried dependencies. Max cites Log4j as critical infrastructure that suffered a massive exploit yet remained basically unfunded.

teaRank Goes Beyond Dependencies: A version of Google's PageRank ranks projects daily, but experts warned dependency data alone could be gamed. The calculation takes hours and runs off chain, initially on a single node run by Tea.

Incentives Backed by Stake: Users and maintainers "steep" tokens into the protocol. Max also wants breaking semantic versioning to get you slashed, and has a future idea to slash stake over reported security problems.

Control That Shifts to Community: Tea will initially hold much of the governing power, but the protocol is programmed to reduce those rights over time. Onboarding projects are encouraged to form DAOs that decide how their tokens are distributed.

Launching the Package Manager Early: Max says Tea's package manager shipped too early, with design flaws and too much scope. It has since been refocused as a cross-platform package runner, similar to npx or pipx.

q: What is teaRank and how does it work?
a: Max Howell describes teaRank as the ranking engine that values open source projects relative to each other using dependency data and other factors. In his words, "we use a version of Google's PageRank to figure out the value of open source projects" [19:43]. It has to recalculate once a day for all of open source, with the work done off chain because doing it on chain would be too expensive.

q: Why don't donations solve open source funding?
a: Max argues that large enterprises depend on so many packages, 50,000 in his example, that they have no practical way to compensate them all. He said "part of the reason donations don't work is because these big enterprises" [08:55] rely on that many projects, and he sees Tea's crypto-based automation as the way to handle it.

q: What is steeping in the Tea protocol?
a: Steeping is Tea's riff on staking, where participants put tokens on a project and place them at risk. Max explained that users "and open source maintainers have to steep into the system to show that they are committed to the" [07:27] security of the network.

q: How did Homebrew first become popular?
a: Max Howell says Homebrew went unnoticed for six or seven weeks until he wrote a detailed Stack Overflow answer to a question from Simon Willison and pitched the tool at the end. His lesson from that moment is that with developers, "They trust the other developers they talk to." [30:08]

q: How is the Tea package manager different from Homebrew?
a: Max admits that early on he had no good answer when people asked what was wrong with Brew, since he sees nothing majorly wrong with it. He has since repositioned the product, saying "the tea package manager is now more of a package runner." [24:27] It is a cross-platform single binary for running open source tools, creating environments and writing scripts.

c73f5aff-67a6-4bfb-bd5c-29009dba04cb
s8-bonus-the-real-time-metadata-graph-moving-beyond-passive-data-catalogs-to-automated-event-driven-governance-with-shirshanka-das-co-founder-of-datahub-ceo-of-acryl-data

From Productivity Tool to Governance: DataHub began as an internal LinkedIn data discovery tool. GDPR work around 2016 showed it held the key to compliance, drawing more investment and growing it into an enterprise-wide data graph.

Community Before Commercials: To open DataHub to contributions, the team rewrote the front end and built a new ingestion framework, then helped users succeed. The community grew from about 200 people to 9,000 data practitioners.
Delaying Fortune 50 Deals: Despite inbound interest from big companies, Acryl held off signing Fortune 50 customers until its cloud product's stability and capabilities were ironed out.
Five Lists Shape the Roadmap: Planning draws on sales prospects, existing customers, technical debt, market-leader bets and the open source community, an approach Das credits to Jyoti Bansal.

One-Way and Two-Way Doors: Design reviews ask whether a decision can be reversed. Shortcuts that can be redone later are typically taken higher in the stack, while deeper platform choices get as much scalability as possible.

q: What problem led to the creation of DataHub?
a: Shirshanka Das saw that LinkedIn's data scientists and ML engineers struggled to find and choose the right data. As he put it, "people just didn't know where all the data lived and which" [03:40] data to use for their analysis.

q: What is the difference between DataHub and Acryl Cloud?
a: Shirshanka Das explains that DataHub is the open source metadata platform he built at LinkedIn, while Acryl Cloud is the commercial offering that adds capabilities on top of it. With the cloud product, "you get data discovery, data observability, and data governance integrated into one unified" [05:41] product.

q: What scaling challenges did Acryl face after DataHub left LinkedIn?
a: Shirshanka Das says the team had to add efficiency measures for the cloud and handle high-scale, time-oriented metadata from jobs such as Spark and Airflow runs. He noted that "There's a lot of time series metadata that comes in, like every single" [16:12] Spark job and Airflow task produces it.

q: What does shift left mean for metadata management?
a: Shirshanka Das describes it as moving metadata collection to where data is created, such as when building a dbt model, writing a DAG or checking in a schema. His pitch is to "just put the metadata right there along with it" [19:34], supported by tools that help teams do that.

q: What mistake do technical founders often make with customers?
a: Shirshanka Das says technical founders can quickly picture a solution on a sales or customer call and then underestimate how long it will take, partly because the team lacks the founder's context. His advice to his earlier self is that "being able to say no more often, being able to say we'll do that later, not right now." [27:02]

s8-e24-bypassing-the-wrapper-trap-to-engineer-model-agnostic-enterprise-rag-and-compliance-guardrails-with-jon-ricketts-co-founder-ceo-of-writerly

Three Product Iterations: Writerly began with foundation model APIs and prompt templates, built in 10 to 12 weeks mostly on UI and UX. It moved to a beta, then a commercial version with vertical products.

Ekom Pairs Data With Models: Ekom pulls in data from sources like Google, SEMrush, Ahrefs and SE Ranking, then instructs the language model to optimize product descriptions at scale for sellers with large catalogs.

Patience Over Chasing Competitors: With new application-layer companies appearing constantly, Ricketts says merely keeping up is a fool's errand. The team chose to let its data guide what to build and to focus on technical architecture.

Generalists First, Then Specialists: Ricketts hires the best possible generalists early, then uses them to identify the specialists needed where the company is investing. Culturally, the team tends to defer to domain experts while respecting consensus.

A Costly Vendor Contract: Terms with a tech stack provider fell through the cracks, leaving a rate probably five to six times what was needed. The team negotiated friendlier terms and learned that delegation still requires attention to detail.

q: What does Ekom by Writerly do for e-commerce businesses?
a: Ekom is a vertical product that came out of Writerly and applies generative AI to e-commerce, informed by search data sources. Jon Ricketts said "we help those that are selling digitally, particularly those with large product catalogs, be able to automate a lot of their product descriptions" [07:17].

q: How was the first version of Writerly built?
a: Jon Ricketts described a first iteration that took 10 to 12 weeks, with most of the work in the UI and UX. In his words, "we were APIing into foundation models and just discovering what we could do from a prompt engineering perspective to create templates" [05:28].

q: How does Writerly decide what goes on its product roadmap?
a: Ricketts said the roadmap reflects user data, customer conversations and analysis showing a large enough market, while the company influences prioritization. He explained that they have purposefully opened "our roadmap up to our customers and the users that we're serving" [08:38].

q: Was Writerly built to scale from the start?
a: Yes, Jon Ricketts said Writerly and products like Ekom were built to scale from day one, to avoid a damaging refactor later. He summed up the business and technical decision as preferring to "rather have it and not need it than need it and not have it" [12:41].

q: What mistake did Writerly make with a third-party tech vendor?
a: Ricketts said the terms of what the company was getting for its money fell through the cracks while the team was heads down building. The result was a provider "at a contracted rate that was probably five to six times what we really needed" [15:49], and the company later worked out friendlier terms.

s8-bonus-engineering-conversational-natural-language-engines-for-elasticsearch-and-overthrowing-the-sql-middleman-with-tim-tutt-co-founder-ceo-of-clearquery

A Feature Became the Product: ClearQuery began as a natural-language question feature in an insider threat product. When a pitch audience asked to buy just that, the team spent another three months building it out on its own.

Elasticsearch Chosen for Scale: The MVP used React, Node.js, Python for intent understanding and Elasticsearch for storage and analytics. Picking Elasticsearch was deliberate, based on the founders' large-scale government search work.

Answers Without Knowing the Question: An early customer said analysts didn't always know what to ask. The team built automated insights, which highlights interesting statistics as soon as data is uploaded.

Plan for Unexpected Questions: A large customer's unusually structured data led to invalid or missing responses. The team revamped error handling, added ways to collect user feedback and began tracking much more logging data.

Bootstrapped on Customer Revenue: Tutt said the roadmap followed customer needs and revenue. The company has 25 people, no outside capital and, at the time of the interview, was exceeding $10 million in ARR that year.

q: Why was ClearQuery created?
a: Tim Tutt had been the technical middleman in government work, writing queries for analysts and returning answers in a repeating cycle. He and his co-founder asked, "wouldn't it be great if we could just get ourselves out of the way, effectively automate ourselves out of a job" [03:42].

q: What tech stack was used to build the ClearQuery MVP?
a: Tutt said ClearQuery is a React web application with a Node.js backend, and the initial MVP used Python for intent understanding and some entity extraction. On the data side, he explained, "We leveraged Elasticsearch very heavily as our workhorse for storing data and running a lot of the analytics" [07:33].

q: What is ClearQuery's automated insights feature?
a: It grew out of customer feedback that analysts didn't always know where to begin with their data. Tutt explained, "What automated insights does is actually analyzes your data for you" [11:40], then presents interesting statistics as soon as the data is uploaded.

q: What mistake did the ClearQuery team learn from?
a: A large customer's data was structured differently than expected, and users' questions sometimes got invalid responses or none at all. Tutt said, "that actually caused us to go back and do a big revamp in terms of how we handled some of those error cases" [17:42].

q: What advice does Tim Tutt give young entrepreneurs?
a: Tutt advises founders to just start, without waiting for an idea to be fully formed and finished. He urges them to get "it into the hands of customers as soon as you possibly can, because those customers will tell" [23:42] you what you're missing.

s8-bonus-the-multi-vendor-telemetry-playbook-scaling-collaboration-intelligence-and-the-road-to-an-hp-acquisition-with-alfredo-ramirez-co-founder-ceo-of-vyopta
Services Before Product: Starting amid the 2007-2008 financial crisis, Vyopta built custom live-video applications to earn revenue and limit the co-founders' risk instead of raising money for an MVP.

Pivot With Customers in Hand: Vyopta pivoted to Unified Communications Performance Management, proved it with upsells in 2015 and raised a Series A in 2016. Ramirez says comfort with services revenue delayed the move.

Roadmap in Concentric Circles: Vyopta began with reliable, high-quality video, then expanded to voice and beyond. As Teams and Zoom gained share during the pandemic, it accelerated coverage beyond its Cisco focus.

Partners Need Real Commitment: Leaning on large resellers that hadn't invested in training led to poorly sold enterprise deals and a "big black eye." Vyopta now favors a smaller partner set that builds real competency.

One Codebase, Faster Growth: Putting its cloud product on-premise for large customers created two codebases. After retiring the on-prem one, Ramirez says new and expansion ARR has been doubling quarter over quarter.

q: What does Vyopta do?
a: Vyopta focuses on what Alfredo Ramirez calls collaboration intelligence, helping enterprises deliver more reliable, better experiences on live video and voice. As Ramirez put it, "We're all about making collaboration work from anywhere." [02:36]

q: How did Vyopta get started during the 2008 financial crisis?
a: Alfredo Ramirez and his co-founders started with a services business, building custom software that brought live video into functions like customer service, court hearings and distance education. The goal was to reduce risk, and Ramirez described the thinking as "Let's just go ahead and generate some revenue, get some customers on board." [06:27]

q: What is Vyopta's user experience score for collaboration?
a: It is a score that lets large IT teams quantify the service they provide to users and expose where problems are, rather than only checking that the technology is running. Ramirez said, "we have developed an algorithmic score that leverages the data we collect from different collaboration technologies" [12:35].

q: Why did Vyopta rebuild its platform?
a: Ramirez said the early .NET and SQL Server architecture didn't scale in cost or work effectively as a multi-tenant cloud solution, and the company decided in 2019 to invest in a rebuild. In his words, "we migrated to a modern microservices, big data lake architecture to support the scale and cost" [09:50].

q: What would Alfredo Ramirez do differently if he started Vyopta again?
a: Ramirez would pivot from custom application work to the product much sooner, saying the team got too comfortable with services revenue. He reflected, "I'd say if we could have pivoted sooner, we could have been much further along" [19:24].

s8-e23-the-multimodal-data-blueprint-structuring-the-unseen-80-of-enterprise-visual-data-without-metadata-tagging-with-will-gaviria-co-founder-of-coactive-ai
Visual Data Meets SQL: Coactive brings unstructured visual data into structured tools like SQL, offering search, dynamic tagging and analytics for both technical and non-technical users.

A Two-Stage MVP: Core functionality took about three months in a Jupyter notebook. Roughly three more went into a React and FastAPI web app after demos showed the notebook confused non-technical stakeholders.
Choosing Category Creation: Rather than plug into existing workflows, Coactive chose to create a new category, then aligned the team by reading Play Bigger in a company-wide book club.

Enterprise Table Stakes Early: Beyond returning results from terabytes in seconds, Coactive prioritized security and reliability from the start, including early certification work and internal and external SLAs.
Culture as a Product: Before hiring anyone, Will and Cody wrote down their culture and published it on GitHub, where it has a commit history and people can submit pull requests.

q: What does Coactive AI do?
a: Will Gaviria describes Coactive as an enterprise B2B SaaS that unlocks the value of visual content for uses such as search and analytics. He said it brings that data "into the world of structured data such as SQL and other big data tools" [03:01].

q: How does Coactive's dynamic tagging differ from static tags?
a: Gaviria explained that users control the tags, including how they are defined and how they evolve, and can version them much like code. The goal is to move people from static tags to "a world where tags are like a living and breathing thing" [03:52].

q: How was the first version of Coactive built?
a: Gaviria said the first stage used Python, Spark, scikit-learn and PyTorch in a Jupyter notebook, followed by a web application built on React and FastAPI. With less off-the-shelf AI software in 2021, he noted that "we had to build an in-house vector database when one didn't exist" [06:42].

q: How does Coactive decide what to build on its roadmap?
a: Gaviria said the team listens to customers, works out what success they will pay for, and builds a roadmap to deliver it. He credits company advisor Ken Coleman with the idea that "customers don't buy a product, they buy success" [10:38].

q: What would Will Gaviria do differently if he started Coactive again?
a: Gaviria would put even more weight on the founding hunch that AI should be accessible, a lesson reinforced by the simplicity of ChatGPT's interface. As he put it, "If there's anything I'll do differently now is I will double down" [24:24].

s8-bonus-bypassing-brittle-custom-scripts-implementing-automated-multi-tenant-configuration-backups-and-vulnerability-patching-at-scale-with-andrew-kahl-of-backbox
Automation for Network Upkeep: BackBox automates keeping enterprise network devices compliant, patched and running, and lets a network that goes down be brought back as it was configured.

Loyalty Signaled a Strong Base: BackBox's heritage was network backup and recovery. In due diligence, customer loyalty, retention and service levels that customers rated above some large enterprise vendors stood out to Kahl.

Building a Demand Engine: At acquisition there was no marketing department, SEO or lead generation, just one or two big events a year. Most investment went into go-to-market, including building out a North American sales team.

Paid Search Before Messaging: Early growth capital went heavily into paid search and Google ads before messaging, buyers and competitors were clear. The fix was to pause, ask customers why they buy, and build that into the messaging.
Make Hard Calls Faster: Kahl wanted to respect what was built, but in hindsight would have moved three to six months sooner on tough decisions about investment, people or strategic direction.

q: What does BackBox do?
a: BackBox does network automation, helping ensure devices on a corporate network are compliant, patched and kept up and running. Andrew Kahl compares it to reconnecting and securing devices on a home network, but says of BackBox, "We do it for the enterprise at scale." [03:43]

q: Why was BackBox an attractive company to acquire?
a: Andrew Kahl points to a good product, strong retention and service that impressed customers during due diligence. What excited him "is the absolute customer loyalty and the solid product that they have." [05:00]

q: How did BackBox change its go-to-market after the acquisition?
a: Andrew Kahl says the company had relied on one or two large events a year for leads, and that "there was no consistent demand engine." [06:40] The new team worked on a marketing plan, target regions and messaging, and built out a North American sales organization.

q: What marketing mistake did Andrew Kahl make at BackBox?
a: Kahl says the company misapplied some investment before its messaging and target buyers were nailed down: "we spent a lot of money very early on in paid search words and Google-based advertising." [12:49] The team paused, talked to customers about why they buy and reworked the messaging, which then produced the results they wanted.

q: What is the future vision for BackBox?
a: Andrew Kahl said of the product, "I want us to be really a network automation platform." [13:38] He describes a central piece of IT infrastructure where customers can see when devices are compliant or at risk, with APIs that align with other critical systems and tools.

s8-bonus-the-data-asset-revolution-moving-beyond-imperative-task-pipelines-to-declarative-orchestration-with-pete-hunt-co-founder-of-react-ceo-of-dagster-labs

The Pivot to Data Assets: Users called Dagster the best orchestrator, but not good enough to leave Airflow. Software-defined assets replaced task sequences with declarative code, and 75% of customers used the feature within a year.

Caveman Planning for Roadmaps: Dagster Labs collected 300 project pitches from across the company. Executives ranked every one against company goals, which made themes clear and prioritization decisions trivial.
A Late Bet on Serverless: Six weeks before the 1.0 launch, the team added a fully hosted option despite security and abuse risks. Hunt says Dagster Cloud Serverless was a huge success.

Check Intuition With Customers: Hunt's next idea, having Dagster configure ETL tools much like Terraform, took a top engineer over a month and didn't land. He says he should have run it by customers much earlier.

Stress Test Before Launch: Early on, a design partner with tens of thousands of pipelines pushed the system. Now the team defines an SLA, stresses new features until they break, and optimizes if they can't handle customer scale.

q: What is Dagster and what is it used for?
a: Dagster is an open source data orchestrator from Dagster Labs, used by data engineers to produce clean, usable data assets. Pete Hunt describes it as "a Python library framework and system for building and operating data pipelines" [02:44].

q: Why did Dagster move from task-based pipelines to software-defined assets?
a: Pete Hunt explains that everyone was building pipelines as sequences of tasks, and "that is not how developers think of the problem" [10:40]. With software-defined assets, developers write declarative code describing how to build each data asset, which helps them trace broken data back to the code that produced it.

q: How did Dagster Labs build its product roadmap?
a: Hunt ran what he calls caveman planning: make a big list of everything to do, sort it by priority and work through it in order. As he put it, "step one was we solicited pitches from everyone in the organization" [13:22], and the executive team then triaged all 300 against company goals.

q: How does Dagster Labs test new features for scale?
a: Hunt says the team instruments each new feature, decides on an SLA and how to measure it, then stresses the system to find where it breaks. "And if it breaks at a sufficiently high load, we are happy with it and we ship it" [18:02]; otherwise, they keep optimizing.

q: What did Pete Hunt learn from a feature that didn't land with customers?
a: Hunt championed a feature that let Dagster configure ETL tools such as Fivetran or Airbyte, but customers didn't respond as expected. He still believes startups require intuition, but says "it is important to do your best to try to objectively check that your" [22:44] intuition isn't wrong, ideally with customers before spending months prototyping.

s8-e22-the-identity-orchestration-blueprint-unifying-multi-cloud-security-and-bypassing-legacy-app-refactoring-with-eric-olden-co-founder-ceo-of-strata-identity

Interviews Before Code: Strata waited almost nine months before writing code and ran close to 150 interviews about customers' most painful problems. Eric Olden advises open-ended questions, because leading ones invite confirmation bias.

Orchestrators Near the Apps: Strata, built on Go, deploys identity orchestrators close to applications across public, private and hybrid environments. They work in concert, so one policy can secure workloads on both Azure and AWS.

The Dozen-Customer Test: Olden asks early customers how they'd spend a metaphorical dollar. Of 12, he likes about six who love the product, three who show how to expand it, and two or three who mark what Strata won't build.

No Salespeople for Two Years: The early team of six covered software, product, operations, sales engineering and marketing. Olden left sales out so market feedback reached the people building the product without being diluted.

Security and Scale From Day One: Stateless sessions, no single point of failure and no passwords were designed in early. The executable is under 30 MB, and capacity grows by adding more orchestrators.

q: What does Strata Identity do?
a: Strata provides identity orchestration, an abstraction layer that decouples applications from infrastructure so they can use different identity systems without being rewritten. Co-founder and CEO Eric Olden compares it to virtualization, saying "what we're building is the VMware of identity" [03:41].

q: How does Strata manage identity across multiple clouds?
a: Strata deploys orchestrators, typically near the applications being secured, on whichever cloud runs the workload. Olden explained that the company can "make all of these identity orchestrators work in concert with one another" [05:39], so the same policy can apply on Azure and AWS.

q: How did Strata Identity approach building its MVP?
a: Olden said the team spent months asking people about their problems before coding, and built the platform on Go for performance and security. In his words, "we built our MVP actually waited almost nine months before we started" [04:18] writing code.

q: Why are there no passwords in Strata's software?
a: Olden noted that most security breaches involve compromised passwords, so Strata designed them out and relies on alternatives such as passkeys, multi-factor authentication, OpenID Connect and SAML. As he described the decision, "we said, look, there'll never be a password in" [18:35] Strata software.

q: What mistake from a previous company shaped how Eric Olden built Strata?
a: At Symplified, Olden's team supported both SaaS and on-premises versions, which spread them thin and left customers running old software. Despite the millions in on-premises revenue, he said, "what it wound up costing us was a lot more than the revenue that we got" [23:02].

s8-bonus-edtech-scale-engine-bypassing-video-bootcamps-with-live-code-execution-and-ai-guided-mentorship-rails-with-barak-glanz-co-founder-of-coddytech

Practice Over Goal-Oriented Courses: Coddy teaches code through practice and borrows from Duolingo, using streaks, achievements and leaderboards to make learning a daily habit instead of a course people abandon after two or three months.

A Deliberately Small MVP: The first version paired an online Python compiler with a short beginner course bought through Fiverr. It was free, and the team added content, languages and libraries in small steps to confirm demand.

Freemium Built on Daily Limits: Coddy stayed free with a cap on daily usage, which suits the vast majority of users. Power users who want hours of unlimited learning can upgrade to premium for $10 per month.

B2B Detour Cost Three Months: Despite believing in B2C, the team followed experienced businesspeople and pitched an unready product to American institutes. Nothing sold, and billing was delayed. University sales later worked well.

Bootstrapped and Data-Driven: The three founders spend less than they earn and report about 20% monthly growth in newly acquired customers. They built an internal analytics tool, RapidSight, inspired by Monday's BigBrain, to guide decisions.

q: What is Coddy.tech and how does it teach coding?
a: Barak Glanz describes Coddy as "an online platform focused on teaching code in a practice-driven way." [03:17] It is fully gamified with features such as streaks, achievements and leaderboards, with the aim of turning code learning into a daily habit.

q: How did Coddy build its MVP?
a: Barak Glanz said the team started with a very minimal product: "we built an integrated compiler for Python" [04:50]. They paid someone on Fiverr to create a short beginner Python course, then sent it to people to try for free to check for demand.

q: How does Coddy's freemium pricing model work?
a: Barak Glanz explained that the team kept the product free for everyone, "but we put a limitation over the daily usage" [07:52]. Power users who want to learn without limits, sometimes for two or three hours a day, convert to premium at $10 per month.

q: Why did Coddy stick with B2C instead of becoming a B2B platform?
a: Barak Glanz said experienced businesspeople urged a B2B approach, and the team listened "even though deep inside we knew this is a mistake" [13:31]. About three months of selling to American institutes produced no sales, though selling to university computer science faculties later began working well once the product had matured.

q: What is the junior problem Coddy wants to solve?
a: Barak Glanz said fresh grads and people with little experience "struggle to find their first position in tech companies." [15:40] His vision is that once Coddy has millions of users, it can spot talented coders and connect them with interested tech companies.

s8-bonus-the-college-matchmaking-engine-replacing-opaque-university-rankings-with-predictive-culture-analytics-and-david-hurwitt-founder-ceo-of-troove

Alumni Patterns Drive Matching: Troove uses data science and AI to find the academic and social patterns behind graduates' happiness and success, then turns them into a digital filter that shows new students how well they fit a school.

National Coverage From Day One: The MVP took about a year. Troove bought public data on roughly 4,000 U.S. colleges so students could match with any of them, then supplements a signed school's data with about 400 surveys.

Free for Students, Paid by Schools: After beta, Troove revisited charging consumers but kept the service free to families. With early-stage capital hard to raise and consumer features costly to build, it doubled down on selling to schools first.

Beta Exposes the Friction: Higher ed timing mattered, since most students have applied soon after the new year. Friction also varied: a SUNY school signed beta contracts in about 10 days, while a much smaller private school struggled.

Correct Hiring Mistakes Quickly: A business development hire was accomplished but not an early-stage fit and wasn't delivering the results Hurwitt wanted. He ended it decisively rather than bleed capital trying to avoid admitting the mistake.

q: What inspired David Hurwitt to start Troove?
a: A college visit with his daughter went badly, and Spotify and Yelp then quickly improved the mood and found them a great dinner. Hurwitt realized their matching was "profoundly more effective than this quarter million dollar decision about where she was going to go to college" [05:12].

q: How does Troove match students with colleges?
a: Troove learns from each school's graduates which academic and social patterns mattered to their happiness and success, then uses them as a filter for prospective students. As Hurwitt explained, "take the existing users. The largest part of every school are the graduates." [05:38].

q: Is Troove free for students and families?
a: Yes, the service is free to students and their families and is paid for by schools. Hurwitt tied this to unequal graduation outcomes, saying "we want to levelize the playing field with technology." [11:26].

q: How was the first version of Troove built?
a: It took about a year, during which Hurwitt, a non-coder, built a network, raised angel capital and ran a beta with three schools in Western New York. He wanted students to know that "from day one, they'd be able to match with any school in the country" [06:49].

q: What advice does David Hurwitt have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Hurwitt advises listening to others only to a point, and pairing passion with a thoughtful strategy and plan. In his words, "trust yourself, trust your instincts, and let that passion flow out of you." [24:58].

s8-e21-the-hubspot-of-inventory-overthrowing-netsuite-lock-in-and-automating-multi-channel-supply-chain-rails-with-jared-ward-founder-ceo-of-luminous

Build From Inside the Customer: Jared took a Director of Supply Chain job at a brand matching his ideal customer, openly building Luminous there. The MVP tackled one module at a time and took almost a year to get past beta.

Simple Concepts Hide Complexity: Inventory management looked easy on paper, so the team replaced SkuVault with its own build. It was so hacky that they had to rebuild it all, teaching Jared to scope the work and study the market first.

Prove It, Then Scale: Jared spent $70,000 to $100,000 of his own money on an MVP that ran as separate single-tenant instances per client. CTO Brendan turned it into a one-codebase SaaS product in his first three months.

Backwards B2B Design Won: Luminous built invoicing and a B2B portal very differently from big ERPs like NetSuite. It became the most adopted feature, with some companies running 2,000 invoices a year through it.

The Margin Report Flop: Building from an employee's first-draft Google Sheet produced what Jared calls the worst feature they've built. Even the client who inspired it didn't use it, so every feature now starts with the problem being solved.

q: What is Luminous and who is it for?
a: Founder and CEO Jared Ward describes it this way: "Luminous is an all-in-one supply chain and inventory solution for the modern e-commerce brand" [02:37]. He sees a gap for a system of record that does for e-commerce inventory what HubSpot did for SMB CRM.

q: How did Jared Ward build the Luminous MVP?
a: Jared joined a direct-to-consumer, multi-channel brand as its director of supply chain and was transparent that building Luminous was his main motivation. His pitch included a promise to "save you a crap ton of money as your director of supply chain" [05:27], and the product was then built one module at a time around that brand's needs.

q: Why is building inventory management software harder than it looks?
a: Jared says inventory management was his biggest underestimation, even though "conceptually inventory management is simple" [07:49]. The team's first version was built in such a hacky way that it had to be rebuilt.

q: How does Luminous handle B2B wholesale and invoicing?
a: Luminous has its own invoicing tool and B2B portal, which can support inventory in multiple countries and different client pricing tiers. Jared says the design was the opposite of the large ERPs, "But at the end of the day, it's actually been our most adopted feature." [15:56]

q: How does Luminous decide what to build next?
a: Jared credits CTO Brendan with teaching him to research the market, say no, and shape a roadmap. He recalls Brendan responding to big ideas by asking, "But why would we build that right now?" [10:16]

s8-bonus-engineering-text-to-video-ai-automation-and-scaling-to-millions-of-users-with-vikram-chalana-co-founder-ceo-of-pictory

Simplicity Over Flexibility: Pictory deliberately made more choices for users, since they weren't professional video editors. The goal was that anyone who can use PowerPoint should be able to use the product easily.

Cloud Rendering's Lasting Cost: Rendering video in the cloud let anyone use Pictory from any computer or browser, without heavy hardware. The trade-off later proved expensive, and Vikram says the company is still paying for it.

Finding the Creator Market: The MVP took about nine months, but finding the right market took a year. Enterprises wouldn't commit, partly because their marketing was agency-heavy, while creators brought strong traction.
A Public, Voted Roadmap: Pictory published its roadmap and let customers vote on the features they wanted. That input, along with community polls, helps define what the team builds.

Scaling Under Pressure: Growing from 50 to 5,000 customers in three months was an intense server scaling exercise. A later growth surge showed that systems already in place weren't meant to scale and had to change.

q: What problem led to the creation of Pictory?
a: Vikram Chalana saw content marketing shift toward video, yet at his previous company of about 350 employees, only one person was equipped to make videos. After finding tools like Adobe Premiere and Camtasia complicated, he said, "I felt like there has to be a better way" [03:59].

q: How was the Pictory MVP built and how long did it take?
a: A small team started in fall 2019, using a wide range of AWS tools with a Python backend and React frontend. Vikram said that "we were able to launch our first MVP in production by June of 2020" [04:19].

q: How did Pictory find product-market fit?
a: Pictory first targeted larger enterprises, which showed enthusiasm but didn't want to commit when it came time to buy. Vikram's team then explored adjacent markets, and as he put it, "we finally found this traction with the creator segment" [08:59].

q: What is the future of Pictory's AI video platform?
a: Vikram described integrating ChatGPT and generative AI, exploring voice cloning, avatars and automatic script generation, and moving upmarket to serve larger companies. He also wants to use video performance to guide new videos, saying "what we're hoping to build in the future is a feedback loop about videos" [17:03].

q: What advice does Vikram Chalana have for young entrepreneurs?
a: Vikram encourages founders to pursue their ideas fully, because the experience is invaluable whether or not they succeed. He also warns them to be ready to pivot: "don't get too attached to your initial idea or your initial sense of the market" [19:33].

s8-bonus-the-bare-metal-database-revolution-engineering-c-thread-per-core-systems-and-overthrowing-the-jvm-with-dor-laor-co-creator-of-kvm-ceo-of-scylladb

A Pivot Born From Benchmarks: While showing that databases ran faster on their new operating system, the team found Cassandra didn't. They traced this to its Java implementation and pivoted to building a database.

Shard-Per-Core in Modern C++: ScyllaDB runs one thread per processor with a shared-nothing design. The team first built the Seastar library and a basic HTTP daemon that handled millions of requests per second on one machine.

Compatibility Set the Early Roadmap: The first job was matching Cassandra's API, with better performance, so users could migrate without client-side code changes. Unique features and DynamoDB compatibility came later.
