Overshooting on Scale: The team ran a billion-operations-per-second benchmark that Dor says no one needs. It also built TCP kernel bypass, then never used it in production.
Commit to SaaS Earlier: Dor wishes ScyllaDB had shifted to a cloud-native, as-a-service model much sooner. He also says the team working on that service started too small for its goals.

q: Why was ScyllaDB built in C++ instead of Java?
a: Dor Laor says the team found Cassandra, written in Java, had a scalable design but weaker per-unit economics in its implementation. In his words, "Java is a great language for management application," [04:41] but not for infrastructure, so ScyllaDB was written in modern C++.

q: What is ScyllaDB's shard-per-core architecture?
a: It is a shared-nothing design in which a server with 20 processors runs 20 threads that all do the same work. Dor explains that "The shard per core is a notion where you run one thread on one processor." [06:24]

q: How did ScyllaDB decide what to build first after its MVP?
a: Dor says API compatibility with Cassandra made the early roadmap easier, since users needed to migrate without changing client code. As he put it, "We just needed to implement the API and in a much better way than the origin" [08:29].

q: What was the biggest mistake in ScyllaDB's early history?
a: Dor points to the company's first project, a new operating system meant to compete with Linux for virtualization workloads, and says the team was slow to recognize the problem. He admits, "The whole original project was a mistake and it was relatively hard to recover from it." [13:51]

q: What advice does Dor Laor give young founders?
a: He recommends finding someone you fully trust and can share everything with. He also suggests testing good advice against an opposing view: "try to receive another advice, a counter advice that have an opposite outcome" [21:25], then decide between the two.

s8-e20-extracting-context-from-chaos-implementing-real-time-nlp-semantic-parsing-and-automated-action-item-routing-with-artem-koren-of-sembly-ai

Many Pieces Before Viable: Sembly's MVP needed to attend, record, transcribe, diarize, analyze and present meetings. Starting in 2019, transcription was unsolved and diarization generally unavailable, so the team had to innovate on the fly.

Skeleton First, Then Build Out: A professional shop built the basic SaaS framework on a Postgres, Django and React stack. A core team of about five developers in Ukraine, guided closely by Artem, took it further, with an MVP in roughly six or seven months.

Enterprise Fit Wasn't Usability: Sembly first targeted large companies, but individual users found it confusing. A pivot to a simple, polished individual experience came first, and features were added once uptake grew.

Scaling for Top-of-Hour Spikes: Meetings tend to start and end at the same times, and activity drops after work hours. Docker and Kubernetes often weren't enough, so Sembly built custom scaling to handle peaks and manage cloud costs.

Build Telemetry Earlier: Sembly added telemetry much later than was optimal, leaving the team flying blind on what was failing, why and who was affected. It now tracks the user journey, including languages, call length and feature use.

q: What is Sembly AI and how does it work?
a: Artem Koren describes Sembly AI as an AI teammate or meeting assistant that joins Microsoft Teams, Google Meet or Zoom calls and afterward produces a transcript, notes, tasks and other insights. In his words, "It's an application that you invite to your online meetings." [02:42]

q: Why was building an AI meeting assistant MVP so difficult?
a: Artem Koren said Sembly had to get recording, transcription, diarization, analysis and presentation all working together before the product was usable. When development began in 2019, he recalled, transcription "was an unsolved problem. Diarization was generally not available." [07:43]

q: Why did Sembly AI shift its focus from enterprises to individual users?
a: Artem Koren explained that the product was styled for large companies, and once it reached their users, many found it hard to understand and didn't know what to do with it. The team pivoted to a version "where we made the experience, the user experience, very simple, very intuitive, very easy" [09:34].

q: How did Sembly AI handle scalability as it grew?
a: Artem Koren said the team built with scale in mind but prioritized real features over a complex scalability test suite, so growing traffic revealed the weak spots. "With every growth spurt, we would identify kind of the next weakest link in the environment" [13:11], he said, and the team then patched it.

q: What advice does Artem Koren give founders about product-market fit?
a: Artem Koren advises taking all advice with a grain of salt, while listening widely and checking whether people show growing enthusiasm for what you're building. He urges founders to "pay attention to those like very intuitive indicators that there's a pull for your product." [22:46]

s8-bonus-the-45m-github-for-docs-experiment-engineering-git-style-version-control-for-asynchronous-business-teams-with-adam-nathan-co-founder-ceo-of-almanac

Templates as the Skateboard: Almanac started with the Almanac Core, a free template repository. Nathan estimates it drew hundreds of thousands of users in year one while the team worked toward a much bigger product.

Selling Before Building: To test Handbooks, the team used a landing page, a Figma prototype and a couple hundred dollars of ads. Nathan recalls 30 or 40 customers entering credit cards within a month, against a goal of 100 in three months.

Suggested Changes for Living Docs: Anyone can mark up a private layer of a document and submit it to the owner, who merges it or sends it back. This addressed wikis that teams found hard to maintain and trust.

Pulling the Andon Cord: Facing low retention and quality complaints, Almanac spent about four months only fixing existing features. It added 24/7 on-call and weekly batched releases, and Nathan says it now has net negative churn.

Avoiding the Art Project: Nathan once had engineers build his idea from PRDs, only to find nobody wanted it. Now the team tests ideas cheaply; the landing page headline he thought was best recently placed last out of 10 variants.

q: What is Almanac and what problem does it solve?
a: Almanac is a wiki and document workflow tool that Adam Nathan likens to GitHub for business teams, with asynchronous feedback and approvals. Nathan describes it as "a single source of truth for teams of all kinds, remote, distributed, in person" [02:46].

q: How do Almanac Handbooks keep company documentation up to date?
a: Anyone in the company can create a private layer on a document, suggest changes and submit them to the owner for approval. Nathan described living documentation "where anyone in the company could update it as things, as context progressed" [11:22], while control stayed with the owner.

q: How did Almanac validate demand before building Handbooks?
a: The team put up a landing page, made a Figma prototype and ran a small amount of ads, then asked people to pay after only a demo or conversation. As Adam Nathan put it, "The trick was that customers had to sign up for the product" [11:59] before they had access to it.

q: How did Almanac fix its product quality and retention problems?
a: Borrowing Toyota's Andon cord concept, the team stopped its roadmap, refactored the product piece by piece, started an on-call program and moved to weekly releases. Nathan said that "for probably four months, we did nothing but just fix existing features" [17:09].

q: What startup mistake does Adam Nathan warn founders about?
a: Nathan calls it the art project mistake: building your own vision without checking whether people want it. In his words, "the point of a business isn't to build an art project" [21:50], and he says talking to people is the way to check.

s8-bonus-overcoming-100x-ai-code-velocity-and-enterprise-vulnerability-noise-with-idan-plotnik-co-founder-ceo-of-apiiro

Inventory Before Everything Else: Apiiro's core is a graph-based inventory of code components and their relationships. Third-party scanner data and its own risk engine are layered on top to form a "risk graph" for prioritizing fixes.

An MVP That Reveals Unknowns: The first version scanned two languages with a custom static analysis engine, surfacing things like APIs writing sensitive data to logs. Customers connected their source control through a read-only API.

Go Broad, Then Deep: Customers' varied stacks and scanners pushed Apiiro to integrate widely. Its workflow engine then expanded from prioritizing and remediating risk to prevention, including blocking pull requests and builds.

Scale Came Through Iteration: Microservices and Kubernetes weren't enough for enterprises with 150,000-200,000 code repos. Apiiro also had to support on-prem and SaaS, while analyzing code history and each new commit in near real time.

Don't Hold Every Role: Idan says he brought in a CRO at least six months too late and wrongly believed he could be CEO, VP of product and VP of marketing at once. He felt the size of that mistake when Moti joined as chief product officer.

q: What problem does Apiiro solve for application security and development teams?
a: Apiiro is an application security posture management (ASPM) platform that enriches alerts from existing tools with context, calculates risk and finds code owners. Idan Plotnik felt the pain as a GM at Microsoft, where, he said, "Most of these alerts were not relevant, were not reachable in the code, were not" [04:18].

q: What did the first version of Apiiro do?
a: Idan Plotnik's team built its own static analysis engine and started by scanning two languages, exposing sensitive data written to logs, deprecated frameworks and code that could be deleted. He described the aha moment as "just showing them things that they don't know" [07:35].

q: What is the core technology behind Apiiro's risk graph?
a: Apiiro maps every code component and the relationships between them, then adds data from third-party scanners and its own risk engine. Idan Plotnik was clear about what matters most: "But the foundation of our success is the inventory." [10:49]

q: How does Apiiro scale for large enterprises that need on-prem deployment?
a: Idan Plotnik said the microservices and Kubernetes foundation was scalable but not enough, and getting there took time and a lot of learning. Some customers will not expose code to the cloud, which means a design that is, in his words, "very challenging architecture to support both on-prem private clusters and" [17:06] fully software as a service.

q: What advice does Idan Plotnik give founders about launching a startup?
a: Idan Plotnik advises founders not to launch until they have customers who will publicly advocate for what they built, a mistake he says he made at a previous startup. Do not launch, he warned, "if you don't have real customers" [27:21].

s8-e19-the-124m-scale-up-playbook-engineering-contextual-ai-and-b2b-invoice-orchestration-engines-to-kill-procurement-friction-with-yann-ravel-sibillot-co-founder-ceo-of-flowie

Merging Both Sides of Invoicing: Flowie brings procure-to-pay and order-to-cash into one platform to ease communication between companies. Yann likens it to an agent that handles invoice validation and payment inside your tools.

Figma Before Real Software: The first version was a Figma with automation that clients could use as if it were a true environment. A demo followed, with React.js on the front end and some Node.js on the back.

An Early Event-Based Bet: Because invoices are sensitive, the team relied on Auth0 for authentication and built an event-based Kotlin backend on GCP. Yann calls it a big investment for a startup that is already paying off.

Reorder the Carpaccio Slices: Yann cuts the client's pain into thin slices, then reorders them so each small, continuously deployed piece has the biggest possible client impact. The product can end up very different from where it started.
Users Before Beautiful Code: Flowie focused too much on craftsmanship principles and code beauty. Having no technical debt is good, Yann says, but getting live users matters more at first.

q: What is Flowie and what problem does it solve?
a: Flowie is a platform for communication between companies around invoices, born from a problem Yann Ravel-Sibillot had as CTO of an Italian restaurant group. Describing the product, Yann said "you will merge the process of procure to pay and order to cash" [03:15] within the same platform.

q: How did Flowie build its MVP?
a: Yann started with clients and a narrow focus on communication between companies, before moving on to a demo and an event-based backend. As he put it, "we started with a Figma. Nothing more than that." [04:02]

q: What is the elephant carpaccio approach to building a product?
a: Yann describes the client's pain as an elephant that can't be solved all at once, so you slice it thinly and order the slices by client impact. In his words, you "will cut it like a carpaccio very thin slice" [05:52].

q: What mistake did the Flowie team make early on?
a: Yann says the team focused too much on craftsmanship and a clean codebase instead of getting a live user. He explained, "It's good to not have any technical debt, but we were more thinking about the beauty" [11:38] of the code.

q: What is Yann Ravel-Sibillot's advice for finding product-market fit?
a: Yann advises finding several clients who share a problem, even if they describe it differently, then building something as simple as possible with no code before expanding. He said to "find clients that have a common problem, not one, at least two, three is better, five is perfect." [15:19]

s8-bonus-bypassing-the-excel-accounting-trap-architecting-high-throughput-bank-api-connectors-and-rule-matching-engines-with-danielle-shaul-of-nilus

Build the Software You Wanted: At Fundbox, Danielle Shaul's team had to build financial workflow tools in-house. Nilus, co-founded with Daniel, who came from PayPal, turns that roadmap into a product for other finance teams.

Data Pipelines Came First: The MVP took about six months, after a year of validation. Its base layer was bank integrations, data pipelines, and validation and completeness checks so customers get up-to-date, verified data.

Microservices for a Rainy Day: Nilus chose microservices over a monolith despite a harder start and heavy tooling needs. Shaul expected a monolith would eventually hit limits on what the system could do.

Test Willingness to Pay Early: Research was not the same as selling. The team learned to ask early whether people would pay, how much, whether the product would help day to day, and how many hours it would save.

In-Office Team With FinTech Roots: The team of about 20 is almost entirely from FinTech, and roughly half previously worked with Shaul. Nilus traded a global talent pool for in-person whiteboard brainstorms, and recognizes standout work weekly.

q: What is Nilus and what does it do?
a: Nilus is a platform that helps finance teams gather information across banks and payment processors, get insights and automate their workflows, including month-end close. Danielle Shaul, its co-founder and CTO, describes it simply: "Nilus is a financial operations platform." [08:25]

q: Why did Danielle Shaul start Nilus?
a: While at Fundbox, an SMB lender, Shaul found no existing software to automate financial workflows, so the team built everything internally. She says, "So I kind of now building the software I wish I had back in the days." [04:14]

q: How many banks does Nilus connect to, and how?
a: Shaul says Nilus connects to banks through APIs, SFTP, screen scraping and other methods, then builds algorithms on top of that data. In her words, "To this day, we're connected to over 20,000 different banks" [05:40].

q: Why did Nilus choose microservices instead of a monolith?
a: Shaul wanted to avoid eventually hitting the limits of what a monolithic system could do, even though microservices took time to get right and required a lot of tooling. She explains, "But I knew that I'm making this investment for a rainy day." [12:45]

q: What mistake did Nilus make during early customer validation?
a: Shaul says that despite a lot of customer research, the team did not discuss selling early enough, and research proved different from trying to sell. Selling is what answers questions such as "will people pay for it? How much will they pay for it?" [14:56]

s8-bonus-the-mark-cuban-backed-playbook-turning-short-form-videos-into-interactive-games-without-code-with-dan-projansky-caroline-strzalka-co-founders-of-overplay
Born From a Bike Video: Dan wanted to play a mountain bike trail he saw on YouTube as a video game. The bigger idea became letting anyone who can make a video add an interactive gaming layer to it.

A Part-Time, Rough MVP: Dan and one developer took about six months to reach a playable iOS version. Adding Android made it a team of three, and Dan thinks it took almost a year to reach the App Store.

Motion Controls Needed Second Screens: Authoring pitch or roll inputs moves the phone so much that creators can't see their video. The team extended the MVP timeline so a second screen could show the video while the phone acts as a remote.

Balancing Users Against Vision: Overplay weighs resources, research, user feedback, monetization and original vision on its roadmap. Dan warns that listening only to users can miss big leaps, yet admits he has been slow to drop ideas users didn't want.

Hiring Mandarins-in-the-Shower People: A phrase from UX designer Luis became an internal check for wacky, creative thinkers. The fully remote team is international, with the two founders as its only Americans.

q: What is Overplay and how does it turn a video into a game?
a: Overplay lets creators add interactive game inputs, such as tap, pitch or roll, on top of video. Dan Projansky explained that "anyone who can make a video can now add an interactive gaming layer to it" [03:52].

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Overplay?
a: Dan Projansky built the first iOS version with one other developer while both worked on other projects. Dan said, "we spent about six months before we had the first playable version" [06:02], and he thinks it was almost a year before the original product reached the App Store.

q: Why does Overplay use a second screen for game authoring?
a: Games can be authored directly on a device, but motion inputs make that hard to do well. As Dan put it, "the inputs that you're doing actually move your phone" [08:10], so a second screen shows the video while the phone serves as a remote.

q: What is the future vision for Overplay?
a: Caroline Strzalka expects Overplay to appear across many platforms and be used by both everyday creators and brands. She also described a big idea "around having interactive games on top of live events" [26:42], such as racing along with a Formula One driver, with possibilities in sports and concerts too.

q: What advice do Overplay's founders have for new entrepreneurs?
a: Dan Projansky says you had better love what you're building, because it will take a long time and be harder than you expect. Caroline Strzalka warned that it takes three times "more time and often three times more money than you think it will" [35:06].

s8-e18-bypassing-the-gps-crutch-engineering-level-4-contextual-ai-and-multi-floor-autonomous-robots-with-ritukar-vijay-co-founder-ceo-of-ottonomy

MVP Built to Be Piloted: Ottonomy's co-founders and early members built robots in guest rooms in three to four months during lockdowns. The bar was a product that could be piloted at a customer site, even if it didn't look its best.

Function Before Polish: With limited budget and people, the team prioritized the complete delivery use case, including seamless indoor and outdoor navigation. It never compromised on sensors, using 3D lidars and cameras from day one.

A Joke Sparked Ottobots 2.0: At an airport deployment, an engineer joked that the robot should move sideways to avoid crowds. A design sprint two weeks later led to robots that can crab walk and make zero radius turns.

Balance Founder Archetypes: An early investor's AI-based tool placed the four co-founders in four different quadrants. Ottonomy kept using it as the team grew, weighing archetype alongside technical competence.

Perfect Slowed Deployment: After a successful MVP test, it took almost six months to reach a deployed product. Vijay believes redefining "perfect" could have saved about three months and brought customer learnings sooner.

q: What does Ottonomy build?
a: Ottonomy, co-founded by CEO Ritukar Vijay, makes robots for last-leg delivery and operates in North America, Europe and the Middle East. In Vijay's words, "Ottonomy builds autonomous delivery robots meant for hyper-local deliveries of food and beverage, retail and packages" [02:32].

q: How did Ottonomy build its first delivery robot MVP?
a: Ritukar Vijay says the co-founders and a few early members designed the robots and made micro-assemblies in their guest rooms, finishing in three to four months during lockdowns. His definition was clear: "So our thought process was that an MVP should be in a form" [05:03] that could be piloted at a customer location.

q: Why can Ottonomy's Ottobots 2.0 move sideways?
a: Ritukar Vijay traces the idea to an airport deployment, where an engineer joked, "I wish the robot could have moved sideways to avoid that crowd" [09:01]. The team started exploring it in a design sprint two weeks later, and the resulting version can crab walk and make zero radius turns.

q: What mistake did Ottonomy make after its MVP?
a: Ritukar Vijay says chasing a perfect product slowed the move from a successful customer test to deployment, noting "it took almost six months for us to, you know, get to a deployed product" [14:30]. The lesson was to stay agile and get product versions in front of customers sooner.

q: How did Ottonomy approach building its team?
a: Ritukar Vijay warns that startups often keep hiring similar people because the frequency seems to match. He argues that "you need to have complementary skill sets to have a wonderful team" [10:42], and Ottonomy has used an AI-based archetype tool to see which types of people it needs.

s8-bonus-shattering-the-compliance-audit-toil-engineering-an-automated-devops-system-of-record-and-binary-provenance-engine-with-mike-long-co-founder-ceo-of-kosli

Keeping the Receipts: Kosli records what's running in production and links it to commits, builds, tests, security scans and approvals, giving regulated teams searchable proof for auditors without slowing developers down.

Funded From a White Paper: A Norwegian bank funded a roughly three-month proof of concept based on a two-page white paper. Mike says nearly every early technical choice was wrong, but the result was enough to demo and move toward early customers.

COVID Forced a SaaS Pivot: The plan was on-prem software funded by big financial institutions, but they paused innovation projects. Kosli built a SaaS version in 2020, picked up four or five fintechs and raised a pre-seed.

Outgrowing Git as a Database: Viewing a file's history meant traversing the whole repository, which became extremely slow at volume. Kosli moved to an append-only document database, with a transparency log as an option.

Go to the US Early: Mike says Kosli was two and a half years in before focusing on the US. He rejects the win-local, then Scandinavia, then Europe sequence and urges founders to get to the US as early as possible.

q: What is Kosli and what problem does it solve?
a: Kosli is a DevOps tool for regulated industries such as banking, healthcare and medical devices, where teams face heavy manual work around audit, compliance and security. Mike Long says these teams need a delivery process and proof they followed it: "Essentially, they need to keep the receipts." [03:30]

q: How was the first version of Kosli built?
a: Mike Long's early choices were Git for storage, JavaScript for the application and Python for the client tools in CI pipelines. JavaScript was dropped before the first customer demo, and Mike says they "replaced six weeks of JavaScript coding with one week of Python coding." [07:18]

q: Why did Kosli stop using Git as its database?
a: Git worked until volumes grew large, then history lookups became extremely slow. Mike Long explained that to see a file's history, "you actually have to traverse the entire repo's history." [11:58] The team moved to an append-only document database.

q: Why did Kosli switch from an on-prem plan to SaaS?
a: COVID-19 meant large financial institutions were not running innovation projects, so funding development through them no longer worked. Mike Long said he and his co-founder James decided, "okay, let's take this thing and turn it into a SaaS product." [09:12]

q: Can Kosli show what was running in an environment at a past date?
a: Mike Long says Kosli can automatically treat environments such as Kubernetes clusters, Docker containers and S3 buckets much like version control, so teams can see changes over time and compare systems. As he put it, "what was running on Christmas Day is a question we can answer." [16:15]

s8-bonus-the-intranet-of-human-memory-architecting-decentralized-plms-and-blockchain-secured-memory-stacks-with-suman-kanuganti-co-founder-ceo-of-personalai

Personal Models Over LLMs: Personal.ai builds each person a time-bound long-term memory, then a personal language model on top. Its own implementation does not depend on a large language model, on CTO Sharon Zhang's advice to ground it in individual data.

AI in the Loop: To address a cold start problem, the team shifted from human-to-AI chat to human-to-human messaging, where your AI drafts a reply you can review and edit. They also worked to make training passive.

Finding the First Market: Early ethnographic studies ranged widely. The team later narrowed to personal brands such as solopreneurs, coaches and thought leaders, who have their own data and may serve 100 to 10,000 people.

Capital-Efficient Model Building: Kanuganti says the company built a fundamentally different set of models, personal language models, with $8 million raised, in contrast to the huge raises common in AI.

Limited Capital Demands Focus: Building the technology while serving early customers was extremely difficult. The team eventually dropped some use cases, telling customers it would not support speech because meeting transcription was not its focus.

q: What is Personal.ai?
a: Suman Kanuganti describes Personal.ai as an AI version of an individual, grounded in that person's facts, opinions, thoughts and voice. On ownership, he said, "They own it, not only the data, but also the model for everyday use" [02:49].

q: Why does Personal.ai use a personal language model instead of a large language model?
a: Kanuganti said co-founder and CTO Sharon Zhang advised that the product had to be grounded in small amounts of data belonging to one individual. As he recounted her advice, "you cannot start with a large language model because fundamentally we need to ground this" [04:36].

q: How did Personal.ai change its user experience after the first version?
a: Kanuganti explained that people wanted an augmented experience rather than a replacement, so the team moved beyond simple human-to-AI chat. The product shifted "to actually a human to human communication tool with like AIs in the loop" [07:11], where the AI drafts responses that the user can review and edit.

q: Who is Personal.ai's first target market?
a: Kanuganti said the first market is personal brands, including solopreneurs, small business owners, coaches and thought leaders who serve relatively small communities rather than millions of followers. Of this group, he said, "But they have their moat and their moat is their personal data" [10:50].

q: How could personal AI change data privacy for apps and online services?
a: Kanuganti envisions services calling your personal AI instead of collecting your data into their own platforms, giving users control while still delivering personalization. He put it this way: "imagine opening an app and the service provider makes an API call to you" [19:51].

s8-e17-the-science-of-legal-optimization-engineering-predictive-data-and-ai-engines-for-law-firms-with-dr-jay-sarmaz-co-founder-of-truveai

Consulting Didn't Scale: Jay Sarmaz and co-founder Zech were doing legal analytics consulting and could handle only about 10 projects a year. That limit led to Truve, aimed at serving thousands of law firms.

Out-of-the-Box Law Firm Metrics: Truve tracks performance from marketing to settlement with prebuilt metrics, so firms don't need data analysts to build dashboards. It integrates with 20+ technologies, including five large case management systems.

From Tableau to Real MVP: The first version was Tableau embedded in a web page, built in about four to five weeks. Tableau didn't scale for this use, so the team built a React and JavaScript app on AWS in about three months.

Holding Back Demand: Truve had more interest than it could handle and chose to limit new clients until the product matured. It built closely with beta and large firms, whose problems smaller firms shared.
Hire for EQ, Too: Sarmaz says some bad hires came from favoring capability over emotional intelligence. He would spend more time on hiring and move poor culture fits out sooner, though not harshly.

q: What is Truve.ai and what does it do for law firms?
a: Jay Sarmaz, Truve's co-founder and CEO, says "Truve is a data and intelligence platform for law firms." [02:43] It shows the performance of a firm's operation from marketing to settlement, using out-of-the-box metrics and its own visualization technology.

q: What is Truve's Case Value Estimator?
a: Sarmaz describes the Case Value Estimator as a product with an AI model, "which is an AI model that allows personal injury law firms or workers' compensation law firms" [03:49] to work with case values. He says it started as a response to the data advantage of large insurance companies, including their Colossus platform from the 1980s.

q: Why did Jay Sarmaz start Truve?
a: Sarmaz was doing legal analytics consulting when law firms were going through digital transformation during COVID and didn't know what to do with their data. He and his co-founder Zech saw that consulting couldn't scale: "We can only do, I don't know, 10 of these projects a year." [04:58]

q: How was the first version of Truve built?
a: Sarmaz's team built data pipelines for a few clients and put dashboards on top, and he says the "First version of our product was literally this Tableau visualization embedded into a web page," [05:48] which took about four to five weeks. After the May 2022 spin-off, they built a new MVP in about three months with React, JavaScript and AWS.

q: What hiring mistakes did Truve's founder learn from?
a: Sarmaz says some bad hires came from weighing skill over emotional intelligence: "I remember a few times where we focused more on the capability, so more on the IQ of the person than the EQ of the person." [13:56] He now would put more time and attention into the hiring process.

s8-bonus-the-remote-analytics-pivot-engineering-behavior-telemetry-to-fight-developer-burnout-and-the-yc-to-acquisition-playbook-with-reza-farahani-co-founder-of-wfhomie

Sloppy Where It's Reversible: WFHomie's MVP used Firebase and React, with Google authentication built to last. To skip a super admin UI, the team edited frequently changed data in a Google Sheet that fed the platform directly.

Ship What Gets Used Tomorrow: The long-term vision stayed fixed, but near-term sprints came from customer requests plus usage analytics such as Mixpanel. A feature released today had to be used the next day.

Junior-Only Hiring Backfired: Reza, who calls himself semi-technical, planned to manage junior developers and save money, but founder duties left no time to train them. WFHomie moved to a senior-junior mix, hiring for at least two years.

A Hit Exposed the Architecture: A customer-requested Slack app took off and hit bottlenecks, including timeouts. The team patched it over several sprints while building a full replacement, migrating from serverless to a dedicated server.

Build or Be Bought: WFHomie wasn't in core HR, payroll or hiring. Facing a next raise to build one of those, it became a strategic buyout for GoCo, which did core HR and could offer WFHomie's product to all its customers.

q: What is WFHomie?
a: WFHomie was a platform built to help remote workers stay engaged with their workplace, which Reza Farahani links to both mental health and productivity. As Reza described it, "it's an employee engagement platform for remote teams" [02:39].

q: How was the WFHomie MVP built?
a: After design work led by Reza's co-founder, a former UI/UX designer, the first version was built in React on Firebase because both developers already knew it. Reza recalled that it was "me and another engineer kind of like build everything from ground up" [04:45].

q: How did WFHomie decide what to build next?
a: Reza Farahani relied on customer conversations and analytics showing how people used the product, while keeping a long-term vision in mind. On near-term features, he said "we wanted to make sure if a feature gets released today, it's going to be" [08:20] used the next day.

q: What scaling problem did WFHomie face with its Slack app?
a: The Slack app, which included the Kudos feature, became such a hit that it created bottlenecks, and responses could time out. Reza traced it to an architecture decision made without detailed enough requirements, saying "we needed to migrate everything to a dedicated server" [15:36].

q: Who acquired WFHomie and why?
a: GoCo, which offered a core HR product, acquired WFHomie as it faced the choice of raising another round to build into a core area or being bought. Reza explained that "when it came to the acquisition, we were a strategic buyout for GoCo" [17:37].

s8-bonus-the-just-in-time-access-playbook-automating-identity-governance-and-eliminating-enterprise-security-debt-with-alex-bovee-co-founder-ceo-of-conductorone

Workflows Before UI Polish: ConductorOne accepted an inconsistent UI in year one to make access reviews and self-service provisioning reliable, since those workflows touch many employees at a customer.

Integrations Set the Timeline: A working end-to-end prototype took about three months, but getting a customer live took roughly a year because identity governance needs broad integration coverage and robust workflows.
Pausing the Roadmap for Customers: Prompted partly by feedback that filters were slow, the team paused its roadmap for three or four months to clean up UI inconsistencies and improve responsiveness.

Earn the Right to Scale: About a year and a half in, Bovee added go-to-market people and process before massive product-market fit. His lesson: first learn to repeatedly generate pipeline, qualify deals and sell.

Building a Compound Platform: ConductorOne laid foundations early to sell multiple products to the same buying center. At recording, two were on the market and a third was due in about three or four weeks.

q: What is ConductorOne and what problem does it solve?
a: Alex Bovee describes it this way: "ConductorOne is a modern identity governance solution." [02:38] It addresses the trouble cloud-forward companies have managing permissions, access and related compliance, including over-provisioned users and unused licenses.

q: How long did it take to build the ConductorOne MVP, and what tech stack did it use?
a: Bovee had functional prototypes within a few months, but said "it took us about a year to get really alive" [04:34] with the first customer. The team went all in on AWS and chose DynamoDB to handle high transaction and read volumes across many integrations and potentially millions of entitlements.

q: What trade-offs did ConductorOne make in its first version?
a: Bovee said the biggest cut was UI polish, which left the look and feel inconsistent across parts of the application. The priority was dependable workflows, because as he put it, "The product can be beautiful, but if the workflow piece doesn't work, it kind of doesn't really matter." [07:24]

q: How does ConductorOne decide what to build next?
a: Bovee said the company holds firm on its long-term vision of securing workforce identity while letting customer feedback shape short-term priorities. In his words, "We've always been very, very, very customer driven, customer success focused." [09:26]

q: What is Alex Bovee's advice on when a startup should scale?
a: Bovee advises doing things in non-scalable ways until you know what works, whether in engineering, marketing or sales. Reflecting on his own premature go-to-market scaling, he said, "you really do have to earn the right to scale because scaling necessarily" [13:25] is very expensive and comes with a lot of overhead.

s8-e16-the-death-of-static-api-docs-engineering-interactive-real-data-code-walkthroughs-to-kill-developer-churn-with-job-rietbergen-co-founder-former-ceo-of-alphadoc

Prototypes Before Product: Alphadoc sketched in Miro, ran screen-share customer calls, then spent two weeks on Figma prototypes. They tested demand with those, videos, a marketing site and a long lead form.
Beyond Docs-as-Code: To reach product people and technical writers as well as developers, V1 used a WYSIWYG editor with APIs and visual flow charts, accepting that it might not fit some audiences.
Roadmap From Weekly Conversations: The team speaks with about 15 to 20 people or companies each week, shares insights in Slack, collects them in Productboard, and reviews the roadmap monthly.

Lambda's Early-Stage Trade-Off: Building around AWS Lambda functions made the product very scalable, but warm-up time felt slow to some users. The team soon chose an approach better matched to its stage.

Qualify and Charge Sooner: Rietbergen let anyone try the product without a clear path to revenue for too long. He would now ask for credit cards sooner and give two or three customers everything they wanted first.

q: What problem does Alphadoc solve?
a: Alphadoc aims to make it easier for companies to onboard developers onto their products and sell into them through a self-serve, bottom-up motion, serving both technical and business audiences. Job Rietbergen describes it as "solving an engineering problem with a commercial mindset." [12:29]

q: How is Alphadoc different from a docs-as-code approach?
a: Rietbergen says the first version stepped away from keeping everything next to the codebase so that less technical users could take part, with an editor for pulling in APIs and creating visual flow charts. As he explained, "we made the decision to make more of a WYSIWYG," [06:43]

q: How does Alphadoc decide what to build next?
a: Rietbergen's team gathers insights from weekly customer calls, lead forms and in-product chat, then looks at the roadmap once a month. He said they wanted it shaped by users, including "people that are actually also willing to commit payment." [07:54]

q: What scaling problem did Alphadoc hit with AWS Lambda?
a: Rietbergen says the Lambda-based design could handle large volumes, but the functions needed to warm up. It was very scalable, "but actually it was slow for some of our users" [11:23], so the team moved to an approach that better matched its phase.

q: What would Job Rietbergen do differently if he started Alphadoc again?
a: Rietbergen would put more effort into giving two or three customers everything they wanted, building a few use cases before going into the open. He would also "start asking people to take out their credit card" [17:05] sooner, to test whether people actually want the product.

beyond-bots-daniel-jordan-wayflyer

Repayments Flex With Sales: Wayflyer advances working capital to e-commerce businesses and takes a share of daily revenue, such as 10%, so payments shrink when sales slow. It charges a fee rather than interest, which merchants can build into margins.

Buying Beat Building: Daniel's team built its own transaction classification and entity extraction, then saw Ntropy pulling ahead on data sources and features. Wayflyer migrated to Ntropy, though only after months of continuing its in-house work.

LLMs Behind the Scenes: Wayflyer isn't building a ChatGPT-style product. It uses LLM output to structure data, enriching every transaction through Ntropy for underwriting and predicting a customer's industry from product titles, descriptions and images.

Low Touch, Still Human: Wayflyer connects directly to customers' source systems to cut back-and-forth and questions, but still offers a person to talk to by phone. Daniel notes that business finances are personal, especially when founders still run them.

Efficiency Drives the Roadmap: Daniel prioritizes data integrations, analytics and monitoring so Wayflyer can fund more stores within its risk thresholds. Since money is a commodity, the aim is a good price without making customers jump through hoops.

q: How does Wayflyer's merchant cash advance work?
a: Wayflyer advances money to e-commerce businesses for costs like inventory in return for a share of their future revenue, charged as a fee rather than an interest rate. Daniel Jordan explained that a merchant's "payments back to us is proportional to how much business you're doing" [03:07].

q: Why does Wayflyer focus on funding e-commerce businesses?
a: Daniel Jordan said the founders saw that direct-to-consumer brands with strong demand struggled to get financing from banks. Six months into the company, the pandemic sent demand soaring, and in his words, "COVID was the biggest boost for the e-commerce industry ever" [07:16].

q: Why did Wayflyer switch to Ntropy instead of building transaction enrichment in-house?
a: Daniel Jordan's team had been building its own transaction classification and entity extraction, but Ntropy had data from many more sources and kept adding features. "Eventually, I realized that there was no point in us trying to do it ourselves anymore" [05:58], he said.

q: How is Wayflyer using large language models?
a: Wayflyer uses LLM output internally, including enriching banking transactions through Ntropy for underwriting and predicting a customer's industry from product data. Daniel Jordan sees the big benefit for finance as "turning unstructured data into structured data" [09:36].

q: What impact will AI have on the finance industry?
a: Daniel Jordan expects AI to turn finance upside down, mainly by increasing competition against large incumbents that are robust but slow to innovate. He said that "AI and software in general is going to enable people to start targeting" [21:01] specific products and niches.

s8-bonus-the-15m-bootstrapped-pivot-tech-ifying-private-capital-markets-and-engineering-a-compliance-first-os-for-investment-bankers-with-david-frank-founder-ceo-of-stonehaven
One Stack, Shared Economics: Stonehaven moved affiliates off their separate tech setups onto one platform, gaining economies of scale to build infrastructure none of them would individually justify.

Salesforce Backbone, Custom Interface: Stonehaven built on Salesforce for its data backbone but developed its own UI. Onboarding affiliates then required a data team able to migrate CRMs, documents and spreadsheets at scale.

Turning Contract Terms into Code: A decision tree with about 150 variables produces client term sheets. Turning them into contracts was still manual, and the team was investing heavily that summer to automate it.

Bootstrapped with Global Teams: With no external equity financing, Stonehaven built a roughly 30-person team, including developers in Eastern Europe and about a dozen people in India supporting data, mandate management, finance and more.

Features Can Cost Speed: Adding complexity to workflows slowed parts of the code, a problem Frank called hidden. The team went back to re-architect many tools and was just finishing much of that optimization.

q: What is Stonehaven and who is it built for?
a: Stonehaven is a fintech capital markets platform and U.S. broker-dealer that supports investment bankers and placement agents with an operating system and a collaboration network. David Frank said the idea grew from experience in the market, where "we saw a real gap for small and medium-sized investment banks and placement" [04:45] agents.

q: How did Stonehaven build the first version of its platform?
a: David Frank and his team used Salesforce as the backbone, designing a data model and fields to support the entire deal journey. They built a custom front end because, as Frank put it, "Salesforce does not have great user interface from our perspective" [08:07].

q: How does Stonehaven handle compliance and legal workflows for broker-dealers?
a: Stonehaven has built compliance, legal, due diligence, finance and operations into its tech stack, replacing back-and-forth emails, spreadsheets and PDFs. David Frank said the goal is "a clean workflow where three clicks and you're done" [10:36], which also helped his internal team scale faster.

q: How has Stonehaven scaled without raising outside equity?
a: David Frank credits offshore teams as part of the reason, alongside a U.S.-based team. He explained, "Part of the reason we've been able" [17:07] to stay bootstrapped is a dedicated development team in Eastern Europe, and the company also has about a dozen people in India.

q: What advice does David Frank give young entrepreneurs about funding and market size?
a: Frank said he would have brought in the right outside investors early, while cautioning against raising too much and diluting too fast. He also warned that big markets bring huge competitors and advised "finding a narrow enough niche that you can become very strong at" [26:19] before expanding.

s8-bonus-shattering-mvp-pitfalls-engineering-disciplined-scalable-architectures-for-early-stage-startups-with-max-walker-co-founder-of-piton-labs

Build Less, Pick Boring: Max advises building as little software as possible, since much of it will change or be replaced. A Google form and email blast may be enough to start, and boring technology beats shiny, over-engineered choices.

Plan to Hand Off: Piton Labs builds early products and then moves on, so it also helps clients hire. It writes job recs, runs interviews and trains clients to take over, a need that surfaced when clients asked what happens after Piton leaves.

Hire Proven Builders: Piton looks for former founders, early lead engineers and open source creators. Max says building something from the ground up is the only thing he's found that correlates with taking ownership on a small, autonomous team.

Scaling People Was Harder: Landing first customers and revenue was pretty easy, but growing beyond the two co-founders was not. The 2021 hiring market was fierce, and Piton quickly learned that hiring good-but-not-great people undercut its value.

React Quickly but Purposefully: When a client's loan underwriting system went down almost immediately at launch, the team didn't panic or roll everything back. They rate limited, fixed the issue and had it working as expected within an hour.

q: What is Piton Labs and what does it do?
a: Piton Labs, co-founded by Max Walker, helps early-stage startups build their product, team and technology strategy before handing them off. Max explained, "We jump in at very, very early stages for a lot of businesses" [03:53].

q: How much should a startup build for its MVP?
a: Max Walker recommends a minimalist approach, such as testing with a Google form and an email blast if that covers what the product needs to do. Even though more building would mean more revenue for Piton, he said that "most of the time, that's really building as little as possible" [07:39].

q: What does Piton Labs look for when hiring software engineers?
a: Beyond the usual checks on skill and being reasonable to work with, Max looks for people who have created something themselves, such as former founders or major open source project starters. He asks whether they have started something "from the ground up, built it with your own two hands, and been really passionate" [13:29].

q: How should an engineering team respond when a production launch fails?
a: Max described a client's financial services system that went down almost immediately, where his team rate limited traffic, found the problem and corrected it without panicking. His lesson is that "you need to react quickly, but you need to react purposefully" [21:18].

q: What advice does Max Walker give first-time founders facing rapid growth?
a: Max advises focusing on what is broken now and writing down future problems somewhere to revisit later. As he told one young client, "you need to separate your concerns into the things that are urgent problems right now" [29:12].

s8-e15-the-b2b-cash-collection-tech-problem-eradicating-manual-invoice-friction-and-predictably-reducing-dso-with-alex-louisy-co-founder-ceo-of-upflow

Collection Before Financing: Upflow began as a B2B lending idea, until finance teams and CEOs said they needed to borrow because customers paid late. The team chose to fix on-time payment first, then add modern payments and financing.

Workflows Beat Reconciliation: The team spent heavily on matching payments to invoices, but users found that time-consuming yet manageable. The bigger pain was organizing workflows and chasing unpaid invoices, which became the cash collection engine.

Charging Changes the Feedback: When Upflow told free users they would have to pay, the feedback shifted. Some apparent power users left, others emerged, and Alex now urges founders in their space to monetize as early as possible.

Native Integrations for Scale: Customer-fed data pipelines worked early on, but 1-2% errors became a nightmare as customers grew. Native connections to financial systems improved accuracy and led to distribution partnerships, mostly in the US.

Fix Unit Economics Early: At Y Combinator, a partner said Upflow's price was too low for its outbound sales to CFOs: sell low-touch or raise prices. Within two or three months, the team raised prices significantly and refined its go-to-market.

q: What does Upflow do?
a: Upflow helps B2B companies turn outstanding invoices into cash in the bank by improving analytics, workflows and payment methods. In Alex Louisy's words, "Upflow is a software company that aims at helping B2B companies to manage their cash collection" [02:34].

q: How did Alex Louisy come up with the idea for Upflow?
a: Alex and his team first set out to offer simpler, faster financing to B2B companies. User interviews revealed that late payment drove the need to borrow, with finance leaders saying "we want to borrow money because we just can't get paid on time by our customers" [05:02].

q: How did Upflow solve its data scalability problem?
a: Upflow needs all of a customer's invoices, transactions and payments, and its early pipelines for receiving that data did not scale. Alex described the shift to native integrations: "We would actually connect natively to their systems" [15:42].

q: What was Upflow's biggest mistake?
a: Alex says it was a go-to-market mistake: the team focused on users and product without planning how to sell it. He admitted, "The one thing that we didn't really think about was GTM" [20:25].

q: When should a B2B SaaS startup start charging users?
a: Alex found that paying users gave very different feedback from free users once Upflow made the switch. He encourages founders in a space like Upflow's "to try to monetize as early as possible" [10:59].

beyond-bots-bryce-crawford-meow

Costco of Financial Services: Meow believes most financial services are commodities, so the winner will be whoever provides them at the lowest cost, at scale, to a wide set of customers. It is not a bank, but offers startups checking and treasury services.

Leverage Through Software: Bryce says Meow has around $1.3 billion in assets under management with 16 people. To work within tight banking margins, it scales through automation and software rather than headcount, while driving down service and operating costs.

Cleaning Up Transaction Data: Meow uses Ntropy to turn cryptic checking account transaction text into readable details like merchant name, spend category, website and logo. The relationship runs both ways, as Ntropy is also a Meow customer.

Cheaper, Faster Onboarding: Bryce estimates manual business verification at a legacy bank could cost $100 over a multi-week period. Digital identity tools might cut that to $10 or even $5 and work much faster.

Customers Before LLMs: Meow is cautious about hunting for AI use cases. With product-market fit in core areas, it can watch what emerges, try tools from companies like Ntropy with low effort, and add what actually solves customer problems.

q: What is Meow and why does it call itself the Costco of financial services?
a: Meow is a fintech, not a bank, that offers checking accounts and treasury services to venture-backed startups. Bryce Crawford explains the Costco comparison by saying "we really truly believe that most financial services are commodities" [01:18], so low cost at scale wins.

q: How does Meow use Ntropy?
a: Meow uses Ntropy on its checking account to clean up transaction data so customers can see the merchant, category and website and review their spend more easily. As Bryce puts it, the job is "taking a lot of dirty text that comes through on transaction data" [02:32].

q: How can a fintech pass more value to customers when banking margins are so tight?
a: Bryce Crawford says Meow focuses on bringing down both the cost of its services and its operating costs. The company concentrates on "scaling as much as possible through automation and software, not through people" [04:09].

q: How could large language models help startups understand their burn and revenue?
a: Bryce sees room for LLMs to give customers a qualitative analysis of their transaction, treasury and burn data, potentially by generating code that produces a human-readable answer. His example question was "why did my burn increase over the past three months?" [08:15].

q: What impact will AI have on finance, according to Meow's CTO?
a: Bryce Crawford sees more immediate impact in analysis, workflows, policy documents, and Excel and code productivity, which carry less regulatory scrutiny. For areas like algorithmic investment advice, he expects "a collaboration between the public sector and" [12:27] the private sector to shape what is allowed.

s8-bonus-the-real-time-infrastructure-masterclass-bypassing-http-streaming-failures-to-deliver-exactly-once-data-sync-at-global-scale-with-matthew-oriordan-co-founder-ceo-of-ably

Four Pillars of Real-Time: Ably focused on low latency, integrity, availability and dependability. Keeping latency under 100 milliseconds meant building globally distributed edge infrastructure rather than running in a single region.

Nine Months Became Three Years: Matthew's deck suggested reaching market in nine months, but building a novel distributed system took three years. He thinks it was the right call, though he'd hesitate to recommend that path.

Better Tech Wasn't Enough: At launch, many developers recognized Ably's tech was better but stuck with familiar tools. Engineers with critical, high-scale or integral real-time needs were the ones who valued the difference.

Don't Let Customers Design APIs: Ably avoids building whatever API a customer requests, to prevent a "Frankenstein" product. Expansion ideas come largely from calls where the team sees customers solving problems in unexpected ways.

Two Sales Motions, Mixed Signals: After the Series B, adding sales-led selling alongside product-led growth created internal conflict. One red flag was hearing a customer called "lost" because they had signed up through self-service.

q: What is Ably and what does it do?
a: Ably is a real-time experience platform for developers, powering features such as live chat, delivery tracking, document collaboration and multiplayer games. Co-founder and CEO Matthew O'Riordan explains, "we provide APIs that power live and collaborative experiences" [02:34].

q: Why does real-time infrastructure need to be globally distributed?
a: Matthew O'Riordan says latency becomes perceptible beyond about 100 milliseconds, and data traveling between distant regions such as Australia and the US can exceed that. As a result, Ably built edge infrastructure because it "can't have the service in a single region. It's got to be globally distributed." [05:54].

q: How long did it take to build the first version of Ably?
a: It took three years, even though Matthew's original deck suggested nine months, because the team had to design a novel distributed system to stand apart from existing options. Comparing it to railway infrastructure, Matthew said, "you can't launch railway infrastructure half-baked. You have to kind of do it properly." [08:38].

q: How does Ably decide which APIs to build?
a: Early on, Ably looked at the feature sets of existing real-time products and aimed to do them better, and later drew on customer insight and its own view of where the industry was going. Matthew cautions that "you should not ask your customer what API you should build" [11:37], preferring to watch how customers actually solve problems.

q: What mistake did Ably make after its Series B?
a: Ably added a sales-led motion alongside its developer-first, product-led one, which left people unsure whether to sell to new signups or help them succeed. Matthew's conclusion is that "it's always make customers succeed when it comes to developers." [23:40].

1bfd3dc1-fb8f-4696-bdf9-23fed81bcbdb
s8-e14-beyond-static-dora-dashboards-deploying-real-time-git-metadata-parsing-and-policy-as-code-engines-with-dan-lines-of-linearb

Slides Before SaaS: Ori scripted pulls from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket APIs, and Dan presented the metrics in slide decks to about 10 to 15 design partners. That validation led to a real-time SaaS platform, which took about six months to build.

Two-Thirds Enhance, One-Third Innovate: LinearB puts about two-thirds of its roadmap into improving existing features through betas, designs and usability sessions. The rest goes to new ideas tried with design partners.

Free Tool, New Persona: A free metrics tool for engineering managers drew thousands of teams but hit a cap. LinearB shifted its bottom-up motion to developers, a far larger audience, which forced sales, product and marketing to adapt.

Scale With the Customer: LinearB didn't try to build an endlessly scalable product from day one. Early customers had roughly 20 to 50 engineers, and the product progressively matured as organizations with thousands of engineers came on.

Hire for Change Resilience: Dan screens for character, resilience and adaptability. The technical founders brought in trusted past colleagues and sought go-to-market hires who could innovate in sales and marketing.

q: What is LinearB and what does it do?
a: Dan Lines describes LinearB as a software delivery management system, usually brought into engineering teams by a VP of engineering. He said the first thing it does is "allow engineering leaders to create a metrics program for their" [02:57] software organization, and it has since added resource allocation, delivery estimates and pull request automation.

q: How did LinearB build its first MVP?
a: Co-founder Ori wrote scripts that pulled metrics such as cycle time, release frequency and PR size from code hosting APIs. Dan Lines would take that data and "put it into a slide deck for our first few" [05:52] design partners before the team built a SaaS platform.

q: How does LinearB decide what goes on its product roadmap?
a: Dan Lines says listening to customers is the most important thing. At LinearB, he explained, "it's probably like a two-thirds, one-third thing" [09:11], with two-thirds going to enhancing the current feature set and one-third to innovation.

q: Why did LinearB shift its free tool from engineering managers to developers?
a: The free tool for engineering managers reached thousands of teams, but Dan Lines said that "as we learned, there's kind of a cap to that go to" [16:45] market motion. Developers vastly outnumber managers, so LinearB changed its bottom-up motion to serve them as well.

q: Did LinearB build its product to scale from day one?
a: No, Dan Lines said the type of customer changed at each stage, from organizations with 20 to 50 engineers to some with thousands. As he put it, "we never took the philosophy of from day one, let's make this endlessly scalable" [14:00].
